Tightened information control to the point of punishing the viewing of South Korean dramas with execution (Amnesty International report).
Sends troops and artillery shells to Russia and receives technology in return.

intent.read: No country's words and deeds align more closely. Pyongyang treats its nuclear arsenal as a given rather than a subject of negotiation and has cut off contact with South Korea. The one opening is that Kim Yo Jong's statement did not name the United States directly, and that opening faces Washington alone.

watch.t: How the party plenary meeting report refers to the United States and South Korea
Signs of preparation for a seventh nuclear test
Whether statements begin to name the United States directly

uncertain: Mongolia's and North Korea's 2025 military spending could not be confirmed in SIPRI data and has been left blank. With no IMF data for North Korea, its GDP uses the Bank of Korea's estimate of nominal GNI (about $33.8 billion).

The U.S. figure of 5,042 nuclear warheads comes from an automated summary of the SIPRI Yearbook 2026 summary PDF (the press release has no country-by-country table). China's 620 and North Korea's roughly 60 were confirmed in the press release.
The size of the North Korean force deployed to Russia rests on Ukrainian claims (about 8,500 additional troops; estimates of 30,000 to 50,000) and has not been independently verified.
North Korea's official reaction to the transfer of its prisoners of war has not yet been confirmed.

MNG.leader: President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh, Prime Minister Nyam-Osor Uchral (took office March 30, 2026)
MNG.situation: Mongolia has gone through political turmoil, with three changes of prime minister in the year after June 2025, and after Prime Minister Zandanshatar resigned in March 2026, Uchral took office promising mining reform. While keeping up its "third neighbor" diplomacy between China and Russia, Mongolia is widening its economic ties with Russia, gaining SCO partner status in September and bringing an interim trade agreement with the EAEU into force in July. Its dependence on Russian fuel and the deadlock in price talks over the Power of Siberia 2 gas pipeline are the main variables.

mil.note: A small force focused on UN peacekeeping; Mongolia maintains its nuclear-weapon-free status.

pol.stability: Unstable, with frequent changes of prime minister; because the president is limited to a single term, a reshuffling of power is set for 2027.
pol.next_election: Presidential election, June 2027 (Khurelsukh cannot run again)

econ.note: An economy dependent on coal and copper exports, heavily reliant on exports to China and imports of Russian fuel.

recent.text: An interim trade agreement between the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and Mongolia entered into force.
President Khurelsukh met President Putin at the SCO summit in Bishkek, and Mongolia obtained SCO partner status.
At the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Prime Minister Uchral discussed a stable fuel supply with Russia's energy minister.

watch: China-Russia price talks on the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline and whether a route through Mongolia is finalized
Coalition stability and the shape of the 2027 presidential race
Fuel supplies amid Russian restrictions on exports of petroleum products

gs.core: Independence and democracy between two giants.
goals: "Third neighbor" diplomacy (the United States, Japan, South Korea, the EU)
Mining export revenue
Neutrality
give: Dependence on Russian fuel
Mineral exports to China
never: Entry of either neighbor's troops
Sovereignty
gs.summary: Even amid political turmoil that has brought three prime ministers in a year, Mongolia is trying to secure room to maneuver through its "third neighbor" diplomacy. Yet SCO partner status and the EAEU trade agreement are widening its economic ties with Russia.
gs.contra: Political instability unsettles its long-term foreign policy.

hist.meaning: A buffer steppe between two giants.

episodes.t: The Mongols built a world empire
Mongolia declared independence from the Qing and, with Soviet backing, set up a revolutionary government
The Battle of Khalkhin Gol: Soviet and Mongolian forces stopped the Japanese army
Democratization, and "third neighbor" diplomacy

hist.learned: That leaning on one giant to escape the other cost it dependence. Hence its search for third neighbors since 1990.
hist.read: Mongolia's room for independence depends on relations between China and Russia. The closer the two are, the narrower Mongolia's options.

drivers.why: Its geography as a landlocked country trapped between two giants explains nearly everything.

uncertain: Mongolia's and North Korea's 2025 defense spending could not be confirmed in SIPRI data and was left blank. With no IMF data on North Korea's GDP, the Bank of Korea's estimate of its nominal GNI (about $33.8 billion) was used.

USA.leader: President Donald Trump (Republican), Vice President JD Vance
USA.situation: Through reciprocal state visits with China, to Beijing in May and Washington in September, the Trump administration is pursuing a tariff truce (through January 2027) and "strategic stability," and it has floated arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip, unsettling allies. After the Supreme Court ruled the IEEPA tariffs unlawful in February, Washington moved to Section 122 (10 percent) and then, from July 24, imposed Section 301 "forced labor" tariffs on 60 countries (12.5 percent on South Korea and Japan, 10 percent on Taiwan and the EU, and an additional 12.5 percent on China). With the Iran war that began in late February and the Hormuz crisis still unresolved, it is pressing South Korea to send troops, has unilaterally scaled back the combined U.S.-South Korea exercises, and is seeking a summit with Kim Jong Un before year's end.

mil.note: The world's largest defense budget. U.S. Forces Korea remains at 28,500 troops, but scaled-back combined exercises and the diversion of forces to Hormuz have made the U.S. posture in Asia less coherent.

pol.stability: The midterms are approaching amid continuing institutional clashes, from the expansion of presidential power to the courts' checks on tariffs.

econ.note: Trade policy is highly uncertain as the legal basis for tariffs has shifted from IEEPA to Section 122 to Section 301.

recent.text: Section 301 forced-labor tariffs on 60 countries took effect: 12.5 percent on South Korea, Japan, and China and 10 percent on Taiwan and the EU.
President Trump ordered the U.S.-South Korea Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise scaled back on the grounds that it sent a hostile signal to North Korea.
Special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met President Putin in Moscow and then President Zelensky in Kyiv in an effort to revive three-way talks, but no breakthrough followed.
President Trump held a summit with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in New York, and the two reaffirmed their tariff agreement and cooperation through the Quad.
Xi Jinping's state visit concluded. The two countries extended their tariff truce by two months and set up a new AI dialogue channel, and Washington said its Taiwan policy had not changed.

President Zelensky said the United States had proposed preparing and hosting a three-way technical-level meeting of Ukraine, Russia, and the United States in the United Arab Emirates, though no date was set; the Kremlin reiterated that it is not seeking a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to rearm.

President Trump rejected an Iranian road map that offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days in exchange for the release of $12 billion in frozen assets, the lifting of oil sanctions, an end to the naval blockade, and a halt to hostilities including in Lebanon. The Wall Street Journal reported that he is considering resuming bombing after the November midterms.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed to have seized a U.S. military unmanned underwater vehicle (REMUS 600) in the Strait of Hormuz and to have targeted 19 vessels it said were in violation over two days; Washington rejected the claim that advanced equipment had been seized. (The rerouting of 122 merchant ships was announced by U.S. Central Command on September 25.)

The Treasury Department ran a campaign to isolate Iran across some 50 countries. In response, the United Arab Emirates suspended all flights by Iranian airlines and cut off transactions with Bank Melli, and Turkey and Oman barred Mahan Air.

David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, said President Trump had asked Xi Jinping at their Washington summit whether China would be interested in buying American weapons, and that a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, put on hold after the May summit in Beijing, still has no approval date.

watch: The outcome of the November midterms and the continuity of foreign policy
How a U.S.-China "grand bargain" would affect arms sales to Taiwan and commitments to allies
Whether the Iran war and Hormuz crisis shift burdens onto Asian allies and change the posture of U.S. Forces Korea
USA.alliances_note: Quad: foreign ministers met in New Delhi on May 26; no date set for a leaders' summit. AUKUS: retained after a 2025 Pentagon review; construction of the U.K.'s SSN-AUKUS submarines is to begin in 2027. U.S.-Japan: alliance and tariff agreement reaffirmed at the September 22 summit. U.S.-South Korea: friction over South Korean investment in the United States and contributions in Hormuz; UFS scaled back.

gs.core: To protect the homeland and preserve dominance in the Western Hemisphere while ensuring that no country surpasses the United States. That country is China.
goals: Keep China from overtaking the United States in advanced semiconductors and AI
Lighten the U.S. burden by handing allies primary responsibility for their own defense
Bring manufacturing and energy supply chains back home
give: Primary responsibility for allied defense, such as Europe's defense against Russia and South Korea's conventional deterrence of North Korea
Rhetorical formulations on Taiwan (such as not supporting independence)
Part of Ukraine's territory in a settlement of the Russia-Ukraine war
Damage to alliance relationships in the course of trade negotiations
never: Transfer of core technologies to China
The dollar's reserve-currency status and command of the oceans
Leaving unchecked nuclear and missile capabilities aimed at the homeland (Iran's nuclear program, North Korea's ICBMs)
gs.summary: The 2026 National Defense Strategy ranks homeland defense first, deterring China second, and allied burden sharing third, and it enshrines U.S. dominance in the Western Hemisphere as the "Trump Corollary" to the Monroe Doctrine. Rather than defending every front in Eurasia directly, the United States is handing primary responsibility to regional allies and shifting toward the role of an offshore balancer that holds the balance with decisive capabilities in nuclear weapons, sea power, and technology. Where it defines a threat as one to the homeland, however, it uses force directly, as in the Iran war.
gs.contra: The more Washington leaves to its allies, the greater their autonomy and their incentive to go nuclear, and the narrower the range of what the United States can control. The tariff truce with China is in constant tension with technology controls on China.

hist.meaning: An island-like continent guarded by two oceans. Because it lies outside Eurasia, it could become Eurasia's balancer.

episodes.t: The Monroe Doctrine declared the Western Hemisphere off-limits to interference by the European powers
The United States entered both world wars when a would-be hegemon rose in Eurasia
The Truman Doctrine and containment kept the Soviet Union from dominating Eurasia
The Nixon Doctrine asked Asian allies to take primary responsibility for their own defense
The fall of Saigon: South Vietnam collapsed two years after the Paris Peace Accords

hist.learned: That domination of Eurasia by a single power endangers the United States, and that ground wars in the Eurasian interior become quagmires (Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan).
hist.read: The United States has swung periodically between isolation and intervention. The retrenchment of the Nixon Doctrine years in the 1970s gave way to Reagan's rearmament in the 1980s. The retreats were not permanent, but allies paid a heavy price during them.

drivers.why: The geography of two oceans grants freedom of choice, and the shift in relative power brought on by China's rise sets the priorities. Domestic politics, including isolationist sentiment, governs how far intervention goes.

signals.t: After the Beijing summit, the White House announced that it had affirmed with China a shared goal of North Korean denuclearization.
Asked at the White House whether he expected to meet Kim Jong Un later this year, Trump replied, "Yeah, I will be."
The National Defense Strategy handed South Korea primary responsibility for conventional deterrence of North Korea.
Unilaterally scaled back the Ulchi Freedom Shield combined exercise.
Backed South Korea's pursuit of uranium enrichment and nuclear-powered submarines.
The House strengthened a provision in its version of the NDAA barring funds for reducing U.S. Forces Korea; the White House opposed the provision.
Approved $11.1 billion in arms sales to Taiwan.
Deployed Navy and Marine Corps systems to the Luzon Strait and Japan's southern islands.
When Xi called for U.S. opposition to Taiwanese independence, Trump said Xi understood his position.
Annual equipment licenses for Samsung and SK hynix plants in China, valid for 2026 only
Lutnick said memory chipmakers would have to pay a 100 percent tariff or build plants in the United States
Section 232 semiconductor proclamation: 25 percent tariff on certain advanced chips
$252 million penalty on Applied Materials over exports to SMIC routed through a South Korean entity
Enforcement guidance on Blackwell chip licenses for overseas subsidiaries of Chinese companies

In his annual testimony before the House Financial Services Committee, the Treasury secretary said the United States was running the largest economic isolation campaign in world history against Iran and its enablers, and was no longer managing the Iranian threat but ending it.

Testifying before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations said he had secured 136 co-sponsors for a Security Council resolution condemning Iran's attacks on its neighbors and its weaponization of the Strait of Hormuz.

In budget testimony before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the under secretary of commerce for industry and security pledged to break companies of the habit of treating export controls as a cost of doing business, citing as enforcement results a penalty for illegally diverting chipmaking equipment and indictments over servers with advanced chips diverted through Southeast Asia.

intent.read: In its rhetoric, Washington holds to denuclearization, the alliance, and deterrence over Taiwan. Its money and forces, however, are moving in two directions: on the Korean Peninsula it is cutting costs and opening the door to a deal with North Korea, while around Taiwan it is stepping up arms sales and deployments. The Trump administration also treats both the peninsula and Taiwan as objects of bargaining.

watch.t: The U.S. Forces Korea provision in the final NDAA
The scale of the spring 2027 combined exercises
Whether a Trump-Kim meeting takes place — forecast of a U.S.-North Korea summit by June 2027 (f22)

uncertain: Saudi Arabia's July 22 civil nuclear cooperation agreement with the United States (linked to the Abraham Accords) was left out of recent developments because its only source is Wikipedia.

The figure of 5,042 U.S. nuclear warheads comes from an automated summary of the SIPRI Yearbook 2026 summary PDF (the press release has no country-by-country table). China's 620 and North Korea's roughly 60 were confirmed in the press release.
Details of 2026 policy changes on AUKUS could not be confirmed (reports say it is proceeding). Whether a Quad leaders' summit will be held this year is undecided.

Timing of the 50 percent U.S. tariff on Canada: an Al Jazeera article of August 23 gives August 22, while one of September 8 says July, so the accounts conflict. The legal basis (presumably Section 301) was not confirmed in the original sources either.
Date of the Sheinbaum-Trump call: the original source gave the date as Wednesday, September 18, but September 18, 2026, is a Friday, so the date is given as Wednesday, September 16.
Lula-Trump call: reported by Bloomberg on August 21 and by Asharq Al-Awsat on August 22. The date is given as the 21st.
The exact date of the Caribbean strike that killed four (reported September 20; the strike itself presumably on the 19th) and the cumulative death toll (230-plus) are estimates.

Course of the Iran war: fighting appears to have flared again in July after the June 15 U.S.-Iran agreement to halt operations, but the state of ceasefire negotiations as of September is unclear (there are reports of a meeting between Trump and an Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly).
It could not be confirmed whether Russia has formally accepted the U.S.-proposed three-way technical-level meeting in the UAE, or when it will be held.

EUR.leader: Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission; António Costa, president of the European Council; Kaja Kallas, high representative for foreign affairs and security policy; Mark Rutte, NATO secretary-general
EUR.situation: On July 23 the EU adopted its 21st package of sanctions against Russia, freezing the assets of 94 banks and targeting 41 shadow-fleet vessels and crypto-assets, and it is disbursing a €90 billion loan to Ukraine for 2026–27. Yet by early September only €11.55 billion had been paid out, and with Ukraine's Defense Ministry facing a €23 billion funding gap, the idea of tapping frozen Russian assets has resurfaced. Europe is wary of the U.S.-led peace talks and is raising defense spending quickly.

mil.note: SIPRI puts total European defense spending at $864 billion (up 14 percent from the previous year), of which the 29 European NATO members account for $559 billion. The warhead count combines Britain's 225 and France's 370.

pol.stability: Sanctions on Russia and aid to Ukraine are holding, but member states remain divided over using frozen assets and other questions.

econ.note: Figures cover the 27 EU member states (IMF); energy prices and the Hormuz crisis weigh on growth.

recent.text: The first €3.2 billion of the €90 billion loan for Ukraine was disbursed.
The EU adopted its 21st sanctions package against Russia, targeting finance, the shadow fleet, refineries and crypto-assets.
The European Commission maintains that €90 billion is enough for now, but Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland are again pushing to use €210 billion in frozen Russian assets.
The European Commission disbursed an additional €3.3 billion in defense funding to Ukraine.

watch: A 22nd sanctions package and whether agreement is reached on using frozen Russian assets
Whether Europe is shut out of the U.S.-mediated peace talks or given a role in security guarantees
The gap in financial support for Ukraine after 2027

gs.core: Defending Europe against Russia's military threat, and building the strength to stand on its own without the United States.
goals: Ukraine's survival as a state, which means preventing a Russian victory
A surge in defense spending and the rebuilding of its defense industry
Keeping sanctions on Russia in place
give: The timing of Ukraine's NATO membership
Some economic ties with China (to the extent of de-risking)
De facto acceptance of the reality of occupation, short of legal recognition
never: Legal recognition of borders changed by force
Being shut out of negotiations on Ukraine
The credibility of NATO's Article 5
gs.summary: Europe has accepted that the United States is shifting the burden onto it and has begun to rearm; it is responding with a €90 billion loan for Ukraine and a 21st sanctions package against Russia. But decisions come slowly and divisions among member states run deep, so its defensive aim, to avoid being dragged along by U.S.-led negotiations, outweighs any offensive one.
gs.contra: Funding for rearmament is short, which has revived the debate over using frozen Russian assets. Energy prices driven up by the Iran war are squeezing both budgets and public opinion.

hist.meaning: A collection of peninsulas and islands. Division is the default; integration has advanced when there was an external threat and an American umbrella.

episodes.t: The Congress of Vienna: a balance of power that averted a great war for roughly 100 years
Both world wars began in Europe
The founding of NATO: Europe entrusted its hard security to the United States
The Suez crisis: Britain and France backed down in the face of U.S. opposition
The Yugoslav wars: Europe could not end the fighting until the United States intervened

hist.learned: Never again war among themselves. Economic integration made war impossible, but for security Europe leaned on the United States.
hist.read: As Jean Monnet put it, "Europe will be forged in crises." Integration advances only when a crisis reaches its peak. Yet as Suez and Yugoslavia showed, Europe has never taken decisive military action without the United States.

drivers.why: The military gap left by decades of relying on the United States for security defines its strategy, and the need for consensus among 27 states sets its pace.

uncertain: Whether the EU leadership (von der Leyen, Costa, Kallas) and the NATO secretary-general (Rutte) remain in office has not been rechecked directly against reporting from September 2026.

IND.leader: Prime Minister Narendra Modi (head of state: President Droupadi Murmu)
IND.situation: Since its four-day air war with Pakistan in May 2025, India has kept up a hard line toward Pakistan and held the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance. At the same time, it is trying to repair relations with China, hosting the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September 2026 and securing Xi Jinping's first visit to India in seven years, and it patched up its tariff dispute with the United States through a trade agreement in February 2026. Amid the energy crisis set off by the Iran war, it is leaning more heavily on Russian crude and pressing ahead with its policy of strategic autonomy.

mil.note: The world's fifth-largest military spender by SIPRI's count; its 2025 clash with Pakistan led to large increases in air force procurement and operating budgets.

pol.stability: The Modi government's political base is solid, with the BJP winning power in West Bengal for the first time in the 2026 state assembly elections, among other gains.

econ.note: Growth is among the highest of the major economies, but the oil shock from the Iran war and the trade balance pose downside risks (IMF figures are on a fiscal-year basis).

recent.text: India and China held the 25th round of Special Representatives talks on the boundary question, discussing an "early harvest" in boundary delimitation and stabilizing the Line of Actual Control (LAC).

The Court of Arbitration constituted under the Indus Waters Treaty, with the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) serving as its registry, ruled that India's decision to hold the treaty "in abeyance" is invalid, but India rejected the court's jurisdiction.
Modi and Xi Jinping met on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi and agreed to work toward a fair and reasonable settlement of the border dispute.
BRICS leaders adopted the New Delhi Declaration, criticizing unilateral tariffs and urging restraint on the parties to the Middle East conflict, though without naming the United States directly.
An Indian destroyer (identified as INS Kolkata) and a Pakistani patrol vessel collided in the Arabian Sea, the first direct military contact between the two since May 2025.

watch: Whether the India-Pakistan maritime collision leads to accidental escalation, given the absence of a hotline
Progress in boundary delimitation talks with China and how far India opens its economy to China
Energy import costs and dependence on Russian crude as the Iran war and the Hormuz blockade drag on

gs.core: Strategic autonomy: rising as an independent great power that belongs to no bloc.
goals: High growth and a manufacturing base (supply chains that replace China)
Deterring Pakistan and keeping freedom of action against terrorism
Primacy in the Indian Ocean
A stable border with China
give: The volume of Russian crude purchases
Terms of trade with the United States
Border management agreements with China
never: Third-party mediation on Kashmir
A break in the strategic relationship with Russia
Joining a formal alliance
gs.summary: India profits by keeping up relations with the United States (the Quad), Russia (energy and arms), and China (inviting Xi Jinping as BRICS chair) all at once. It is hard-line toward Pakistan but has stabilized the border with China to avoid simultaneous crises on two fronts.
gs.contra: India needs relations with every great power at once, but if the U.S.-China rivalry intensifies, it will be forced to choose.

hist.meaning: A subcontinent ringed by the Himalayas and the Indian Ocean. Invaders came through the northwestern passes, and on the seaward side it sits at the center of the Indian Ocean.

episodes.t: Partition, independence, and mass bloodshed
A crushing defeat in the border war with China exposed the limits of Nehru's nonalignment
After signing a friendship treaty with the Soviet Union, India won the Bangladesh war
Nuclear tests

hist.learned: The 1962 defeat bred deep distrust of China and drove military modernization. The year 1971 taught the value of enlisting a great power when needed.
hist.read: India forms no alliances but enters quasi-alliances when it must (the 1971 treaty with the Soviet Union). Its current participation in the Quad follows the same pattern.

drivers.why: Growing national power raises the value of strategic autonomy, and the memory of 1962 sustains distrust of China.

uncertain: Details of 2026 policy changes on AUKUS could not be confirmed (reports say it is proceeding). Whether a Quad leaders' summit will be held this year is undecided.
IMF figures are taken from the DataMapper (labeled WEO April 2026); India's are on a fiscal-year basis. The July 2026 revised projections are not reflected.

SIPRI Yearbook 2026 nuclear warheads: India about 190, Pakistan about 170 (total inventories, extracted by tool from the summary). Rechecking the breakdown (stockpiled vs. deployed) against the original is recommended.

September 15 India-Pakistan naval collision: Pakistan identified the Indian ship as INS Kolkata, but India has not confirmed the ship's name, and the location of the collision (Pakistan's EEZ or international waters) is also disputed.

PAK.leader: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif (President: Asif Ali Zardari; real power: Field Marshal Asim Munir, Chief of Defence Forces)
PAK.situation: Pakistan faces a two-front security crisis: tensions persist with India to the east, while to the west it is fighting the Afghan Taliban, against whom it declared all-out war in February 2026. It raised its profile in the Iran war as a mediator of the U.S.-Iran ceasefire, and in August 2026 it signed a trilateral mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey modeled on NATO's Article 5 (the Mecca Pact). At home, the concentration of power in Field Marshal Munir, the imprisonment of Imran Khan, a surge in militant violence in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and dependence on an IMF program all converge.

mil.note: Orders for Chinese fighter jets and missiles after the 2025 clash with India pushed military spending up 11 percent.

pol.stability: The 27th Amendment and legislation passed in August expanded Field Marshal Munir's powers, entrenching military-centered rule, but its foundations of legitimacy are weak.

econ.note: The fourth review of the $7 billion IMF Extended Fund Facility (EFF) is under way in September, and the oil shock and rising poverty (about 29 percent) weigh on the economy.

recent.text: Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, with a clause treating an attack on one as an attack on all.
Parliament passed a bill expanding the powers of Chief of Defence Forces Munir.
PNS Hunain collided with an Indian destroyer near the area of the SEASPARK-26 exercise in the Arabian Sea, and each country summoned the other's diplomats.

Citing an Afghan-launched drone attack the previous day, Pakistan on September 24 struck 10 sites in Afghanistan, including Kandahar, Paktia, and Khost. The strikes followed the September 18 terrorist attack on police headquarters in Kohat in the northwest (31 killed) and are regarded as the worst clash between the two countries since February 2026.

watch: Wider fighting with the Afghan Taliban and the TTP, and closures of border trade
Accidental clashes with India at sea and along the Line of Control, and the dispute over Indus waters
Whether Pakistan passes the IMF review, and fiscal and foreign-exchange pressure from energy prices

gs.core: Preserving the military's role in running the state, and deterring India.
goals: Maintaining nuclear and conventional deterrence against India
Keeping out militants from Afghanistan
Economic survival on IMF and Gulf money
Maximizing its usefulness to Saudi Arabia, China, and the United States
give: The scope of cooperation with Washington, such as mediation with Iran
The level of its relations with the Afghan Taliban
The civilian veneer of domestic politics
never: Its claim to Kashmir
Nuclear capability
The military's political supremacy
gs.summary: Field Marshal Munir's regime is pursuing a strategy of being a useful partner. Mediating the Iran ceasefire demonstrated its usefulness to the United States, and the Mecca Pact made it a security asset for Saudi Arabia. At the same time, it must manage the Afghan front to the west and the Indian front to the east.
gs.contra: Two fronts and a fragile economy. Its international visibility cannot mask domestic instability such as the imprisonment of Imran Khan and violence in Balochistan.

hist.meaning: A country wedged between India and Afghanistan, and a great-power frontline state.

episodes.t: Partition and independence
Pakistan lost East Pakistan (Bangladesh's independence)
As a U.S. frontline state, Pakistan backed the Afghan mujahideen
After the Soviet withdrawal, Pakistan came under U.S. sanctions (the Pressler Amendment)
Nuclear tests

hist.learned: The trauma of the 1971 breakup made nuclear deterrence of India an absolute. The strategy of surviving by selling its usefulness to great powers also hardened then.
hist.read: Pakistan was abandoned once its usefulness ran out (1990). And the Taliban it nurtured have now become its enemy. The usefulness strategy has always brought blowback.

drivers.why: The regime's interest in preserving the military's role in running the state shapes both its deterrence of India and its balancing among the great powers.

uncertain: SIPRI Yearbook 2026 nuclear warheads: India about 190, Pakistan about 170 (total inventories, extracted by tool from the summary). Rechecking the breakdown (stockpiled vs. deployed) against the original is recommended.

September 15 India-Pakistan naval collision: Pakistan identified the Indian ship as INS Kolkata, but India has not confirmed the ship's name, and the location of the collision (Pakistan's EEZ or international waters) is also disputed.

IDN.situation: Under the banner of its "free and active" foreign policy, Indonesia continues to hedge between the United States and China. In August 2026 it held a joint sailing exercise with the Chinese navy in waters east of Taiwan while also hosting a senior Pentagon official. At home, student protests over fuel prices, a weak rupiah and the free-meals program flared again, and in September, amid the threat of a downgrade from emerging to frontier status in MSCI indexes and doubts about fiscal credibility, Prabowo abruptly fired his finance minister.

mil.note: Military spending jumped 28 percent in 2025, one of the largest increases in Southeast Asia.

pol.stability: An overwhelming coalition majority in parliament gives the government a stable institutional base, but economic grievances keep bringing protesters into the streets.

econ.note: Growth is holding at around 5 percent, but the key variables are the weak rupiah, confidence that the 3 percent deficit ceiling will be respected, and the risk of capital flight.

recent.text: Student protests against fuel price hikes, the weak rupiah and a poorly run free-meals program spread to Jakarta and other cities.
MSCI kept Indonesia in its emerging-markets index but maintained its warning of a downgrade to frontier status.
A joint sailing exercise with Chinese naval vessels in waters east of Taiwan raised concern in the region.
Prabowo dismissed Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa and appointed Deputy Minister Suahasil Nazara to replace him.

watch: Fiscal discipline under the new finance minister, and stability in the rupiah and capital markets
How expanding military cooperation with China affects Jakarta's position on sovereignty in the Natuna Sea
Whether protests over the economy spread again

gs.core: A nonaligned, independent ("free and active") foreign policy and domestic development.
goals: High growth and industrialization through resource processing
Preserving the bargaining power that comes from neutrality amid great-power rivalry
Sovereignty over the Natuna waters
give: Military exchanges with both the United States and China
Terms of external economic engagement
never: Joining either side's alliance
Sovereignty over the Natuna exclusive economic zone
gs.summary: The Prabowo government hedges by, for example, holding a joint sailing exercise with the Chinese navy and hosting a senior Pentagon official in the same month. As confidence in its public finances wavers, its room to maneuver abroad is narrowing too.
gs.contra: Fiscal instability and recurring protests weaken the leverage of its neutral diplomacy.

hist.meaning: The world's largest archipelago, straddling the Malacca, Sunda and Lombok straits that link the Indian and Pacific oceans.

episodes.t: Declaration of independence
Hosted the Bandung Conference, the forerunner of the Non-Aligned Movement
After the September 30th Movement, power passed to the Suharto regime
The Asian financial crisis brought down Suharto's 32-year rule

hist.learned: The Bandung tradition of joining no bloc, and the memory of 1998: an economic crisis can bring down a regime.
hist.read: Indonesia's foreign policy depends on economic stability at home. Its current fiscal instability is the biggest variable.

drivers.why: Domestic economic and political stability determine how much latitude its foreign policy has, and the Bandung tradition of nonalignment sets its direction.

VNM.leader: To Lam, general secretary of the Communist Party and state president (Prime Minister Le Minh Hung)
VNM.situation: Power in Vietnam has become concentrated in one man: after the 14th Party Congress in January 2026, General Secretary To Lam also took on the state presidency in April. Hanoi is managing relations with Beijing, issuing a joint statement with China in April, while openly protesting Chinese construction in the Paracel Islands and sharply expanding land reclamation at its own outposts in the Spratlys. It is broadening cooperation with Western partners through state visits to Australia and New Zealand, and pursuing a 10 percent growth target.

mil.note: Military spending rose 27 percent in 2025, and the fortification of Spratly outposts is accelerating.

pol.regime: Communist one-party state (general secretary also serves as president)
pol.stability: With power consolidated around To Lam, short-term stability is very high.
pol.next_election: National Assembly election and 15th Party Congress, 2031

econ.note: The government targets 10 percent growth, but the IMF forecasts around 7 percent; U.S. tariffs and curbs on transshipment are the key variables.

recent.text: The National Assembly elected General Secretary To Lam as state president and Le Minh Hung as prime minister.
Satellite imagery showed a major expansion of land reclamation and construction at Vietnamese outposts in the Spratly Islands.
To Lam made state visits to Australia (August 9–12) and New Zealand, discussing deeper comprehensive strategic partnerships.
Hanoi lodged a formal protest over China's construction of what appears to be a radar facility in the Paracel Islands, demanding an immediate halt.

watch: The construction race and maritime friction with China in the Paracels and Spratlys
Slowing export growth under U.S. tariffs and transshipment rules
Whether the reform drive endures after To Lam's consolidation of power

gs.core: Communist Party rule, and sovereignty that is not subordinate to China.
goals: High growth (a 10 percent target) and attracting supply chains
Defending its South China Sea claims (Spratly reclamation)
Balancing among the major powers
give: Managing relations with China at the level of joint statements
Expressions of ideological affinity
never: Its sovereignty claims to the Paracels and Spratlys
Allowing foreign military bases (the "Four No's" policy)
gs.summary: Under To Lam's one-man rule, Vietnam practices "bamboo diplomacy." It manages relations with China through joint statements while sharply expanding reclamation in the Spratlys and widening partnerships with the United States, Australia and India.
gs.contra: Concentrated power speeds decision-making but also widens the room for missteps in dealing with China.

hist.meaning: A long coastline on China's southern flank, with a history of resisting China that spans 2,000 years.

episodes.t: The Battle of Bach Dang River freed Vietnam from Chinese rule
Repelled three Mongol invasions
Defeated France at Dien Bien Phu, then fought the United States to achieve reunification
China invaded despite Vietnam's treaty of alliance with the Soviet Union
South Vietnam fought China in the Paracels (1974), and unified Vietnam fought it in the Spratlys (1988)

hist.learned: To stand up to China without crossing the line, through tribute and careful management of relations. And the memory of 1979: an alliance does not guarantee security. The "Four No's" policy, including the refusal to host foreign military bases, grew out of this.
hist.read: Vietnam has always combined armed resistance with tributary diplomacy. Today's bamboo diplomacy carries that tradition into the present.

drivers.why: Its geography as China's southern coastline and the memory of 2,000 years of resistance produce a strategy of standing firm without crossing the line.

PHL.situation: As ASEAN chair in 2026, the Philippines is pushing to conclude a code of conduct for the South China Sea, yet its clashes with China at Scarborough Shoal and Second Thomas Shoal are intensifying instead. On September 25, Chinese navy and coast guard vessels openly blocked a Philippine resupply mission bound for Second Thomas Shoal, the first such blockade since a provisional arrangement in 2024. At home, the feud between the Marcos and Duterte clans has peaked with impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte and a warrant for her arrest.

mil.note: SIPRI's 2025 figure for the Philippines could not be confirmed, so the 2024 value is used. The Philippines is bolstering deterrence by expanding joint exercises with the United States and Japan.

pol.stability: The rivalry between the Marcos and Duterte camps has spilled into the courts and impeachment proceedings, leaving politics sharply polarized.

econ.note: Growth has slowed to around 4 percent, and dependence on imported energy leaves the economy exposed to oil shocks.

recent.text: The day after Foreign Minister Wang Yi warned at an ASEAN meeting in Manila of bitter consequences, vessels from the two countries faced off again at Scarborough Shoal.
A court issued an arrest warrant for Vice President Sara Duterte on charges of threatening to kill the president (a Senate impeachment trial is also under way).
A Chinese coast guard vessel rammed a ship of the Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources 54 nautical miles west of Palawan, inside the Philippine exclusive economic zone (EEZ).

Chinese warships (including two Type 022 missile boats) and coast guard vessels blocked a Philippine resupply mission bound for Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal with dangerous maneuvers, forcing it to abort, the first open blockade since the provisional arrangement of July 2024.

watch: A renewed resupply attempt at Second Thomas Shoal and the threshold for invoking the U.S.-Philippine Mutual Defense Treaty
Progress in code of conduct (COC) negotiations under the Philippines' ASEAN chairmanship
How the vice president's impeachment and criminal case shape the 2028 presidential race

gs.core: Maritime sovereignty and domestic political stability.
goals: Giving effect to its South China Sea rights (the 2016 arbitral ruling)
Strengthening the U.S. alliance
Concluding an ASEAN code of conduct (as 2026 chair)
give: Adjusting how resupply missions are carried out
Economic cooperation with China
never: Withdrawing the BRP Sierra Madre from Second Thomas Shoal
Abandoning the arbitral ruling
gs.summary: The Marcos government is pushing back with the U.S. alliance and a transparency strategy that publicizes footage of Chinese conduct. China's blockade of the September 25 resupply mission broke the 2024 provisional arrangement, raising the risk of clashes again.
gs.contra: The domestic feud with the Duterte clan casts doubt on whether the country's foreign policy line will survive the 2028 presidential election.

hist.meaning: An archipelago forming the eastern edge of the South China Sea; once an American colony and a U.S. base.

episodes.t: Became an American colony after the Spanish-American War
Signed a Mutual Defense Treaty with the United States
U.S. forces withdrew from Subic Bay Naval Base
China's occupation of Mischief Reef came to light
The Scarborough standoff: after a U.S.-brokered agreement on simultaneous withdrawal, only the Philippines pulled back, and China stayed

hist.learned: That when U.S. forces left Subic in 1992, China occupied Mischief Reef in 1995. That is why Manila is now widening U.S. access to its bases again.
hist.read: In the 2012 Scarborough standoff, only one side honored the withdrawal agreement. When the weaker party kept its word first, the stronger one took the space.

drivers.why: Its geography on the eastern rim of the South China Sea and the power gap with China make the U.S. alliance indispensable; dynastic politics undercuts the continuity of its foreign policy.

uncertain: Philippine military spending: SIPRI's individual 2025 figure could not be confirmed, so the 2024 value (about $6.1 billion, from World Bank/SIPRI series) is used.

AUS.situation: In its April 2026 National Defence Strategy, Australia committed to raising defense spending to around 3 percent of GDP by 2033, and it is accelerating expanded U.S. rotational deployments and the AUKUS nuclear-submarine program. In July its alliance treaty with Papua New Guinea (the Pukpuk Treaty) entered into force, giving Australia its first new alliance in more than 70 years, since ANZUS, and extending its security cooperation across the Pacific. In September, nuclear-capable B-52s deployed to RAAF Base Tindal. While naming China as its principal threat, Canberra is diversifying its partnerships with Vietnam, India and others.

mil.note: Its forces are small, but AUKUS and forward-deployed U.S. forces are making it an increasingly important allied hub in the region.

pol.stability: Since its landslide in the 2025 election, the Labor government has held a stable majority.

econ.note: Heavily dependent on commodity exports and Chinese demand, but its fiscal and financial health is sound by the standards of advanced economies.

recent.text: The mutual defense treaty with Papua New Guinea (the Pukpuk Treaty) entered into force.
The first U.S. B-52 bombers arrived at the upgraded RAAF Base Tindal in the Northern Territory.
At a meeting between Defence Minister Richard Marles and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Washington announced that it would accelerate the expansion of U.S. forces in Australia.
At the UN General Assembly, Albanese formally launched Australia's bid for a nonpermanent seat on the Security Council for 2029–30.

watch: Domestic opinion on the AUKUS submarine timeline and expanded U.S. forward deployments
Balancing trade with China against security
Competition with China for influence among Pacific island nations (PNG, the Solomon Islands and others)

gs.core: Preventing a China-dominated order in the Indo-Pacific, with the U.S. alliance as the axis.
goals: AUKUS nuclear-powered submarines
Defense spending at around 3 percent of GDP by 2033
A security network among Pacific island nations (the alliance treaty with PNG)
give: Normalizing trade with China
Part of its defense procurement
never: The U.S. alliance
Chinese military bases in Pacific island nations
gs.summary: Australia has named China as its principal threat and fortified its southern line of defense by expanding U.S. rotational deployments, accelerating AUKUS and bringing the alliance treaty with PNG into force.
gs.contra: It names China as its principal threat, yet China is also its largest trading partner.

hist.meaning: An island continent at the southern edge of Eurasia. It has bought security by allying with distant great powers.

episodes.t: The fall of Singapore and the bombing of Darwin: Britain could not protect Australia
The ANZUS Treaty shifted the axis of its security to the United States
AUKUS

hist.learned: That a protector may fail to protect (1942). So Australia switched to a stronger one.
hist.read: Whenever Australia has sensed its protector weakening, it has moved quickly to a new protector or to self-reliance.

drivers.why: Its isolation as an island continent demands alliances with distant great powers, and the memory of 1942 has shaped its choice of protector.

uncertain: Details of 2026 AUKUS policy changes could not be confirmed (reports say the program is still proceeding). Whether a Quad summit will be held this year has not been decided.

AFG.situation: The Taliban regime has been in a de facto all-out war with Pakistan since February 2026, and tensions rose again in late September when Pakistan struck as far as Kandahar, the supreme leader's base.

recent.text: A Pakistani airstrike hit a drug rehabilitation hospital in Kabul, killing some 260 civilians.
Pakistan struck 10 sites, including Kandahar, and the Taliban government said four civilians had been killed.
The Afghan Taliban's defense ministry claimed to have killed 28 militants who had crossed from Pakistan into Nuristan province and captured 32; Pakistan dismissed the claim as baseless.

uncertain: Whether members of the Taliban cabinet, including Prime Minister Hasan Akhund, remain in office in 2026 was not checked.

BGD.situation: The BNP won a landslide in the February 2026 election, making Tarique Rahman prime minister; relations with India are strained over the extradition of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.

recent.text: Tarique Rahman was sworn in as prime minister, launching the first elected government since the 2024 uprising.
The government said it would link Rahman's visit to India to the question of Hasina's extradition.

MMR.leader: President Min Aung Hlaing (commander in chief: Ye Win Oo)
MMR.situation: After the general election, Min Aung Hlaing took office as an "elected" president in April 2026, but in substance this extends military rule, and civil war continues on the Kachin and Arakan fronts.

recent.text: Min Aung Hlaing became president after being elected by parliament and handed the post of commander in chief to Ye Win Oo.
The Kachin Independence Army (KIA) repelled a military breakout attempt around Bhamo (Banmaw), and the Arakan Army (AA) captured outposts around Sittwe (according to resistance sources).

uncertain: September battlefield reporting on Myanmar relies on a resistance-side summary (Substack). The International Crisis Group (June) assessed that the military had regained some of the initiative, so perspectives differ.

THA.situation: Bhumjaithai became the largest party in the February 2026 election, relaunching Anutin's coalition government; the border ceasefire with Cambodia is holding but remains fragile.

recent.text: At a leaders' retreat with Singapore in Bangkok, the two countries launched a future-oriented strategic partnership.
The Thai military warned of a full-scale response to any Cambodian attack while urging de-escalation through dialogue.

uncertain: Armed clashes on the Thailand–Cambodia border, June–September 2026: no reports of large-scale fighting were found, but smaller incidents may have been missed.

KHM.situation: Since the 2025 border fighting with Thailand, a ceasefire under the December 27 joint statement has held, but the conflict remains unresolved because of Thailand's scrapping of a maritime boundary MOU and disputes over occupied areas.

recent.text: Initiated UN conciliation proceedings over the maritime boundary dispute with Thailand.
At a forum in Hanoi, Prime Minister Hun Manet said the ceasefire with Thailand was holding but fragile.

uncertain: Whether armed clashes occurred on the Thai-Cambodian border between June and September 2026: no reports of major fighting were found, but small incidents may have been missed.

MYS.situation: Describing his government as stable, Anwar is weighing an early 16th general election (GE16), while keeping to quiet diplomacy with China in the South China Sea.

recent.text: Anwar raised the possibility of holding GE16 early.
Anwar instructed the People's Justice Party (PKR) to close ranks and prepare for the general election.

SGP.situation: Sitting at the gateway to the Strait of Malacca, Singapore balances between the United States and China and is preparing to take over the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027.

recent.text: At a leaders' retreat with Thailand, the two sides agreed to cooperate on energy, supply chains, and coordination around the ASEAN chairmanship.

LKA.situation: Dissanayake's leftist government is pursuing economic recovery under an IMF program, and with its approval ratings slipping, it began a series of nationwide rallies in September.

recent.text: President Dissanayake began a tour of rallies across the country to win back flagging support.

NPL.leader: Prime Minister Balen Shah (Balendra Shah), Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP)
NPL.situation: In the March 2026 election that followed the 2025 Gen Z protests, the RSP won 182 of 275 seats, making Balen Shah the youngest prime minister in the country's history; he is pushing anti-corruption reforms.

recent.text: Balen Shah took office as prime minister.
The new government arrested a former prime minister, holding him responsible for the deadly crackdown on the 2025 protests.

LAO.leader: President Thongloun Sisoulith (Prime Minister: Sonexay Siphandone)
LAO.situation: After the party congress and general election in early 2026, President Thongloun and Prime Minister Sonexay were re-elected; debt to China and economic hardship remain structural weaknesses.

recent.text: At the first session of the 10th National Assembly, President Thongloun Sisoulith and Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone were re-elected.

PNG.situation: The Pukpuk Treaty, a mutual defense pact with Australia, entered into force in July 2026, giving Papua New Guinea its first alliance and enlarging its role as Australia's breakwater against China's push into the Pacific.

recent.text: The Pukpuk Treaty with Australia entered into force.
The two countries' defense ministers advanced measures to implement the Pukpuk Treaty (recruitment and integration of personnel).

NZL.situation: Luxon's center-right coalition faces a general election on November 7, and in foreign policy New Zealand is tightening its security ties with Australia and the United States.

recent.text: Vietnam's general secretary and president, To Lam, made a state visit to New Zealand after Australia.
Prime Minister Luxon set the general election for November 7, 2026.

GBR.leader: Prime Minister Andy Burnham (Labour; took office July 20, 2026) / King Charles III
GBR.situation: After a rout in the May local elections, Starmer announced his resignation on June 22, and Burnham won the Labour leadership contest in July to become Britain's seventh prime minister in a decade. Abroad, London is keeping up support for Ukraine (including handing over Storm Shadow design data) and its target of defense spending at 3.5 percent of GDP, but gilt yields have climbed to their highest since 2008, sharply reducing fiscal headroom. In the fallout from the Iran war, the bases at Akrotiri in Cyprus and Diego Garcia came under attack, and in August Iran-linked hackers shut down a power plant for four days.

mil.note: A nuclear power, Britain has decided to rejoin NATO nuclear sharing by acquiring 12 F-35As. The gap between what the Ministry of Defence requests and what the Treasury allocates remains wide, however.

pol.regime: Constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system
pol.stability: Labour's parliamentary majority is solid, but its poll numbers have collapsed, and the surge of Reform UK is increasing pressure for a change of government.
pol.next_election: The next general election must be held by August 2029 at the latest

econ.note: Soaring energy prices and rising gilt yields are estimated to have cut fiscal headroom to about £8 billion, making the October 28 budget a test.

recent.text: Prime Minister Starmer announced his resignation after the local election rout and mounting pressure within the party.
Andy Burnham, winner of the Labour leadership contest, took office as prime minister and appointed John Healey chancellor of the exchequer.
Prime Minister Burnham said he would keep the pledge to raise defense spending and create 500,000 defense and aerospace jobs by 2030.
It was disclosed that a cyberattack by Iran-linked hackers had shut down a British power plant for four days.
Gilt yields rose to their highest since the 2008 financial crisis, and analysts estimated that fiscal headroom had been cut in half.

watch: How the October 28 budget balances higher defense spending against the fiscal rules, and how the gilt market reacts
Whether the Hormuz maritime mission that Britain agreed to lead jointly with France actually gets under way
Whether the crackdown on Russia's shadow fleet and Iranian cyber retaliation spill over into security on British soil
uncertain: Details of 2026 policy changes on AUKUS could not be confirmed (reports say it is proceeding). Whether a Quad leaders' summit will be held this year is undecided.

IISS active-duty troop numbers are taken from a Wikipedia compilation (mixing the IISS 2024–2026 editions): U.K. 141,100 / France 203,900 / Germany 179,850 / Poland 173,000. They could not be cross-checked against the original Military Balance 2026. Poland's defense ministry has said it has more than 220,000 active-duty troops.

FRA.leader: President Emmanuel Macron / Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu (reappointed October 10, 2025)
FRA.situation: In a parliament with no majority, Prime Minister Lecornu is hanging on, surviving one no-confidence threat after another. Ahead of the 2027 presidential election, the National Rally (RN) leads in the polls. In March, Macron announced an increase in nuclear warheads and a plan for extended deterrence across Europe, and France agreed to lead a Hormuz maritime mission with Britain, though the mission has stalled. Having missed its 2026 deficit target, the government has proposed €54 billion in spending cuts.

mil.note: The EU's only nuclear power; in March 2026 it announced an increase in warheads and the Europeanization of nuclear deterrence (talks with Germany and Britain).

pol.stability: A minority government faces a no-confidence threat with every budget and, with the presidential election approaching, is squeezed from both the far right and the far left.
pol.next_election: Presidential election: first round April 18, 2027; runoff May 2, 2027

econ.note: The government has pledged €54 billion in cuts to bring the 2027 deficit down to 5 percent of GDP, but with fuel prices driven up by the Middle East and rising interest costs, it is unclear whether the plan will pass.

recent.text: The French navy seized the Russian shadow-fleet tanker Deliver near Sicily, its fifth boarding since September 2025.
An appeals court shortened Marine Le Pen's ban from public office, clearing the way for her to run in the 2027 presidential election.
France said it would soon launch a maritime security mission in the Strait of Hormuz with Britain, but actual deployment had been delayed as of August.
Prime Minister Lecornu acknowledged that the 2026 deficit target would be missed and unveiled the outline of a €54 billion austerity budget for 2027.

watch: Whether a no-confidence motion passes during October's budget debate and brings down the government
The shape of the 2027 presidential race, especially whether the RN candidate is Le Pen or Jordan Bardella, and whether the center unites behind one candidate
Whether Europeanizing nuclear deterrence leads to actual deployments or agreements with Germany and others
uncertain: Active-duty IISS troop numbers are taken from a Wikipedia table (mixing the 2024–2026 IISS editions): Britain 141,100 / France 203,900 / Germany 179,850 / Poland 173,000. They have not been cross-checked against the original Military Balance 2026. Poland's Defense Ministry says it has more than 220,000 active personnel.

The figure of 370 French nuclear warheads is the total inventory, including retired warheads awaiting dismantlement, in a table in the summary of the SIPRI Yearbook 2026. SIPRI puts France's military stockpile at 290, the same as in the 2025 edition. Because France stopped disclosing its stockpile in March 2026, both figures are SIPRI estimates.

DEU.leader: Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) / President Frank-Walter Steinmeier
DEU.situation: With military spending of $114 billion in 2025, Germany ranked fourth in the world, and by stationing a permanent armored brigade in Lithuania it has become the center of European rearmament. In September's state elections, the AfD took 43.8 percent in Saxony-Anhalt; in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the AfD came first and the CDU fell below 5 percent; and in Berlin, the Left Party finished first. These were the worst results ever for parties in government, and they have badly sapped the momentum of Merz's coalition. Berlin formally blamed Russia for an incident involving explosive-laden drones at Leipzig airport, stepping up its response to Russian hybrid warfare.

mil.note: The world's fourth-largest military spender by SIPRI's count. Germany has no nuclear weapons but takes part in NATO nuclear sharing (U.S. B61 bombs) and is a party to talks on French nuclear deterrence.

pol.stability: The CDU-SPD coalition is holding, but the AfD is at or near the top of national polls at around 30 percent, and there is a risk that forming governments in the eastern states will become paralyzed.
pol.next_election: Bundestag elections in 2029 (regular schedule). The Federal Convention will elect the next federal president on January 30, 2027

econ.note: Europe's largest economy, but stagnation persists: manufacturing is losing more than 10,000 jobs a month, and the economy is vulnerable to energy price shocks.

recent.text: Germany signed a bilateral defense cooperation agreement with Poland.
Germany for the first time formally blamed Russia for an incident involving explosive-laden drones near Leipzig/Halle airport. Russia retaliated by closing the Goethe-Institut.
In the Saxony-Anhalt state election, the AfD won a landslide 43.8 percent but fell short of a majority. The CDU managed only 17.2 percent.

The AfD came first in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the CDU failed to clear the 5 percent threshold, and in Berlin the Left Party finished first for the first time. Merz acknowledged the results as a disaster but declared that the coalition would continue.

watch: Whether the firewall against the AfD holds as governments are formed in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
The Merz coalition's reform agenda and pressure on the SPD to walk away
How quickly the Lithuania brigade reaches full strength, and the spread of Russian hybrid attacks (drones, sabotage)
uncertain: IISS active-duty troop numbers are taken from a Wikipedia compilation (mixing the IISS 2024–2026 editions): U.K. 141,100 / France 203,900 / Germany 179,850 / Poland 173,000. They could not be cross-checked against the original Military Balance 2026. Poland's defense ministry has said it has more than 220,000 active-duty troops.
The Federal Convention that elects Germany's next federal president will meet on January 30, 2027 (set by the Bundestag president on February 26, 2026); Steinmeier's term ends on March 18, 2027.

POL.leader: President Karol Nawrocki (PiS-aligned) / Prime Minister Donald Tusk (Civic Coalition)
POL.situation: A frontline state on NATO's eastern flank, Poland put 4.7 percent of GDP into defense in 2025 and 5 percent in 2026 and is building Europe's largest land army. In July, a Russian cruise missile came down near Lublin, and in September a Mi-8 helicopter from Kaliningrad violated its airspace; such provocations have become routine. At home, the cohabitation clash between President Nawrocki and the Tusk government has deepened, leading to a presidential veto of EU defense loans (SAFE) and a push for constitutional change.

mil.note: At 4.7 to 5 percent of GDP, its defense spending is the highest share in NATO. The defense ministry says active-duty personnel exceed 220,000 (a figure that differs from the IISS count).

pol.regime: Parliamentary system (directly elected president with veto power)
pol.stability: A cohabitation arrangement pits the president against the government. Veto politics is paralyzing legislation, and the right-wing opposition is regrouping.

econ.note: Among the fastest-growing large EU economies; rising defense spending is propping up growth while adding to the fiscal burden.

recent.text: Poland signed a bilateral defense cooperation agreement with Germany.

President Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle after the Ukrainian president decorated a unit that claims the legacy of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), straining relations with Ukraine.
A cruise missile believed to be Russian came down near Lublin, and NATO fighter jets were scrambled.
Nawrocki launched a constitutional commission to strengthen presidential powers; the Tusk government declined to take part.
A Russian Mi-8 helicopter from Kaliningrad violated Polish airspace for 42 seconds, and Poland expanded its air defenses in the east.

watch: Whether Russian missile, drone, and helicopter incursions lead to discussions under NATO's Article 4 or Article 5
Whether Nawrocki's vetoes continue to block defense procurement (including SAFE) and judicial reform
The regrouping of the right-wing opposition ahead of the 2027 elections, and the Tusk coalition's poll numbers
uncertain: IISS active-duty troop numbers are taken from a Wikipedia compilation (mixing the IISS 2024–2026 editions): U.K. 141,100 / France 203,900 / Germany 179,850 / Poland 173,000. They could not be cross-checked against the original Military Balance 2026. Poland's defense ministry has said it has more than 220,000 active-duty troops.

ITA.leader: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni / President Sergio Mattarella
ITA.situation: The Meloni government is stable, having set the record as the longest-serving cabinet since World War II, but a budget deficit stuck at 3.1 percent has dashed hopes of exiting the EU's excessive deficit procedure, and ahead of the 2027 election it faces pressure from rivals further to the right.

recent.text: The Meloni cabinet became the longest-serving Italian government since World War II.
Italian Air Force fighters shot down a drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace (as part of NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission).

ESP.leader: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez / King Felipe VI
ESP.situation: The Sánchez government is shaken by corruption scandals and a minority position in parliament but is holding on. Spain is the NATO member most reluctant to embrace the 5 percent target, yet its economy is growing faster than any other large eurozone economy.

recent.text: During the UN General Assembly, Prime Minister Sánchez publicly criticized the Trump administration, continuing his confrontational line toward Washington.
Spanish F-18s scrambled after detecting an aerial target over Ukraine near the Romanian border (a NATO eastern-flank mission).

uncertain: The item in Spain's recent developments on criticism of the United States at the UN General Assembly was confirmed only at the level of a headline.

NLD.leader: Prime Minister Rob Jetten (D66, took office February 23, 2026) / King Willem-Alexander
NLD.situation: A three-party minority cabinet of D66, the VVD and the CDA took office without a confidence-and-supply agreement with the opposition, the first such case since 1918, leaving an unstable arrangement that must find a fresh majority for every bill. As host of the NATO summit in The Hague, the Netherlands maintains its line on deterring Russia and raising defense spending.

recent.text: The Jetten cabinet (a D66-VVD-CDA minority coalition) took office.

SWE.leader: Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson (outgoing, caretaker) → new parliament opened September 28; vote on Magdalena Andersson as prime minister after September 29 / King Carl XVI Gustaf
SWE.situation: In the September 13 election, the left-wing bloc won narrowly, 176 seats to 173, and Prime Minister Kristersson announced his resignation; parliament could vote on a new prime minister as early as September 29. Conflict with the Center Party over bringing the Left Party into government makes coalition-building shaky, but the defense course set since NATO accession is expected to keep cross-party support.

recent.text: The Social Democrats became the largest party, and the left-wing bloc won a majority (176 seats).
Prime Minister Kristersson announced his resignation. Parliament's vote on a prime minister could come as early as September 29.

Sweden's new parliament opened on September 28 and elected a speaker; because the speaker can nominate a candidate for prime minister only after September 29, the vote on Andersson has not yet taken place (left-wing bloc 176 seats, right-wing bloc 173).

uncertain: Sweden's next prime minister will be confirmed by a parliamentary vote after September 29. Andersson is the favorite, but the question of the Left Party joining the government could cause delays.

FIN.leader: President Alexander Stubb / Prime Minister Petteri Orpo
FIN.situation: Finland has finished building about 200 kilometers of fence and sensors along its 1,340-kilometer border with Russia and is preparing for the Russian buildup near that border. In the spring, Ukrainian drones knocked off course by Russian electronic warfare strayed into Finnish airspace. Finland is a key frontline state on the Baltic and Arctic fronts.

recent.text: Warnings emerged that Russia is redeploying large forces (up to about 100,000 troops) toward the Finnish border.
The trial of the captain of the Fitburg, in the case of damage to undersea cables in the Gulf of Finland, opened at the Helsinki District Court.

NOR.leader: Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre / King Harald V
NOR.situation: Since the closure of Hormuz, Norway has gained weight as a key energy supplier to Europe. It is NATO's northern front line, facing Russia's Northern Fleet in the Arctic and the Barents Sea.

recent.text: Støre attended the European Arctic summit in Rovaniemi, where leaders discussed linking Arctic and Baltic security.

ROU.leader: President Nicușor Dan / interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan; confirmation vote pending on Prime Minister-designate Siegfried Mureșan (around September 29–30; about 170 seats secured, 233 needed)
ROU.situation: After the Bolojan cabinet fell to a no-confidence vote in May over austerity disputes, Prime Minister-designate Mureșan faces a confirmation vote with a minority coalition of the PNL, USR, and UDMR (170 seats, against the 233 needed for confirmation), and passage is uncertain. Along the Black Sea and Danube borders, Russian drone incursions continue, and Romania shot down a drone on September 24.

recent.text: The Bolojan government fell in a no-confidence vote (281 in favor).
Romanian forces shot down a drone suspected to be Russian.

Prime Minister-designate Mureșan submitted his three-party PNL-USR-UDMR cabinet list and governing program to parliament, but with about 170 seats secured, he is 63 short of the 233 needed for confirmation; the vote will be held at a joint session of both chambers on September 30, and the outcome is uncertain.

uncertain: Romania's confirmation vote on the Mureșan cabinet is expected around September 30; with 170 seats against the 233 needed, passage is uncertain. If it fails, the interim Bolojan arrangement will continue.

HUN.leader: Prime Minister Péter Magyar (Tisza; took office May 9, 2026) / President Tamás Sulyok
HUN.situation: In the April general election, Tisza won 141 of 199 seats, a two-thirds supermajority, ending Orbán's 16 years in power. Hungary has swung to a pro-EU course, recovering EU funds that had been frozen and lifting its veto on EU support for Ukraine.

recent.text: Péter Magyar took office as prime minister, ending the Orbán era.
With Hungary's veto lifted, the EU approved 6.6 billion euros in military aid to Ukraine through the European Peace Facility (EPF), which had been blocked since 2023.

uncertain: Military spending is not listed for Hungary, Serbia, or the three Baltic states because they do not appear among SIPRI's top 40 countries for 2025.
It could not be verified whether Hungary's president (Tamás Sulyok) remains in office after the Magyar government took power. Magyar's camp has called for his resignation.

GRC.leader: Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis / President Konstantinos Tasoulas
GRC.situation: Tensions with Turkey in the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean have flared again, and Mitsotakis visited Kastellorizo, declaring that Greece takes orders from no one on defense and sovereignty. Defense cooperation with Israel is also provoking Ankara.

recent.text: Mitsotakis warned Turkey that Greece does not take orders on matters of defense and sovereignty.
Mitsotakis visited the island of Kastellorizo, off the Turkish coast, sending a message to Ankara.

SRB.leader: Acting President Ana Brnabić (speaker of the National Assembly, since September 27, 2026); Prime Minister Đuro Macut. Aleksandar Vučić is running for prime minister in the October 25 snap parliamentary election
SRB.situation: After nearly two years of antigovernment protests that followed the 2024 collapse of a canopy at the Novi Sad railway station, Vučić called a snap parliamentary election for October 25. He has given up the presidency to run for prime minister, aiming to shift his power base. The youth-led protest movement is formally taking part in the election.

recent.text: Vučić called a snap parliamentary election for October 25.

Serbian President Vučić resigned to run for prime minister in the October 25 snap election, and his ally Ana Brnabić, the speaker of the National Assembly, became acting president; just before stepping down, he pardoned 49 people, including 23 jailed in connection with the protests.

Vučić said the first round of a presidential election must be held before the end of the year under the constitution's 90-day deadline; analysts see a close race in the October 25 parliamentary election between the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and the student-led movement's list (Students Are Winning).

uncertain: Hungary, Serbia and the three Baltic states are not on SIPRI's 2025 list of the top 40 spenders, so no military spending figure is given.

EST.leader: Prime Minister Kristen Michal / President Alar Karis (President-elect Ülle Madise takes office October 12)
EST.situation: Estonia, a frontline state whose border runs through Narva, saw a Russian drone strike the Auvere power plant in March; in May, a stray drone was shot down in its airspace. On September 2, parliament elected Ülle Madise as the next president.

recent.text: Parliament elected Ülle Madise president (she takes office October 12).
A Romanian F-16 shot down a stray drone over Estonia.

uncertain: Estonia's presidency passes from Karis to Madise on October 12. The results of Latvia's parliamentary election (October 3) and Bosnia's general election (October 4) are not yet in.

LVA.leader: Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List, took office May 2026) / President Edgars Rinkevics
LVA.situation: Latvia heads into an October 3 election in which Kulbergs's United List holds the lead. In response to migration pressure, sabotage and airspace violations by Russia and Belarus, NATO sent additional German Eurofighters for the election period.

recent.text: Two drones that had strayed off course entered Latvia, and one of them exploded at an oil storage facility.
Elections to the Saeima (parliament) are scheduled for October 3.

uncertain: Estonia's presidency passes from Karis to Madise on October 12. The results of Latvia's election (October 3) and Bosnia's election (October 4) are not yet known.

LTU.leader: Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius (Social Democrat, confirmed June 30, 2026) / President Gitanas Nausėda
LTU.situation: A frontline state bordering the Suwałki corridor between Belarus and Kaliningrad, Lithuania hosts a permanent German armored brigade (about 4,800 troops). On September 15, NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that had entered from the direction of Belarus. In June, Prime Minister Inga Ruginienė resigned, making her successor the third Social Democratic prime minister since the 2024 election.

recent.text: Parliament confirmed Sinkevičius as prime minister, following Ruginienė's resignation.
NATO (Italian) fighter jets shot down a drone that had entered from the direction of Belarus over eastern Lithuania.

CZE.leader: Prime Minister Andrej Babiš (ANO) / President Petr Pavel
CZE.situation: The Babiš government is continuing the Czech-led initiative to procure artillery shells for Ukraine but has cut off state financing for it. It is at odds with the pro-Western President Pavel, and the head of Czech intelligence has warned that a Russian attack on Europe could come within months rather than years.

recent.text: The head of Czech intelligence warned that a Russian attack on Europe could come within months.

DNK.leader: Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen (third term; appointed June 3, 2026) / King Frederik X
DNK.situation: In the snap election in March, the Social Democrats posted their lowest vote share since 1903, but Frederiksen won a third term at the head of a four-party minority coalition. The crisis sparked early in the year by U.S. pressure to annex Greenland was settled, for now, by the U.S.-Denmark-Greenland security agreement of September 22. Washington gained an expansion of Pituffik Space Base and two new bases, and non-NATO countries may not base forces in Greenland without the consent of the parties to the agreement.

recent.text: A Russian corvette fired flares at a Danish navy helicopter near Gedser in the Baltic Sea.
The U.S.-Denmark-Greenland security agreement was signed at the UN General Assembly. It allows the expansion of Pituffik and new bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, and it has no expiration date.

CAN.leader: Prime Minister Mark Carney (Liberal; won an outright majority through by-elections in April 2026)
CAN.situation: After trade talks with the United States broke down in late August, Canada answered the 50 percent U.S. tariff by imposing about $20 billion in retaliatory tariffs on September 8, entering a full-scale trade war. Having secured a majority in April, the Carney government stands on a stable domestic footing, but national unity faces a test ahead of the October 19 Alberta referendum on separation.

mil.note: By SIPRI's count, military spending rose 23 percent in 2025 from the previous year to 1.6 percent of GDP, 16th in the world

pol.stability: As a majority government, it has a stable base in Parliament, but the trade war with the United States and Alberta separatism weigh on it

econ.note: Because about three-quarters of exports go to the United States, a prolonged tariff war would hit manufacturing and agriculture hard

recent.text: At the USMCA joint review, the United States declined to extend the agreement for 16 years, shifting it to annual reviews through 2036

Trade talks with the United States collapsed, and Carney said the U.S. proposal set unfair terms that would have constrained even Quebec's cultural protections and Canada's ability to sign its own free trade agreements
Carney rebutted criticism from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and said Canada would resume talks when the United States is ready
Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs of 15 to 50 percent on about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods across some 700 product lines, including steel, home appliances, farm machinery, and dairy products

The same day, the United States hit back by banning imports of Canadian dairy products, motorcycles, and alcoholic beverages (effective September 29), excluding Canada from federal procurement, and threatening to block sales by Bombardier

watch: Whether talks resume before or after the U.S. import ban takes effect on September 29
The result of the October 19 Alberta referendum (on a question to begin the separation process)
Whether the annual USMCA reviews and a bilateral U.S.-Mexico deal leave Canada isolated

MEX.situation: Since the killing of CJNG boss "El Mencho" in February, the Sheinbaum government has eased U.S. pressure for military intervention through a hard-line security policy and extraditions to the United States. Washington has refused to extend the USMCA and is maintaining tariffs of 50 percent on steel and aluminum and 25 percent on non-originating autos; the two countries resume trade negotiations in Washington on September 28.

mil.note: Military spending jumped 71 percent in 2024, then fell by a third in 2025; folding the National Guard into the military has enlarged the armed forces

pol.stability: The ruling party's dominance gives the government a firm base, but cartel violence and sovereignty disputes with Washington are ever present
pol.next_election: Federal midterm elections, June 2027 (presidential election in 2030)

econ.note: With exports overwhelmingly dependent on the U.S. market, the annual USMCA review and product-specific tariffs are the biggest variables for growth

recent.text: Washington's refusal to extend the USMCA for 16 years triggered a regime of annual reviews; Mexico said it supports an extension
U.S. forces shot down three cartel drones near the border with a laser weapon
After her 22nd call with Trump, Sheinbaum said a trade deal was making progress, and talks were set to resume in Washington on September 28
