Mexico stayed out of the U.S.-led anti-cartel coalition, the Shield of the Americas, but its major cartels are among the 24 groups on the coalition's list of narco-terrorist organizations

watch: Whether steel and auto tariffs come down at the September 28 trade talks in Washington
The possibility of unilateral U.S. strikes on cartels on Mexican soil
The CJNG succession struggle after El Mencho's death and deteriorating security
uncertain: Mexico's figure of 301,000 active-duty troops is an IISS number cited by Wikipedia; whether it includes the absorbed National Guard could not be confirmed in the original source

BRA.leader: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (Workers' Party)
BRA.situation: Ahead of the October 4 first round of the presidential election, Lula, seeking a fourth term, and Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, are locked in a statistical tie in hypothetical runoff polling (47 percent to 45 percent). When Washington imposed 25 percent Section 301 tariffs in July, Lula hit back in the name of defending sovereignty and has held firm in refusing to join the U.S.-led Shield of the Americas.

mil.note: Investment in naval technology development and rising personnel costs lifted military spending 13 percent in 2025, making Brazil the largest spender in South America

pol.stability: A polarized, neck-and-neck presidential race, compounded by infighting on the Supreme Federal Court (STF) and the Banco Master scandal, makes for high uncertainty
pol.next_election: Presidential and general elections: first round October 4, 2026; runoff October 25, 2026 (inauguration January 1, 2027)

econ.note: Modest growth is expected amid U.S. Section 301 tariffs (beef, coffee and aircraft parts exempted) and high interest rates

recent.text: The United States announced 25 percent tariffs on a wide range of Brazilian goods under Section 301 of the Trade Act (effective July 22); Brazil responded with its reciprocity law and a WTO complaint
Lula launched his campaign for a fourth term, putting national sovereignty front and center
In a call of about 80 minutes with Trump, Lula asked to reopen tariff negotiations
The release of messages between Justice Alexandre de Moraes and banker Daniel Vorcaro fueled conflict and investigations within the Supreme Court

Ahead of Brazil's October 4 first-round vote, a Datafolha poll (September 22–23) put Lula at 40 percent and Flávio Bolsonaro at 36 percent, with a hypothetical runoff at 47 to 45 percent, within the margin of error. At the UN on September 23, Lula said that Brazil is no one's backyard.

watch: Vote shares in the October 4 first round and whether a runoff is held on October 25
Post-election instability, including refusal to accept the result and conflict with the judiciary
Negotiations over U.S. Section 301 tariffs and allegations of election interference

VEN.leader: Acting President Delcy Rodríguez (sworn in January 5, 2026; recognized by the United States as head of state in March)
VEN.situation: With Nicolás Maduro, captured in a U.S. military operation on January 3, awaiting trial in New York, the Rodríguez transitional government is cooperating with Washington and has opened up the oil sector, signing an oil agreement in late August covering 65 billion barrels of reserves. Twin earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 on June 24 caused heavy loss of life. No election timetable has been set, and the UN notes that the machinery of repression remains intact.

mil.note: There is no SIPRI estimate because Venezuela has not disclosed military spending for years; Defense Minister Vladimir Padrino López was replaced in March

pol.regime: Transitional authoritarian regime (led by remnants of chavismo, under U.S. patronage)
pol.stability: Outwardly stabilized under U.S. patronage, but fragile given its lack of legitimacy, the unsettled election timetable and earthquake damage
pol.next_election: Presidential election date not set (government–opposition negotiations under way)

econ.note: Sanctions relief and the U.S. oil agreement are expected to revive oil output, but earthquake recovery is a heavy burden

recent.text: A U.S. air strike (reported June 12–13) killed Tren de Aragua leader "Niño Guerrero" in Bolívar state
Twin earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck the Yaracuy area, killing thousands and leaving tens of thousands missing
Under U.S. sponsorship, the government (represented by Jorge Rodríguez) and the opposition (Dinorah Figuera) began negotiating a path to elections, with María Corina Machado excluded
Trump announced an agreement giving the United States a stake in 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves
In her first UN speech, Rodríguez pledged to hold elections, and she met Trump in New York

After a second round of U.S.-backed government–opposition talks, Delcy Rodríguez's transitional government released 39 political prisoners; the same day, rallies in Caracas and elsewhere demanded Machado's safe return and a presidential election.

watch: Whether a presidential election date is set, and Machado's return and candidacy
Implementation of the U.S. oil agreement and the pace of the recovery in output
Whether the machinery of repression, including the military and the colectivos, is dismantled, and Maduro's trial
uncertain: Venezuela earthquake death toll: estimates vary widely—Wikipedia lists 1,719+ (with some 46,000 missing), while ABC News (September 23) reported more than 6,500—so the recent developments section says "thousands."
Venezuela's GDP of $99.7 billion and 2026 growth of 4.0 percent are IMF DataMapper figures; statistics during the transition are of low reliability
Venezuela's military spending is left blank because it is not reported to SIPRI
The exact date of the Caribbean strike that killed four people (reported September 20; the strike itself probably on the 19th) and the cumulative death toll (230+) are estimates

ARG.situation: Under austerity and a strong-peso policy, the economic slowdown continues, and the poverty rate rose again to 32.3 percent in the first half of the year, adding to the burden on Milei's path to reelection in 2027.

recent.text: Took part in a meeting of the Shield of the Americas, a U.S.-led anti-cartel coalition
The national statistics agency (INDEC) reported a first-half poverty rate of 32.3 percent, reversing the downward trend

COL.leader: President Abelardo de la Espriella (took office August 7, 2026)
COL.situation: The hard-right de la Espriella has scrapped Petro's "total peace" negotiations, shifted to a campaign to crush armed groups and a pro-U.S. course, and signaled that he will break off relations with Cuba and Nicaragua.

recent.text: He was elected after defeating leftist Iván Cepeda in the runoff by about 250,000 votes
Taking office in Cali, he said dialogue had been completely exhausted and announced a hard line against armed groups and Colombia's entry into the Shield of the Americas

CUB.leader: Miguel Díaz-Canel, president and first secretary of the Communist Party
CUB.situation: A U.S. energy blockade in place since January has exhausted fuel supplies and caused repeated collapses of the power grid, creating a humanitarian crisis, while Trump openly names Cuba as the next target for regime change after Venezuela.

recent.text: The United States imposed additional sanctions, including on nine state-owned companies in mining, metals and construction
In his UN speech, Trump said freedom was coming to Cuba; Díaz-Canel retorted that the threat is not Cuba but the blockade

Trump said the United States and Cuba would make a deal and that military action would not be needed; Cuba's foreign minister condemned the oil blockade as collective punishment but said Havana is open to dialogue without preconditions.

uncertain: Cuba's GDP is left blank because the IMF does not publish it

CHL.leader: President José Antonio Kast (took office March 11, 2026)
CHL.situation: The hard-right Kast government is pushing reforms to crack down on organized crime and immigration, drawing criticism as illiberal. The macroeconomy, by contrast, is relatively stable.

recent.text: Kast unveiled a legislative agenda to strengthen the fight against organized crime

PER.situation: Fujimori, Peru's ninth president in 10 years, took office after a razor-thin runoff victory, promising iron-fisted security (a mega-prison, faceless judges), but fears of an authoritarian relapse and political instability persist.

recent.text: In the presidential runoff, Fujimori defeated leftist Roberto Sánchez by fewer than 50,000 votes
Taking office, she signaled hard-line security policies and the deportation of undocumented migrants

uncertain: The exact date of Peru's runoff (in June) could not be confirmed

PAN.situation: After the Supreme Court in January struck down CK Hutchison's concession to operate ports on the canal as unconstitutional, Maersk and MSC have been operating the ports of Balboa and Cristóbal on an interim basis, and Panama is walking a tightrope between Chinese retaliation through ship inspections and customs measures and pressure from the United States.

recent.text: Mulino visited the Balboa terminal, urged China to ease tensions, and said Panama is preparing a permanent tender for the ports
China is seeking the extradition of one of its businessmen linked to the canal ports dispute, and Panama must decide by early November

ECU.situation: As gang violence rises again, Noboa declared roughly his 20th state of emergency in September, and since March Ecuador has been conducting ground strikes near the Colombian border jointly with U.S. forces.

recent.text: A bombing in Cascales, near the Colombian border, during a joint U.S.-Ecuadorian operation sparked controversy over a strike on a civilian farm
Declared a 60-day state of emergency in eight provinces (Decree 498) and a nighttime curfew in four

NIC.leader: Co-Presidents Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo
NIC.situation: With the co-presidency of husband and wife Ortega and Murillo in control of the judiciary, the legislature, and the electoral council, Ortega declared in July that there would be no more elections, deepening the confrontation with the United States.

recent.text: In a speech marking the anniversary of the Sandinista revolution, Ortega declared that there would be no more elections, and Secretary of State Rubio condemned the statement
The State Department denounced legislation passed by Nicaragua's National Assembly as a sham and announced countermeasures

uncertain: The exact date of the State Department statement on Nicaragua (September) and the content of the legislation it targeted could not be confirmed because the original could not be accessed

BOL.situation: Amid fuel shortages and economic crisis, nationwide blockades and protests in May and June forced the president to take refuge in Sucre. A 90-day state of emergency restored order, but the IMF projects that the economy will contract in 2026.

recent.text: Amid marches and road blockades led by Evo Morales, President Paz relocated to Sucre
Paz declared a 90-day national state of emergency, and all blockades were lifted on June 23

uncertain: Whether Bolivia's 90-day state of emergency (declared June 20) has expired or been extended could not be confirmed

EGY.leader: President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi (Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly)
EGY.situation: With Hormuz shut by the Iran war, ships have crowded into the Suez Canal, lifting canal revenue back to its highest level since late 2023. Passing an IMF program review has eased pressure on foreign exchange, but heavy debt and war-driven energy costs remain a burden. To the south, Sudan's civil war and the dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) compound Cairo's security concerns.

mil.note: $2.5 billion in nominal dollars per SIPRI (the dollar figure is understated because of the pound's devaluation). Troop numbers are baseline figures from the IISS Military Balance; the 2026 edition figure could not be confirmed.

pol.stability: The military-centered regime is entrenched, and crackdowns on dissidents continue

econ.note: IMF April 2026 WEO (fiscal-year basis). Passing the IMF review in July released $1.8 billion; inflation was 14.3 percent in June. Suez revenue is forecast at $5.8 billion to $6 billion in 2026 ($4.1 billion in 2025).

recent.text: The United States imposed a 12.5 percent tariff on Egyptian goods, citing allegations of forced labor.
Two tankers were damaged in a drone attack at the port of Damietta.
The IMF approved a program review, releasing $1.8 billion ($7.3 billion in total so far).
Suez Canal revenue in July rose 42 percent from a year earlier to $505 million, the highest since December 2023.
Cairo advanced a new argument against Ethiopia in the GERD dispute; the next day Ethiopia dismissed it as colonial thinking.

watch: Whether the Houthi threat at the southern end of the Red Sea derails the recovery in Suez traffic
Spillover onto the southern border from Sudan's civil war and Ethiopia's Tigray war
Debt repayment and the inflation path under the IMF program

SIPRI 2025 defense spending (Egypt $2.5 billion, Ethiopia $530 million, Nigeria $2.1 billion, South Africa $3.2 billion) are nominal-dollar values from the SIPRI database (April 2026); the figures for Ethiopia and Egypt may be understated because of currency devaluation.

NGA.leader: President Bola Tinubu (Vice President Kashim Shettima)
NGA.situation: Ahead of the January 2027 general election, the Tinubu government is sharply increasing defense spending to fight armed groups and bandits in the north. The president spent nearly a month in Europe from August 30, and the vice president delivered the UN address in his place. On the strength of reforms, the economy is expected to grow in the 4 percent range, and the central bank cut interest rates sharply in September.

mil.note: SIPRI: defense spending rose 55 percent in 2025, to $2.1 billion. Troop numbers are the IISS baseline figure; the 2026 edition figure could not be confirmed (Wikipedia gives more than 230,000).

pol.stability: Elections function, but the collapse of security in the north and the president's prolonged absence are sources of instability
pol.next_election: Presidential and National Assembly elections, January 16, 2027

econ.note: IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2026. The central bank cut its benchmark rate from 26.5 percent to 23 percent on September 22.

recent.text: Tinubu left for Europe and stayed until late September; Vice President Shettima delivered the September 23 address to the UN General Assembly.
Analysts noted that the government is stepping up its response to insurgency and violence through military reform and higher defense spending ahead of the 2027 election.
Thirty-seven detainees died at a Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) detention facility in Minna, Niger State, prompting the formation of a federal commission of inquiry on September 22.
The central bank cut its benchmark rate by 3.5 percentage points, from 26.5 percent to 23 percent.

watch: Opposition consolidation ahead of the January 2027 election (the ADC coalition: Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi)
Bandit attacks in the northwest and ISWAP/Boko Haram offensives in the northeast
Controversy over the president's health and absences

SIPRI 2025 defense spending—Egypt $2.5 billion, Ethiopia $530 million, Nigeria $2.1 billion, South Africa $3.2 billion—are nominal-dollar values from the SIPRI database (April 2026); Ethiopia's and Egypt's may be understated because of currency devaluation.

Nigeria's presidential election date of January 16, 2027, is based on Wikipedia and INEC's revised timetable (whether it falls on the same day as the National Assembly elections needs to be rechecked).

ZAF.situation: The ANC-led Government of National Unity (GNU), a 10-party coalition, has held together for two and a half years, but Ramaphosa is fighting impeachment proceedings over the Phala Phala scandal in the courts. After excluding South Africa from the G20, the United States in September imposed visa sanctions on officials over the country's land and race policies. The November 4 local elections will be the GNU's first test. Meanwhile, unemployment has soared to 33.6 percent.

mil.note: SIPRI: the largest spender in sub-Saharan Africa, but spending fell 1.2 percent from the previous year and is 19 percent lower than in 2016. Troop strength is the IISS baseline figure; the 2026 edition's figure could not be confirmed.

pol.stability: The coalition is holding, but impeachment proceedings against the president coincide with a succession fight within the ANC

econ.note: IMF April 2026 WEO (the Treasury projects 1.5 percent growth and the central bank 1.4 percent). Unemployment stood at 33.6 percent in the second quarter; there has been no load shedding (rolling blackouts) for more than 400 days.

recent.text: Ramaphosa obtained an interim order halting the impeachment inquiry until judicial review of the Phala Phala report is complete.
Parliament's impeachment committee decided to appoint Thuli Madonsela as evidence leader.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced visa restrictions on South African officials, citing racial discrimination and land expropriation without compensation.
Ramaphosa skipped the UN General Assembly, citing health reasons.

watch: ANC and DA vote shares in the November 4 local elections, and whether the GNU survives
The outcome of the judicial review of the Phala Phala report and the resumption of impeachment proceedings
Deteriorating relations with the United States (tariffs, visa sanctions, exclusion from the G20)
uncertain: IISS active-duty troop numbers for Egypt (438,500), Nigeria (143,000), South Africa (73,650), and Ethiopia (503,000) are baseline figures from earlier editions of the Military Balance and could not be checked against the 2026 edition.

SIPRI 2025 defense spending figures for Egypt ($2.5 billion), Ethiopia ($530 million), Nigeria ($2.1 billion), and South Africa ($3.2 billion) are nominal dollar values from the SIPRI database (April 2026); Ethiopia's and Egypt's may be understated because of currency devaluation.

ETH.situation: The Prosperity Party won a landslide in June's general election, taking 438 seats, but on September 22 full-scale fighting erupted in Tigray, Amhara and Afar, pushing the country back toward civil war. Seven armed groups, including the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and Amhara Fano militias, have formed an antigovernment coalition, and Tigrayan forces have seized the airports at Mekelle, Axum and Shire. The government accuses Eritrea of backing the coalition, raising a serious risk of interstate war entangled with Ethiopia's quest for an outlet to the Red Sea.

mil.note: About $530 million in nominal dollars per SIPRI (the dollar figure is small because of the birr's collapse). The 503,000 troop figure is a 2025 estimate; whether it matches the 2026 IISS edition could not be confirmed.

pol.stability: Highly unstable, with full-scale fighting in three northern regions and the formation of an armed antigovernment coalition

econ.note: IMF April 2026 forecast (fiscal-year basis). GDP in dollar terms has shrunk sharply since the birr was floated.

recent.text: Prime Minister Abiy's Prosperity Party won a landslide in the general election, taking 438 seats in the lower house.
A government airstrike hit a residential compound in the Daero area of Mekelle (documented by Human Rights Watch).
Suspicions of Ethiopian involvement in Sudan's civil war grew after the Sudanese government claimed to have shot down RSF drones launched from Ethiopian territory.
Seven armed groups, including the TPLF and Fano, formed an antigovernment coalition; the same day, full-scale fighting began in Tigray, Amhara and Afar.
The Tigray Defense Forces (TDF) seized the airports at Mekelle, Axum and Shire, and the African Union called for renegotiating the Pretoria agreement.

watch: Whether Eritrea enters the war directly, and the question of the port of Assab
Whether the Fano-TPLF coalition widens the front and puts pressure on Addis Ababa
The standoff with Egypt over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD)
uncertain: IISS active-duty figures (Egypt 438,500, Nigeria 143,000, South Africa 73,650, Ethiopia 503,000) are baseline values from earlier editions of the Military Balance and have not been checked against the 2026 edition.

SIPRI 2025 defense spending (Egypt $2.5 billion, Ethiopia $530 million, Nigeria $2.1 billion, South Africa $3.2 billion) are nominal-dollar values from the SIPRI database (April 2026); the figures for Ethiopia and Egypt may be understated because of currency devaluation.
The date of Kenya's presidential election (August 2027) and Ethiopia's next general election (2031) are inferred from constitutional cycles.

SDN.leader: Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the military's top leader (chairman of the Sovereignty Council), and Prime Minister Kamil Idris / RSF: Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo (Hemedti)
SDN.situation: The civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF is in its fourth year; with the front shifting to Kordofan and Blue Nile, there are signs it could spill over into Chad and Ethiopia.

recent.text: The army carried out its first drone strike on Chadian territory, near Mourdi, hitting an RSF convoy of about 200 vehicles and destroying dozens of them.
The RSF attacked a gold market in North Kordofan, killing five, and Burhan stressed a Sudanese-led peace.
RSF drones struck targets including a facility for displaced people in El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, killing two and wounding 20, the second such attack in a week.

uncertain: Sudan: whether the government has returned to Khartoum (or remains in Port Sudan as the administrative capital) could not be confirmed, so the capital's coordinates are set to Khartoum.

DZA.situation: Africa's biggest defense spender ($25.4 billion), Algeria began intervening in the Sahel when it sent fighter jets abroad for the first time since 1973 during an attempted coup in Niger.

recent.text: The day after the attempted coup in Niger, Algeria deployed fighter jets and support aircraft to Niamey.

MAR.leader: King Mohammed VI (Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch; a new prime minister has yet to be named)
MAR.situation: The PAM finished first in the September 23 election but fell short of a majority, opening coalition negotiations; turnout was low, at 38 percent.

recent.text: In the election, the PAM won 97 seats, the RNI 66 and the PJD 54 (up from 13 in 2021); turnout was 38 percent.

The PAM became the largest party with 97 seats in Morocco's September 23 election (RNI 66, Istiqlal 65, PJD 54; turnout about 38 percent), but as of September 27 the king had not yet appointed a new head of government.

uncertain: Morocco: a new prime minister (the names mentioned as PAM candidates include Fouzi Lekjaa and Fatima Zahra Mansouri) appears not to have been named as of September 27.

LBY.leader: West: Government of National Unity (GNU) Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah and Presidential Council head Mohamed al-Menfi / East: Khalifa Haftar (Libyan National Army, LNA) and the government of Osama Hammad
LBY.situation: With the country still split between east and west, the rival sides agreed on August 30, under UN mediation, to a road map for unified elections within 24 months.

recent.text: Fawzi al-Mansouri, the LNA's intelligence chief, was killed by a car bomb.
Rival factions signed an agreement at the UN office in Tripoli to hold presidential and parliamentary elections within 24 months.

uncertain: Libya: Dbeibah is listed as prime minister of the western GNU, but Wikipedia lists the premiership as disputed.

KEN.situation: Ahead of the August 2027 presidential election, Ruto has set out on a reelection push built on nationwide development projects and his broad-based government.

recent.text: Ruto stepped up his campaign, framing the 2027 election as a vote against tribalism and exclusion.

uncertain: Kenya's presidential election date (August 2027) and Ethiopia's next general election (2031) are inferred from constitutional cycles.

COD.situation: Despite the U.S.-brokered Washington Accords and the Doha Framework negotiated in Qatar, fighting between government forces and M23 continues in the east, and an Ebola outbreak is spreading on a large scale.

recent.text: The government and M23 agreed on a road map for phased negotiations at talks in Switzerland.
The ruling party held a march calling for a referendum on amending the constitution, and confirmed Ebola cases reached 7,672 (3,699 deaths).
There were reports that an attempted mutiny within M23 aimed at ousting military commander Sultani Makenga had been put down, and fighting continues in the Minembwe highlands, Masisi, and Walikale.

RWA.situation: Amid allegations that it backs the M23 rebels, Rwanda is sparring with the Democratic Republic of the Congo over implementation of the lifting of its defensive measures under the Washington agreement.

recent.text: The Joint Security Coordination Mechanism reconvened in Geneva to review progress on neutralizing the FDLR and lifting Rwanda's defensive measures.

SOM.leader: President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud (term extension disputed)
SOM.situation: After the president extended his term to five years through constitutional amendment, the opposition, insisting that his term expired on May 15, clashed with the government, and al-Shabaab controls large parts of south-central Somalia.

recent.text: Federal forces entered Baidoa and forced the president of South West State to resign.
U.S. Africa Command carried out airstrikes against al-Shabaab.

MLI.situation: A fuel blockade by JNIM has left the capital, Bamako, dependent on convoys, and since a joint JNIM-FLA offensive in April, Russia's Africa Corps and government forces have been pushed out of the north.

recent.text: JNIM attacked the army base at Dioura, killing 120 to 150 soldiers (the figures are disputed).
Some 900 fuel tankers entered Bamako under military escort.

NER.situation: An August 29 coup attempt was put down with the help of Russia's Africa Corps and Algeria, but security is deteriorating further under offensives by JNIM and the Islamic State Sahel Province.

recent.text: Troops led by special forces attacked the presidential palace, Air Base 101 and state broadcasting, but the presidential guard and Russian forces put down the assault.
JNIM claimed to have captured a checkpoint near Niamey.

BFA.situation: With JNIM's offensive continuing across much of the country, the junta has broken off relations with France and tilted toward Russia.

recent.text: Burkina Faso severed diplomatic relations with France.

JOR.situation: Jordan is coming under Iranian missile and drone attacks because it is a U.S. ally, while it regards Israel's expansion in the West Bank as the greater threat.

recent.text: Amid continuing Iranian strikes, the king appointed a new chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
At the United Nations, the king denounced Israel's expansion in the West Bank as a war crime.

uncertain: The intensity of fighting in the Iran war in August and September (an Iranian attack on U.S. forces in Jordan in late August, IRGC claims of attacks on U.S. warships in early September, etc.) has been confirmed only at the headline level.

LBN.leader: President Joseph Aoun; Prime Minister Nawaf Salam
LBN.situation: A ceasefire reached in June, after Israel's ground offensive in March, had effectively stopped working by September. About 600 square kilometers of the south remain under Israeli occupation, and Hezbollah refuses to disarm.

recent.text: Through Trump's mediation, a partial truce was announced under which Hezbollah would not attack northern Israel and Israel would not strike Beirut. A ceasefire agreement between the Israeli and Lebanese governments had been reached on June 3, but Hezbollah rejected it.
Prime Minister Salam appealed at the United Nations for help disarming Hezbollah, and President Aoun condemned Israeli attacks on aid workers.

After a Hezbollah drone attack, Israeli forces struck several villages in southern Lebanon with helicopters and tanks; the ceasefire has effectively stopped working, and trilateral talks are deadlocked over disarmament.

YEM.leader: Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Leadership Council (Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani) / Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi
YEM.situation: The 2022 truce has collapsed and the civil war has reignited; the Houthis have seized Mocha and Perim (Mayun) Island, tightening their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

recent.text: The Houthis launched simultaneous attacks on cities in southern Saudi Arabia, and government forces mounted a counteroffensive toward Sanaa.
The Houthis seized the port of Mocha and Perim Island and declared navigation safe for all ships except Saudi vessels.

uncertain: Yemen's GDP of $7.9 billion (IMF, 2025) is of low statistical reliability because of the conflict. Eritrea's GDP of $2.3 billion is based on IMF figures as reported by Worldometer.

QAT.leader: Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani
QAT.situation: Iranian missile and drone attacks have damaged Qatar's LNG facilities, and the IMF projects the economy will contract 8.6 percent in 2026. Qatar has cast itself as a mediator between the United States and Iran.

recent.text: Speaking at the UN, the emir said the Gulf was going through one of its most dangerous phases and called for the reopening of Hormuz and a diplomatic solution.

OMN.situation: Iranian attacks on the ports of Duqm and Salalah, which U.S. forces use, have shaken relations between Iran and Oman, until now the Arab country closest to Tehran.

recent.text: As fighting over Hormuz intensified, relations between Iran and Oman deteriorated, and mediation by Oman and Qatar made no progress.

KWT.situation: Since the war began, Kuwait's airport, refineries and power plants have come under concentrated Iranian attack, and with the Hormuz blockade cutting off its export route, its economy is expected to contract.

recent.text: A drone hit Terminal 1 at Kuwait International Airport, killing one person and injuring 63.

ERI.situation: Since Ethiopia named it as a backer of an armed antigovernment coalition, Eritrea has become one of the two parties to a potential interstate war over the port of Assab.

recent.text: The Ethiopian government accused Eritrea of supporting a rebel coalition; Eritrea denied the charge.

uncertain: Yemen's GDP of $7.9 billion (IMF, 2025) is of low statistical reliability because of the conflict. Eritrea's GDP of $2.3 billion is based on IMF figures as reported by Worldometer.

flashpoints.status_ko: In the fifth year of full-scale war, Russia is pressing its offensive toward Kostiantynivka and Dobropillia while Ukraine mounts local counterattacks around Kupiansk, Chasiv Yar, and elsewhere. Every short truce—at Easter in April, on Victory Day in May, and on September 5–8—ended with a return to fighting. Washington is trying to reconvene three-way U.S.-Russia-Ukraine technical talks in the UAE, but Moscow is holding to its demand for all of the Donetsk region.

last_major_event.text: A massive Russian drone attack (295 drones across the country overnight) killed seven people in Kyiv; the same day, Russia and Ukraine confirmed plans to resume three-way talks with the United States.

flashpoints.name_ko: Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
flashpoints.status_ko: The war that began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026, is now in its seventh month. After an April ceasefire and a June 17 memorandum of understanding effectively collapsed on July 8, the United States reimposed its naval blockade. In Hormuz, Iran is trying to control passage by attacking merchant ships and laying mines, while the U.S. military escorts transits; U.S. Central Command said on September 25 that it had turned back 122 merchant vessels since the blockade began. Ship-tracking data and U.S. government statements diverge sharply on how much traffic is getting through. Ship-tracking data in early September showed between five and 12 vessels a day, roughly 10 percent of the peacetime level of about 100. Yet U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on September 28 that about 13 million barrels a day were passing through, and the ship-tracking firm Kpler counted 19 tankers transiting in the week to September 27. On September 25, Iran put forward a roadmap for reopening the strait within seven days, but President Trump rejected it on September 26. On the nuclear front, Natanz and other sites have been destroyed again, but about 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent has been beyond IAEA verification since June 2025.

last_major_event.text: Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the strait would not reopen until seven conditions were met; a tanker was hit in the strait the same day.

flashpoints.status_ko: The Israel-Hezbollah war, which reignited in March alongside the Iran war, has left Israeli forces occupying about 55 villages south of the Litani River, and fighting continues under a nominal ceasefire. In Gaza, an agreement on the phased disarmament of Hamas was announced on July 31, but whether Israel will formally accept and implement it remains unclear.

last_major_event.text: The Board of Peace announced an agreement on the phased disarmament of Hamas and a phased Israeli withdrawal.

flashpoints.status_ko: The peace treaty initialed at the White House in August 2025 remains unsigned because Armenia has not first amended its constitution, as Azerbaijan demands. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan's ruling party won the June parliamentary elections but fell short of the seats needed to change the constitution. Construction has yet to begin on the 43-kilometer Meghri section of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), for which only about $400 million in initial U.S. funding has been secured, while Turkey and Azerbaijan are pursuing a parallel Kars-Dilucu railway that bypasses Armenia.

last_major_event.text: Pashinyan's ruling party won Armenia's parliamentary elections but fell short of the majority needed to amend the constitution.

flashpoints.status_ko: Under Ahmed al-Sharaa's transitional government, Syria has entered a phase of integration and reconstruction: in August the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) disbanded and merged into the government army, and the United States lifted Syria's designation as a state sponsor of terrorism. Tensions persist, however, as Israel keeps troops in the south and in August struck as far afield as an air base in Idlib. Much depends on whether U.S.-mediated de-escalation talks between Israel and Syria bear fruit.

last_major_event.text: The dissolution of the SDF and its integration into the Syrian army were announced.

flashpoints.status_ko: Ukraine is repeatedly striking Novorossiysk, the Black Sea Fleet's new base, and tankers of Russia's shadow fleet with drones, Neptune missiles, and uncrewed surface vessels. The fleet has effectively been pushed out of Sevastopol, and with even Russia's crude export ports now within Ukraine's reach, the risks to Russian seaborne logistics have grown.

last_major_event.text: Ukraine struck the port and air defenses at Novorossiysk.

flashpoints.status_ko: Since the Justice Mission-2025 encirclement drills in December 2025, no named large-scale exercise by the People's Liberation Army (PLA) had been confirmed through September 2026, and Chinese military aircraft entered Taiwan's air defense identification zone (ADIZ) 125 times in August, less than half the monthly average for 2024–25. Gray-zone pressure, however, has become routine, from coast guard incursions around Kinmen and Dongsha (Pratas) to the announced integration of Kinmen and Xiamen. Amid U.S.-China summitry, Trump has treated arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip and Taiwan's Legislative Yuan has cut the defense budget, eroding the political foundations of deterrence.

last_major_event.text: The PLA's Justice Mission-2025 exercise (December 29–30) rehearsed encircling Taiwan, including a port blockade and live fire.

flashpoints.status_ko: At its Ninth Party Congress, North Korea designated South Korea a permanently hostile state and severed inter-Korean links, and its ballistic missile launches have surged in 2026 to nine rounds involving 15 or more missiles. Trump, pursuing a meeting with Kim Jong Un before the end of the year, unilaterally scaled back the joint South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise. Seoul has floated a plan to trade a nuclear freeze for sanctions relief, but Pyongyang rejects denuclearization as an agenda item altogether. The expanding deployment of North Korean troops to Russia, now including drone operators, is fueling concern that Moscow will pay Pyongyang back with military technology.

last_major_event.text: North Korea launched a hypersonic intermediate-range missile from the Wonsan area; South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said it flew more than 700 kilometers.

flashpoints.status_ko: For 11 months since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's remarks on a Taiwan contingency in November 2025, China has maintained a ban on exports of dual-use items and rare earths to Japan, a halt to imports of Japanese seafood, and curbs on travel to Japan. Military pressure has continued as well—fire-control radar lock-ons by fighter jets, live-fire drills near Okinotori, and joint Chinese-Russian bomber flights—and leader-level channels are effectively frozen. Japan is responding by building up its defenses and deepening cooperation with Australia and other partners.

last_major_event.text: China's Commerce Ministry announced a total ban on exports to Japan of dual-use items with military applications, including rare earths.

flashpoints.status_ko: After spending a record number of days in the waters contiguous to the Senkakus in 2025, the China Coast Guard has continued to enter the islands' territorial waters repeatedly in 2026. On June 10 and July 7, the two countries' coast guards faced off in territorial waters around Japanese fishing boats, sharpening a contest over who enforces the law there. A deliberate armed clash is unlikely, but the risk of an accidental one is ever present.

last_major_event.text: Chinese and Japanese coast guard vessels faced off around a Japanese fishing boat in Senkaku territorial waters, and the Japan Coast Guard drove the Chinese ships away.

flashpoints.name_ko: Structures in the Korea-China Provisional Measures Zone (PMZ), Yellow Sea
flashpoints.status_ko: South Korea and China have been at odds over the aquaculture facilities (Shenlan 1 and 2) and a management platform that China installed in the PMZ. After the January summit in Beijing between Lee Jae-myung and Xi Jinping, China moved and dismantled the management platform, which the South Korean government called "meaningful progress." But the aquaculture facilities and many observation buoys remain, and cases of the China Coast Guard obstructing South Korean ocean surveys have piled up, so concerns about gray-zone encroachment have not been laid to rest.

last_major_event.text: After the South Korea-China summit, China began moving and dismantling its management platform in the PMZ.

flashpoints.status_ko: The China Coast Guard maintains a constant presence and blocks Philippine vessels, and buoys and floating platforms apparently installed by China were spotted in late May 2026, heightening fears that artificial structures will go up on the shoal. Standoffs resumed in July right after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi warned of bitter consequences, and in late September a Philippine-led multinational exercise was held nearby.

last_major_event.text: The China Coast Guard said it had expelled two Philippine vessels from waters near Scarborough Shoal.

flashpoints.status_ko: Under a provisional arrangement reached in July 2024, Philippine resupply missions to the BRP Sierra Madre had proceeded without interference. On September 25, 2026, however, 17 Chinese navy, coast guard, and maritime militia vessels blocked a resupply mission, effectively ending the arrangement. China says the Philippines failed to obtain prior approval; Manila counters that it has no obligation to seek it. The risk of renewed confrontation is high.

last_major_event.text: Chinese navy and coast guard ships stopped a Philippine resupply mission 60 nautical miles short of the shoal, forcing it to abort.

flashpoints.status_ko: New construction, including what appears to be a radar installation, has been spotted in the Paracels, which China has controlled since 1974, prompting a formal protest from Vietnam in August. Vietnam is also expanding land reclamation in the Spratlys, and the two countries are now competing to fortify the islands.

last_major_event.text: Vietnam's Foreign Ministry demanded that China immediately halt its new construction in the Paracels.

flashpoints.name_ko: India-Pakistan (Kashmir, the Arabian Sea, and the Indus)
flashpoints.status_ko: The ceasefire that ended the four-day conflict of May 2025 is holding, but India continues to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance. In late August the Court of Arbitration constituted under the treaty ruled the suspension invalid, but India does not recognize the court's jurisdiction. On September 15, warships from the two countries collided in the Arabian Sea—their first direct military contact since 2025—and with no naval hotline or incidents-at-sea agreement between them, the risk of accidental escalation is high.

last_major_event.text: An Indian destroyer and a Pakistani patrol vessel, PNS Hunain, collided in the Arabian Sea.

flashpoints.status_ko: Relations have been stabilizing since the 2024 agreement on troop disengagement in eastern Ladakh, and the 25th round of Special Representatives talks in August 2026 discussed which parts of the boundary delimitation could be settled first (an "early harvest"). At a meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September, Modi and Xi agreed to pursue a fair settlement of the border, but both sides' large troop deployments and China's dam on the upper Brahmaputra remain unresolved.

last_major_event.text: At their summit, Modi and Xi agreed to pursue a fair and reasonable settlement of the border dispute.

flashpoints.status_ko: After clashes in July and December 2025, a ceasefire was reached in a joint statement on December 27 and is holding, but both Thailand and Cambodia call it fragile. Tensions persist over Thailand's cancellation in May of the 2001 memorandum of understanding on maritime boundaries, Cambodia's launch of UN conciliation proceedings in June, and the return of residents to the Ban Nong Chan area, and in September the Thai military warned of a full-scale response.

last_major_event.text: The Thai military warned that it would respond with full force to any Cambodian attack.

flashpoints.status_ko: Min Aung Hlaing became president in April 2026 following elections, but the move is seen as having changed only the outward form of military rule. The junta has regained some of the initiative through conscription and Chinese support, and northern Shan State has stabilized under Chinese-brokered ceasefires, but fighting continues on the Kachin (Bhamo), Rakhine (Sittwe), and Karen fronts.

last_major_event.text: The Kachin Independence Army repelled a junta attempt to break through around Bhamo, and the Arakan Army captured several outposts around Sittwe (according to resistance forces).

flashpoints.status_ko: Since Pakistan declared open war on the Taliban government on February 27, 2026, airstrikes and border clashes have recurred, and a March airstrike on a hospital in Kabul killed more than 260 civilians. Mediation by Qatar, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and China has failed to produce a lasting ceasefire, and on September 24 Pakistan extended its airstrikes as far as Kandahar, citing a terrorist attack on a police headquarters and drone attacks launched from Afghanistan.

last_major_event.text: Pakistan carried out airstrikes in Afghanistan's Kunar and Helmand provinces; the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan said at least 10 civilians were killed, most of them children.

flashpoints.status_ko: With traffic through Hormuz effectively paralyzed by the Iran war, the Strait of Malacca has become even more important strategically to Asia's energy supply chains. In April, Indonesia's finance minister floated the idea of charging transit fees, then dropped it after the Foreign Ministry objected, but the remark alone pushed up shipping insurance premiums. Piracy and armed robbery incidents in the strait are among the most numerous in Asia.

last_major_event.text: Shipping insurance premiums rose after Indonesia's finance minister floated, then withdrew, the idea of a Malacca transit fee.

flashpoints.name_ko: Baltic Sea, Kaliningrad, and the Suwałki Gap
flashpoints.status_ko: Russian provocations on NATO's eastern flank have multiplied since the start of September. A Russian warship fired flares at a Danish helicopter (September 14), NATO shot down a drone over Lithuania (September 15), and an Mi-8 helicopter from Kaliningrad violated Polish airspace (September 23–24). Kaliningrad's GPS-jamming antennas now number 36 and are disrupting signals in seven countries. Courtroom and maritime standoffs over severed undersea cables and the crackdown on the shadow fleet also continue.

last_major_event.text: In a diplomatic note to NATO member states, Russia claimed that NATO was preparing to blockade Kaliningrad and warned that, in the event of a blockade, it could use all weapons, including nuclear ones.

flashpoints.name_ko: NATO's southeastern airspace (Romania and the Black Sea)
flashpoints.status_ko: Whenever Russia strikes southern Ukraine, drones and missiles stray across Romania's Danube border. On September 24, Romania shot down a drone suspected of being Russian, and on September 25 Romanian F-16s and Spanish F-18s were scrambled. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed intelligence that Russia is planning hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries that support Ukraine.

last_major_event.text: Romanian forces shot down a drone suspected of being Russian.

flashpoints.status_ko: The Greenland crisis, set off by Trump's threats of annexation, was brought into an institutional framework on September 22, when the United States, Denmark, and Greenland concluded a security agreement. Washington gained an expansion of Pituffik and two new bases, a right of consent over any base established by a non-NATO country, and the power to screen foreign investment. Because the agreement remains in force even if Greenland becomes independent, some observers conclude that it has established de facto U.S. security sovereignty over Greenland. The risk of armed conflict has receded, but the sovereignty dispute lies dormant.

last_major_event.text: The United States, Denmark, and Greenland signed an open-ended security agreement (expanding bases and excluding non-NATO countries).

flashpoints.status_ko: In Serbia, after nearly two years of antigovernment protests, Aleksandar Vučić has given up the presidency to run for prime minister in early elections on October 25, aiming to move the center of power to the premiership. In Bosnia, the October 4 general election puts Republika Srpska's separatist course after Milorad Dodik to the test. The question of Serbs in northern Kosovo also remains unresolved, and tensions could rise over this cycle of elections.

last_major_event.text: Vučić resigned as Serbia's president to run for prime minister in the October 25 elections.

flashpoints.name_ko: Russian and Iranian hybrid attacks (Germany and the U.K.)
flashpoints.status_ko: After explosive-laden drones, apparently targeting transport aircraft bound for Ukraine, were found near Leipzig/Halle Airport in August, Germany on September 1 formally named Russia as the culprit for the first time. Britain summoned Russian diplomats, and it emerged that Iran-linked hackers had knocked a British power plant offline for four days. At sea, retaliation for the crackdown on the shadow fleet continues, including a Russian warship firing warning shots at a British yacht.

last_major_event.text: The German government formally attributed the explosive drone incident at Leipzig airport to Russia.

flashpoints.name_ko: Regime change in Venezuela under U.S. pressure
flashpoints.status_ko: After U.S. forces captured Nicolás Maduro on January 3, Washington recognized Delcy Rodríguez's interim government and set up an arrangement under which it effectively oversees Venezuela's oil sector. Armed conflict has subsided, but no election timetable has been set, the apparatus of repression remains intact, and the damage from a major earthquake in June has compounded matters, leaving the transition unstable.

last_major_event.text: Acting President Rodríguez promised elections in a speech at the UN and met with Trump in New York.

flashpoints.name_ko: Strikes on drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific (Operation Southern Spear)
flashpoints.status_ko: U.S. military strikes on vessels suspected of carrying drugs, which began in September 2025, have continued for more than a year, and the cumulative death toll has passed 230. The campaign has expanded to strikes on land in Venezuela and Ecuador, and because the United States has not released its evidence, it continues to draw charges of extrajudicial killing.

last_major_event.text: A U.S. strike on a suspected drug boat in the Caribbean killed four people.

flashpoints.status_ko: Since January the United States has been intercepting tankers bound for Cuba and threatening tariffs on countries that supply it with fuel, plunging the island into a humanitarian crisis marked by fuel shortages, the collapse of the power grid, and rising infant mortality. The Trump administration has named Cuba as the next target for regime change and keeps adding sanctions, while talks between the two countries drag on without result.

last_major_event.text: Trump said in his UN speech that freedom is coming to Cuba; Miguel Díaz-Canel hit back, demanding an end to the blockade.

flashpoints.status_ko: Trump has vowed land strikes on the cartels, but no U.S. military strike on Mexican territory has been confirmed to date, and Mexico has eased the pressure for U.S. military intervention by killing El Mencho and carrying out large-scale extraditions. The border is being militarized, with U.S. forces shooting down cartel drones with lasers, and Mexico has stayed out of the Shield of the Americas.

last_major_event.text: U.S. forces used a laser weapon to shoot down three cartel drones near the border.

flashpoints.status_ko: After Panama's Supreme Court in January struck down as unconstitutional CK Hutchison's concession to operate the ports of Balboa and Cristóbal, Denmark's Maersk and MSC took over interim operations. China retaliated with inspections of Panama-flagged ships and stricter customs checks on agricultural products, and the sale of CK Hutchison's ports business to a BlackRock consortium is held up by a Chinese antitrust review.

last_major_event.text: China is reportedly seeking the extradition of a Chinese businessman tied to the ports dispute, and Panama must decide by early November.

flashpoints.status_ko: With the Transitional Presidential Council dissolved in February, Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé governs alone, while gangs control most of Port-au-Prince and about 1.5 million people are internally displaced. The UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force (GSF) has deployed only about 1,000 of its authorized 5,550 personnel, and a vote on extending its mandate looms ahead of its September 30 expiry. On December 13, Haiti is scheduled to hold its first elections since 2016.

last_major_event.text: The Gang Suppression Force announced its first large-scale deployment outside Port-au-Prince, to the Artibonite department.

flashpoints.status_ko: After talks broke down in late August, the United States imposed 50 percent tariffs and Canada retaliated with tariffs on about $20 billion worth of goods, turning the dispute into an all-out trade war between allies. Washington escalated with a ban on imports of Canadian dairy products and alcohol (effective September 29) and exclusion from government procurement, and an October 19 referendum related to Alberta's separation adds to the tension.

last_major_event.text: As Canada's retaliatory tariffs took effect, the United States hit back the same day with an import ban and exclusion from procurement.

flashpoints.name_ko: Ecuador: gang violence and joint operations with U.S. forces
flashpoints.status_ko: With the homicide rate at about 49 per 100,000 people, President Daniel Noboa's government again declared a 60-day state of emergency in September. Since March it has conducted ground strikes alongside the U.S. military near the Colombian border, drawing controversy over errant strikes, while a proposal to allow foreign military bases was rejected in a 2025 referendum.

last_major_event.text: Noboa declared a 60-day state of emergency in eight provinces and a nighttime curfew in four.

flashpoints.status_ko: Since the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) captured El Fasher in October 2025, the front has shifted to Kordofan, where El Obeid is under siege, and to Blue Nile. The war is spilling across borders: the army has struck RSF convoys inside Chad with drones, and RSF drones are alleged to be launching from Ethiopian territory. Five-way mediation by the AU, the EU, IGAD, the Arab League, and the UN has made no progress.

last_major_event.text: The army used drones to strike a convoy of about 200 RSF vehicles near Mourdi, Chad, destroying dozens of them.

flashpoints.name_ko: Sahel jihadist insurgency (Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger)
flashpoints.status_ko: JNIM has been blockading fuel supply routes into Mali's capital, Bamako, for a year, and in April a joint offensive by JNIM and the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) drove government forces and Russia's Africa Corps out of the north. In Niger, an attempted coup on August 29 was put down with Russian and Algerian support, while mutual assistance within the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) failed to work.

last_major_event.text: JNIM attacked a military base at Dioura, Mali, killing 120 to 150 soldiers.

flashpoints.name_ko: Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (M23 and Rwanda)
flashpoints.status_ko: After M23 seized Goma and Bukavu in 2025, the Washington Accords (DRC-Rwanda) and the Doha Framework (DRC-M23) followed, but implementation has been slow. Despite an August negotiating roadmap and the deployment of ceasefire monitors, government-aligned forces launched offensives toward Minembwe and Walungu, and an Ebola outbreak has deepened the humanitarian crisis.

last_major_event.text: The Washington Accords' Joint Security Coordination Mechanism reconvened in Geneva to review implementation of the commitments on the FDLR and on Rwanda's defensive measures.

flashpoints.name_ko: Horn of Africa (Tigray war and Ethiopia-Eritrea)
flashpoints.status_ko: On September 22, full-scale war broke out in Tigray, Amhara, and Afar between Ethiopian government forces and an antigovernment coalition including the TPLF and Fano militias, effectively bringing down the order established by the Pretoria agreement. The Ethiopian government accuses Eritrea of aiding the rebels, and that charge, coupled with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's demand for an outlet to the Red Sea (the port of Assab), has raised the risk of war between Ethiopia and Eritrea.

last_major_event.text: Tigray Defense Forces seized the airports at Mekelle, Axum, and Shire.

flashpoints.name_ko: Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb (Houthis and Yemen's civil war)
flashpoints.status_ko: Alongside the Iran war, the Houthis have stepped up attacks aimed at Saudi Arabia, and with Yemen's civil war reignited they have seized the port of Mocha and Perim Island. The Houthis say they will target only Saudi vessels, but the risks to shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait have grown, and Saudi Arabia's crude export route, rerouted to the Red Sea to avoid Hormuz, is under threat as well.

last_major_event.text: The Houthis claimed to have attacked Aramco facilities around Riyadh; the Saudi-led coalition denied it and said it had struck Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis.

flashpoints.status_ko: With the Hormuz blockade diverting Saudi crude through the East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea, and ships heading north through Suez to escape the Houthi threat, the canal's traffic and toll revenue have rebounded. Transits reached 1,340 in July, up 27 percent from a year earlier, and 2026 revenue is projected at $5.8 billion to $6 billion. Egyptian ports themselves have come under threat, however, as the drone attack on the port of Damietta showed.

last_major_event.text: Suez Canal revenue for July reportedly reached $505 million, the highest since December 2023.

flashpoints.status_ko: Amid the standoff between the Government of National Unity in Tripoli and Khalifa Haftar's forces in the east, a UN-brokered roadmap for unified elections within 24 months was signed on August 30. It needs the approval of the House of Representatives and the High Council of State within a month, and sources of instability remain, including the assassination of the Libyan National Army (LNA) intelligence chief in August and a drone attack on the Zawiya refinery.

last_major_event.text: The rival factions signed a UN-brokered agreement to hold presidential and parliamentary elections within 24 months.

flashpoints.status_ko: When Israel recognized Somaliland in December 2025, Somalia reacted in January 2026 by cancelling all its agreements with the UAE. Armed clashes have broken out in Mogadishu over the extension of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term, while Puntland and Jubaland are moving to break away and al-Shabaab is expanding its reach.

last_major_event.text: U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) carried out airstrikes against al-Shabaab.

flashpoints.name_ko: U.S.-China chip rivalry and Korean fabs in China
flashpoints.status_ko: At the end of 2025, the United States revoked the validated end-user (VEU) status of Samsung's Xi'an plant and SK hynix's plants in Wuxi and Dalian, issuing equipment import licenses valid only for 2026. The licenses prohibit expansion and upgrades, but the process transitions the two companies carried out around the time the licenses were issued—236-layer NAND at Xi'an and DDR5 at Wuxi—could become a point of contention when the licenses come up for renewal for 2027. With State Council Decree No. 835 (April 2026), China created a legal basis for sanctioning companies that comply with U.S. controls. The U.S.-China summit in September extended the tariff truce to January 10, 2027, but chip controls were not on the agenda.

last_major_event.text: The U.S.-China summit extended the tariff truce to January 10, 2027; chip export controls were left off the agenda.

forecasts.q: A full ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, signed by both sides, takes effect
forecasts.basis: All three short-term ceasefires of 2026 ended in renewed fighting, and Russia has not softened its demand that Ukraine hand over the rest of Donetsk Oblast still under Ukrainian control.

forecasts.q: Trilateral technical-level talks among the United States, Russia, and Ukraine actually take place (at any venue)
forecasts.basis: On September 25, Russia and Ukraine agreed to trilateral talks with the United States, but neither the venue (the UAE has been mentioned) nor the agenda has been settled, and Russia launched a large-scale drone attack the same day.

forecasts.q: A U.S.-Iran ceasefire takes effect and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is officially announced
forecasts.basis: On September 25, Iran put forward a roadmap for reopening the strait within seven days, but Trump rejected it. There are also reports of a U.S. plan to resume airstrikes after the November midterm elections.

forecasts.q: The United States officially announces the resumption of large-scale airstrikes on mainland Iran
forecasts.basis: The case for: Trump's September 23 threat to annihilate Iran and reports of plans to resume bombing after the midterms. The case against: oil prices hovering around $100 a barrel and the room for negotiation after the election.
forecasts.s: U.S. resumes strikes on mainland Iran

forecasts.q: Trump and Kim Jong Un hold a summit
forecasts.basis: Trump has said he wants a meeting this year and has scaled back the Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise, but North Korea rejects denuclearization as an agenda item, calling it unrealistic.

forecasts.q: North Korea conducts its seventh nuclear test
forecasts.basis: North Korea has sharply stepped up its missile launches, but having restored relations with both of its patrons, China and Russia, it would pay a high price for a nuclear test at this point.

forecasts.q: China conducts a named, large-scale joint exercise encircling Taiwan
forecasts.basis: There has been no named large-scale exercise since December 2025, and U.S.-China summit diplomacy is under way. Triggers could include Taiwan's National Day address in October.

forecasts.q: A new incident in which China blocks a resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal is publicly reported
forecasts.basis: China's blocking of a resupply mission on September 25 effectively ended the provisional arrangement of July 2024, and the Philippines says it will keep resupplying the outpost without Chinese approval.
forecasts.s: Second Thomas Shoal resupply blocked again

forecasts.q: Indian and Pakistani forces engage in interstate fighting that causes casualties
forecasts.basis: Warships of the two countries collided in the Arabian Sea on September 15, but both sides avoided escalation. A major terrorist attack would sharply raise the probability of fighting.

forecasts.q: Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban agree to a formal ceasefire
forecasts.basis: Mediation by Qatar, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and China has failed to produce a lasting ceasefire, and airstrikes on Kandahar in late September raised tensions again.

forecasts.q: The U.S.-China tariff truce is extended again before it expires or is replaced by a comprehensive agreement
forecasts.basis: Reciprocal state visits by the U.S. and Chinese leaders in May and September established a framework of strategic stability, and Xi Jinping has said the two should meet again soon.

forecasts.q: Prime Minister Takaichi and President Xi Jinping hold a China-Japan summit
forecasts.basis: China's economic retaliation is in its 11th month, and Takaichi has not retracted her remarks on a Taiwan contingency. The APEC meeting China hosts in November is the only opening.

forecasts.q: Brent crude's final closing price of the year is below $90 a barrel
forecasts.basis: On top of the Hormuz blockade, the September shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and its restart at reduced volumes have blocked supply routes twice over. If the forecast on a U.S.-Iran ceasefire and the reopening of Hormuz (f03) comes true, this one is likely to come true as well.

forecasts.q: By the end of 2027, the United States formally revokes its approval of H200-class AI chip exports to China, or lowers the approved volume through regulation, license conditions, or legislation (a de facto halt resulting from Chinese import restrictions or a company's production stoppage does not count)
forecasts.basis: Approval was announced in December 2025; the January 2026 rule capped volumes at 50 percent of U.S. domestic sales and collected a 25 percent levy in the form of a tariff; in May, licenses were granted to about 10 Chinese companies with a cap of 75,000 units per customer. China blocked imports, then allowed them on a limited basis from August (about 13 percent of the cap). A bill restricting the exports is pending in Congress. The current administration has tightened export controls when the trade truce was faltering and loosened them during truce periods (the H20 was re-approved three months after its 2025 ban), so the path most likely to lead to revocation is retaliation if the truce breaks down · The AI variable in the Taiwan Strait issue

forecasts.basis: The March 2026 strikes on data centers in the UAE and Bahrain were the first cases · The AI variable in the Iran issue
forecasts.void: The forecast's condition had already been met when it was created (a renewed attack on a data center in Bahrain in April 2026, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' claim of further strikes in July, and Russia's attack on a data center in Kyiv in September). Because it could not discriminate, it has been voided and excluded from accuracy scoring. A new forecast on disruptions to South Korean chip production from a helium shortage (f45) takes its place.

forecasts.q: By the end of 2027, North Korea states explicitly in its official media that it has applied AI or automation technology to the Nuclear Trigger (the state's comprehensive nuclear weapons management system) or to its nuclear counterattack command system
forecasts.basis: Announcements about delivery systems do not count (Kim Jong Un's February 2026 reference to AI in connection with the KN-25, which may have pointed to the production process, and May reports of an AI-guided cruise missile), nor does repetition of the law's wording that a strike is launched "automatically"; only an explicit statement that AI or automation technology has been applied to the command-and-control system counts. Nuclear powers have rarely stated officially that their nuclear command and control is technically automated (in 2011 the commander of Russia's Strategic Missile Forces confirmed that the Perimeter system exists and is on combat duty, but Moscow has never officially described how automated it is) · External variable X7 in the Korean Peninsula issue (shrinking human judgment and delegated authority)
forecasts.s: North Korea states AI use in nuclear command

forecasts.basis: Even while Qatar's helium production was halted for several months in 2026, no production disruptions at South Korean chipmakers were reported (thanks to inventories, recycling, and diversified sourcing). Qatari helium began shipping via Jeddah in August. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix hold four to six months of helium inventory. If this forecast comes true, it would signal that the assessment that a helium shortage amounts to no more than a cost burden was wrong · The AI variable in the Iran issue
