Japan-North Korea normalization that leaves out the abduction issue
South Korea alone acquiring latent nuclear capability
items.ext: A Taiwan crisis is a crisis for Japan (Okinawa). U.S. retreat opens the door to a debate on Japan's own nuclear weapons.
items.want: That Seoul maintain U.S.-Japan-South Korea cooperation and coordinate with Japan before pursuing latent nuclear capability
items.onrec: Tokyo would support a phased freeze (A1) if medium- and short-range missiles are included in what is frozen. If South Korea opens the door to a conditional latent nuclear capability (A3b), Japan would use it as a pretext to "normalize" its own reprocessing.
items.lever: Prior coordination on latent nuclear capability (a joint Japanese-South Korean norm); a joint demand that medium- and short-range missiles be included in any agreement with North Korea

F1: The threat remains, but it is familiar
F5: If only ICBMs are limited, Japan is left with the threat from medium- and short-range missiles
F3: Some welcome it; most fear it

intent.read: In words, Tokyo keeps its non-nuclear principles, but the language has weakened, and it is accelerating moves to acquire counterstrike capabilities and raise defense spending. It is leaning toward "keeping the door open" rather than toward nuclear armament. This is the basis for the judgment that Japan could move first in nuclear dominoes (F3).

watch.t: Wording on the non-nuclear principles in the revised three security documents (f19)
Changes in reprocessing and plutonium policy
How much of the U.S.-Japan extended deterrence consultations is made public

reads.t: "Armed stalemate" (F1) is the only future that none of the deciding powers rejects.
reads.d: That is why it is the most likely. Everyone is somewhat dissatisfied, but no one is willing to pay the cost of breaking it.

reads.t: Of the three powers with the greatest say (the United States, China, and North Korea), two (the Trump administration and North Korea) prefer "a U.S.-North Korean deal without South Korea" (F5), and China can accept it.
reads.d: For South Korea, exclusion is a risk as real as war. This future was hidden because, among the four futures first sketched, it had been folded into armed stalemate (F1).

reads.t: North Korea holds the key to managed coexistence (F2). And what North Korea rejects is not a freeze but contact.
reads.d: North Korea fears South Korean information more than South Korean weapons. That is why a freeze (A1) comes before exchanges (A2). Because North Korea rejects exchanges, only the legal framework should be prepared; exchanges that return something to people, such as family reunions or the repatriation of detainees, should be opened separately as deals with something given in return (A7). For the same reason, the information tools (A6) become the most expensive card South Korea holds.

reads.t: Nuclear dominoes (F3) is no one's preference. It comes from fear.
reads.d: It is a future that the countries' preferences alone do not capture. External variables such as a U.S. retreat open this path. It also marks a limit of this method, which gauges futures by preferences.

reads.t: South Korea's leverage lies in "the things that cannot be implemented without South Korea."
reads.d: The practical work and funding of sanctions relief, the scale of joint exercises, a joint Japanese-South Korean norm on latent nuclear capability, and information tools aimed at the North. South Korea should make these conditional on its participation in a U.S.-North Korean deal, showing both Washington and Pyongyang that a deal without South Korea will not work. This is the tactic for turning a deal without South Korea (F5) into managed coexistence (F2).

syn.note: Preferred, Acceptable, Uncomfortable, and Rejected are provisional judgments of how readily each country's leadership would accept that future through 2030. A country's weight as a deciding power is rated by how hard it would be for a future to come about if that country opposed it.

intent.note: Each country's intentions are checked first against costly actions rather than words. For each country, dated signals are sorted into words and deeds, and a judgment is made on whether the two match.
intent.read: North Korea and Russia are the countries whose words and deeds match most closely. In the United States and Japan, actions are running ahead of words, toward retreat and toward preparation, respectively. China's words and deeds point in opposite directions: it talks of denuclearization while embracing North Korea. A recheck against these intent indicators found no signal yet that would change the judgments in the table of preferred futures. If the signals change, both the preference judgments and the probabilities of the futures will be revised.

items.def: An actual reduction of U.S. Forces Korea, or a formal weakening of the extended deterrence commitment
items.flips: C2 (the risk of exclusion grows), C5 (an independent nuclear arsenal ranks last)
items.why: If the United States pulls back from the Korean Peninsula, it becomes easier for a U.S.-North Korean deal to bypass South Korea (F5↑), and doubts about extended deterrence open nuclear debates in South Korea and Japan (F3↑).
items.sign: The USFK provision is dropped from the final NDAA, or a troop reduction is announced

items.def: The Korean Peninsula becomes an item in a U.S.-China deal that also covers Taiwan · an extreme form of world scenario A
items.why: The risk of war falls (F4↓), but the signal that allies' interests can be traded away heightens anxiety in South Korea and Japan (F3↑), and the Korean question is handled over South Korea's head (F5↑).
items.sign: A joint U.S.-China document includes language "opposing" Taiwan independence or wording on U.S. Forces Korea

items.def: A blockade or quarantine of Taiwan, or armed conflict · the same event as world scenario D
items.why: U.S. Forces Korea is drawn off to Taiwan, and North Korea gains an incentive to open a "second front" on the Korean Peninsula. Pyeongtaek and Osan become targets whether South Korea wants it or not (F4↑, F3↑).
items.sign: Exercises around Taiwan shift to maritime inspections or drills to cut off energy shipments

items.t: An end to the Russia-Ukraine war and a shrinking North Korea-Russia trade
items.def: North Korea's exports of troops and artillery shells stop after the war ends or after a long ceasefire
items.flips: C3 (the favorable case in which freeze negotiations open), C2 (the risk of a deal without South Korea also grows)
items.why: With its income from Russia cut off, a cash-strapped North Korea could turn toward negotiations. It is almost the only external variable that could move things in a favorable direction. But because its negotiating partner would likely be the United States alone, the probability of a deal without South Korea (F5) rises as well.
items.sign: A Russia-Ukraine ceasefire holds for more than a month, and the return of North Korean troops is reported

items.t: Cracks in North Korea's internal control
items.def: Cracks such as mass defections, market unrest, or elite defections become visible from outside
items.flips: The shape of an upheaval (peaceful transition or bloodshed)
items.why: The influx of information is less a trigger than a slow variable that determines the shape of an upheaval when it comes. East Germans watched West German television for decades, but the system fell only after the Soviet Union withdrew its backing.
items.sign: Defector arrivals in South Korea exceed 1,000 a year, or reports of executions and purges in border areas surge

items.def: Xi Jinping's incapacitation or a power struggle becomes visible
items.why: The ongoing military purge (the expulsion of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli) signals consolidation rather than instability. Because China's policy of keeping North Korea as a buffer rests on interests that do not change with the leader, a change in China's leadership would have only a weak effect on the Korean Peninsula. The risk lies in the succession of the 2030s.
items.sign: No succession lineup emerges at the 2027 Party Congress, or an unusual vacuum appears at the top of the leadership

items.t: Shrinking human judgment and delegated authority
items.def: Official documents confirm that the U.S.-South Korean combined command-and-control system has cut human approval steps between AI target identification and strike authorization or has predelegated strike authority, or North Korea states explicitly that it has applied AI or automation to the Nuclear Trigger or its nuclear counterattack command system (by the end of 2030). The public unveiling of AI weapons (North Korea's February 2026 reference to AI in the KN-25 and May reports of an "AI-guided" cruise missile, and the U.S.-South Korean adoption of AI decision support) is treated as a baseline that has already occurred. The AI mentioned in connection with the KN-25 may refer to the production process rather than guidance.
items.why: What destabilizes a crisis is not the announcement of a technology but the shrinking of the human judgment that screens out false alarms and the widening of predelegation (the 1983 Petrov false alarm). Right after Iran's supreme leader was killed, North Korea wrote the delegation of nuclear-use authority into its constitution (no causal link has been established). If these changes overlap on both sides, the likelihood of sudden upheaval (F4), including accidental clashes, rises, and the trust-building that managed coexistence (F2) requires becomes harder. Nuclear dominoes (F3) does not move, because it is a matter of alliance credibility, not AI.
items.sign: North Korean media explicitly mention AI or automation in the Nuclear Trigger system; the United States and South Korea announce changes to strike-authorization procedures

reads: With the exception of an end to the Russia-Ukraine war and a shrinking North Korea-Russia trade (X4), every variable moves probability away from managed coexistence (F2) toward a deal without South Korea (F5), nuclear dominoes (F3), and sudden upheaval (F4). The more the outside world is shaken, the greater the chance of extremely bad outcomes.

The value of reversible insurance (a conditional latent nuclear capability, A3b) therefore rises. And if managed coexistence is the aim, Seoul must move quickly while the window is open. That window falls around China's 2027 Party Congress, the U.S. decision on U.S. Forces Korea, and the end of the Russia-Ukraine war.

Some external events have already happened. Iran's being attacked without nuclear weapons and losing its leader has become, for North Korea, a second lesson after Libya. Denuclearization is treated as having effectively disappeared from the negotiating agenda through 2030, and a freeze is set as the ceiling.

The AI variable (X7) is defined not by announcements but by changes in the structure of authority. Both the U.S.-South Korean side and North Korea have already unveiled AI weapons, but no clear rise in the probability of crisis has been detected since. Rather than creating new probabilities on the Korean Peninsula, AI raises the likelihood of accidental clashes to the extent that it shrinks the role of human judgment.
external.note: The likelihoods and conditional probabilities are provisional judgments. Because the variables overlap, they should not be added or multiplied. The table shows which way the futures tilt on the assumption that a given variable occurs.

client.name: The government of the Republic of Korea
client.note: The goals and their order are derived from the Constitution of the Republic of Korea and the government's official statements; the order is Clisa Geopolitics' interpretation. The preamble of the Constitution commits the nation "to ensure security, liberty and happiness for ourselves and our posterity forever," and Article 10 guarantees the right to pursue happiness. The well-being of the country's own citizens is thus already built into the South Korean government's goals.

goals.d: Deter war and protect citizens' lives
goals.src: Constitution, Article 5(2) (mission of the armed forces) and Article 66(2) (independence and territorial integrity of the state)

goals.t: A seat at the table and diplomatic autonomy
goals.d: Avoid being shut out of decisions on the Korean Peninsula; preserve the alliance and the country's foreign policy options
goals.src: Constitution, Article 66(2); address to the UN General Assembly, September 2026 (pledging to help resume U.S.-North Korean dialogue)

goals.d: Protect markets, supply chains, energy, and the country's credit standing
goals.src: Preamble of the Constitution ("security, liberty and happiness"); the state's basic duties of governance

goals.d: Preserve the legal basis for unification and the framework of inter-Korean relations
goals.src: Constitution, Articles 3 and 4 and Article 66(3)

goals.d: Protect citizens, including separated families, detainees and abductees, and North Korean defectors
goals.src: Constitution, Article 10 (right to pursue happiness and the state's duty to guarantee fundamental rights)

ranked.t: Build up conventional deterrence (A5) and secure a conditional latent nuclear capability (A3b) as insurance. In freeze negotiations, concentrate less on a seat at the opening stage than on securing a seat at the table for the implementation and peace-regime stages that follow a U.S.-North Korean agreement (A1). The cards to play early are not sanctions relief but tension-reducing steps, such as adjusting joint U.S.-South Korean exercises or restoring inter-Korean liaison channels; information tools aimed at the North (A6) serve as bargaining chips within this package.

A humanitarian exchange that offers something in return (A7) contributes substantially to protecting citizens (G5) at low cost, so it should be pursued in parallel whenever an opening appears. Because North Korea rejects special-relationship coexistence (A2), only its legal framework should be prepared for now.
Staying the course (A0) is the baseline for comparison. It incurs small losses on the two highest-priority goals: national security (G1) and a seat at the table and diplomatic autonomy (G2).
Nuclear sharing or the redeployment of tactical nuclear weapons adds to deterrence, but Washington is unlikely to accept it, and it would invite Chinese retaliation.

Maximum pressure (A4) ranks low even when judged by the South Korean government's own goals. China and Russia plug the gaps in sanctions, so its effect is small; it runs against the current of U.S. negotiations, leaving South Korea bypassed; and it closes the door to freeze negotiations.
An independent nuclear arsenal ranks last, because it would cost the alliance (G2) and the economy (G3) irreversibly. It should be reconsidered if U.S. extended deterrence actually collapses.

rank2.tension: Stronger deterrence (A5) and freeze negotiations (A1) are in tension with each other. North Korea can cite A5 as evidence of hostility and reject A1. This procedure does not settle how to align the pace of building deterrence with the timing of opening negotiations.
rank2.undecided: How to weigh the possibility of unification (G4) and the protection of citizens (G5) against security (G1) and diplomacy (G2) is for the South Korean government to decide. Here the goals are ordered G1 > G2 > G3 > G4 ≈ G5, following the order of the constitutional provisions and government statements.

human.note: This section reviews the rankings from the strategy evaluation from the standpoint of individual lives. It does not filter the rankings; it states where they change and by how much. The judgment belongs to readers and the South Korean government.

items.client: Switching off the information tools could be traded for restored communication lines or resumed dialogue.
items.clisa: Limit the price of switching them off to things that return to people: reunions, confirmations of whether relatives are alive, and the repatriation of detainees.
items.cost: One bargaining chip becomes narrower in use.
items.gain: The access to information that North Koreans lose is converted into gains for separated families and detainees. It remains true that the interests of different people are being traded.

items.client: A second-ranked option, pursued in parallel when an opening appears.
items.clisa: Raise it into the top-ranked package and open it at the same time as freeze negotiations (A1). The number of surviving separated-family members will fall to about 20,000 by 2030, and that loss is irreversible.
items.cost: The domestic political cost of giving North Korea something in return, and the burden of the sanctions-exemption procedure.
items.gain: The relationships dimension for separated families could rise from 0 to 50 (confirmation of whether relatives are alive, and letters). The benefit would go directly to the six detainees and to the families of abductees.

items.clisa: Keep the ranking as it is, but add food and health aid to North Korea through UN channels to the agenda of freeze negotiations (A1).
items.cost: Small. The negotiating agenda grows by one item.
items.gain: Partly eases the burden on the livelihoods of North Koreans squeezed by the arms race.
None. Viewed in terms of what it means for people, the ranking stays the same.

rows.name: Managed competition
rows.why: If Washington and Beijing manage tensions, the United States gains room to deal directly with North Korea. A deal without South Korea (F5) rises the most.

rows.name: Armed multipolarity
rows.why: If all the major powers arm, nuclear debates open in South Korea and Japan. Nuclear dominoes (F3) rises and managed coexistence (F2) falls.

rows.name: Protracted linked wars
rows.why: If the wars in Ukraine and Iran drag on, the North Korea-Russia alignment hardens. Armed stalemate (F1) becomes most entrenched.

rows.name: Taiwan Strait crisis
rows.why: A crisis in the Taiwan Strait opens a second front on the Korean Peninsula. It is the same picture as the cross-strait crisis (X3) among the external variables.

rows.name: Internal fracture in one pole
rows.why: If either China or Russia is shaken from within, North Korea, which leans on that pole, is shaken too. Sudden upheaval (F4) rises.

world.note: These are the probabilities of each future for the Korean Peninsula on the assumption that each of world scenarios A through E on the World Order tab occurs. The values are set so that, weighted by the probabilities of the world scenarios, they match the baseline probabilities under the current trend to within one percentage point (a total-probability check). They are judgment estimates by the analyst.

ranked.t: A direct deal with Washington that leaves South Korea out is the best move. The core of the exchange is de facto acceptance of its nuclear status and a scaling back of joint exercises and U.S. strategic assets; sanctions relief is a side item (the formula entrenched since Kim Yo Jong's statement of July 2020).

There is precedent for North Korea accepting multilateral formats only when they were co-proposed by the United States or hosted by China. Sitting down with the South as a separate, hostile state would be considered only if the cost of exclusion grew.
If a deal with Washington is blocked, North Korea stays the course (N0).
Limited armed provocations (N4) are a way to shake up the game when negotiations stall.
Costly, because it would mean losing China.
Inter-Korean exchanges rank last: they would let in information, the greatest threat to the regime.

counter.read: North Korea's response estimated in Step 5 (dealing with Washington alone and leaving South Korea out) is also supported by precedent. What has been revised is the content of the exchange and the conditions for multilateral participation. Since the collapse of the Hanoi summit, North Korea has put withdrawal of hostile policy and recognition of its nuclear status ahead of sanctions relief, and whether it sits down in a multilateral format depends not only on the agenda but on who convenes it and how the South's status is defined. Part of the price North Korea wants (joint exercises) falls in an area where South Korea has a say, but the decision rests mainly with Washington.

ranked.t: The best move is to lead a four-country freeze framework while propping up North Korea, because Washington and Pyongyang bypassing China (K2) is the outcome Beijing dislikes most.
If a four-party freeze framework does not materialize, China keeps propping up North Korea as it does now.
A direct U.S.-North Korean deal lowers tensions, but China is left out.
Open pressure on South Korea backfires by fostering U.S.-Japan-South Korea solidarity.
Pressure on North Korea ranks last because it shakes the buffer.

counter.read: China's best move overlaps with South Korea's at one point: both dislike a direct U.S.-North Korean deal "without South Korea" or "without China." But because precedent shows that China has not been a guarantor that brings North Korea to the table (the dual suspension China proposed in 2017 was carried out bilaterally by Washington and Pyongyang in 2018, without China), it is more realistic to use a four-party framework not as a way to open negotiations but as a way to guarantee South Korea a seat at the table in the peace-regime stage after a U.S.-North Korean agreement.

pairs: South Korea
A5 + A1 + A3b (as a party to freeze negotiations)
North Korea
N1 direct U.S.-North Korean deal without South Korea → fallback N2 multilateral freeze

K1 four-country freeze framework + propping up North Korea
twoway.equilibrium: The current equilibrium lies between "a deal without South Korea" and "armed stalemate." North Korea's best move (N1, a direct U.S.-North Korean deal without South Korea) and the Trump administration's preferences point to the same place. That is why a deal without South Korea (F5) is put at 22 percent.
twoway.zopa: There is a narrow space where the interests of the three countries overlap. South Korea wants to avoid being shut out, and China does not want Washington and Pyongyang to bypass it. But since February 2026, North Korea has said it will not deal with the South regardless of the agenda, and the only multilateral formats in which it has sat with South Korea in the past were ones co-proposed by the United States or hosted by China. The realistic area of overlap is therefore a four-party framework for the implementation and peace-regime stages after a U.S.-North Korean agreement. The price for South Korea is consent to adjusting joint exercises, the practical work and funding of sanctions relief, and the restraint China will demand on Taiwan and THAAD.
traps: Nuclear dominoes (F3) is no one's preference, but it is a security dilemma that builds up from each party's rational moves. North Korea's nuclear buildup (N0), South Korea's latent capability (A3b), and Japan's preparations justify one another. Designing the latent capability to be conditional, pursued within a joint U.S.-South Korean framework, and transparent is the mechanism for breaking this cycle.

The harder South Korea tries to insert itself alone into the U.S.-North Korean channel, the more firmly North Korea shuts it out. This is the paradox: Seoul's unilateral efforts invite its own exclusion.

ai.t: AI compresses decision time, and North Korea answers by delegating authority
ai.stake: AI-enabled surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting threaten the survivability of North Korea's leadership and its mobile launchers. Historically, the weaker side has responded not with preemptive strikes but with automatic retaliation, delegated authority, and dispersal (the Soviet Perimeter system of the 1980s). Article 3 of North Korea's 2022 law on its nuclear forces policy provides that if the command-and-control system over its nuclear forces is endangered by an attack from hostile forces, a nuclear strike will be launched automatically and immediately in accordance with a predetermined operational plan. "Automatically" here means predelegation, not technical automation. Article 89 of the revised constitution, adopted by the Supreme People's Assembly in March 2026 and made public in May, provides that the chairman of the State Affairs Commission may delegate the authority to use nuclear weapons. It was adopted shortly after Iran's supreme leader was killed (February 28), but no causal link between the two events has been established.
ai.moves: What raises the risk is less AI itself than the shrinking of the human judgment that screens out false alarms and misjudgments (the Petrov false alarm and Able Archer 83, both in 1983). AI's effect therefore concentrates on raising the likelihood of sudden upheaval (F4), including accidental clashes, and on making it harder to build the trust that managed coexistence (F2) requires. Because there are also many precedents in which better reconnaissance increased transparency and stabilized crises (Cold War reconnaissance satellites and arms control verification), the introduction of AI is not in itself treated as destabilizing. The driver of nuclear dominoes (F3) is the credibility of alliances, not AI, so the AI variable does not raise its probability (external variable X7).
ai.lever: In the second quarter of 2026, South Korea accounted for about 83 percent of the world's supply of high-bandwidth memory (HBM): SK Hynix 50 percent, Samsung 33 percent. Yet when allies have used chokepoints in supply chains as instruments of coercion, it has backfired. Japan's 2019 export controls against South Korea spurred South Korean localization and alternative sourcing. Even the Netherlands (ASML) and Taiwan (TSMC), which hold chokepoints of their own, managed only to improve their terms with Washington in exchange for investment pledges. South Korea, too, did not wield HBM as leverage in negotiations over U.S. export-control exemptions (validated end-user status) and chip tariffs; HBM's defensive value worked indirectly, through the interests of American AI companies. HBM is a passive defense that raises the cost of U.S. coercion, and an asset whose value may erode as Washington presses for local production and Micron expands capacity in the United States. Because South Korea's AI base depends on American equipment and design tools and on what is in effect a single buyer (Nvidia), its leverage and its dependence sit in the same place.

The frequency of drills and the launch threshold of the Nuclear Trigger (the state's comprehensive nuclear weapons management system)

brief.q: Amid North Korea's nuclear program and great-power deal-making, what should South Korea do?
brief.a: Seoul should strengthen conventional deterrence and, as insurance, build a latent nuclear capability — enrichment and reprocessing within the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty — while tying its pace to whether North Korea freezes its program. In any negotiation over a freeze, Seoul should secure a seat at the table for the implementation and peace-regime stages that would follow a U.S.-North Korean agreement. The cards it plays early should be steps that lower tensions, such as adjusting joint U.S.-South Korean exercises or restoring inter-Korean liaison channels.
brief.eq: North Korea's best move and the Trump administration's preferences both point toward a direct deal between Washington and Pyongyang that leaves Seoul out. What Pyongyang wants most in return is de facto acceptance of its nuclear status and a scaling back of joint U.S.-South Korean exercises — and since February 2026, it has said it will not deal with the South.
brief.human: Even if these recommendations are carried out, South Koreans' life-and-safety score on the personal well-being index is likely to fall below its 2026 level. The largest gain would come in personal relationships, as separated families meet again and exchange news.

items.name: 1991: the Basic Agreement, simultaneous UN membership, and the Joint Declaration on Denuclearization
items.format: Bilateral inter-Korean talks (high-level talks). The agenda was mutual recognition of each other's systems, nonaggression, and exchanges, with the Joint Declaration on the Denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula (December 31, 1991) running in parallel. The sequence: North Korea announced its intention to join the United Nations (May 28, 1991), the two Koreas joined simultaneously (September 17, 1991), and the Basic Agreement was signed (December 13, 1991) and took effect (February 19, 1992).
items.outcome: It took effect, but its implementing bodies, such as the Joint Military Commission, were soon neutralized, and it became a dead letter with the 1993 dispute over nuclear inspections and North Korea's announced withdrawal from the NPT.
items.why: North Korea accepted simultaneous membership because, with Chinese and Soviet veto cover gone, it wanted to avoid being treated unfavorably at the United Nations. The Basic Agreement itself had no nuclear provisions, so the inter-Korean framework could not cope with the inspection issue.
items.differs: North Korea then negotiated with Seoul on the premise of a special relationship within one nation; today its constitution defines the South as a hostile state and excludes it from the category of compatriots.

items.name: 1994: the Geneva U.S.-North Korean Agreed Framework
items.format: Bilateral U.S.-North Korean talks (Geneva): a freeze of graphite-moderated reactors in exchange for two light-water reactors and heavy fuel oil. South Korea was not a party to the negotiations, but through KEDO it paid 70 percent ($3.2 billion) of the reactor costs ($4.6 billion); Japan paid $1 billion, and the United States had no designated share.
items.outcome: After the June 1994 crisis in which Washington considered striking Yongbyon, Jimmy Carter's visit to Pyongyang (June 15) produced agreement on a freeze, and the framework was signed on October 21. The plutonium facilities stayed frozen for about eight years, but the framework collapsed with the October 2002 allegations of uranium enrichment, the lifting of the freeze and expulsion of inspectors in December 2002, and North Korea's announced withdrawal from the NPT on January 10, 2003.
items.why: The freeze was limited to the verifiable Yongbyon facilities, leaving enrichment as a detour, and construction of the light-water reactors fell far behind schedule. During the crisis, President Kim Young-sam's opposition to the use of force effectively constrained a unilateral U.S. strike.
items.differs: North Korea then had not yet acquired nuclear weapons, so the freeze targeted "future capability"; today it has written its nuclear status into its constitution and declared it irreversible.

items.name: The Four-Party Talks (the two Koreas, the United States, and China; Geneva)
items.format: Jointly proposed at the U.S.-South Korean summit on Jeju in April 1996. Six plenary sessions were held, from the first in Geneva on December 9, 1997, to the sixth on August 5–9, 1999, with two subcommittees, on tension reduction and on a peace regime. The chair rotated, determined by lot.
items.outcome: The talks lapsed without an agreed document. Substantive negotiations moved to bilateral U.S.-North Korean talks, which produced a moratorium on long-range missile tests at the Berlin talks in September 1999.
items.why: North Korea delayed acceptance for more than a year and, once at the table, insisted on putting the withdrawal of U.S. forces from South Korea on the agenda, which Seoul and Washington refused. The Taepodong launch of August 31, 1998, shifted the focus to missiles.
items.differs: The United States was then a co-proposer; the current four-party idea is a South Korean government initiative, and even South Korea's own foreign ministry has distanced itself from it, calling it an idealistic plan that had not been agreed on.

items.name: The Six-Party Talks (the September 19 Joint Statement and the February 13 agreement)
items.format: The two Koreas, the United States, China, Japan, and Russia, hosted by China (Beijing). Launched after a U.S.-China-North Korea three-way meeting in April 2003. The Joint Statement of September 19, 2005, set out nuclear abandonment in exchange for energy aid and normalization of relations, along with a separate forum on a peace regime among "the directly related parties"; the agreement of February 13, 2007, laid down an action-for-action sequence: closure of Yongbyon within 60 days in exchange for 50,000 tons of heavy fuel oil, then disablement and declaration in exchange for the equivalent of 950,000 tons.
items.outcome: The process went as far as the disablement of Yongbyon, the submission of a declaration on June 26, 2008, and removal from the list of state sponsors of terrorism on October 11, 2008, but the verification protocol collapsed in December 2008 when North Korea refused to put sampling in writing, and in April 2009 North Korea announced it was leaving the talks. The peace-regime forum provided for in the September 19 statement was never convened.
items.why: The core issues were disagreement over the scope of verification (facilities beyond Yongbyon and sampling) and the dispute over sanctions on Banco Delta Asia (BDA). As the talks broke down, Washington warned it would halt heavy fuel oil shipments while China and Russia announced they would keep supplying aid, splitting the pressure front.
items.differs: It was a framework in which North Korea nominally accepted the goal of denuclearization; today North Korea rejects denuclearization as an agenda item altogether.

items.name: 2017: China's dual suspension proposal and THAAD retaliation
items.format: Proposed by Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in March 2017: a halt to North Korean nuclear and missile activities in exchange for a halt to large-scale joint U.S.-South Korean exercises (dual suspension), with denuclearization and a peace treaty pursued in parallel. In the same period, China imposed informal economic retaliation over the THAAD deployment.
items.outcome: Washington did not accept it, and on October 31, 2017, North Korea rejected it, calling dual suspension "irresponsible behavior." Yet in 2018 essentially the same exchange was carried out bilaterally by Washington and Pyongyang, without China, through North Korea's testing moratorium and Trump's suspension of exercises.
items.why: North Korea saw China's mediation proposal as a framework that would constrain its nuclear status, and Washington refused to make alliance exercises an object of exchange.
items.differs: China is now mentioning denuclearization less (Xi Jinping in September 2025; the U.S.-China outcome document of September 2026), so its position on North Korea's nuclear status is closer to Pyongyang's than it was in 2017.

items.name: 2018: the Panmunjom Declaration and the September 19 military agreement
items.format: Bilateral inter-Korean summits. Article 3, Paragraph 3 of the Panmunjom Declaration committed the two Koreas to pursue "trilateral meetings involving the two Koreas and the United States, or quadrilateral meetings involving the two Koreas, the United States and China" toward declaring an end to the war and concluding a peace treaty. The September 19 Pyongyang military agreement contained conventional tension-reduction measures such as buffer zones in and around the DMZ.
items.outcome: The three- or four-party talks were never convened, even though both Korean leaders had signed the declaration. North Korea scrapped the military agreement on November 23, 2023, South Korea suspended it in full on June 4, 2024, and the Lee Jae-myung government announced in August 2025 that it would restore it.
items.why: Implementation of the inter-Korean agreements became subordinate to the U.S.-North Korean nuclear talks, and after the collapse at Hanoi, North Korea openly dismissed the South's role as "mediator."
items.differs: In 2018, North Korea used the South as a channel for dialogue; today it excludes the South as a partner in dialogue.

items.name: 2018: the Singapore U.S.-North Korean summit
items.format: A bilateral U.S.-North Korean summit. It declared four principles — new relations, a peace regime, efforts toward complete denuclearization, and the repatriation of remains — without defining a sequence for implementation.
items.outcome: It produced only an agreement in principle. At a press conference, Trump announced a halt to joint U.S.-South Korean exercises, and the South Korean government was reported to have been caught by surprise.
items.why: The top-down, leader-to-leader approach left the definition and sequencing of denuclearization to working-level talks, and alliance exercises were used as a bargaining chip without adequate coordination with South Korea.
items.differs: Trump's second administration is repeating the pattern, ordering exercises scaled back in August 2026, but North Korea now rejects any agreement that includes language on denuclearization.

items.name: 2019: the collapse of the Hanoi summit and Kim Yo Jong's statement of July 2020
items.format: A bilateral U.S.-North Korean summit. North Korea offered the permanent dismantlement of the nuclear-material production facilities at Yongbyon and a written pledge to halt nuclear and long-range missile tests, and demanded the lifting of five of the 11 UN sanctions resolutions. Washington presented a one-page document proposing comprehensive dismantlement, including facilities beyond Yongbyon, warheads, and missiles, in exchange for sanctions relief.
items.outcome: The summit collapsed without agreement. On July 10, 2020, Kim Yo Jong called the idea of reviving the bargain of "the partial lifting of sanctions versus the permanent dismantlement" of Yongbyon a "pipedream" and said the formula of negotiations should change to "withdrawal of hostility versus resumption of DPRK-U.S. negotiations."
items.why: The "partial" relief North Korea sought was economically the core of the sanctions, while Yongbyon was only part of its overall capability, so the values the two sides placed on the deal were far apart. North Korea had no alternative ready for Washington's demand for a comprehensive deal.
items.differs: On September 22, 2026, South Korea's president publicly proposed a freeze in exchange for sanctions relief, but North Korea has already discarded the very formula of trading for sanctions.

items.name: 2019: U.S.-North Korean working-level talks in Stockholm
items.format: Bilateral U.S.-North Korean working-level talks (North Korea's delegation led by Ambassador Kim Myong Gil). Washington said it had brought "creative ideas"; North Korea demanded the complete and irreversible withdrawal of hostile policy as a precondition and set a year-end deadline.
items.outcome: The talks broke down the same day. North Korea's Foreign Ministry called them "sickening negotiations," and Pyongyang rejected a proposal to resume two weeks later.
items.why: North Korea preferred leader-level bargaining to working-level negotiations, and it parted ways with Washington over the sequence, insisting that the hostile policy be withdrawn first.
items.differs: The working-level channel has not been restored since, and contact today is limited to letters and remarks between leaders.

items.name: The hostile two-state line and the 2026 four-party and freeze proposals
items.format: North Korea: the declaration of "two belligerent states" at the December 2023 plenary meeting; the designation of the South as a hostile state in the constitution in 2024; at the Ninth Party Congress in February 2026, the statement that the DPRK has "nothing to discuss with the ROK, the most hostile entity," along with conditions for Washington (respect for its nuclear status and withdrawal of hostile policy); and the removal of the goal of unification from the constitution in March 2026. South Korea: Minister Chung Dong-young's proposal at the Ulaanbaatar Dialogue on June 4, 2026, for four-party talks among the two Koreas, the United States, and China (later expanded to Mongolia, Japan, and Russia); the June 26, 2026, plan for three stages — freeze, reduction, denuclearization — preceded by U.S.-North Korean dialogue; and the president's proposal at the United Nations on September 22, 2026, of a freeze in exchange for sanctions relief.
items.outcome: In August 2026, the foreign minister called the four-party idea an idealistic notion not agreed on within the National Security Council. In August 2026, Trump ordered exercises scaled back and claimed that Kim Jong Un had responded positively, but on September 24, 2026, Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui reaffirmed that North Korea's nuclear status is irreversible and said sanctions and military pressure are incompatible with dialogue. Denuclearization was left out of the outcome document of the U.S.-China summit of September 24, 2026.
items.why: North Korea demands recognition of its nuclear status and the withdrawal of hostile policy from the United States alone, and excludes the South regardless of the agenda.
items.differs: This is the current phase itself. In November 2025, Washington formalized its support for South Korean enrichment, reprocessing, and nuclear-powered submarines, lowering the cost to the U.S.-South Korean alliance of pursuing latent nuclear capability; North Korea denounced it as laying a springboard for South Korea's development into a "quasi-nuclear weapons state."

items.name: 2015: the August 25 inter-Korean high-level agreement (the loudspeaker exchange)
items.format: Inter-Korean high-level contact (Panmunjom). The sequence was an expression of regret by the North over the mine provocation, followed by the South's halting loudspeaker broadcasts "unless an abnormal case occurs."
items.outcome: North Korea lifted its quasi-state of war, returned its submarines to port, and agreed to resume family reunions.
items.why: The loudspeakers exposed North Koreans to information the regime could not control, so the cost to the North was high, and leaving a condition for resumption in place preserved their exchange value.
items.differs: A high-level inter-Korean channel was working then; today North Korea has closed its channels for dealing with the South altogether.

checks.reason: Given that every negotiating track over more than 30 years has collapsed within one to eight years, the judgment that an "armed stalemate" will continue is supported by the historical frequency (base rate). But 1994–2002 was a period in which a U.S.-North Korean agreement and an armed stalemate held at the same time, so the two scenarios are not mutually exclusive. And in the precedents of "a U.S.-North Korean agreement without South Korea" (1994, 2018), South Korea was left out only at the table; it still shouldered costs (70 percent of KEDO's light-water reactor costs) and adjustments to exercises.

Exclusion is a recurring fact (Geneva in 1994, the 2018 announcement halting exercises, the August 2026 order to scale them back). But as the June 1994 consideration of striking Yongbyon shows, the risk of war concentrates in the crisis phase just before negotiations collapse, and at that point South Korea's opposition to the use of force worked as a de facto veto. The real loss from exclusion was not losing a seat at the negotiating table but bearing costs without a voice.

The four-party framework operated once, in 1997–99, but North Korea insisted on the withdrawal of U.S. forces from South Korea, and the substantive result came bilaterally between Washington and Pyongyang (Berlin, 1999); the three- or four-party peace talks agreed in writing in 2005, 2007, and 2018 were never convened. At Hanoi, even a concession bigger than a freeze (the dismantlement of Yongbyon) failed to win partial sanctions relief, and North Korea discarded that formula in 2020. On the other hand, in the August 25, 2015, agreement, loudspeaker broadcasts worked as an actual bargaining chip, and U.S. support for enrichment and reprocessing in November 2025 lowered the cost to the U.S.-South Korean alliance of pursuing latent nuclear capability.

At Hanoi, North Korea offered the dismantlement of Yongbyon — a bigger concession than a freeze — and a written pledge to halt tests, yet failed to win the lifting of five sanctions resolutions. Kim Yo Jong's statement of July 2020 dismissed reviving the bargain of partial sanctions relief for the dismantlement of Yongbyon as a "pipedream" and changed the formula to "withdrawal of hostility versus resumption of DPRK-U.S. negotiations," and the February 2026 Party Congress and Choe Son Hui's statement of September 24, 2026, make recognition of nuclear status and withdrawal of hostile policy preconditions. Sanctions relief is not the best outcome North Korea itself has put forward.

North Korea sat with South Korea in the Four-Party Talks of 1997–99 and the Six-Party Talks of 2003–08, but in both cases the format was co-proposed by the United States or hosted by China. Since February 2026, North Korea has said it will not deal with the South regardless of the agenda, and it refused even right after South Korea's president proposed a freeze in exchange for sanctions relief. Simultaneous UN membership in 1991 is a precedent in which North Korea, its great-power cover gone, accepted a "two states" framework to avoid exclusion.

A shared interest in avoiding exclusion is supported by Kim Jong Un's five meetings with Xi Jinping between March 2018 and June 2019 and by the Panmunjom Declaration's reference to "trilateral ... or quadrilateral" meetings. But in the Four-Party Talks China was only one of the rotating chairs; as the Six-Party Talks broke down (December 2008), it sided with the North by continuing to supply heavy fuel oil; and the 2017 dual suspension, after North Korea rejected it, was carried out bilaterally by Washington and Pyongyang without China. As for the price, China put a real cost on South Korea's security choices through informal economic retaliation over THAAD.

checks.claim: Forecast (at least one four-party consultation by the end of 2027: 15%)
checks.reason: Over the past 30 years, the four-party framework was convened only once, in 1997, and even then it took more than a year after the U.S.-South Korean joint proposal for North Korea to accept. The peace talks agreed in writing in 2005, 2007, and 2018 were never held, not even in 2018, when both Korean leaders had agreed. Today, North Korea's exclusion of the South, the foreign ministry's dismissal of the idea as idealistic, and Washington's silence all coincide; the upside factors are the president's UN proposal, the omission of denuclearization from the U.S.-China outcome document, and the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November.

precedents.insight: Since 2020, North Korea's demand has shifted from "sanctions relief" (a matter for the Security Council, where Washington and Beijing hold the keys) to "withdrawal of hostile policy" (joint exercises and strategic assets, matters for the U.S.-South Korean alliance). This means that part of the price North Korea wants lies within the scope of South Korea's consent; but the precedents of 2018 and August 2026, in which Trump raised halting or scaling back exercises first, out of step with Seoul's announcements, show that this power of consent does not translate directly into a seat at the table. South Korea's historical leverage has been not a seat at the table but a veto over the use of force (1994) and cost-sharing (70 percent of KEDO), and North Korea, too, accepted a "two states" framework in 1991 out of fear of exclusion.
