links.work: Carl von Clausewitz, On War, Book 3, Chapter 16, "The Suspension of Action in War," 1832
links.idea: Military action can stop for long periods when both sides believe that waiting serves them better, or when defense is stronger than attack. Such a suspension is not peace but a tense equilibrium that can break at any moment.
links.fit: It supports the judgment that armed stalemate is the most likely future. For both Seoul and Washington and for Pyongyang, the cost of changing the status quo exceeds the cost of waiting, and the defensive advantages on the Korean Peninsula (artillery near Seoul, the U.S. reinforcement system) prolong the suspension.
links.limit: Clausewitz also saw suspension as a temporary phenomenon arising from imperfect information and fear. Unlike the conventional suspension he analyzed, a suspension under nuclear weapons tends to permit low-intensity provocations (see the stability-instability paradox below).
sources: Carl von Clausewitz, Vom Kriege, Book 3, Chapter 16 (1832); English translation by Michael Howard and Peter Paret, On War, Princeton University Press, 1976

links.work: Glenn H. Snyder, "The Balance of Power and the Balance of Terror", in Paul Seabury (ed.), The Balance of Power, 1965
links.idea: The more stable mutual deterrence is at the nuclear level, the more room there is for conventional and local provocations beneath it (the stability-instability paradox).
links.fit: It qualifies the label "armed stalemate." Stalemate is not calm: as with the sinking of the Cheonan and the shelling of Yeonpyeong Island in 2010, local clashes can become more frequent under nuclear deterrence. The 37 percent probability means only the absence of full-scale war; it says nothing about the frequency of low-intensity clashes.
links.limit: The empirical evidence for the paradox is mixed. The 1999 Kargil conflict is often cited as the classic case, but systematic evidence that provocations became more frequent after acquiring nuclear weapons is sensitive to case selection.
sources: Glenn H. Snyder, "The Balance of Power and the Balance of Terror," in P. Seabury ed., The Balance of Power (San Francisco: Chandler, 1965), pp. 184-201

links.work: Virginia Page Fortna, 『Peace Time: Cease-Fire Agreements and the Durability of Peace』, 2004
links.idea: Analyzing cease-fires in interstate wars that ended between 1946 and 1994, Fortna showed that demilitarized zones, explicit outside guarantees, and joint commissions for handling disputes lengthen the duration of cease-fires. Arms control provisions had no clear effect.
links.fit: The Korean armistice regime has all of these — a demilitarized zone, the Military Armistice Commission, and a de facto outside guarantee in U.S. Forces Korea — which supports the judgment that the stalemate will last.
links.limit: Those elements are eroding. North Korea withdrew from the Military Armistice Commission in the 1990s, and the 2018 September 19 military agreement became effectively void in 2023–2024. With the institutional skeleton of the armistice weakened, past durations cannot simply be extended.

links.work: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, 17–31 (the Peace of Nicias, 421 BC)
links.idea: Sparta's allies — Corinth, Boeotia, Megara, and Elis — rejected the peace that Athens and Sparta concluded. Alienated by an agreement that did not reflect their interests, they sought new alliances, and the peace collapsed within a few years.
links.fit: It supports the judgment (C2) that exclusion is a matter not of having a seat at the table but of whether South Korea's interests are reflected, and goes a step further: an agreement that leaves out the interests of an excluded party falters at the implementation stage.
links.limit: Corinth and the others had their own military forces and an alternative alliance (Argos). South Korea has no alliance alternative to the United States, so a threat to defect carries little credibility.
sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, 5.17-5.31; Robert B. Strassler ed., The Landmark Thucydides, Free Press, 1996

links.work: Ryu Seong-ryong, Jingbirok (The Book of Corrections, written from the late 1590s to around 1604), passages on the Ming-Japanese peace negotiations (1593–1596)
links.idea: During the Imjin War, Shen Weijing of Ming China and Konishi Yukinaga of Japan negotiated a peace while excluding Joseon. Toyotomi Hideyoshi demanded the cession of four of Joseon's eight provinces and a prince as hostage; after the intermediaries distorted each side's terms, the investiture negotiations collapsed in 1596, and the second invasion (Jeongyu War) followed in 1597.
links.fit: It is a precedent in which even Ming China, Joseon's suzerain and protector, bypassed the injured party to strike a deal, supporting the judgment that exclusion is a risk as serious as war. The territory and people of the excluded country became items on the bargaining table.
links.limit: Joseon was then on the verge of military collapse, and its relationship with Ming was one of tributary investiture, not a treaty alliance. Moreover, the harm of exclusion in this case appeared not as an unfavorable agreement but as the failure of the agreement and a second invasion.
sources: Ryu Seong-ryong, Jingbirok, translated into modern Korean by Lee Jae-ho, Yeoksaui Achim, 2007

links.work: Glenn H. Snyder, "The Security Dilemma in Alliance Politics", World Politics 36(4), 1984
links.idea: Allies move between two risks, abandonment and entrapment; the closer an ally clings to the alliance to reduce the risk of abandonment, the greater the risk of entrapment and the weaker its bargaining power within the alliance.
links.fit: Exclusion is a form of abandonment. The theory adds a qualification: the earlier South Korea declares its support for Washington in order to win a seat at the table, the more Washington will treat Seoul's consent as already secured, and the less incentive it will have to reflect South Korea's interests when decisions are made.
links.limit: Snyder's model assumes relative symmetry between allies. In a highly asymmetric alliance such as that between Seoul and Washington, the weaker side's threats to defect struggle to gain credibility, and the model's equilibrium tilts to one side.
sources: Glenn H. Snyder, "The Security Dilemma in Alliance Politics," World Politics 36(4), 1984, pp. 461-495

links.work: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence, Chapter 2, "The Art of Commitment," 1966; The Strategy of Conflict, Chapter 8, 1960
links.idea: The credibility of extended deterrence comes from devices that bind the protector to its commitment so it cannot back out (such as tripwire forces) and from threats that leave something to chance — the risk that events slip out of control.
links.fit: The judgment ranking stronger conventional deterrence (A5) first is supported, in that South Korea's own capabilities fill the gap when North Korea's ICBM capability against the United States shakes the credibility of the U.S. commitment. At the same time, a tension emerges: adjusting joint exercises, proposed as an early card, loosens what Schelling calls the binding device, so this card and stronger conventional deterrence (A5) may erode each other's effects.
links.limit: Schelling's theory of commitment grew out of Cold War Europe (the garrison in West Berlin). The argument that tripwires lose their force when an adversary can strike the protector's homeland was the logic behind France's independent nuclear arsenal in the 1960s.
sources: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence, Yale UP, 1966, ch. 2
Thomas C. Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict, Harvard UP, 1960, ch. 8

links.work: Stephen J. Stedman, "Spoiler Problems in Peace Processes", International Security 22(2), 1997; Barbara F. Walter, 『Committing to Peace』, 2002
links.idea: The greatest dangers in peace processes arise in the implementation stage after signing, when groups left out of the agreement become spoilers. Walter argued that credible outside guarantees are decisive for the implementation of negotiated settlements to civil wars.
links.fit: It supports the judgment that gives priority to a seat at the table in the implementation and peace-regime stages over the stage that opens negotiations. Implementation is where agreements actually succeed or fail, and at that stage South Korea carries weight both as a contributor to the costs and as a potential spoiler.
links.limit: Both studies draw mainly on cases of civil-war termination. They do not transfer neatly to interstate nuclear negotiations or to a peace regime for a divided nation, and if South Korea is seen as a spoiler, the cost to its alliance with the United States rises.
sources: Stephen J. Stedman, "Spoiler Problems in Peace Processes," International Security 22(2), 1997, pp. 5-53
Barbara F. Walter, Committing to Peace: The Successful Settlement of Civil Wars, Princeton UP, 2002

links.work: Ryu Seong-ryong, Jingbirok, opening of Volume 1 (Sin Suk-ju's dying advice) and the passage on the 1590 envoys' reports
links.idea: On his deathbed, Sin Suk-ju urged King Seongjong not to lose peaceful relations with Japan (gyorin, "neighborly relations"). Yet when Hwang Yun-gil and Kim Seong-il went to Japan as envoys in 1590, they gave contradictory reports on the likelihood of a Japanese invasion, and the court, swayed by factional considerations, chose the optimistic view.
links.fit: It bears on the judgment that puts tension-reducing measures and the restoration of liaison channels among the early cards. Joseon's tradition of neighborly relations treated standing channels with a powerful neighbor as an instrument of security.
links.limit: The channel existed, yet it did not prevent the invasion of 1592. It is a counterexample showing that a channel by itself offers no protection when the interpretation of what it yields is captive to domestic politics.
sources: Ryu Seong-ryong, Jingbirok, Volume 1; "Jingbirok" entry, Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr

links.work: Sunzi, The Art of War, "Maneuvering" (Chapter 7)
links.idea: When you surround an army, leave an outlet free (圍師必闕); do not press a desperate foe too hard (窮寇勿迫). An enemy with no way out fights to the death.
links.fit: It supports the judgment (C4) that maximum pressure (A4) ranks low even when judged by the South Korean government's goals. Pressure with no way out maximizes resistance and provocation, not submission.
links.limit: Sunzi's context is battlefield tactics. And if the "outlet" for North Korea becomes recognition of its nuclear status, it collides head-on with South Korea's goals, so the form any outlet takes has to be designed separately.
sources: 『孫子兵法』 軍爭篇; Samuel B. Griffith tr., Sun Tzu: The Art of War, Oxford UP, 1963, ch. VII

links.work: Nicholas L. Miller, 『Stopping the Bomb: The Sources and Effectiveness of US Nonproliferation Policy』, 2018
links.idea: U.S. sanctions actually imposed on nuclear programs already under way succeeded in only three of 22 cases (about 14 percent). Sanctions threats were most effective when the target depended on the United States for trade or security, and before a program began.
links.fit: North Korea, which has virtually no dependence on the United States and already possesses nuclear weapons, belongs to the type on which sanctions work least. This supports the judgment that the expected effect of maximum pressure is low.
links.limit: UN sanctions in 2016–2017 sharply cut North Korea's exports to China, so the economic blow itself was large. But it did not lead to a change in nuclear policy, and since 2023, North Korean-Russian military cooperation has weakened the sanctions net, further reducing the efficiency of pressure.
sources: Stephan Haggard & Marcus Noland, Hard Target: Sanctions, Inducements, and the Case of North Korea, Stanford UP, 2017

links.work: Nicholas L. Miller, Stopping the Bomb, 2018 (the South Korean and Taiwanese cases)
links.idea: In the 1970s, South Korea and Taiwan tried to develop nuclear weapons, but both gave up once the U.S. Congress wrote sanctions into law in the mid-1970s and the threat became credible. No country firmly aligned with the United States has launched a new nuclear weapons program since the late 1970s.
links.fit: It supports the judgment that ranks an independent nuclear arsenal last. Heavily dependent on the United States, South Korea is the type on which sanctions threats work best, and the Park Chung-hee government's program was halted along this path.
links.limit: The effect depends on the degree of dependence. If Washington lowers the value of dependence by reducing its troops or weakening its commitment, the weight of the sanctions threat falls with it.

links.work: Alexander Lanoszka, 『Atomic Assurance: The Alliance Politics of Nuclear Proliferation』, 2018
links.idea: The main trigger for allies to seek nuclear weapons is doubt about the protector's commitment, especially changes in posture such as troop reductions, and allies tend to stop when the protector restores its posture.
links.fit: It shows that the judgment ranking an independent nuclear arsenal (A3a) last holds only on the condition that U.S. Forces Korea and the extended deterrence commitment remain in place. Among the 2030 futures, the threshold for crossing into "nuclear dominoes" (F3, 19 percent) is likely to lie in changes to the U.S. posture rather than in South Korean public opinion.
links.limit: The cases center on Cold War West Germany, South Korea, and Japan. A situation in which North Korea can strike the U.S. homeland differs from the conditions of Cold War alliances.
sources: Alexander Lanoszka, Atomic Assurance: The Alliance Politics of Nuclear Proliferation, Cornell UP, 2018

links.work: Kenneth N. Waltz, "The Spread of Nuclear Weapons: More May Be Better", Adelphi Paper 171, 1981
links.idea: Because nuclear weapons raise the costs of war to extremes, they breed caution among their possessors, so gradual proliferation can bring stability.
links.fit: By Waltz's logic, mutual nuclear deterrence between the two Koreas might actually create stability, which contradicts the judgment that ranks an independent nuclear arsenal (A3a) last.
links.limit: Sagan countered, drawing on organization theory, with the risks of accidents and miscalculation by new nuclear states. Waltz's model also leaves out the costs South Korea would pay in the process of arming — NPT withdrawal, sanctions, and a rift in the alliance — and the risk of a preemptive strike during the development period.
sources: Kenneth N. Waltz, The Spread of Nuclear Weapons: More May Be Better, Adelphi Papers 171, IISS, 1981
Scott D. Sagan & Kenneth N. Waltz, The Spread of Nuclear Weapons: A Debate, W. W. Norton, 1995

links.work: Maximilian Horster, "The Trade in Political Prisoners between the Two German States, 1962-89", Journal of Contemporary History, 2004
links.idea: Between 1963 and 1989, West Germany bought the release of 33,755 East German political prisoners with goods and cash, at a price per prisoner that started at about 40,000 marks and rose over time, for a total of some 3.5 billion marks (with estimates as high as 8 billion marks); it also paid for exit permits for about 250,000 people.
links.fit: It supports the judgment to raise a humanitarian exchange with something given in return (A7) into the top-ranked package. It is a precedent in which exchanges that returned something to people, between hostile halves of a divided nation, were kept separate from political relations and lasted for decades.
links.limit: Critics charged that East Germany turned the practice into a source of hard currency, creating an incentive to make arrests. It also differs from the Korean case in that intermediaries from the churches and institutional frameworks such as the 1972 Basic Treaty between the two German states supported the exchange. North Korea has tied even family reunions to political conditions, and they have been cut off since 2018.

links.work: Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace, Section 1, Preliminary Article 6, 1795
links.idea: Even in wartime, hostile acts that would make mutual trust impossible in a future peace — employing assassins or poisoners, breaking terms of surrender, inciting treason in the enemy state — are not permitted.
links.fit: It qualifies the judgment that uses information tools as bargaining chips. By Kant's standard, means close to inciting the overthrow of the regime are something to refrain from voluntarily, before any exchange, and must be distinguished from channels through which people obtain outside information. C6, which limits the price to things that return to people, is in line with this distinction.
links.limit: Kant's article is based on trust between states; the human rights perspective of people's right to information lies outside its framework. And because North Korea defines the very influx of outside information as a hostile act, the distinction may not be accepted by the other side.
sources: Immanuel Kant, Zum ewigen Frieden (1795), First Section, Sixth Preliminary Article; Korean translation by Lee Han-gu, Yeongu pyeonghwaron, Seokwangsa

links.work: Kim Il Sung, "On Eliminating Dogmatism and Formalism and Establishing Juche in Ideological Work," December 28, 1955; Supreme People's Assembly law "On the DPRK's Policy on the Nuclear Forces," September 8, 2022
links.idea: Juche proclaims independence in ideology, self-reliance in politics, and self-defense in national defense, and since the military-first (Songun) era has placed military power at the center of the state's existence. The 2022 law defined nuclear forces as a means of the state's existence and declared that there would be no denuclearization negotiations, and at the end of 2023 North Korea defined relations with the Republic of Korea as those between "two states hostile to each other."
links.fit: It supports the judgment that North Korea's best move is a direct deal with Washington that leaves South Korea out, with recognition of its nuclear status at the center of the exchange. In the discourse of independence, South Korea is not a negotiating partner in its own right, and nuclear weapons are presented as a status, not a bargaining item.
links.limit: Ideological texts and laws serve both external propaganda and domestic cohesion, and they have at times diverged from actual negotiating behavior. In 2018, three inter-Korean summits were held, and North Korea used South Korea as a channel to the United States.
sources: Kim Il Sung, Kim Il Sung jeojakjip (Collected Works), vol. 9, Workers' Party of Korea Publishing House, 1980 (speech of December 28, 1955)
https://www.ncnk.org (English translation of the September 8, 2022 law on the nuclear forces policy)

links.work: James D. Fearon, "Rationalist Explanations for War", International Organization 49(3), 1995
links.idea: When the other side has no incentive to keep its promises in the future (the commitment problem), even rational actors refuse a bargain. When one side makes concessions that are hard to reverse and the other makes concessions that are easy to reverse, a deal is hard to reach.
links.fit: It explains the judgment that North Korea puts recognition of its status and a scaling back of joint exercises and strategic assets ahead of sanctions relief. Sanctions relief is easily reversed; giving up nuclear weapons is hard to reverse (Libya's renunciation in 2003, followed by the regime's collapse in 2011, is the case North Korea cites again and again).
links.limit: The same logic qualifies the judgment. Scaled-back joint exercises can be reversed (they resumed after the 2018 suspension), and so can North Korea's moratorium on nuclear and ICBM tests. An exchange in which both sides' concessions are reversible amounts to managing a stalemate rather than resolving it, and it collapses just as easily.
sources: James D. Fearon, "Rationalist Explanations for War," International Organization 49(3), 1995, pp. 379-414

links.work: Zuo zhuan (The Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals), Duke Xi, Year 5 (655 BC): the remonstrance of Gong Zhiqi
links.idea: Gong Zhiqi, a minister of Yu (虞), warned that if Yu let Jin (晉) pass through its territory, its neighbor Guo (虢) would fall and Yu would fall with it, remonstrating that "the sideboards and the wheels of a cart depend on each other; when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold" (輔車相依 脣亡齒寒). Since entering the Korean War in 1950, China has described its relationship with North Korea through this metaphor.
links.fit: It supports the judgment that China's priority is the survival of the North Korean regime (the buffer) and that its role as a guarantor of denuclearization comes below that. A country intent on preserving a buffer is limited in how far it can pressure the buffer state to come to the table.
links.limit: "Lips and teeth" is also rhetoric. China established diplomatic relations with South Korea in 1992 over North Korea's objections and joined sanctions on North Korea in 2017. China's strategy on the peninsula also aims not only to preserve the buffer but to drive a wedge between Seoul and Washington, so in a four-party framework at the peace-regime stage, China could use the seat it gains there as a channel for putting U.S. Forces Korea and the alliance on the agenda.
sources: 『春秋左氏傳』 僖公五年; James Legge tr., The Chinese Classics vol. V, The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen, 1872

links.work: Joint Statement of the Fourth Round of the Six-Party Talks (September 19, 2005), Item 4; the Four-Party Talks on peace on the Korean Peninsula (1997–1999)
links.idea: The September 19 Joint Statement provided that "the directly related parties will negotiate a permanent peace regime on the Korean Peninsula at an appropriate separate forum," separating denuclearization from a peace regime. Earlier, the Four-Party Talks of 1997–1999 among the two Koreas, the United States, and China had ended without results despite several plenary sessions.
links.fit: It supports the judgment (C8) that the real value of a four-party framework lies in guaranteeing South Korea a seat at the table in the peace-regime stage after a U.S.-North Korean agreement. There is already a precedent for separating peace-regime negotiations into a separate forum.
links.limit: The main reason the Four-Party Talks failed was North Korea's insistence on the withdrawal of U.S. forces from South Korea and on a U.S.-North Korean peace treaty. As with the "three or four parties" wording of the October 4, 2007 declaration, the very range of participants can become a subject of negotiation, leaving room for South Korea or China to be left out.

theory.insight: The earlier judgment (C2) treats exclusion from negotiations as a risk for South Korea and proposes "securing" a seat at the table in the implementation stage as the remedy. Set side by side, classical and historical cases show that agreements that bypassed the local party with the most at stake were likely to be concluded but did not last. The Peace of Nicias (421 BC) collapsed because of alienated allies; the Ming-Japanese peace talks (1593–1596), conducted without Joseon amid the deceptions of intermediaries, broke down and led to a second invasion; and the Agreed Framework (1994) collapsed in 2002 under an arrangement in which South Korea paid the costs but had no part in the decisions. The F5 future (a deal without South Korea, 22 percent) therefore needs to be treated in terms of both the probability that it happens and the probability that it lasts, and an exclusionary deal is likely to have a path that leads back to F1 (armed stalemate). Moreover, the way an excluded South Korea actually gained weight was not by demanding a seat but through cost-sharing and the capacity to obstruct. In 1953, Syngman Rhee unilaterally released some 27,000 anti-communist prisoners of war, shaking the armistice, and Washington granted the U.S.-South Korean Mutual Defense Treaty as the price of his accepting it. South Korea's leverage lies in explicitly linking what it can provide or block at the implementation stage (cost-sharing, inter-Korean projects, enforcement of sanctions within South Korean jurisdiction, the conduct of joint exercises) to a seat at the table. But as Snyder's alliance dilemma shows, this capacity to obstruct wears down the relationship with Washington; in 1953, the United States even considered a plan to remove Rhee (Operation Everready). How far to push this linkage is the hidden variable in the top-ranked package.
uncertain: The exact number of cease-fires in Fortna's (2004) sample and the failure-rate figures could not be confirmed (the summary contains no figures).

The direction of the conclusions of Mehta and Whitlark, "The Benefits and Burdens of Nuclear Latency" (International Studies Quarterly 61(3), 2017) — whether latency provides deterrence or invites coercion — could not be confirmed from the original, so it was left out of the link to A3b.
The sample size in Walter (2002) and the figures for the effect of third-party guarantees could not be confirmed.
Estimates of the total West Germany paid for the release of East German political prisoners vary, from about 3.5 billion marks to as much as 8 billion marks.
Jingbirok is thought to have been completed around 1604, but the exact year could not be confirmed.
The official source for the formulation of China's Korean Peninsula priorities as "no war, no chaos, no nukes" (不战、不乱、无核) could not be confirmed, so it was left out of the links.
The number of captives repatriated by the monk Samyeong (Yujeong) in 1604–1605 (a Joseon precedent for humanitarian exchange) could not be confirmed, so it was left out of the links.

The level at which Operation Everready (1953) was considered, and the exact timing and conditions of the promise of the U.S.-South Korean Mutual Defense Treaty, were not checked against the original FRUS documents.

items.q: Do you agree that South Korea should also possess nuclear weapons?
items.read: Support for an independent nuclear arsenal has not fallen below a majority once in 13 years. Other organizations' 2026 surveys point the same way: the Asan Institute for Policy Studies found 80.0 percent, the East Asia Institute 69.1 percent (on the premise that the North Korean nuclear threat persists), and the Seoul National University Institute for Peace and Unification Studies 61.1 percent.
items.caveat: Because question wording and methods differ by organization, producing results spread between 51 and 80 percent, the different surveys have not been joined into a single time series. Some surveys also find that support drops sharply when costs such as sanctions or a weakened alliance are presented alongside the question (Asan Institute for Policy Studies).
sources: Asan Institute for Policy Studies survey, February 7–11, 2026 (1,000 respondents), as cited by Segye Ilbo, April 13, 2026
East Asia Institute and Hankook Research survey, July 20–21, 2026 (1,547 respondents), as cited by Korea JoongAng Daily, August 12, 2026
Seoul National University Institute for Peace and Unification Studies, 2026 Unification Perception Survey (July 2026, 1,200 respondents), as cited by Hankook Ilbo, September 28, 2026

publics.read: Clisa Geopolitics ranks an independent nuclear arsenal (A3a) last, but a majority of the public stands on the other side. Because the domestic political cost of publicly pledging to forgo nuclear weapons is high for any government, a conditional latent nuclear capability (A3b) serves as a buffer that absorbs public demand without damaging the alliance. If Washington concludes an agreement that limits only ICBMs while leaving South Korea out (the condition for reconsidering C5), it will become harder for the government to contain the debate over nuclear armament, since public opinion already leans toward it.
publics.watch: If support stays above a majority even on questions that present the costs, that would mean the public wants nuclear weapons knowing the price, and the assumption that A3b alone can absorb public demand will be revisited.

congress.t: Conditions on cutting U.S. troops in Korea and transferring wartime operational control
congress.stage: The fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) bars the use of funds to reduce U.S. Forces Korea below 28,500 troops or to complete the transfer of wartime operational control in a way that departs from the plan Seoul and Washington agreed. On July 22, 2026, the House passed a bill extending the same conditions through fiscal 2027, and the Senate Armed Services Committee's version would require the defense secretary's certification before the transfer could be completed at all.
congress.power: Through appropriations and the NDAA, Congress attaches conditions to any presidential decision to cut troops or transfer operational control. The conditions lift 60 days after the defense secretary certifies and submits an assessment.
congress.votes: The House passed the bill 216–212, with 209 Republicans, six Democrats, and one independent voting yes. In the Senate, a July 14 vote to take up the bill stalled at 50–46, short of the 60 votes needed.
congress.sides: Both the House bill and the Senate Armed Services Committee version keep the commitment to roughly 28,500 U.S. troops in Korea among their provisions on strengthening the alliance.
congress.next: House and Senate negotiators will settle the final text. Fiscal 2027 spending continues under a stopgap through December 11.

speakers.note: No floor remarks on cutting U.S. troops in Korea or transferring wartime operational control were found in the House or Senate record between July 1 and October 5, 2026. The conditions entered the NDAA as statutory text rather than through floor debate; they were drafted by the House Armed Services Committee (Chair Mike Rogers; ranking Democrat Adam Smith) and the Senate Armed Services Committee (Chair Roger Wicker; ranking Democrat Jack Reed).

congress.t: The timetable for transferring wartime operational control
congress.stage: The government told the National Assembly on September 10 that it aims to complete verification of full operational capability at the Security Consultative Meeting (SCM) in November. On September 16, the nominee for defense minister said that once verification is complete, the two defense ministers will set a year for the transfer and recommend it to their presidents.
congress.power: The transfer of wartime operational control is settled by agreement between Seoul and Washington and does not require the National Assembly's consent. The Assembly scrutinizes it through its annual parliamentary audit and through questioning.
congress.sides: Ruling-party members pressed for a swift transfer. A People Power Party member criticized the government, pointing to differences between Seoul and Washington and to the cancellation of counteroffensive drills in the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise.
congress.next: The parliamentary audit in October; the 58th SCM in November.

quotes.body: Plenary questions to the government (foreign affairs, unification and security)
quotes.ex: My understanding is that the Defense Ministry's goal is to finalize a target year for the transfer of wartime operational control at next month's Security Consultative Meeting and recommend it.
quotes.full: 전작권 환수는 군사주권의 최종적인 확립이지요? 그리고 한반도 평화 시대를 여는 출발점이라고 저는 생각합니다.  다음 달 한미 안보협의회의에서 전작권 전환 목표 연도를 확정해 건의하는 것이 국방부 목표로 알고 있는데요. 맞습니까?

quotes.body: Plenary questions to the government (foreign affairs, unification and security)
quotes.ex: Building a system in which we can fight on our own and take responsibility whenever war breaks out, and so securing the capability to command in war and recovering wartime operational control
quotes.full: 그렇습니다. 튼튼한 한미동맹을 바탕으로 북한의 핵 위협에 대해서는 고도화된 확장억제를 신뢰 가능한 수준으로 지속시켜 가면서 우리의 첨단 재래전력과 미국의 전략 핵억제력이 결합된 CNI 전략을 추구하되 그러나 언제든지 전쟁이 일어나면 우리가 스스로 싸울 수 있고 책임질 수 있는 체제를 갖추는 것, 그래서 전쟁지휘능력을 확보하고 전작권을 회복하면서 동시에 국제사회의 신뢰를 바탕으로 핵추진잠수함을 도입하여 우리의 전략적 타격능력을 강화시키는 것입니다. 동시에 우리는 평화와 자주국방의 기틀을 튼튼히 하는 것 이것이 우리 안보의 대강이라고 생각합니다. 맞지요?

quotes.body: Plenary questions to the government (foreign affairs, unification and security)
quotes.ex: I think the more important question is not who exercises wartime operational control but how to safeguard the security of the Republic of Korea.
quotes.full: 그렇게 중요하지요. 그런데 보세요. 이렇게 한미동맹은 자주국방을 안정적으로 추진할 수 있는 울타리를 제공했는데 여기를 위해서 자주국방의 역량을 키우는 것은 당연히 중요합니다.  그런데 이렇게 한미동맹과 자주국방은 독립적인 관계가 아니에요. 표에 보시면, PPT에 보시면 뫼비우스의 띠와 같습니다. 그래서 전작권이 자주성과 굴종의 잣대가 되거나 전작권 전환 그 자체가 목적이 되면 안 되고요, 전작권을 누가 행사하느냐가 중요한 게 아니라 대한민국의 안보를 어떻게 지킬 것인가 그게 더 중요한 문제라고 생각하는데 어떻게 생각하십니까?

quotes.body: Plenary questions to the government (foreign affairs, unification and security)
quotes.ex: If we say ‘no thanks’ without weighing our national interest and practical gains, they will say ‘no thanks’ right back when we are in trouble.
quotes.full: 그렇지요. 그래서 죽고 사는 문제를 함께 공유해야 되는 동맹이 필요에 의해서 도움을 요청할 때 국익과 실리도 따져 보지 않고 ‘노 땡스’라고 하면 우리가 어려울 때 그들도 바로 ‘노 땡스’ 합니다.  전작권 전환 등 한미동맹의 문제를 단순히 국방의 지휘관이 누구냐 이런 데 한정시키면 안 돼요. 국가안보와 국민의 삶을 총체적으로 살피고 총리로서 전시에 내가 무슨 역할을 해야 되는지 대통령은 뭘 하는지 그리고 군인이 혼자 지휘하는 게 아니고 국가통수기구 양국 간에 합의해서 전시에 통제한다는 것을 잘 알고 앞으로 고민해 주셨으면 좋겠습니다.

items.pv: As I said this morning, I will pick up where I left off on the transfer of wartime operational control. A conditions-based transfer probably needs no explanation for anyone else here. But in several of your written answers, Nominee Kang Shin-chul, you said that on the FOC assessment, agreement would be reached at this SCM…

Nominee, let me ask about the transfer of wartime operational control as well. Put the slide up, please. (Referring to the slides) In answer to our question, the nominee replied that he agrees with the principle of a conditions-based transfer of wartime operational control. Right? Next slide. He also said he shares current Minister Ahn Gyu-back's view of the problem…

When the U.S. House passed its fiscal 2027 NDAA, didn't it bar the use of funds if the transfer of wartime operational control proceeds differently from the plan Seoul and Washington agreed in advance, until the secretary of war certifies to Congress that it serves U.S. interests and that consultations with the ally are complete? In other words…

speakers.note: Members are ranked by the number of questions they asked on this issue, according to the records of the National Defense, Foreign Affairs and Unification, and Intelligence committees and of plenary sessions. Procedural remarks by committee chairs and answers from government officials are excluded, a short exchange between government answers counts as one question, and opening greetings are omitted. For each member, 30 percent of their questions (rounded down; at most three, at least one) are excerpted, chosen by how often the issue's keywords appear and no more than one per meeting; the rest are listed by date with a link to the original record. Excerpts are translated from Korean.

congress.t: Aid to North Korea and a resolution condemning North Korean land mines
congress.stage: The unification minister told the National Assembly that the government is preparing to send medical equipment to North Korea and has obtained a UN sanctions exemption (September 17). On September 29, the National Defense Committee sought to adopt a resolution condemning the North Korean land mine incident but failed to do so after the ruling and opposition parties could not agree on a clause calling for a review of aid to North Korea already in the works.
congress.power: The National Assembly can cut the budget, and inter-Korean agreements that impose a heavy fiscal burden require its consent.
congress.votes: The budget passes by simple majority, so the Democratic Party (161 seats) can protect the government's proposal on its own.
congress.sides: The People Power Party demanded a review of aid to North Korea alongside the condemnation; the Democratic Party rejected that clause, saying the resolution should focus on condemning the North. Both parties agreed that North Korea was responsible and had violated the armistice agreement.
congress.next: The parliamentary audit in October; review of the 2027 budget (constitutional deadline: December 2).

quotes.role: Member, Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee

quotes.full: 오늘 국방위를 통해서 군사분계선 남쪽 10m에서 우리 장병들 사상, 중상자가 나고 희생이 됐습니다. 그래서 이것은 명백히 북한이 설치한 지뢰에 의한 것임이 판명이 났습니다. 그래서 이것은 정전협정 위반일 뿐만 아니라 도발로 간주가 됩니다. 그래서 우리 국방위원들은 여야 할 것 없이 북한을 규탄해 왔습니다. 그리고 다 규탄에 동의를 했고요. 그래서 저희 제안에 대해서 국방위 행정실에서 예전 사례를 가지고 초안을 잡았습니다. 저는 아주 명쾌히 잘 잡았다고 봅니다.  먼저 국방위에서 북한에 대한 강력한 규탄 하는 내용이 나와 있고요. 재발 방지 대책을 요구하는, 강력히 촉구하는 것도 나와 있고. 우리 장병 안전 대책을 마련하도록 우리 정부와 군에 요구하는 사항도 나와 있고요. 그리고 국제사회에도 이런 것들을 알려서 북한의 천인공노한 이런 것들을 알리는 내용도 나와 있습니다. 그리고 장병들 치료·회복에 최선을 다해 달라는 촉구도 나와 있고요. 그리고 또 국민의힘에서 요구했던 만약에 북한이 사과를 하지 않는다면 그에 상응하는 조치를 정부는 강력히 하도록 촉구하는 것은 국민의힘 의견을 받아서 포함을 시켰습니다.  그런데 유감스럽게도 거기에 하나 더 요구해서 현재 추진 중인 대북 지원을 재검토하라는 항목을 포함시켜야 된다고 국민의힘은 요구합니다. 현재 추진 중인 대북 지원 사항은 없습니다. 지금 남북한은 모든 통신선이 끊어지고 모든 게 돼 있는데 추진 중인 대북 지원을 재검토하라는 것은 말이 되지도 않고요. 또 국방위에서는 북한의 규탄에 포커스를 맞추는 겁니다. 우리 정부의 대책은 다음에 또 요구를 해도 되는 것인데 현재 추진 중인 대북 지원 재검토를 넣지 않으면 규탄 결의안을 받지 않겠다는 것은 저는 생떼를 쓰는 트집이라고 봅니다. 그러면 규탄을 안 하겠다는 겁니까? 그러면 그 항목, 정부의 대책 요구는 다 빼 버리고 북한을 규탄한 내용만 일단 여기서 하시지요, 그러면.  중요한 것은 우리가 모처럼 여야가 합의를 해서 한목소리를 지금 내고 있지 않습니까. 온통 신문도…… 지금 ‘여야가 공동으로 규탄한다’ 이런 메시지가 북한에 가야 되는 것이고요. 또 북한은 다시는 이런 걸 못 해야 되는 것인데 한 문구를 가지고 이걸 넣어 주지 않으면 못 하겠다는 게 뭔 말입니까, 도대체? 도대체 북한을 규탄하는 겁니까, 안 하는 겁니까?

quotes.ex: The basic position of the People Power Party members is that we must get an apology from North Korea and a promise that this will not happen again.
quotes.full: 민주당에서 대북 결의안을 같이 채택하자라고 이야기를 했고요. 그와 관련해서 우리 국민의힘 위원들도 원칙적으로 동의했기 때문에 워딩과 관련돼서 의견들을 죽 나눴습니다. 그 과정에서 저희들이 요구하는 부분과 관련돼서 받아 줄 수 없다고 하기 때문에 저희들은 이걸 채택하기가 어렵다라는 말씀을 드립니다.  왜냐하면 오늘 보고한 내용이나 민주당 위원님들이 이야기한 내용 그다음에 답변한 내용들을 보면 이번 이 사고는 북한이 MDL 이남에 대해서 의도적으로 내려와서 지뢰를 매설한 거고 그 매설한 지뢰에 의해서 우리 장병이 다친 겁니다. 이건 이미 다 시인을 한 것 아닙니까? 그러면 북한의 정전협정 위반이고 이 부분들과 관련돼서 북한의 사과와 재발 방지를 약속받아야 된다라는 것이 기본적인 우리 국민의힘 위원들의 생각입니다.  이것이 안 될 경우에는 지금 우리 정부 차원에서 추진하고 있는 통일부를 비롯한 일부에서 진행하고 있는 북한에 대한 인도적 지원과 관련된 부분들이 예산에 반영되고 하는 과정들이 있습니다. 이런 부분들을 일체 할 수 없다라고 하는 부분들이 한 부분이고요. 북한이 도발을 먼저 했고 우리 MDL 이남에 지금 지뢰가 매설되어 있는 이 상황들을 복구하기 위한 군사적 조치를 우리가 단호하게 해야 됩니다. 그런 부분들을 포함시켜 달라고 이야기를 하는 겁니다.  예를 들어서 대북 확성기 방송은 다 철수해 가지고 할 수 없다라고 하는데 그건 그렇지 않거든요. 정부가 바뀔 때마다 확성기는 여러 번 철수가 됐다가 다시 설치도 하고 했습니다. 정말 북한이 도발한 것을 우리 정부가 인정을 하고 북한에 대한 제대로 된 사과를 받아 내고 그들의 행동이 변화를 가져오게 하기 위해서는 우리 정부 차원에서 단호한 입장을 보여야만 북한의 행동의 변화를 끌어낼 수 있다고 생각합니다. 그런 내용들이 포함되지 않는다면 우리가 그 결의문에 동의할 수 없다라는 이야기를 분명히 말씀드립니다.  이상입니다.

items.pv: Only roads that vehicles can use — they don't go into unverified minefields. But a battalion commander runs into an unverified minefield, it has snowed, the minefield can't be identified, and he says, I'll go first, step only where I step. That in itself is nonsense, which is why I am checking. What does that even mean?…

The accident happened while they were clearing a path to confirm, with evidence in hand, that mines were being laid beyond the Military Demarcation Line. Then they must have prepared for that operation for a long time. The ones who went in… surely it wasn't only the 18? Many more troops, along the routes or our detected…

Minister, first I'd like to ask about the resin anti-personnel mine confirmed today. Representative Chun Ha-ram asked about this earlier, but this was buried, not swept in by water, correct? It was in the ground, wasn't it? And judging from a text the Joint Chiefs of Staff sent a moment ago, the wounded soldiers… a wooden-box mine…

A swift and thorough investigation into the mine incident… the call to move swiftly came on the 29th. What were you doing in the meantime? The president said nothing either. And now you say it is because the area falls under UN Command jurisdiction. Then why say anything now? Why speak at all? The UN…

Minister, based on the scientific verification so far, the military considers a North Korean mine the most likely explanation, correct? So there is no reason for you to rule out North Korea or to tiptoe around it, is there, Minister? I don't think the Lee Jae-myung government, and the military in particular, has any reason to tiptoe around it. Right now the incident…

speakers.note: Members are ranked by the number of questions they asked on this issue, according to the records of the National Defense, Foreign Affairs and Unification, and Intelligence committees and of plenary sessions. Procedural remarks by committee chairs and answers from government officials are excluded, a short exchange between government answers counts as one question, and opening greetings are omitted. For each member, 30 percent of their questions (rounded down; at most three, at least one) are excerpted, chosen by how often the issue's keywords appear and no more than one per meeting; the rest are listed by date with a link to the original record. Excerpts are translated from Korean.

strategies.title: The Taiwan Strait: What should South Korea prepare for, and what should it promise, in a Taiwan contingency?
strategies.recipient: Government of the Republic of Korea
facts: In the Justice Mission-2025 exercises on December 29–30, 2025, the People's Liberation Army deployed 130 aircraft on the first day (90 of them crossing the median line), along with 27 naval vessels and 29 coast guard ships. It fired 27 rockets into Taiwan's contiguous zone, and the declared exercise zones disrupted 941 civilian flights. The drills came days after Washington approved $11.1 billion in arms sales to Taiwan on December 18.

On May 8, 2026, Taiwan's Legislative Yuan, where the Kuomintang (KMT) and the Taiwan People's Party hold a majority, passed the government's request for a NT$1.25 trillion special defense budget only after cutting it to NT$780 billion. The cuts eliminated funding for some 200,000 domestically produced drones, the T-Dome air defense network, and serial production of Strong Bow (Chiang Kung) interceptor missiles. Local elections are scheduled for November 28, and the presidential election for January 2028.

In the Han Kuang exercises in August, Taiwan for the first time rehearsed evacuating the president in the event of a decapitation strike and practiced responding to a blockade. The same month, China's Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration, citing a typhoon, demanded that ships in international waters of the Taiwan Strait comply with its navigation controls. Taiwan refused.

After Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told the Diet on November 7, 2025, that a Taiwan contingency could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, China advised its citizens to avoid travel to Japan (Chinese visits to Japan fell 60 percent in January), halted seafood imports, imposed export controls on dual-use items and rare earths in January 2026, and sanctioned Japanese politicians in March. The dispute is not yet over.

In January 2026, the United States concluded a trade agreement with Taiwan ($250 billion in Taiwanese semiconductor and technology investment; tariffs cut from 20 percent to 15 percent), and in July it deployed Navy and Marine Corps systems to the Luzon Strait and Japan's southern islands. At the White House summit on September 24, when Xi Jinping asked Washington to oppose Taiwanese independence, Trump said that Xi understood his position.

Since 2023, more than half of China's full generals have been purged. As of August 2026, only six active-duty full generals were appearing in public, and 21 theater command posts stood vacant. On September 21, Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were expelled from the Party and the military.

Ahead of President Lee Jae-myung's state visit to China in January 2026, Beijing pressed Seoul to make its position on Taiwan clear. Seoul kept the language of the 1992 joint communiqué establishing diplomatic relations, in which it "respects the position of the Chinese side." Washington's 2026 National Defense Strategy names China as the top challenge and expects South Korea to play a larger regional role; Seoul remains cautious about U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) being sent to a Taiwan contingency (so-called strategic flexibility). About 5,000 South Koreans live in Taiwan (2021).

On September 28, David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, said that no date had been set, even after the summit, for approving a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan that has been on hold since May. Washington has made no public concessions on Taiwan, but it is holding back the arms sale.

law.title: What South Korea has already promised
points: In the 1992 joint communiqué establishing diplomatic relations with China, South Korea recognized the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China and stated that it "respects the position of the Chinese side that there is but one China." Seoul respected the one-China position; it did not recognize it.

Article III of the 1953 Mutual Defense Treaty between the Republic of Korea and the United States treats an armed attack in the Pacific area on territory under the administrative control of either party as a common danger. Taiwan is not South Korean territory, so there is no automatic obligation to intervene. The picture changes, however, if USFK bases on South Korean soil come under attack, because Article III could then apply.

In the January 2006 agreement on strategic flexibility, South Korea "respects" the necessity for strategic flexibility of U.S. forces in Korea, and the United States "respects" South Korea's position that it shall not be involved in a regional conflict in Northeast Asia against the will of the Korean people.
law.result: Through these two "respects," South Korea has preserved its ambiguity as a matter of law. The trouble is that in a crisis this ambiguity can no longer hold, and Seoul will be forced to choose in an instant. Option A1 below, designing conditional rear-area support in advance, would turn the two "respects" of the 2006 agreement into concrete procedures before a crisis comes.

client.name: Government of the Republic of Korea
client.note: The goals and their order are the same as in the Korean Peninsula issue. In the Taiwan Strait, national security (G1) involves a gap in deterrence on the Korean Peninsula and the targeting of USFK bases; the economy and national creditworthiness (G3) involve shipping, supply chains, and trade with China; and protection of citizens (G5) involves the safety of South Koreans in Taiwan and of seafarers transiting the strait.

goals.t: A seat at the table and diplomatic autonomy

goals.src: Constitution, Article 66(2); address to the UN General Assembly, September 2026 (pledging to help restart U.S.-North Korean talks)

goals.d: Protect markets, supply chains, energy, and national creditworthiness

people.how: A gap in deterrence on the Korean Peninsula, the targeting of USFK bases, shipping, supply chains, and trade with China
Life and safety, freedom, energy and food
Evacuation in a blockade or armed clash

people.how: Inspections, detention, suspension of sailings
Becoming a battlefield
Mobilization, sanctions, economic shock

alts.name: Maintain strategic ambiguity (staying the course)
alts.desc: Make no public commitments and decide case by case when a crisis comes.

eff.safety: No change in peacetime, but a high risk of improvised decisions in a crisis.
eff.living: No change in peacetime.

alts.loser: South Koreans, forced to decide unprepared in a crisis
alts.esc: Low in peacetime, high in a crisis

G1.t: No preparation for a deterrence gap in a crisis

G2.t: Autonomy preserved, but improvisation in a crisis

G5.t: Plans for nationals and seafarers unclear

alts.name: Designing conditional rear-area support in advance
alts.desc: In peacetime, set up procedures under which South Korea accepts the dispatch of USFK to a Taiwan contingency only on two conditions: prior consultation between Seoul and Washington, and measures to fill any resulting gap in deterrence on the Korean Peninsula. South Korea's own role is capped at rear-area logistics, evacuation of noncombatants, and maritime patrols in the Yellow Sea.

eff.safety: Prevents a gap in deterrence on the Korean Peninsula during a crisis.
eff.living: Slightly raises the risk of Chinese economic pressure.
eff.bond: Creates procedures for evacuating South Koreans abroad.

alts.loser: South Korean companies that do business with China (risk of pressure)

G1.t: Makes filling the deterrence gap a condition

G2.t: A position to set conditions within the alliance

alts.name: An explicit commitment to contribute to the alliance
alts.desc: Formalize the possibility that South Korean forces would take part in operations in a Taiwan contingency, and accept the dispatch of USFK to Taiwan without conditions.

eff.safety: Opens a gap in deterrence on the Korean Peninsula and puts USFK bases on China's target list.
eff.living: Invites economic retaliation beyond what Japan suffered after Prime Minister Takaichi's answer in the Diet.

alts.loser: South Korean companies and workers hit by economic retaliation; residents near bases that become targets

G1.t: Deterrence gap, North Korean opportunism, bases become targets

G2.t: Gains the alliance's trust but loses autonomy toward China

alts.name: A public declaration of neutrality
alts.desc: Formally declare that South Korea will not permit USFK to be sent to Taiwan and will not intervene itself.

eff.safety: Shakes the alliance and weakens deterrence on the Korean Peninsula.
eff.living: Improves relations with China.
eff.freedom: For the people of Taiwan, it sets a precedent that Chinese coercion works.

alts.loser: South Koreans, who bear the risk of a weaker alliance; people in Taiwan, who inherit a precedent of successful coercion

G1.t: Rifts in the alliance weaken deterrence

ev.feas: Low (a South Korean declaration alone can hardly stop how USFK is used)

alts.name: Economic and civilian preparedness
alts.desc: Build up stockpiles of energy, food, and critical minerals; prepare shipping contracts for routes that skirt east of Taiwan and diversify semiconductor supply chains; and draw up plans to evacuate and protect South Koreans in Taiwan and seafarers transiting the strait.

eff.safety: Reduces the risk to South Koreans in Taiwan and to seafarers.
eff.living: Absorbs the shock of a blockade or inspections.

alts.loser: Public finances, which bear the cost of stockpiling

alts.name: A crisis communication channel with China
alts.desc: Set up a South Korea-China defense hotline and procedures to prevent incidents at sea, reducing the risk of miscalculation.

eff.safety: Reduces the risk of accidental clashes.
eff.living: Almost no change.

alts.loser: Hardly anyone

G2.t: A channel to talk to China

responses.note: These responses assume not a loud protest but the most capable adversary's response: one that neutralizes the signals Seoul sends and leaves South Korea with nothing but costs.

rows.CHN: Just before a crisis, uses economic pressure aimed at South Korea alone to extract a declaration of neutrality.
rows.USA: Demands an immediate decision from Seoul in a crisis.
rows.JPN: Sees South Korea as an unreliable partner and concentrates on U.S.-Japan ties rather than trilateral cooperation with Seoul.

rows.CHN: Denounces the move as preparation to intervene over Taiwan, but holds back the kind of large-scale retaliation it imposed on Japan, since pulling South Korea toward neutrality pays better. Just before a crisis, it presses Seoul to narrow the scope of the rear-area support it has promised.
rows.USA: Complains that Seoul has attached too many conditions, but accepts the arrangement as better than ambiguity without procedures.
rows.TWN: Welcomes it but judges that South Korea's steps will have little effect.
rows.JPN: Welcomes it and wants to expand it into trilateral rear-area coordination among the United States, Japan, and South Korea.
rows.PRK: Finds opportunism harder because of the condition that any gap in deterrence on the Korean Peninsula be filled.

rows.CHN: Retaliates more harshly than it did against Japan (rare earths, tourism, sanctions on South Korean companies) and openly declares USFK bases to be targets.
rows.USA: Welcomes it.
rows.JPN: Welcomes it.
rows.PRK: Aligns with China and Russia and steps up provocations.

rows.CHN: Welcomes it and asks for more (withdrawal of THAAD, scaled-back trilateral cooperation with Washington and Tokyo).
rows.USA: Reviews the alliance and uses the declaration to justify cutting USFK.
rows.TWN: Sees it as a precedent of coercion succeeding.
rows.JPN: Bypasses South Korea and cements U.S.-Japan ties.
rows.PRK: Sees the rift between Seoul and Washington as an opportunity.

rows.CHN: Does not react much.
rows.USA: Welcomes it.
rows.JPN: Proposes supply chain cooperation.

rows.CHN: Accepts the channel but also uses it to pressure South Korea in a crisis.
rows.USA: Distrusts it but tolerates it.
rows.JPN: Wary.

responses.lesson: A China that calculates with the greatest care would not retaliate against South Korea the way it did against Japan. In peacetime it would pull Seoul toward neutrality and save its retaliation for a single use just before a crisis. South Korea's risk is therefore concentrated not in peacetime but in the few days before a crisis. To avoid being forced into a decision during those days, Seoul needs to have the procedures for conditional rear-area support (A1) and economic and civilian preparedness (A4) in place in peacetime.

items.means: The People's Liberation Army; gray-zone tools of the coast guard and maritime authorities; economic retaliation; political connections inside Taiwan
items.frame: Taiwan is the unfinished business of the civil war, and unification is a condition of national rejuvenation. Force is a last resort, but it will not be renounced.
goals: Prevent Taiwanese independence and foreign military intervention
Create the conditions for unification before 2049
Pry the United States, Japan, and South Korea away from their commitments on Taiwan
items.strategy: Make pressure below the threshold of war routine (exercises, the coast guard, maritime jurisdiction) to extend de facto control; wait for Taiwan's 2028 presidential election; and press Washington for concessions on the Taiwan language in joint documents.
tactics: December 2025: Justice Mission-2025 exercises (27 rockets inside the contiguous zone, 941 civilian flights affected)
November 2025–March 2026: travel advisory against Japan, halt to seafood imports, rare-earth export controls, sanctions on politicians
August 2026: Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration demands navigation controls in the Taiwan Strait
September 24, 2026: asks Trump to oppose Taiwanese independence
red: A formal declaration of Taiwanese independence
A formal commitment by foreign forces to defend Taiwan
Taiwanese nuclear weapons
items.ext: Sees Washington's transactional bent and rifts among allies as opportunities, and Taiwan's 2028 presidential election as the biggest variable.
items.want: That Seoul hold to the position of the 1992 joint communiqué, keep USFK from being sent to Taiwan, and refrain from public statements on Taiwan
items.onrec: Denounces conditional rear-area support (A1) but holds back large-scale retaliation. Just before a crisis, it would try to extract a declaration of neutrality through pressure aimed at South Korea alone.
items.lever: Supplies of semiconductors and intermediate goods; the conditions South Korea attaches to its consent on how USFK is used; a South Korea-China crisis communication channel

T1: Believes time is on its side
T2: Extends de facto control without war
T4: With the military high command hollowed out, armed conflict would be a gamble
T5: U.S. concessions and a change of government in Taiwan

intent.read: Beijing talks of peaceful unification, but its actions make pressure below the threshold of war routine. Toward South Korea, it has so far stuck to words (demands that Seoul state its position).

watch.t: Actual inspections and detentions by the coast guard and maritime authorities (f24)
Taiwan-related economic measures aimed at South Korea (f27)

items.means: Naval and air forces, arms sales, the alliance network, tariffs and technology controls
items.frame: Taiwan is the linchpin of both the semiconductor supply chain and the first island chain. At the same time, the administration also treats Taiwan as one item in a U.S.-China deal.
goals: Deter a Chinese attempt to unify Taiwan by force
Secure the supply of semiconductors
Share the costs of a war with allies
items.strategy: Keep strategic ambiguity while deterring through arms sales and deployments along the first island chain; manage tensions through summit diplomacy; and leave the Taiwan language in U.S.-China joint documents open to bargaining.
tactics: December 18, 2025: approves $11.1 billion in arms sales
January 2026: trade agreement with Taiwan ($250 billion in semiconductor investment, 15 percent tariffs)
July 2026: deploys Navy and Marine Corps systems to the Luzon Strait and Japan's southern islands; the same month, 10 percent tariffs on Taiwan
September 24, 2026: responds to Xi's call to oppose independence by saying that Xi understood his position
red: A Chinese occupation by force
Loss of the semiconductor supply chain
items.ext: Treats Taiwan as one item in the overall U.S.-China relationship. Reads the purges in the Chinese military as a sign that near-term risk has fallen.

expect.note: Expected values are the 2030 values of each future multiplied by its probability and summed. Each dimension is calculated separately; dimensions are never added together. In this issue, South Korea's choices barely change the probabilities of the futures, so the values under the recommendations are the same as those on the current trajectory.
expect.read: The expected value for life and safety in Taiwan is 71.9, slightly below the 2026 level of 74.3, and it falls to 45.6 in the worst future (armed conflict). Freedom has an expected value of 91.3, but it would be cut sharply in the unlikely event of a blockade or armed conflict. For South Koreans, the expected value for life and safety is 73.9, and 63.9 in the worst future. South Korea's choices barely change these probabilities. What Seoul can do is reduce the price it pays in extreme situations, through economic and civilian preparedness (A4) and procedures for conditional rear-area support (A1).

futures.note: Probabilities and the inputs for each future are judgment estimates; the figures in parentheses are ranges. Because South Korea's choices are judged to make little difference to the future of the Taiwan Strait, no separate probabilities are given for the case in which the recommendations are followed. What South Korea's choices change is the price it pays in each future.

ranked.t: Combine three measures: procedures for conditional rear-area support kept confidential (A1); economic and civilian preparedness, including substitutes for and stockpiles of goods South Korea depends on China for, such as rare earths (A4); and a crisis communication channel with China institutionalized in peacetime (A5). The aim is not to change the probabilities of the Taiwan Strait's futures but to have procedures and preparations in place in peacetime so that Seoul is not forced into a decision on the eve of a crisis. South Korea's point of greatest exposure is not a public statement but the moment rear-area support is actually carried out.
Maintaining today's strategic ambiguity (A0) costs nothing in peacetime but forces improvised decisions in a crisis.
A public declaration of neutrality would improve relations with China, but it would shake the alliance, weaken deterrence on the Korean Peninsula, and still fail to stop USFK from being used.

An explicit commitment to contribute to the alliance ranks last. It would open a gap in deterrence on the Korean Peninsula, invite heavy economic retaliation, and be hard to reverse. The price Japan paid for a single answer by its prime minister in the Diet is the floor.

rank2.tension: Conditional rear-area support (A1) and crisis communication with China (A5) pull against each other. Beijing would read A1 as preparation to intervene over Taiwan and could use the A5 channel as a conduit for pressuring Seoul.
rank2.undecided: How far to accept the use of USFK beyond the peninsula is for South Koreans to decide. These procedures do not settle where, between the two "respects" of the 2006 agreement, the line should be drawn.

human.note: This section revisits the ranking from the strategy evaluation in terms of individual lives. It does not filter the ranking; it states where the assessment differs and by how much. The judgment belongs to readers and to the strategic actor.

items.client: Part of the top-ranked combination (stockpiles, shipping, supply chains, South Koreans abroad).

items.gain: The lives and safety of some 5,000 South Koreans in Taiwan and of seafarers. It prevents irreversible losses if a crisis comes.

items.clisa: Lower still. A public declaration of neutrality would set a precedent that Chinese coercion works, widening the path by which the freedom of people in Taiwan (a score of 93) becomes a bargaining chip.
items.cost: A chance to improve relations with China.

An explicit South Korean commitment would add little to the safety of people in Taiwan, while the price for South Koreans would be high.

conclusions.t: The most likely future through 2030 is continued tension without war (50 percent, range 40–60 percent). But since 2022, Chinese pressure has never returned to its earlier level after a crisis. This "status quo" is therefore one in which gray-zone pressure has become routine, and what South Korea must prepare for is a sudden spike in tension on top of it.
conclusions.why: In the 70 years since 1954, every Taiwan Strait crisis has ended as time-limited coercion, and none has escalated into war. Yet each crisis has left pressure one notch higher in its wake: in 2022 the Chinese military effectively erased the median line in the strait, in 2024 coast guard patrols around Kinmen became routine, and in August 2026 the maritime authorities announced navigation controls.
conclusions.flip: If it is confirmed that China's coast guard or maritime authorities have actually inspected or detained ships (f24 resolves yes), the probability of gray-zone escalation will be raised.

conclusions.t: South Korea's choices will do little to change the future of the Taiwan Strait. What they can change is the price South Korea pays in each future.
conclusions.why: The deciding powers are China, the United States, and Taiwan. South Korea's means of influencing the outcome amount to little more than the conditions on its consent to how USFK is used and its production capacity in semiconductors and other industries.
conclusions.flip: If a case is confirmed in which China's behavior (the intensity of its exercises, its demands on South Korea) changed markedly after Seoul stated a position, this assessment will be reviewed.

conclusions.t: Measured against the South Korean government's goals, the top priorities are to prepare, confidentially, procedures for rear-area support that attach conditions to sending USFK to Taiwan (A1), and economic and civilian preparedness that includes substitutes for and stockpiles of goods South Korea relies on China for, such as rare earths (A4). A crisis communication channel with China (A5) should be institutionalized in peacetime but kept as a supplementary tool that is not expected to work during a crisis.
conclusions.why: China's economic retaliation has come not in response to general statements but in response to visible military steps, such as the THAAD deployment in 2016–2017, or explicit public statements of military involvement in a contingency, such as Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi's answer in the Diet in 2025. After U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taiwan in 2022, the first thing China cut off was military communication channels with the United States. South Korea's moment of greatest exposure is not a public statement but the actual delivery of rear-area support.
conclusions.flip: If Washington rejects a framework of conditional rear-area support and applies pressure by threatening to cut USFK (X1 in the Korean Peninsula issue), the ranking will be reviewed.

conclusions.t: An explicit commitment to contribute to the alliance, formalizing South Korean military participation in a Taiwan contingency (A2), ranks last.
conclusions.why: It would open a gap in deterrence on the Korean Peninsula, invite heavy Chinese economic retaliation, and be hard to undo once made. The retaliation Japan absorbed after a single answer by Prime Minister Takaichi in the Diet in 2025 is the minimum price.
conclusions.flip: If China imposes formal economic retaliation on South Korea over Taiwan (f27 resolves yes), the assumption that Beijing will hold back retaliation against Seoul is wrong, and the assessments of maintaining strategic ambiguity (A0) and a public declaration of neutrality (A3) will be recalculated.

conclusions.t: Measured by individual lives, plans to evacuate and protect South Koreans in Taiwan and seafarers transiting the strait should be carried out first, and a public declaration of neutrality (A3) should rank lower still.
conclusions.why: If a crisis comes, the first irreversible losses fall on South Koreans abroad and on seafarers. A public declaration of neutrality would leave a precedent that Chinese coercion works on South Korea.
conclusions.flip: The weighting would change if the number of South Koreans in Taiwan fell sharply or shipping routes moved away from the waters around Taiwan.

conclusions.t: China's best move is a two-track strategy: avoid using force until Taiwan's presidential election in January 2028, extract concessions from the U.S. administration on joint-statement language and arms sales, and influence the election through Taiwan's opposition. The direction of the Taiwan Strait depends heavily on what deal the U.S. administration strikes with China, but the administration cannot decide that deal on its own.
conclusions.why: The Carter administration's break in relations with Taiwan in 1979 was largely offset by the Taiwan Relations Act, which Congress enacted, and the concession in the August 17, 1982, communiqué to reduce arms sales to Taiwan was cushioned by the Reagan administration itself through the Six Assurances it conveyed separately to Taipei. Because the power to initiate arms sales rests with the executive, however, Congress can slow an administration's concessions to China but can hardly reverse them. Chinese coercion ahead of Taiwan's 1996 and 2000 elections backfired, and Beijing afterward changed its approach, avoiding shows of force right before elections.
conclusions.flip: If China actually moves to blockade Taiwan before the 2028 election (f36 resolves no), the assumption that Beijing will wait until the election is wrong.

twoway.equilibrium: Taiwan's best move (deterrence) and China's best move (waiting and dealing) meet in a tense status quo that lasts until 2028. What follows depends on Taiwan's election and on the deal Washington chooses to make. Hence brokered stability (T5) is put at 20 percent, gray-zone escalation (T2) at 18 percent, and a blockade (T3) at 7 percent.
twoway.zopa: There is no room for a deal on sovereignty. But South Korea, Taiwan, and China all want one thing: no war before the 2028 election. That window is the time South Korea has to put in place procedures for conditional rear-area support (A1) and economic and civilian preparedness (A4).
traps: Taiwan through transactional ties with the United States (W2), and China through election-focused inducements and a deal with Washington (P4), are both trying to win the bargaining in Washington. The variable that will decide the fate of the Taiwan Strait is neither South Korea nor Taiwan but the deal the United States chooses to make.
China's waiting meshes with the Legislative Yuan's cuts to Taiwan's defense budget. The gap in deterrence becomes the reward for waiting.

In 1972, 1982, and 2026 alike, the United States put Taiwan language or arms sales on the table in its negotiations with China. In the past, the Taiwan Relations Act passed by Congress (1979) and the Six Assurances the executive gave Taiwan (1982) offset those concessions; in 2026, no such offsetting mechanism is visible within the executive branch.

ai.t: Semiconductors are Taiwan's shield and its target
ai.stake: For advanced AI chips, most leading-edge wafer fabrication (N3 and N2) and most advanced packaging, the final step, take place in Taiwan. TSMC's Arizona plant has been producing Blackwell wafers since October 2025, but they are shipped back to Taiwan for packaging. In the United States, Amkor's Arizona facility aims to begin advanced packaging in early 2028 and TSMC Arizona before 2029. About half of Taiwan's electricity comes from LNG, leaving it vulnerable to a blockade.
ai.moves: The concentration of chipmaking raises the cost that the United States and the world would bear from a war or blockade, and so strengthens Washington's reasons to intervene. But China has been formally cut off from Taiwan's advanced AI processes since the 2020 Huawei sanctions and TSMC's 2024 halt to producing advanced AI chips for Chinese customers (though there are cases of circumvention), so a cutoff in the supply of advanced AI chips would hurt American AI more than China's. If general-purpose chips are included, however, the damage to Chinese manufacturing would also be severe. A concentration of resources from which one side is already excluded may serve not as a deterrent but as a pressure point against the other side (Japan and the Dutch East Indies in 1941). The U.S. response, too, has taken the form not of stronger defense commitments but of talk of denial — making the facilities unusable in a contingency — and pressure to move production. This analysis therefore does not assume that semiconductors lower the probabilities of armed conflict (T4) or a blockade (T3), and it makes no adjustment to the probabilities for the AI factor. Until U.S. packaging comes online in 2028–2029, the shield will be thickest for the United States and the pressure point most valuable to China. In brokered stability (T5), semiconductors and export controls become bargaining chips in a U.S.-China deal.
ai.lever: With high-bandwidth memory (HBM), South Korea holds a different chokepoint in the same supply chain, but this is less a lever to wield against Washington than a defensive asset that raises the cost of coercion (see the AI variable in the Korean Peninsula issue). In a Taiwan contingency, South Korean chipmakers would become an alternative source of supply, and for the same reason a target of Chinese pressure.
