brief.q: What should South Korea prepare for a Taiwan Strait crisis, and how far should it commit?
brief.a: South Korea should prepare, confidentially, procedures for rear-area support under which it accepts the dispatch of USFK to Taiwan only on two conditions — prior consultation between Seoul and Washington, and measures to fill any resulting gap in deterrence on the Korean Peninsula — and put in place economic and civilian preparedness, including substitutes for and stockpiles of goods it relies on China for, such as rare earths. A crisis communication channel with China should be institutionalized in peacetime, without expecting it to work during a crisis. An explicit commitment to contribute to the alliance, formalizing South Korean military participation in a Taiwan contingency, ranks lowest.
brief.eq: Because Taiwan is concentrating on deterrence and China is biding its time, the two strategies meet in a tense status quo likely to last until Taiwan's presidential election in January 2028. What comes after depends on what deal the U.S. administration makes with China, how far Congress slows that deal, and how Taiwanese voters, who have pushed back against outside pressure in the past, choose.
brief.human: Armed conflict would gravely threaten the lives and safety of people in Taiwan. The first thing South Korea should carry out is its plan to evacuate and protect South Koreans in Taiwan and South Korean seafarers transiting the strait.

items.name: The first Taiwan Strait crisis and the U.S.-Republic of China Mutual Defense Treaty
items.format: Communist China shells Kinmen → the United States signs a mutual defense treaty in December 1954 (excluding Kinmen and Matsu) → in January 1955 Congress passes the Formosa Resolution, delegating discretion to the president → a confidential pledge to defend the offshore islands, linked to the evacuation of the Tachen Islands
items.outcome: Tensions eased in April 1955 when Zhou Enlai signaled a willingness to negotiate at the Bandung Conference.
items.why: By limiting the treaty to the main island and leaving the offshore islands ambiguous, Washington pursued deterrence and the avoidance of escalation at the same time.
items.differs: The United States then enjoyed nuclear superiority and a formal alliance; today there is no treaty, and China's naval and air power approaches that of the United States.

items.name: The second Taiwan Strait crisis (the shelling and blockade of Kinmen)
items.format: Communist China shells Kinmen to cut off resupply (in effect, a blockade of an offshore island) → the U.S. Seventh Fleet escorts resupply convoys → the shelling settles into an informal practice of firing on alternate days
items.outcome: U.S. support for resupply sharply reduced the shelling, and alternate-day exchanges of fire continued, almost as a ritual, until Washington and Beijing established diplomatic relations.
items.why: China used an offshore island rather than the main island as a means of pressure to test American resolve, and the United States responded with escorts rather than direct combat.
items.differs: This is the historical precedent for blockading an offshore island, and since 2024 coast guard "law enforcement" patrols in Kinmen's waters have reproduced the same pattern by nonmilitary means.

items.name: The Shanghai Communiqué
items.format: Nixon's summit with Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai → the United States states that it "acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain there is but one China" → a pledge to withdraw U.S. forces from Taiwan gradually
items.outcome: In exchange for the Taiwan language and the troop withdrawal, Washington gained a strategic alignment against the Soviet Union, laying the groundwork for the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1979.
items.why: For the United States, balancing the Soviet Union was a higher interest than Taiwan, and the ambiguous verb "acknowledges" let it avoid a judgment on sovereignty.
items.differs: The motive for the deal then was a third adversary (the Soviet Union); today China itself is Washington's principal adversary, so the strategic return on concessions in wording is small.

items.name: U.S.-China normalization and the Taiwan Relations Act
items.format: The Carter administration recognizes the People's Republic of China and gives notice that it is unilaterally terminating the mutual defense treaty → in April 1979 Congress enacts the Taiwan Relations Act (provision of defensive arms; non-peaceful means to be considered "of grave concern"; no automatic obligation to intervene) → the treaty lapses in January 1980
items.outcome: Congress partly offset the executive's concessions through legislation, and arms sales became institutionalized.
items.why: A dual structure worked, in which the executive spoke for relations with China and Congress for Taiwan's security.
items.differs: The same dual structure is at work in 2026 (Republican senators have criticized delays in arms sales), but there is no confirmed case of Congress forcing the administration to release a sale it has put on hold.

items.name: The August 17 communiqué and the Six Assurances
items.format: The Reagan administration first conveys the Six Assurances to Taiwan (no date set for ending arms sales, no consultation with China on arms sales, and others) → in the August 17 communiqué, Washington states that it "intends gradually to reduce its sale of arms to Taiwan" → an internal memo makes any reduction conditional on China's peaceful policy
items.outcome: Despite the concession in wording, arms sales continued, and the Six Assurances were later written into a 2016 House resolution and the TAIPEI Act of 2020.
items.why: Washington used a double device: it conceded wording while preserving the substance through a conditional interpretation and the assurances it gave Taiwan (the Six Assurances).
items.differs: In 2026, Trump discussed arms sales with Xi Jinping and put a $14 billion package on hold, calling it a "very good negotiating chip" — a departure from the spirit of the second of the Six Assurances (no consultation with China on arms sales).

items.name: The 1992 Consensus framework and the 2015 Ma Ying-jeou–Xi Jinping meeting
items.format: Talks in Hong Kong between ARATS and the SEF (1992) → Su Chi coins the term in 2000 → exchanges and economic agreements under KMT governments, 2008–2016 → leaders' meeting in Singapore in November 2015, at which the two addressed each other as "Mister"
items.outcome: Two months after the meeting, Tsai Ing-wen won the January 2016 election by a wide margin, and Beijing suspended official communication on the grounds that the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) government did not accept the consensus.
items.why: Ahead of the election, China chose inducements and symbolism over coercion, but it could not change Taiwanese voters' choice.
items.differs: Since Xi linked the consensus to "one country, two systems" in 2019, even the KMT has kept its distance; with KMT chair Cheng Li-wun's visit to China in April 2026, the party-to-party channel is being used again.

items.name: The third Taiwan Strait crisis and Zhu Rongji's warning in 2000
items.format: Lee Teng-hui visits Cornell (June 1995) → missile tests near Taiwan in July 1995 and March 1996 → the United States deploys the Independence and Nimitz carrier groups → Taiwan's first direct presidential election on March 23, 1996
items.outcome: Lee Teng-hui won with a majority, and Chen Shui-bian won in 2000 despite Zhu Rongji's threats; coercion before the elections backfired both times.
items.why: Taiwanese voters answered external threats with a backlash vote, and the United States demonstrated its command of the strait with its carrier deployments.
items.differs: China has since learned to avoid large shows of force right before elections and to hold them after inaugurations instead (Joint Sword-2024A came three days after the 2024 inauguration), and sending U.S. carriers near the strait is now far more dangerous.

items.name: The Anti-Secession Law
items.format: Enacted by the National People's Congress; Article 8 sets out three conditions for using "non-peaceful means" (the fact of secession, major incidents entailing secession, and the complete exhaustion of possibilities for peaceful reunification)
items.outcome: Both Taiwan's ruling party and its opposition objected, and the U.S. secretary of state said the law was "not helpful", but no substantive penalties followed; the law has since remained a legal basis for justifying the use of force.
items.why: Beijing sought to fix its red line in domestic law in response to the pro-independence leanings of the Chen Shui-bian government.
items.differs: The third condition can still be stretched without limit depending on interpretation, and China uses the law to calibrate its justification for external pressure.

items.name: Pelosi's visit and the 2022 exercises encircling Taiwan
items.format: Visit by the speaker of the U.S. House → live fire in seven zones, 11 ballistic missiles (some passing over Taiwan) → eight countermeasures against the United States (suspension of military talks and climate cooperation) → after the drills end, announcement that patrols will become regular
items.outcome: The United States showed restraint, postponing a Minuteman III test launch among other steps, while China left behind a new baseline that effectively erased the median line in the strait.
items.why: Using a senior American visit as its pretext, China both rehearsed a blockade and made its presence routine, while the United States, unlike in 1996, put avoiding escalation first.
items.differs: It confirmed that the first thing China cuts in a crisis is military and diplomatic communication channels.

items.name: The Joint Sword, Strait Thunder, and Justice Mission series of exercises
items.format: Named exercises at each trigger, including Tsai Ing-wen's meeting with Kevin McCarthy, Lai Ching-te's inauguration and speeches, and U.S. arms sales → Strait Thunder-2025A in April 2025 → Justice Mission-2025 on December 29–30, 2025 (simulated blockade of the ports of Keelung and Kaohsiung, 27 rockets)
items.outcome: Eight large-scale exercises have followed since 2022 without turning into an actual blockade, and Trump played down Justice Mission-2025.
items.why: Through short exercises tied to specific triggers, China has repeatedly drilled its blockade capability while avoiding the cost of a head-on clash with the United States.
items.differs: No named large-scale exercise had been confirmed as of August 2026; instead, gray-zone moves asserting jurisdiction, such as maritime authorities' announcements of navigation controls, have increased.

items.name: Trump-Xi summit diplomacy (Busan, Beijing, Washington)
items.format: Busan meeting (trade truce) → Trump's visit to China in May 2026 (Xi: "the Taiwan question is the most important issue in China-US relations"; Trump: "I'm not looking to have somebody go independent") → the $14 billion Taiwan arms package put on hold, with Trump calling it a "very good negotiating chip" → Xi's state visit to the United States on September 24, 2026, with the trade truce extended to January 10, 2027
items.outcome: No formal agreement on Taiwan was issued, but arms sales became an item on the agenda of negotiations with China, and as late as September 23, Rubio said only that the sales remained under review.
items.why: China is using trade and purchases as leverage to win substantive gains on Taiwan language and arms sales, and the Trump administration treats these as items to be traded.
items.differs: Unlike in 1972 and 1982, the executive has produced no safeguard for Taiwan to match its concessions; only pushback from Congress is in evidence.

items.name: South Korea's position on Taiwan and China's response
items.format: 1992 joint communiqué establishing relations (recognizing the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government and respecting its one-China position) → May 2021 Moon Jae-in–Biden statement mentions the Taiwan Strait for the first time → April 2023 Yoon Suk Yeol calls the Taiwan issue, like North Korea, a global issue → January 2026 Lee Jae-myung reaffirms respect for one China before visiting Beijing → June 2026 a director-general at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs reaffirms the language of the communiqué
items.outcome: China responded to the 2021 and 2023 remarks with verbal protests only, warning against "playing with fire" and calling the remarks "unacceptable"; no economic retaliation has been confirmed. Beijing publicly welcomed the reaffirmation in June 2026.
items.why: China manages South Korea's references to general principles with words and steers Seoul's position by publicly rewarding retreats in wording.
items.differs: South Korea avoided taking sides in the China-Japan dispute and agreed at the January 2026 summit to expand defense communication, so part of the foundation for a crisis communication channel already exists.

items.name: China's economic retaliation over the THAAD deployment
items.format: Seoul and Washington decide to deploy THAAD and carry it out → China bans group tours, sanctions Lotte's operations, and boycotts South Korean cars and consumer goods → partial lifting after an agreement to restore relations in November 2017
items.outcome: Total losses were estimated at more than $10 billion, including 3.7 million fewer tourists (about $7.7 billion) and a 17–28 percent drop in Hyundai's sales.
items.why: China treated the deployment of physical military assets, rather than words, as an infringement of its security and used informal, deniable sanctions.
items.differs: In a Taiwan contingency, using USFK assets beyond the peninsula or actually providing rear-area support would fall into the same category of physical acts as THAAD and could invite similar retaliation.

items.name: Takaichi's "survival-threatening situation" remark and China's retaliation against Japan
items.format: Prime Minister Takaichi tells the Diet that an armed attack on Taiwan could constitute a survival-threatening situation → China issues a travel advisory (November 14), halts seafood imports (November 19), and cancels cultural events → ban on dual-use exports (January 6, 2026), rare-earth restrictions (January 8), export ban on 20 defense companies (February 24)
items.outcome: Takaichi did not retract her remark, and the retaliation has expanded step by step for more than 10 months; it remained unresolved as of September 2026 (with provisional antidumping duties on dichlorosilane added in September).
items.why: China treated a third country's head of government publicly spelling out the conditions for military involvement in a Taiwan contingency as crossing a red line, and made Japan pay as an example.
items.differs: With its legal framework for collective self-defense and its proximity to Taiwan, Japan's explicit commitment carries more weight than South Korea's would, but South Korea, which relies on China for about half of its rare earths, is exposed to the same tools.

checks.reason: For 70 years, every crisis in the strait has ended as time-limited coercion, with no case of escalation to war, so the broad direction — no war — is consistent with precedent. Since 2022, however, each crisis has shown a ratchet effect, leaving a new baseline that is never rolled back: the erasure of the median line (2022), routine coast guard patrols around Kinmen (2024), and the announcement of navigation controls by maritime authorities (August 2026). The "tense status quo" of 2030 is therefore likely to have already absorbed what would count today as "intensified gray-zone pressure," blurring the line that separates the tense status quo (T1) and gray-zone escalation (T2) as distinct probabilities.

Since 1992, no South Korean statement or action has changed the military or political outcome in the strait; Yoon Suk Yeol's 2023 remark and the 2026 reaffirmation of wording moved only the bilateral costs between Seoul and Beijing, independent of conditions in the strait. Takaichi's remark likewise failed to change the outcome in the strait and only raised Japan's costs. The precedents support the judgment that a third country's choices change not the outcome in the strait but how its own costs are distributed.

Historically, China has answered statements of principle (2021, 2023) with words, but has answered physical military acts (THAAD) and public statements of the conditions for involvement in a contingency (Takaichi) with economic retaliation lasting months to more than a year. Conditional rear-area support (A1) therefore works only if it is designed but kept confidential. And because China cut military communication channels with the United States immediately after the 2022 crisis broke out, it is hard to assume that a crisis communication channel (A5) would work during a crisis. Judging by the precedent of rare-earth and dual-use export controls against Japan, economic and civilian preparedness (A4) must include supply chain substitution as a core element.

The Takaichi case shows that a third country that publicly committed to involvement in a Taiwan contingency suffered economic retaliation that escalated step by step for more than 10 months, and that the United States did not visibly compensate it. At the same time, the U.S. executive, following 1972 and 1982, again put Taiwan language and arms sales on the agenda of negotiations with China in 2026, so if South Korea made an explicit commitment and Washington then struck a deal with Beijing, South Korea would run a high risk of being stranded with nothing but its commitment. Both precedents are consistent with ranking an explicit commitment to contribute to the alliance (A2) last.

After coercion before the 1996 and 2000 elections backfired, China avoided large shows of force right before elections and turned instead to inducements (the 2015 meeting) and post-inauguration exercises (2024); this precedent supports the judgment that Beijing will wait until the January 2028 election. But in 1972, 1979, and 1982 alike, the executive's concessions in wording were offset by Congress (the Taiwan Relations Act) and by the Six Assurances the United States gave Taiwan, so the executive did not decide America's dealings with China on its own, and Taiwanese voters have been an independent variable, moving against China's intentions. Nor is China waiting passively: it is pursuing the U.S. track and the Taiwanese opposition track in parallel, as when Xi met the KMT chair shortly before Trump's visit to China (April 2026).

China has never actually blockaded Taiwan's main island in 70 years. Given the lesson that coercion before elections backfires and the current opening for dealing with Washington, the judgment that a blockade of the main island lasting seven days or more is unlikely before January 2028 is consistent with precedent. But the 1958 shelling and blockade of Kinmen and the coast guard patrols around Kinmen since 2024 show that blockades and quarantines of offshore islands are a real historical pattern, so the forecast about a blockade of the main island needs to make clear whether its scope includes the offshore islands.

precedents.insight: The only precedent of South Korea suffering Chinese economic retaliation (THAAD) stemmed not from a statement but from a decision about physical military assets. South Korea's point of greatest exposure in a Taiwan contingency is therefore not a public statement but the moment USFK assets are actually used and rear-area support is actually delivered. A further new variable: in 1972, 1982, and 2026 alike, the United States put Taiwan language or arms sales on the table in its negotiations with China, and while Congress and the assurances the executive gave Taiwan offset those concessions in the past, no such offsetting mechanism is visible within the executive branch in 2026.
uncertain: The Taiwan language in the White House's official readout of the September 24, 2026, summit in Washington (only Chinese state media reports confirmed)
Whether and when the $14 billion Taiwan arms package will receive final approval
Whether the PLA has held any named large-scale exercise encircling Taiwan since August 2026
The original wording and exact date of President Lee Jae-myung's "xie xie" (thank you) remark (reportedly made during the 2024 election campaign)
The direct trigger for the June 2026 reaffirmation of the communiqué language by a South Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs director-general
The actual trend in the value of arms sales to Taiwan after the August 17, 1982, communiqué

links.work: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence, chapter 2, "The Art of Commitment," 1966
links.idea: Salami tactics exploit the fact that each slice is too small to justify a major response. If the defender fails to draw a clear line, the slices pile up into a fait accompli.
links.fit: This has the same structure as the judgment that every crisis since 2022 has left behind a new baseline that is never rolled back. And since spikes occur when a slice touches a line someone has committed to, it supports the judgment that what South Korea should prepare for is short spikes on top of constant pressure.
links.limit: Baselines have not been permanent. After the 1958 shelling of Kinmen, China made alternate-day shelling (on odd-numbered days) a routine, but that baseline ended with the establishment of U.S.-China diplomatic relations on January 1, 1979. Accumulated baselines, in other words, have been rolled back by deals between great powers, a path that overlaps with brokered stability (T5). Schelling's model also assumes a defender who draws lines, whereas American strategic ambiguity blurs the line itself, making salami slicing easier.
sources: Schelling, Arms and Influence (Yale University Press, 1966; reissued 2008), ch. 2

links.work: Graham Allison, Destined for War, 2017, and the Belfer Center's "Thucydides's Trap Case File"; critique: Steve Chan, Thucydides's Trap? Historical Interpretation, Logic of Inquiry, and the Future of Sino-American Relations, 2020
links.idea: Allison argues that in 12 of 16 cases over the past 500 years in which a rising power challenged a ruling one, the result was war. Chan criticizes the arbitrariness of the case selection, the classification of the Anglo-American power transition as a peaceful case, and the reliance on a single cause.
links.fit: The base rate of 12 out of 16 (75 percent) covers entire power transitions spanning decades, so it does not directly contradict estimates of 5 percent for armed conflict and 7 percent for a blockade over the roughly four years to 2030. But the base rate suggests that continued tension may be not a stable state in the long run but a transitional phase, so it adds a caveat: the 50 percent for the tense status quo (T1) should not be extended beyond 2030.
links.limit: The number of cases is small and the selection criteria are contested, which makes the base rate itself shaky. Transitions under nuclear deterrence, such as U.S.-Soviet relations in the Cold War, ended without war, and U.S.-China relations are also conducted under nuclear deterrence. Moreover, the Taiwan question is more a territorial and sovereignty dispute than a hegemonic transition, so Allison's framework may misidentify the causal structure.
sources: Andrew Scobell, book review, Political Science Quarterly 137(2), 2022, pp. 405–406

links.work: Dale C. Copeland, 『Economic Interdependence and War』, Princeton University Press, 2015
links.idea: Interdependence promotes peace when leaders expect future trade to continue, but becomes a motive for using force when they expect trade to be cut off (trade expectations theory).
links.fit: This specifies the conditions under which continued tension without war can last. China's rare-earth export controls in April and October 2025 and U.S. semiconductor controls lowered trade expectations, and the late-October 2025 U.S.-China summit agreement, which suspended the controls for a year, partly restored them. Whether that suspension collapses or is extended could be a leading indicator of a shift from the tense status quo (T1) to gray-zone escalation (T2) or a blockade (T3).
links.limit: Copeland's cases concern mainly trade dependence among great powers, and because China's decisions on Taiwan put sovereignty and regime legitimacy first, economic expectations may have limited explanatory power. Cases in which a trade cutoff hastened a decision for war, such as Japan in 1941, coexist with cases in which war did not occur despite almost no trade, such as the United States and the Soviet Union during the Cold War.

links.work: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, chapters 84–116 (the Melian Dialogue), late fifth century BC
links.idea: Athens tells Melos that justice matters only between equals in power, and that the strong do what they can while the weak suffer what they must. Melos, insisting on neutrality, fell, and its adult men were executed.
links.fit: This has the same structure as the judgment that a small state's choices do not change the outcome among great powers, only the price it pays. Melos's choice (clinging to neutrality) was irrelevant to the course of the war but decided the fate of its people.
links.limit: South Korea is not an island polis like Melos but a middle power that hosts U.S. forces, and so a variable in the great powers' calculations. And by placing the disastrous Athenian expedition to Sicily right after the Melian Dialogue, Thucydides can also be read as criticizing the logic of the strong as self-destructive.
sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, 5.84-116 (Perseus Digital Library: https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Thuc.+5.84)

links.work: The Second Manchu Invasion (1636–1637) and Choe Myeong-gil's case for peace — Veritable Records of King Injo, years 14–15 of his reign; Choe Myeong-gil, Jicheon-jip
links.idea: Faced with the tide of the Ming-Qing transition, Joseon's choice between rejecting peace and seeking it could not change the fate of the Ming (which fell in 1644). But the choice to reject peace cost Joseon the surrender at Samjeondo, the crown prince taken hostage, and huge numbers of captives, and Choe Myeong-gil argued for peace to avoid those costs.
links.fit: As the closest precedent in Korean history to the judgment that South Korea's choices will do little to change the future of the Taiwan Strait and will change only the price South Korea pays (C2), it supports that judgment.
links.limit: Joseon was the direct target of a Qing attack, whereas South Korea would not be a direct party to a Taiwan contingency. Moreover, the fact that the Qing subdued Joseon before attacking the Ming shows that a stable rear was a precondition for the great power, which calls for a correction: South Korea's stance may influence China's calculations of timing, at least at the margins. The domestic legitimacy constraint that narrowed the choices — Injo's government had taken power in the name of loyalty to the Ming — also makes conditions different from today's.
sources: Veritable Records of King Injo, Annals of the Joseon Dynasty (National Institute of Korean History): https://sillok.history.go.kr
Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, entry on the Second Manchu Invasion (Byeongja Horan): https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr

links.work: Mark F. Cancian, Matthew Cancian, Eric Heginbotham, 『The First Battle of the Next War: Wargaming a Chinese Invasion of Taiwan』, CSIS, 2023
links.idea: In 24 wargames, one of the conditions that decided the outcome was the use of U.S. bases in Japan, and the report calls Japan "the linchpin." For South Korea, it assumes only a limited role because of the North Korean threat, with a baseline scenario in which only two of the four USFK fighter squadrons are committed to the Taiwan theater (pp. 58–60).
links.fit: Because the military outcome of an invasion scenario hinges more on the use of Japanese bases than on South Korea's choices, it supports the judgment that South Korea's choices will do little to change the future of the Taiwan Strait (C2).
links.limit: These are the assumptions of a single study, and it covers only invasion scenarios, so South Korea's role in shipping and energy routes under a blockade or quarantine (T3) or in the gray zone (T2) is not assessed. Moreover, the assumption of a limited South Korean role came from expert judgment about the South Korean government's reluctance, which also implies that South Korea's choices do change U.S. operational plans at the margins.

links.work: King Gwanghae's dispatch of troops to the Battle of Sarhu (1619) and his handling of Gang Hong-rip — Diaries of King Gwanghae, year 11 of his reign; Yi Min-hwan, Chaekjung illok
links.idea: Gwanghae sent about 13,000 troops at the Ming's demand while trying to avoid a rupture with the Later Jin, and after Gang Hong-rip surrendered, he used Gang as a conduit to keep negotiating with the Later Jin. This confidential, conditional stance was attacked at court as a betrayal of the Ming and became one of the justifications for the Injo Restoration of 1623.
links.fit: This is a precedent from Korean history with the same structure as A1 (confidential, conditional rear-area support). It shows that a confidential, conditional stance can reduce losses in the short run, but also that once exposed, it can be reversed through attacks on its domestic legitimacy and a change of government. It adds a condition: for A1 to rank first, its design must include a domestic consensus that can survive leaks and changes of government (for example, bipartisan briefings at the level of the National Assembly's Intelligence Committee).
links.limit: Whether a secret order to "watch how the situation develops and decide which way to turn" existed, and its wording, are disputed in the sources, and other causes, such as the deposition of the queen dowager and the killing of the king's younger brother, also lay behind the Injo Restoration. The interpretation that the pro-Ming line after the restoration brought on the Manchu invasions of 1627 and 1636 also oversimplifies the causation.

links.work: Eugene Gholz, 『Rare Earth Elements and National Security』, Council on Foreign Relations Energy Report, 2014
links.idea: After the 2010 collision between a Chinese fishing boat and Japanese coast guard vessels, China's restrictions on rare-earth exports to Japan failed to impose heavy costs on supply chains because of rising production outside China, defections by Chinese exporters, and market adjustment. The author predicted that China's market dominance would decline.
links.fit: This qualifies the case for economic and civilian preparedness (A4). Judging by the 2010 case alone, the urgency of substitution and stockpiling may have been overstated. But within weeks of the controls announced on April 4, 2025, automakers in the United States, Europe, and Japan reported production disruptions, and a CSIS assessment in April 2026 also found continuing shortages, including rationing of yttrium. Because concentration at the refining and magnet stages, rather than in raw ore, has deepened since 2010, A4 should target refined and processed goods rather than stockpiles of ore.
links.limit: Gholz's optimistic forecast (increased output by Molycorp and Lynas) was partly undone by later events, such as Molycorp's bankruptcy in 2015. The scope of the controls (including a foreign direct product rule and technology embargoes) and China's administrative enforcement capacity differ between 2010 and 2025.

links.work: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama (The Book of Government), chapter 21, on ambassadors and their treatment, c. 1091 (English translation by Hubert Darke, 1960)
links.idea: Even when there is discord and enmity between kings, envoys have always come and gone, carried out their missions, and not been mistreated. At the same time, the purpose of sending envoys lies not only in the letters they openly carry but in quietly learning about roads, mountain passes, rivers, and provisions, the size and equipment of armies, and the character of the ruler.
links.fit: This broadly supports the judgment that a crisis communication channel (A5) should be institutionalized in peacetime without assuming it will work during a crisis. From the Seljuk vizier's point of view, the peacetime value of an envoy channel lies less in negotiation than in sizing up the other side. A South Korea-China channel would thus be both a tool for Seoul to understand Beijing and a tool for Beijing to probe Seoul's resolve and detect whether A1 exists, which adds a condition: what is not put through the channel must be managed.
links.limit: Unlike the medieval norm that envoys are inviolable, modern China has used refusing calls in a crisis as a means of pressure. It did not answer Clinton's attempts to call after the 1999 bombing of the embassy in Belgrade, did not respond for more than 12 hours after the 2001 Hainan Island collision, and did not answer the defense hotline during the 2023 spy balloon incident. Analysts also point to a structure in which military channels cannot act without the Party's approval.
sources: Nizam al-Mulk, The Book of Government or Rules for Kings, tr. Hubert Darke (Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1960), ch.21, pp.97-

links.work: Glenn H. Snyder, 'The Security Dilemma in Alliance Politics', World Politics 36(4), 1984, pp.461-495
links.idea: Strengthening commitments within an alliance raises the risk of entrapment and reduces bargaining leverage over both the ally and the adversary. Weakening commitments raises the risk of abandonment.
links.fit: An explicit commitment to contribute to the alliance (A2) maximizes the risk of entrapment and exhausts bargaining leverage toward both Beijing and Washington at once, supporting the judgment that it ranks last.
links.limit: Snyder himself held that the alliance dilemma is strong in a multipolar system and weak in a bipolar one. And for South Korea the risk of abandonment is real, in the form of USFK reductions and pressure over defense cost sharing, so if Washington demanded an explicit commitment as the price of keeping the alliance, the cost of ranking A2 last would rise.

links.work: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 1, chapters 24–55 (the Corcyraean alliance and the Battle of Sybota)
links.idea: To avoid breaking the Thirty Years' Peace, Athens concluded only a defensive alliance (epimachia) with Corcyra rather than an offensive one (1.44), and sent a small squadron with orders to fight only in defense. But at the Battle of Sybota, Athenian ships ended up engaging the Corinthians, which became one of the immediate causes of the war (1.49–55).
links.fit: Since entrapment is hard to avoid when forces are on the scene, even if the scope of the commitment is narrowed, it supports ranking A2 last. At the same time, it is a warning that A1 (conditional rear-area support) could also follow a Corcyra-style path to entrapment once it is actually carried out.
links.limit: Athens was a great power directly involved, whereas South Korea is a third country. There was no nuclear deterrence then, and the party that set the limits of the defensive alliance was the stronger one.
sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, 1.24-55 (https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Thuc.+1.44)

links.work: Michael Beckley, 'The Myth of Entangling Alliances', International Security 39(4), 2015, pp.7-48; Tongfi Kim, 'Why Alliances Entangle But Seldom Entrap States', Security Studies 20(3), 2011
links.idea: Beckley finds only five cases among 188 militarized interstate disputes involving the United States from 1948 to 2010 that might count as alliance entanglement (the Taiwan Strait crises of 1954–55 and 1995–96, Vietnam, Bosnia, and Kosovo), and even those are ambiguous. Tongfi Kim argues that because states build loopholes into the wording and design of alliance treaties, entanglement is common but entrapment is rare.
links.fit: The finding that the fear of entanglement is exaggerated reduces the weight of the reasons for ranking an explicit commitment to contribute to the alliance (A2) last. But that two of the few cases Beckley found were Taiwan Strait crises shows that these waters are an exceptional zone of entanglement, and Kim's logic supports the design of A1, which leaves room to get out through conditions and ambiguity.
links.limit: Both studies take the perspective of the United States as patron. Junior allies like South Korea have precedents of using explicit commitments as bargaining chips: in the Brown Memorandum of 1966, Seoul obtained the modernization of its armed forces and economic aid in exchange for sending additional troops to Vietnam. An explicit commitment, in other words, is both a cost and a tradable asset, and the judgment ranking A2 last (C4) did not include that tradability among its criteria.

links.work: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, chapter 21, "Of the Liberty of Subjects," 1651
links.idea: The obligation of subjects to the sovereign lasts only as long as the sovereign has the power to protect them. The end of obedience is protection.
links.fit: This provides the normative grounds for the judgment that, at the level of individuals, plans to evacuate and protect nationals abroad should be carried out first. If the state's external choices cannot change the future of the strait (C2), the duty of protection the state can reliably fulfill comes first.
links.limit: Hobbes was writing about the domestic sovereign order, whereas modern noncombatant evacuations depend on the cooperation of third countries (Taiwan, Japan, the United States). Once a blockade or quarantine (T3) begins, air and sea routes may close and evacuation itself may become impossible, so plans need to be tied to advisories to leave before a crisis. The evacuations from Libya in 2011 and Sudan in 2023 took place under conditions that allowed overland routes or transit through third countries.
sources: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), ch.21 (Project Gutenberg: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/3207)

links.work: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, chapter 21, 1532 (written 1513)
links.idea: When two powers fight, a prince who stays neutral becomes the prey of the winner and earns no gratitude from the loser, so it is better to take one side clearly. Yet Machiavelli also advises never to join a stronger power in attacking a third party unless necessity compels it.
links.fit: This supports ranking a public declaration of neutrality (A3) lower still. At the same time, the caveat against joining the stronger in an attack also fits the judgment that ranks an explicit commitment to contribute to the alliance (A2) last, providing a classical basis for a middle course that avoids both public neutrality and a public pledge to fight.
links.limit: Machiavelli's argument reflects conditions in 16th-century Italy, where neighboring small states became battlefields directly. Switzerland and Sweden survived World War II through neutrality, while Belgium's neutrality was violated in 1914. South Korea would not be a direct belligerent in a Taiwan contingency and lives under nuclear deterrence.
sources: Niccolò Machiavelli, Il Principe, cap. XXI (English translation on Project Gutenberg: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1232)

links.work: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, chapter 3, "Attack by Stratagem," c. fifth century BC
links.idea: Subduing the enemy without fighting is best. The highest form is to attack the enemy's plans (fa mou), next to attack his alliances (fa jiao), next to attack his army, and worst of all to besiege walled cities.
links.fit: It matches the ranking in the judgment that China's best move is a dual track: avoid a turn to force while winning concessions on wording and arms sales from the U.S. administration (fa jiao: weakening Taiwan's patronage), and influence the election through the opposition (fa mou).
links.limit: Sun Tzu's ranking rests on the premise that the enemy can be subdued without fighting. In Taiwan, talks on unification made no progress even under KMT governments (2008–2016), and the Election Study Center's surveys show Taiwanese identity prevailing over the long term, which puts a ceiling on the political track. Hitting that ceiling would create an incentive to move down the ranking in "Attack by Stratagem."
sources: 『孫子兵法』 謀攻篇 (中國哲學書電子化計劃: https://ctext.org/art-of-war/attack-by-stratagem)
Election Study Center, National Chengchi University, trends in Taiwanese/Chinese identity: https://esc.nccu.edu.tw

links.work: M. Taylor Fravel, 『Strong Borders, Secure Nation: Cooperation and Conflict in China's Territorial Disputes』, Princeton University Press, 2008
links.idea: Of China's 23 territorial disputes since 1949, it made concessions in 17 and used force in 6. Force was used when the disputed territory had high strategic value and Beijing judged that its bargaining position was deteriorating. In homeland disputes such as Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau, it made no concessions.
links.fit: This qualifies the dual-track judgment. Taiwan belongs to the category in which China has never conceded, and the strait crises of 1954–55 and 1958 were uses of force amid a perceived deterioration in Beijing's bargaining position. The conditional structure must therefore be spelled out: if the dual track fails in the January 2028 election and no U.S. concessions come, the risk of force rises in steps, and the probabilities of a blockade (T3) and armed conflict (T4) in the latter part of the forecast period to 2030 should be tied to the election result.
links.limit: Fravel's data run mainly through the 2000s, and the sample of homeland disputes is small. With China's military power now incomparably larger than in the 1950s, a different mechanism — force when it has superior capability — may operate instead of force when its position deteriorates.

links.work: Aleksandr Svechin, Strategy (Strategiya), 1923/1927 (2nd edition) (English translation edited by Kent D. Lee, 1992)
links.idea: The side pursuing the positive aim of changing the status quo must spend more resources and manpower than the side defending it. Destruction (sokrushenie) and attrition (izmor) are not dogmas but choices made according to concrete conditions, and strategy combines the preparation for war with the conduct of operations.
links.fit: It supports the interpretation that China, pursuing the positive aim of unification, will choose an attritional path of political, economic, and gray-zone means until the conditions for a strategy of destruction are in place, and it shows that the dual track is not a renunciation of force but a period of preparation until those conditions mature.
links.limit: Svechin wrote about strategy in wartime and did not address peacetime political operations. The Soviet Union adopted Tukhachevsky's line of destruction, and Svechin was executed in 1938. The proposition that a positive aim is costlier also presupposes a cohesive defender; if the U.S. administration opts for a deal, the defender's cost structure changes.
sources: A. A. Svechin, Strategy, ed. Kent D. Lee (Minneapolis: East View Publications, 1992), ISBN 9781879944336

theory.insight: Judgment C2 in this issue treats South Korea's choices as changing not the future but only the price, yet comparison with the classics and with precedent reveals that South Korea's choices are a tradable asset. That the Qing subdued Joseon before attacking the Ming in the Second Manchu Invasion shows that the stance of the rear was a precondition for a great power; the limited role assumed for South Korea in the CSIS wargames was itself an assumption derived from the South Korean government's stance; and the Brown Memorandum of 1966 is a precedent of a junior ally trading an explicit contribution for concrete rewards. Conditional rear-area support (A1), an explicit commitment to contribute to the alliance (A2), and a public declaration of neutrality (A3) should therefore be evaluated not only by their ranking on costs but also by what they could be traded for with both Washington and Beijing — and the timing of such trades overlaps with the phase of dealmaking by the U.S. administration that this issue identifies, that is, the path toward brokered stability (T5). When the baselines in the strait are settled by great-power deals, as the alternate-day shelling of Kinmen from 1958 to 1979 ended with U.S.-China normalization, a third country that has not set the price of its position in advance becomes the object of the deal rather than a participant. And because the cases of King Gwanghae and Corcyra show that the weaknesses of a confidential, conditional stance (A1) lie in leaks, changes of government, and entrapment at the point of execution, the design of A1 should include a bipartisan domestic consensus and a cap on what is carried out.

publics.read: Public opinion in Taiwan gives China no opening for unification talks, and a majority of Americans do not back going to war to defend Taiwan. The judgment that China will choose a deal with the U.S. administration and influence through Taiwan's elections over force (C6) fits this combination: force cannot change Taiwanese opinion, and American opinion leaves room for a deal. The check from Congress that slows the administration's concessions, however, comes less from public opinion than from a bipartisan consensus within Congress.
publics.watch: If, in the Election Study Center's surveys, "maintain status quo, move toward unification" rises above 10 percent or Taiwanese identity falls below 60 percent, China's strategy of influence through elections will be rated more likely to work. If support for defending Taiwan in U.S. surveys regains a majority, the administration's room to make concessions in a deal with China will be judged to have narrowed.

strategies.title: The Russia-Ukraine War: How should Ukraine end the war?
facts: The full-scale war is in its fifth year. Russia is pressing its offensive toward Kostiantynivka and Dobropillia, while Ukraine is mounting local counterattacks around Kupiansk and Chasiv Yar. The short truces at Easter in April, on Victory Day in May, and on September 5–8 all ended with fighting resuming.

A massive Russian drone attack that began on the night of September 24 (295 drones launched across the country overnight alone) killed seven people in Kyiv on September 25. The same day, Russia and Ukraine confirmed that they intended to resume U.S.-mediated trilateral talks. Washington is pushing to restart technical talks in the UAE, but Moscow still insists on securing all of Donetsk Oblast.

Ukraine is repeatedly striking Russia's rear, including Novorossiysk, as well as its shadow fleet, using drones, Neptune missiles, and naval drones. The Black Sea Fleet has in effect been pushed out of Sevastopol.
In December 2025 the EU agreed to lend Ukraine €90 billion over 2026 and 2027, and it finalized the loan in April 2026. A plan to fund the loan with frozen Russian assets fell through.

On January 6, 2026, 35 countries meeting in Paris formalized plans for a multinational force (MNF-U). Its headquarters will be in Paris, France and the United Kingdom will lead it, and its deployment is conditioned on a comprehensive ceasefire taking hold first. U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner took part in the discussions on security guarantees.

Article 73 of Ukraine's constitution allows changes to the country's territory to be decided only by a nationwide referendum. Elections are suspended under martial law, and a major cabinet reshuffle took place in July. Ukraine's Freedom House score is 51 (Partly Free).

Russia launched a massive attack on Ukraine's energy facilities from the night of September 30 into the following day, and from October 1 to 4 it struck bridges in Kyiv one after another. On October 4, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that the United States had proposed technical-level trilateral talks among the United States, Russia, and Ukraine by the end of October and that Ukraine supported the proposal; no Russian agreement has been announced.

law.title: The legal threshold for ceding territory
points: Article 2 of the constitution declares Ukraine's territory indivisible and inviolable, and Article 73 allows changes to that territory to be decided only by a nationwide referendum.

A legal cession of territory is therefore impossible on the government's signature alone. A ceasefire along the current front line that leaves the territory's status unresolved, by contrast, does not touch the constitution.

The 1953 Korean Armistice Agreement is the precedent. The armistice has held for more than 70 years with the territorial question left unresolved, and South Korea prospered in the meantime. But U.S. troops were stationed in South Korea.
law.result: A Korean-style armistice (B1) is open to Ukraine because it does not trip the threshold in Article 73, which requires a referendum for any change to the country's territory. The decisive difference from the Korean case is whether Ukraine has actual troops on its soil, as South Korea has U.S. Forces Korea, to stop a renewed invasion.

responses.lesson: Russia, as the most capable adversary, would not reject a ceasefire outright. It would reject a Korean-style armistice (B1) that brings in a multinational force, accept a ceasefire with monitors alone, leave the security-guarantee mechanism empty, and use the ceasefire to rearm. The heart of a Korean-style armistice (B1) is therefore not the signature but the actual deployment of a multinational force.

reads.d: In 2026 Russia has repeatedly demanded withdrawal from all of Donetsk Oblast as a precondition for a ceasefire, and Vladimir Putin has rejected advice to freeze the current front line. As long as neither side is willing to pay the price of ending the war, the war of attrition will go on.

reads.d: The only thing Russia has accepted is an unarmed civilian monitoring mission. Even if a ceasefire is reached on the current front line, it is therefore more likely to be a Minsk-style ceasefire (U6), without the backing of great-power troops.

reads.d: The greatest danger to Ukraine is that a friendly power such as the United States accepts Russia's territorial demands. The veto that could block this lies with Europe.

expect.note: The expected value is the sum of each future's 2030 score multiplied by that future's probability. It is calculated separately for each dimension, such as safety and freedom, and the dimensions are not combined. The score under the worst future is shown alongside.
expect.read: If the recommendations are followed, the expected value for Ukrainians' life and safety rises from 60.0 to 61.3, and for freedom from 53.2 to 54.1. Both are above the 2026 baseline (safety 52.2, freedom 51), but more than half of the scenarios in which a ceasefire takes hold on the current front line are Minsk-style ceasefires without guarantees, so the risk of a renewed invasion remains built into the expected values. In the worst future (collapse of the front), safety falls to 41.0 and freedom to 30.

futures.note: Probabilities and inputs are judgment estimates; ranges are in parentheses. "If the recommendations are followed" assumes that Ukraine pursues the top-ranked combination (a ceasefire without legal cession, B1; deep strikes, B4; and defense-industrial self-reliance, B5) through 2027. Unlike South Korea, Ukraine is a party that can shape the outcome of this war, so following the recommendations changes the probability of each future itself.

ranked.t: Build the capacity to outlast a stalemate around defense-industrial self-reliance (B5), and aim for a ceasefire without legal cession (B1) on condition that it is backed by great-power troops. Deep strikes (B4) are a means of raising the cost of the war for Russia, but whether they push Russia toward negotiations has not been established, so their effect should be reassessed according to whether the ceasefire terms Russia sets begin to change. Any agreement should impose no caps on Ukraine's troop numbers or missile ranges.
Staying the course (B0) lets Ukraine hold out but costs it territory and population bit by bit.
An all-out counteroffensive would pay off handsomely if it succeeded, but its chances are very slim and the casualties would be heavy.
An agreement that includes territorial concessions ranks last. It would have to clear the referendum threshold in Article 73, it could not be undone, and it would open the door to a renewed invasion.

rank2.tension: Imposing costs (B4) invites Russian retaliatory air strikes, and Washington may call for restraint because of oil prices. Between a United States in a hurry for a ceasefire and a Europe that wants security guarantees first, no set procedure will settle the sequencing of ceasefire and guarantees.
rank2.undecided: How to weigh what a ceasefire would gain against the fate of residents in the occupied territories is for Ukrainians to decide.

human.note: This section revisits the strategy rankings from the standpoint of individual lives.

items.client: The goal of the top-ranked combination.

items.cost: Spends some of the bargaining power needed for the agenda items on territory and security guarantees up front.
items.gain: The benefits go straight to prisoners, children, and their families, and it stops the loss of time that can never be recovered.

items.gain: Eases the toll that service with no end in sight takes on families.

conclusions.t: The most likely future through 2030 is a continued war of attrition (33 percent, range 24–42 percent). The chances of a ceasefire on the current front line total 30 percent, but within that, 12 percent is for a Korean-style ceasefire backed by great-power troops; 18 percent are for a fragile Minsk-style ceasefire without such guarantees.
conclusions.why: Russia has made the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from the rest of Donetsk Oblast a precondition for a ceasefire. The 1953 Korean armistice has held on the strength of the U.S.-South Korean Mutual Defense Treaty and the presence of U.S. troops, but Russia rejects the very presence of Western forces. Ceasefires that relied on monitors alone, without great-power troops, have followed the path of the 2014–2015 Minsk agreements: the fighting went on until the arrangement collapsed.
conclusions.flip: If Russia formally drops its demand for withdrawal from Donetsk Oblast or accepts the deployment of Western troops, the probability of a ceasefire will be raised.

conclusions.t: Measured against the Ukrainian government's objectives, the top-ranked combination is to build the capacity to outlast a stalemate through defense-industrial self-reliance (B5), while aiming for a ceasefire that does not legally cede the occupied territories (B1), on condition that it is backed by great-power troops.
conclusions.why: Even after Russia pulled out of the Black Sea Grain Initiative in July 2023, Ukraine kept exporting grain through a maritime corridor it opened on its own. The episode showed that Ukraine can hold out by its own means without an agreement. Strikes on refineries and export ports in Russia's rear (B4) raise the cost of the war for Russia, but according to a July 2026 report they have instead hardened Putin's resolve, so it has not been established that they push Russia toward negotiations.
conclusions.flip: If the United States and Europe both press Ukraine to accept territorial concessions (moving toward a peace on Russia's terms, U3), the ranking will be revisited.

conclusions.t: Whether a ceasefire lasts depends less on the signing of an agreement than on whether troops are actually deployed along the ceasefire line, and those troops must serve as a tripwire that would draw the great powers into the fight if they were attacked. Because the multinational force Europe is preparing would deploy only after a ceasefire takes hold, however, it cannot serve as a means of bringing one about.
conclusions.why: The 1994 Budapest Memorandum and the 2014–2015 Minsk agreements failed because nothing enforced them. By contrast, every place where a conflict has stayed frozen for a long time, namely the Korean Peninsula, Cyprus after 1974, and Transnistria, has had great-power troops on the dividing line. The multinational force in the Paris Declaration of January 2026 is likewise to be deployed "once a credible cessation of hostilities has taken place."
conclusions.flip: If a ceasefire concluded without a multinational force holds for more than three years, this assessment will be revisited.

conclusions.t: Judged by its effect on individual lives, the first item on the ceasefire agenda should be the return of prisoners of war and of children forcibly deported to Russia.
conclusions.why: They are the people losing the most irrecoverable time in this war.
conclusions.flip: If their return is secured first through a separate channel, the order of the agenda will be revisited.

conclusions.t: Russia's best move is not a ceasefire on the current front line but to keep its deal-making with Washington going while seizing the rest of Donetsk Oblast. The gap between Russia and Ukraine is not the multinational force alone but four issues: territory, a cap on Ukraine's armed forces, legal recognition of the annexed regions, and the exclusion of foreign troops.
conclusions.why: Since the start of 2026 Russia has repeatedly demanded the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from all of Donetsk Oblast as a precondition for a ceasefire, and Putin has rejected advice to freeze the current front line. The only thing Russia has accepted is an unarmed civilian monitoring mission, yet the OSCE monitors of the Minsk period and the EU monitors in Georgia since 2008 merely counted violations; they did not prevent them. The realistic guarantees, therefore, are Ukraine's own armed forces, free of caps on troop numbers and missile ranges, and Western commitments of support after a ceasefire.
conclusions.flip: This assessment will be proved wrong if Russia formally proposes a ceasefire on the current front line or accepts the deployment of armed third-country troops.

If a ceasefire concluded without a multinational force holds for a long time, the assessment that a ceasefire's durability depends on troop deployments (C3) will be revisited.

ranked.t: For now, the best course is to keep the bilateral deal with Washington alive while taking the rest of Donetsk Oblast through a war of attrition. In 2026 Russia has repeatedly demanded withdrawal from all of Donetsk Oblast as a precondition for a ceasefire, and Putin has rejected advice to freeze the current front line.

A ceasefire on the current front line becomes the best move only if Russia concludes that it can no longer bear the cost of taking Donetsk. Even then, it would demand the exclusion of Western troops and a cap on Ukraine's armed forces.
Escalation would unite the West, so the price Russia would pay is high.
Scaling back its territorial demands is blocked by Russia's own constitution and ranks last.

counter.read: The earlier estimate (step 5) and the two-way review took Russia's best move to be a ceasefire on the current front line, but the precedent of the Minsk arrangement and Russia's conduct in 2026 contradict that. The only thing Russia has accepted is an unarmed civilian monitoring mission. In Abkhazia, South Ossetia, and Crimea, where Russia once championed a deferral of legal status, the deferral was later followed by Russian recognition or annexation. For Ukraine, then, a deferral formula is not a symmetrical compromise.
