twoway.equilibrium: For now, the point where the best moves of Ukraine and Russia meet is not a ceasefire but a war of attrition. Ukraine wants a ceasefire without legal cession; Russia wants the rest of Donetsk Oblast. The gap spans four issues: territory, troop caps, recognition of the annexed regions, and the exclusion of foreign troops. A ceasefire on the current front line becomes the likely outcome only if Russia concludes that it cannot bear the cost of taking Donetsk. The probability of a war of attrition (U1) is therefore raised to 33 percent, and a ceasefire on the current front line is split between a guaranteed Korean-style ceasefire (U2) at 12 percent and an unguaranteed Minsk-style one (U6) at 18 percent.
twoway.zopa: There is little room for an agreement both sides could accept. The only thing Russia has accepted is an unarmed civilian monitoring mission, and as the OSCE monitors of the Minsk period showed, such missions only count violations; they cannot stop them. Every freeze that has lasted had great-power troops deployed along the ceasefire line. The realistic guarantees are Ukraine's own armed forces, free of caps on troop numbers and missile ranges, and Western commitments of support after a ceasefire; the question of such caps is itself a central point of contention in the negotiations.
traps: Both sides believe time is on their side. That belief keeps the war of attrition going even when a ceasefire plan exists that both could accept.
If Washington moves to a bilateral deal with Russia, Europe drops out, and the ceasefire amounts to no more than a temporary halt in the fighting without security guarantees.

The deferral of legal status that Russia has championed has, in past cases, led to recognition and annexation. Because the constitutions of both Russia and Ukraine forbid ceding territory, a deferral of legal status is necessary, but for Ukraine that deferral is not a symmetrical compromise.

ai.t: Cheap drones block breakthroughs and limit movement on the front to a slow, grinding advance
ai.stake: To evade jamming, both sides use AI-enabled drones that find their own way over the final stretch to the target. Ukraine has fitted many airframes with modules that track a target and guide the drone autonomously over the last 500 meters, and Russia, too, has used drones with autonomous target selection in combat. The drones the two sides have fielded already number in the millions.
ai.moves: Cheap drones turn the entire battlefield into a zone of surveillance and strikes, making operational breakthroughs and their exploitation difficult. They do not freeze the front entirely, however; they only limit movement to a slow, grinding advance. An attacker willing to absorb heavy losses in manpower can erode defensive lines through infiltration tactics (in 2025 Russia took about 4,300 square kilometers, the largest area since 2022, yet its deepest advance was only around 34 kilometers), and when the relative advantage in communications and electronic warfare shifts, so does the side on the offensive (after SpaceX introduced a whitelist in February 2026 at the request of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense, cutting Russian forces off from Starlink, Ukraine said it had retaken about 400 square kilometers by March). A protracted war of attrition (U1) is a conditional outcome: it holds only as long as the two sides' balance in drones and electronic warfare holds. Drones also push ceasefire violations down to small units at the front, making it hard to distinguish violations ordered from above from uncontrolled local ones (about 78 percent of the 2,299 violations Ukraine recorded during the 2026 Easter truce were by tactical drones at the front). The difficulty of attributing violations already existed under the Minsk arrangement because of limits on the monitors' mandate, and drones and jamming make it worse by neutralizing the means of monitoring itself. By contrast, attacks decided at the center, such as missiles, glide bombs, and long-range one-way attack drones, stopped during the truces, so ceasefire monitoring is more effective when designed around those attacks.
ai.lever: Ukraine's drone industry and battlefield data will remain export assets after a ceasefire. In an unguaranteed ceasefire (U6), however, drone deterrence can deny a swift, maneuver-style reinvasion but cannot deter a creeping reinvasion by an attacker willing to absorb heavy losses, or a limited war (as Russia's grinding offensive of 2025, the Minsk arrangement, and the 1973 Yom Kippur War show). Chinese-made parts account for 38 percent of drone-component imports (first half of 2025), and the funding depends on Europe, so the effort would be hard to sustain without outside supply. The memorandum Russia put forward in June 2025, too, made its preconditions for a ceasefire not a troop cap but territorial withdrawal and, for the duration of the ceasefire, a halt to mobilization, outside aid, intelligence, and satellite communications. The decisive provision, therefore, is less whether troop caps are imposed than whether the agreement guarantees that outside supplies of materiel and communications will continue after a ceasefire.
signs: Whether ceasefire negotiations include provisions for continued outside aid and satellite communications
Changes in the reliance on China for drone components
Front-line movements that signal a shift in the advantage in electronic warfare and communications

brief.q: How should Ukraine end the war?
brief.a: Build the capacity to outlast a stalemate through defense-industrial self-reliance, expanding domestic production of drones and ammunition, and aim for a ceasefire that does not legally cede the occupied territories, on condition that it is backed by great-power troops. Any ceasefire agreement should impose no caps on the size of Ukraine's armed forces or the range of its missiles.
brief.eq: Russia has made the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from the rest of Donetsk Oblast a precondition for a ceasefire, so for now the point where the two sides' best moves meet is a war of attrition. Even if a ceasefire is reached on the current front line, it is more likely to lack the backing of great-power troops and to break down again, as the 2014–2015 Minsk agreements did.
brief.human: The longer the war of attrition lasts, the more casualties mount and the later the children forcibly deported to Russia will come home. The first item on the ceasefire agenda should be the return of prisoners of war and deported children; this is the only channel through which talks have continued even amid the stalemate.

items.name: Budapest Memorandum
items.format: The United States, the United Kingdom, and Russia pledged to respect Ukraine's territorial integrity in exchange for its giving up nuclear weapons. These were "assurances," not legally binding guarantees, and the only recourse in case of a violation was consultation at the UN Security Council.
items.outcome: Rendered a dead letter by Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014; the consultation clause had no practical effect.
items.why: It was a written pledge with no means of enforcement and no obligation of automatic intervention, and the violating party was a signatory with a veto on the Security Council.
items.differs: The understanding that signatures alone do not deter has now become a premise of the negotiations. It is the direct reason Ukraine is demanding binding guarantees rather than assurances, along with a troop presence.

items.name: The Minsk I and II agreements, the Normandy format, and the OSCE Special Monitoring Mission (SMM)
items.format: The Trilateral Contact Group of Russia, Ukraine, and the OSCE was combined with the Normandy format, in which Germany and France mediated. The arrangement was sequenced as a ceasefire, the withdrawal of heavy weapons, a special-status law and local elections, and the restoration of Ukrainian control over the border, and some 700 unarmed civilian monitors oversaw implementation.
items.outcome: Large-scale offensives stopped, but hundreds of thousands of ceasefire violations a year continued (about 310,000 in 2018), and the arrangement ended with the full-scale invasion of February 2022.
items.why: Ukraine insisted on security first and elections later; Russia on elections and special status first and the border later. The dispute over sequencing was never resolved. Because the SMM's mandate required consensus, it operated under a Russian veto; 93 percent of the restrictions on its movement occurred in areas outside government control, and its surveillance drones were jammed and fired on. Some assessments credit its mere presence with raising the threshold for escalation, but there is no quantitative evidence that it deterred violations.
items.differs: Today the front is far longer and drones are the main striking force, so detecting violations and assigning blame with unarmed personnel alone is even harder. And Russia is now a direct belligerent, not a backer of proxies.

items.name: Russia's 2017 proposal for UN peacekeepers
items.format: Putin proposed deploying UN peacekeepers only along the line of contact to protect the OSCE monitors. The West and Ukraine called for a robust mandate covering the whole of the Donbas, including the border.
items.outcome: Collapsed over disagreement on the scope of deployment.
items.why: Deploying only along the line of contact would have entrenched the Russian-controlled areas as a UN-sanctioned frozen conflict, which Ukraine could not accept.
items.differs: It is the only precedent in which Russia itself first proposed a non-NATO UN force, but the design was meant to fix the front line in place. Any plan to use a non-NATO monitoring mission as a bridge is likely to run into the same rift over the scope of its mandate.

items.name: The 2022 Istanbul negotiations and the guarantor-state formula
items.format: Turkey mediated direct talks between Russia and Ukraine. The structure traded permanent Ukrainian neutrality for an obligation on guarantor states, including the permanent members of the Security Council, to come to Ukraine's aid, and the parties discussed deferring the question of Crimea's status for 10 to 15 years.
items.outcome: Stalled at the draft stage on April 15 and effectively died after May.
items.why: Russia made aid from the guarantor states conditional on the prior agreement of all guarantors, Russia included, in effect demanding a veto. The two sides were also far apart on troop caps (85,000 plus 15,000 for Russia's proposal against 250,000 for Ukraine's) and on weapons ranges (40 kilometers against 280 kilometers). Ukraine feared that Russia would use the time to rearm, and the Western guarantor states were unwilling to take on an obligation of automatic intervention.
items.differs: A formula for deferring Crimea's legal status, under which the occupation would be tolerated but sovereignty not recognized, was at one point on the table. Today, however, Russia demands recognition of all four regions it has written into its constitution and the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from the Donbas, so the scope of what would have to be deferred is wider than in 2022.

items.name: Black Sea Grain Initiative
items.format: Russia and Ukraine did not sign with each other; each signed a mirror agreement with Turkey and the United Nations. A Joint Coordination Centre in Istanbul (five members from each of the four parties) inspected ships.
items.outcome: About 1,000 voyages carried some 33 million tons of exports, but on July 17, 2023, Russia refused to extend the deal.
items.why: It worked through a combination of a structure that avoided direct signatures between the belligerents, the control that Turkey, a neutral mediator, exercised over the straits, and a narrow agenda that benefited both sides. It ended because Russia's demands to reconnect the Russian Agricultural Bank to SWIFT and restart the ammonia pipeline were not met.
items.differs: After it ended, exports were sustained not by an agreement but by Ukraine's own naval defenses and a corridor through Romanian territorial waters. This confirmed that a partial agreement can be replaced by self-reliance, but such a mirror structure is hard to apply to the territorial question.

items.name: Prisoner exchanges and short partial truces (the 2025 energy and Black Sea truces; the 2026 Easter and May truces)
items.format: With mediation by the United States and others, the two sides exchanged prisoners and declared a 30-day halt to strikes on energy facilities, a Black Sea ceasefire, a 32-hour Easter truce (April 11–13, 2026), and a truce on May 9–11. There was no formal monitoring body.
items.outcome: Prisoner exchanges continued, numbering 72 by April 2026 and, by June, more than 1,000 people returned on each side cumulatively. The partial truces all ended quickly; during the Easter truce, Ukraine recorded 469 Russian violations in the first six hours and 2,299 by the following morning (about 78 percent of them by drones). The Black Sea ceasefire was never implemented because Russia made sanctions relief a precondition.
items.why: Prisoner exchanges continued because both sides benefited immediately and compliance was easy to verify. Truces without monitoring, by contrast, left violations impossible to prove, and cheap drones made violations extremely inexpensive.
items.differs: Humanitarian issues are the only channel that stays open even during a stalemate, but there is as yet no evidence that it can be widened to territorial and security issues.

items.name: U.S.-led negotiations (the 28-point plan; the Abu Dhabi and Geneva trilateral talks) and the Paris Declaration of the Coalition of the Willing
items.format: In November 2025 a 28-point plan was put forward (a demilitarized buffer zone in the Donbas, a cap of 600,000 on Ukraine's armed forces, a ban on stationing NATO troops, and de facto recognition of Crimea and the Donbas as Russian). Trilateral talks among the United States, Russia, and Ukraine followed in Abu Dhabi in January and February 2026 and in Geneva in February. The Paris Declaration of January 6, 2026, committed to a U.S.-led ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism and to a European-led multinational force to be deployed at Ukraine's request once a ceasefire takes hold.
items.outcome: Deadlocked over territory. The talks were suspended in March because of the war with Iran, and on August 29 Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described them as being in a deep pause and reaffirmed that withdrawal from all of Donetsk Oblast is a precondition for a ceasefire. As of late September, Washington is pushing to resume technical-level trilateral talks in the UAE.
items.why: Russia demands withdrawal from the entire Donbas, the exclusion of Western troops, and recognition of the annexed regions; Ukraine counters that any territorial concession requires the people's approval. In July 2026 Reuters reported that Putin had rebuked aides who advised freezing the current front line and that Ukraine's strikes on refineries had instead hardened his resolve. In December 2025 Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov called European troops legitimate targets, and the only thing Russia has said it would accept is an unarmed civilian monitoring mission (Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko, March 2025).
items.differs: As a precedent still unfolding, it shows that the current gap is not the multinational force alone but four issues: territory (the remaining roughly 20 percent of the Donbas), troop caps, recognition, and the exclusion of foreign troops.

items.name: The 1953 Korean Armistice Agreement and the U.S.-South Korean Mutual Defense Treaty
items.format: The armistice was signed by the United Nations Command, China, and North Korea; South Korea did not sign. It created a demilitarized zone four kilometers wide, overseen by the Military Armistice Commission and the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission (Sweden, Switzerland, Poland, and Czechoslovakia). The Mutual Defense Treaty was signed on October 1, 1953 (Article IV grants the right to station forces).
items.outcome: It has prevented a renewed full-scale war for more than 70 years without any legal disposition of territory. But the inspection teams of the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission withdrew in 1956, and the commission lost its function after the United States abandoned the clause barring the introduction of new weapons in 1957.
items.why: It was signed after two years of attritional fighting, at the point when both sides judged that the cost of further fighting outweighed anything they could gain. South Korean President Syngman Rhee opposed the armistice and accepted it only after the United States promised preconditions such as a defense treaty. Deterrence thereafter rested not on the neutral supervisory body but on the treaty and the roughly 28,500 troops of U.S. Forces Korea.
items.differs: The durability of the Korean-style armistice came not from the absence of legal cession but from the presence of great-power troops. Ukraine has no comparable treaty or stationed forces, and Russia explicitly rejects the stationing of Western troops.

items.name: The UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) and the buffer zone
items.format: A lightly armed UN force was deployed in 1964, and after the Turkish invasion of 1974 its mission expanded to patrolling the 180-kilometer Green Line buffer zone. It now numbers about 730 troops.
items.outcome: It could not prevent the 1974 coup and invasion. Over the following 50 years there has been virtually no fighting, but the division has become permanent.
items.why: The stability after 1974 owed less to the UN force's arms than to the balance of power and buffer structure created by the presence of Turkish troops, and to both sides' interest in the status quo. The UN force was less a deterrent than the manager of a line that had already hardened.
items.differs: A counterexample showing that even an armed third-party force cannot deter a great power's offensive if it is small. What kept the freeze in place was not whether the troops were armed but a structure in which an attack would mean a clash with a great power.

items.name: Russia's "peacekeeping" model (Transnistria, Abkhazia, South Ossetia) and the 2008 six-point plan for Georgia with the EU Monitoring Mission (EUMM)
items.format: After the 1992 ceasefire between Moldova and Russia, Russian troops were stationed as peacekeepers under the Joint Control Commission. Russian-led forces also entered Abkhazia and South Ossetia. After the 2008 war, about 200 unarmed EU monitors were deployed under the six-point agreement mediated by France.
items.outcome: In Transnistria, Russian troops have stayed despite the 1999 Istanbul commitment to withdraw, and the conflict has been frozen for more than 30 years. In Georgia, Russia recognized the two regions after the 2008 war, and the EUMM, denied access to the breakaway areas, operates only outside the boundary lines.
items.why: When one party's troops act as "peacekeepers," the freeze holds, but it becomes a means of entrenching that party's sphere of influence. Unarmed monitors denied access cannot even establish the facts.
items.differs: For Russia, deferring legal status has served not as a symmetrical compromise but as a path to later recognition or annexation. This precedent is why Ukraine deeply distrusts any deferral formula.

checks.reason: The Korean armistice came about at a point when both sides judged that the cost of further fighting outweighed anything they could gain, and it rested on the U.S. defense treaty and stationed troops. In 2026, by contrast, Russia believes it can take the entire Donbas and has rejected advice to freeze the current front line, and negotiations are in a deep pause. A freeze on the current front line without foreign troops to guarantee it is closer to the Minsk model than the Korean one and follows a different path, one in which the war resumes or the division hardens.

Ukraine's success in maintaining exports through its own corridor after the Black Sea deal ended supports the idea that defense-industrial self-reliance (B5) can substitute for an agreement. Deep strikes (B4), on the other hand, have instead hardened Putin's resolve according to a July 2026 Reuters report, so the evidence that imposing costs on Russia leads to negotiations remains weak. In the Korean case of 1953, too, what produced the armistice was a protracted stalemate and the U.S. promise of a defense treaty.

The 1994 Budapest Memorandum and the Minsk agreements, which had signatures but no enforcement, failed, while freezes held in Korea, Transnistria, and Cyprus after 1974, where great-power troops stood on the line; in that sense, the assessment that a ceasefire's durability depends on troop deployments (C3) points in the right direction. But as the UN force in Cyprus in 1974 showed, a small third-party force, even an armed one, did not deter. And because the multinational force in the Paris Declaration deploys only "once a credible cessation of hostilities has taken place," it cannot be what brings a ceasefire about.

In 2026 Russia has repeatedly demanded withdrawal from all of Donetsk Oblast as a precondition for a ceasefire, and Putin has rejected advice to freeze the current front line. The premise that "Russia's best move is also a ceasefire on the current front line" and the diagnosis that "the only gap is the multinational force" are therefore at odds with observed behavior. A non-NATO monitoring mission is the only form Russia accepts (unarmed civilian monitoring), but the precedents of the SMM, the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission, and the EUMM show that such missions count violations without deterring them. Russia's 2017 proposal for a UN force, too, was meant to freeze the line of contact. The Crimea formula in the Istanbul draft does show, however, that deferring legal status was once acceptable to Russia.

Over the past 12 months, the net area newly taken by Russia was about 1,600–2,200 square kilometers, and the front has effectively stalled, which partly supports the view that drones favor the defense. But as the violations during the 2026 Easter truce (2,299 by Ukraine's cumulative count) were mostly by drones, cheap drones make ceasefire violations cheap and deniable, and surveillance drones are jammed, as they were during the SMM. Russia has also consistently demanded caps on Ukraine's armed forces, in Istanbul (85,000 troops, a 40-kilometer range) and in the 28-point plan (600,000 troops). What it puts forward first as preconditions for a ceasefire, however, are territorial withdrawal and a cutoff of outside aid and satellite communications.

precedents.insight: Among the precedents, every freeze that lasted (Korea, Cyprus after 1974, Transnistria) had outside great-power troops deployed on the ceasefire line, while neutral or unarmed monitoring bodies (the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission, the SMM, the EUMM) did little more than count violations. And the deferral of legal status that Russia has championed was in past cases followed by recognition and annexation (Abkhazia and South Ossetia, Crimea), so a deferral formula is hard to regard as a symmetrical compromise.
uncertain: The original Foreign Affairs analysis of the Istanbul negotiations could not be checked directly because of a 403 error; its content was replaced with The New York Times' summary of the draft and an article in The National Interest.
Reuters' July 2026 report that Putin rejected a freeze of the front line rests on three anonymous sources close to the Kremlin.
The detailed terms of the May 2026 truce and who mediated it rest only on a wiki page of low reliability.
Whether the technical-level trilateral talks in the UAE in late September 2026 took place, and on what schedule, has not been confirmed.
DeepState and ISW differ in their territorial tallies, so it is uncertain whether the recent trend is acceleration or stagnation.
How far Russia carried out the withdrawal clause of the 2008 six-point plan, after its 1999 Istanbul commitment, could not be confirmed from primary sources in this review.
The exact wording of the ban on ceding territory in Russia's 2020 amended constitution could not be checked directly in this review.

links.work: V. Page Fortna, 「Scraps of Paper? Agreements and the Durability of Peace」, International Organization 57(2), 2003; 『Peace Time: Cease-Fire Agreements and the Durability of Peace』, Princeton University Press, 2004
links.idea: Of 48 ceasefires in interstate wars between 1946 and 1997, war resumed in 21, while 27 held until the end of the sample period. Full demilitarized zones at least two kilometers wide reduced the risk of renewed war by about 91 percent (hazard ratio 0.09), and no ceasefire explicitly guaranteed by outside states broke down. New peacekeeping or monitoring missions and joint commissions for dispute resolution also had large effects, whereas troop withdrawals and arms control had no significant effect.
links.fit: The framework that separates the Korean model (U2) from the Minsk model (U6) by whether guarantees exist is consistent with this research. But the research also shows that design variables of the agreement, such as the width of the demilitarized zone, joint commissions, and the specificity of the provisions (each one-step increase cuts the risk by about 4 percent), greatly affect how long a ceasefire lasts, beyond guarantor troops. The absence of guarantor troops does not automatically produce a Minsk-style outcome, and fewer than half of all ceasefires broke down; the assessment that "without guarantees, a ceasefire is likely to be no more than a pause" should therefore be made conditional on the quality of the agreement's design.
links.limit: The sample ends in 1997, and it contains almost no cases in which a nuclear-armed great power was itself a belligerent. The finding that "no guaranteed ceasefire failed" rests on few cases and is hard to translate into a probability. The Minsk agreements had the Trilateral Contact Group and the OSCE monitors, but the demilitarized zone was never implemented, and Russia, as a permanent member of the Security Council, can block a UN peacekeeping mission, so some of the tools the research found effective are hard to use in this case.

links.work: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, chapters 18–26 (the Peace of Nicias), late fifth century BC
links.idea: The Peace of Nicias of 421 BC was signed, but key provisions such as the return of Amphipolis were never carried out and major allies refused to join. For the next six years and ten months the two sides merely refrained from invading each other's territory while continuing to clash indirectly. Thucydides wrote that it would be a mistake to regard this interval as peace and that the entire 27 years should be seen as a single war.
links.fit: It supports the view that an unguaranteed Minsk-style ceasefire (U6) is not a separate ending but one phase of the war of attrition (U1). Because much of U6 in the distribution of futures through 2030 contains a path back to U1, it fits the structure of this classic better to state the probability of relapse within U6 than to set U1 and U6 side by side.
links.limit: This was a system of alliances among ancient city-states with no nuclear deterrence, and the peace collapsed in large part because of contingencies such as Athenian domestic politics surrounding Alcibiades and the Sicilian Expedition. It does not follow that every imperfect peace leads to renewed war (some imperfect arrangements have stayed frozen for a long time, such as the dividing line in Cyprus since 1974).
sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5.18–5.26 (trans. R. Crawley and others)

links.work: Alexander Svechin, Strategy (Strategiya), Moscow, 1927 (2nd ed.); English edition ed. Kent D. Lee, East View Publications, 1992
links.idea: Svechin distinguished a strategy of destruction (sokrushenie) from a strategy of attrition (izmor) and held that which was superior depended on concrete conditions. In a strategy of attrition, battles at the front are a means of exhausting the enemy's economic and political rear, and the decision comes less on the battlefield than from the staying power of the nation as a whole.
links.fit: It supports the assessment that a continued war of attrition is the most likely future. Russian military thought has a tradition that treats a strategy of attrition as a legitimate choice, so slow progress at the front may not be read by Russia's leadership as a sign of failure. In this framework, whether a ceasefire comes depends less on the front than on a comparison of the endurance of each side's rear: finances, recruitment, and defense production.
links.limit: Svechin was executed in 1938, and the mainstream of Soviet military thought favored destruction, as in deep operations. Russia's operation in early 2022 was an attempt at a quick victory, so the war of attrition that followed may have been the product of failure rather than a planned choice. Scholars also dispute the conventional view that Svechin advocated a strategy of attrition unconditionally.
sources: Aleksandr A. Svechin, Strategy, ed. Kent D. Lee, Minneapolis: East View Publications, 1992

links.work: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, chapters 12–13, written in 1513, published in 1532
links.idea: Mercenary and auxiliary troops are useless and dangerous, and a principality without its own army is not secure. If auxiliaries lose, you are ruined with them; if they win, you are at their mercy.
links.fit: The assessment that puts defense-industrial self-reliance (B5) at the core of the combination fits this classic exactly. But making the backing of great-power troops a condition for a ceasefire turns the dependence on outside forces that Machiavelli warned against into the key to the negotiations' success, so the whole objective wavers if the guarantors' will weakens. If self-reliance is the core, it would be more logically consistent to treat guarantees as an added benefit rather than a condition.
links.limit: Machiavelli's auxiliaries are armies that fight in place of one's own, whereas a tripwire is a commitment device for deterrence; the structures differ. Unlike a sixteenth-century Italian city-state, modern Ukraine depends on its allies for air-defense interceptors, components for long-range strikes, and intelligence assets, so complete self-reliance is impossible; self-reliance is a matter of degree.
sources: Niccolò Machiavelli, Il Principe, capp. XII–XIII (1532)

links.work: Mao Zedong, On Protracted War (Lun chijiuzhan, 論持久戰), 1938
links.idea: A war in which the weak fight the strong passes through stages of strategic defense, strategic stalemate (xiangchi, 相持), and strategic counteroffensive; the stalemate is the longest and most painful stage but the key to the turnaround. In the meantime, the buildup of one's own strength, the enemy's international isolation, and changes in the international situation create the conditions for reversal.
links.fit: Its structure matches the assessment that puts the capacity to outlast a stalemate first. For Mao, however, holding out was not the goal but a bridge while waiting for outside conditions to change. For this combination to be complete, it must specify what Ukraine's holding out is waiting for (the limits of Russia's finances and mobilization, a change in U.S. policy, a ramp-up of Europe's defense production) and settle on the next move if that change does not come.
links.limit: China could trade space for time thanks to its vast depth and population, whereas Ukraine is at a disadvantage in population and capacity for mobilization. In fact, Japan's defeat was decided less by the strength China accumulated during the stalemate than by an outside event, the entry of the United States into the war.
sources: Mao Zedong, On Protracted War (論持久戰), lectures delivered in May 1938 at the Yan'an Association for the Study of the War of Resistance Against Japan

links.work: Glenn H. Snyder, 「The Security Dilemma in Alliance Politics」, World Politics 36(4), 1984
links.idea: Alliances carry a tension between abandonment and entrapment: strengthening a commitment raises the risk of entrapment, and weakening it raises the risk of abandonment. A patron has an incentive to narrow the scope and automaticity of its commitments to avoid entrapment.
links.fit: A guarantee by great-power troops asks the guarantors to accept the maximum risk of entrapment. According to this theory, the guarantors will try to blur the automaticity of their entry into a war by reducing troop numbers or restricting rules of engagement and areas of deployment; if they do, the condition may be met on paper while the tripwire function weakens. An assessment that sets this condition needs to build the guarantors' incentives into its design.
links.limit: Snyder's model assumes relations among formal allies, whereas Ukraine is not allied. The guarantors' domestic politics (elections, public opinion) may weigh more than alliance logic, and if European countries come to see the Russian threat as a matter of their own security, their incentive to avoid entrapment will diminish.

links.work: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence, chapter 2, "The Art of Commitment," Yale University Press, 1966
links.idea: The U.S. garrison in West Berlin was too small to stop the Soviet army, but it functioned as a commitment device that would leave Washington no way to back down if it were attacked. What mattered was not the military size of the force but its making retreat impossible.
links.fit: It lends theoretical support to the assessment that the troops deployed must be a tripwire that would bring the great powers into the war if attacked. The argument that deployment matters more than signatures likewise mirrors Schelling's logic that the credibility of a commitment comes not from documents but from actions that are hard to reverse.
links.limit: The Berlin garrison sat within an alliance framework that already engaged U.S. military power and nuclear deterrence. Whether a multinational force centered on Britain and France would carry the same automaticity against nuclear-armed Russia is uncertain, and a tripwire without U.S. troops has a weak end to its wire.
sources: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence, New Haven: Yale University Press, 1966, ch. 2

links.work: Dan Reiter & Paul Poast, 「The Truth About Tripwires: Why Small Force Deployments Do Not Deter Aggression」, Texas National Security Review 4(3), 2021
links.idea: Small tripwire forces deter poorly, because casualties among them do not necessarily force the home country to intervene and an attacker can create a fait accompli before reinforcements arrive. Deterrence comes from forces large enough to change the local balance of power. In March 1949, when Kim Il Sung told Stalin that as many as 20,000 U.S. troops were in South Korea (the actual figure was about 7,500), Stalin rejected Kim's plan to invade the South; in 1950, after the withdrawal had left only an advisory group of about 500, he approved it.
links.fit: It qualifies the assessment that the troops on the ceasefire line must serve as a tripwire (C3). A multinational force of symbolic size may not adequately serve even as a tripwire, and deterrence holds only when combined with the Ukrainian army's own capacity for denial. The top-ranked combination, centered on defense-industrial self-reliance (C2), is consistent with this research, so the tripwire and Ukraine's own capacity for denial should be treated as complements, not substitutes.
links.limit: The authors' cases concern deterring the outbreak of war, not sustaining a ceasefire, and because they rest mainly on case studies they offer no statistical base rate. In the Korean case of 1950, other signals, such as Dean Acheson's speech defining the U.S. defense perimeter, were also at work.

links.work: Yu Seong-ryong, Jingbirok (The Book of Corrections, 懲毖錄), written after the Imjin War; included in his collected works in 1633 and published separately in 1647
links.idea: In the Imjin War, Ming forces were decisive in retaking Pyongyang in 1593, but Ming China then negotiated peace with Japan through Shen Weijing and Konishi Yukinaga while shutting Joseon out, and the negotiators on both sides misrepresented the other side's terms to their own courts. After the main Ming forces were withdrawn or scaled back during the peace talks, the investiture negotiations broke down in 1596, and Japan invaded again in 1597 (the Jeongyu War).
links.fit: It shows that even when outside great-power troops are present, if their stay depends on the guarantor's own interests, the guarantor, eager to extricate itself from the war, will agree to an ambiguous truce and draw down its forces. It supports the assessment that the deployment of a multinational force cannot serve as a means of bringing about a ceasefire (C3), and it adds a condition: even after deployment, the force's staying power depends on the guarantor's domestic circumstances and its direct dealings with the aggressor.
links.limit: Ming China was a belligerent, whereas a modern multinational force is a non-belligerent guarantor force that enters after a ceasefire. And the conditions that made it possible to distort negotiating documents within the premodern tributary investiture order differ from those of modern diplomacy.

links.work: Donald W. Boose Jr., 「The Korean War Truce Talks: A Study in Conflict Termination」, Parameters 30(1), 2000
links.idea: At the Korean War armistice talks, the issue of repatriating prisoners of war stalled for about 17 months, from the communist side's rejection of the United Nations Command's proposal for voluntary repatriation in January 1952 until agreement on June 8, 1953. Fighting that continued after the talks began cost the UN forces more than 125,000 casualties and Chinese and North Korean forces about 250,000.
links.fit: The prisoner issue can become an agenda item that holds the entire ceasefire hostage when principles collide. In the Korean War, the prisoner question was not the first agenda item but the last point of contention, and it prolonged the war. If the return of prisoners and children is to be the first item, a structure for implementing it separately (phased exchanges, third-party verification) must be designed alongside it so that this item does not become hostage to the others.
links.limit: The issue in the Korean War was a Cold War propaganda principle: whether to forcibly repatriate prisoners who refused to go home. In the Russia-Ukraine war, prisoner exchanges have recurred even amid the fighting (including the large-scale exchanges after the direct talks in Istanbul in 2025), so the return of prisoners can proceed separately from a ceasefire. At the same time, the fact that many South Korean prisoners of war never returned after the Korean War shows that even a provision for the return of all prisoners will not be carried out without a means of verification.

links.work: Revised Annals of King Seonjo (Seonjo sujeong sillok), entry for the first day of the fourth month of the 38th year of King Seonjo's reign (1605): the Buddhist master Samyeong (Yujeong)'s mission to gather intelligence and repatriate captives
links.idea: In negotiations to reopen relations with the Tokugawa regime after the Imjin War, Joseon made the repatriation of its people taken captive to Japan a prerequisite. In 1605, after an audience with Tokugawa Ieyasu at Fushimi Castle, Yujeong brought back more than 3,000 people. From 1607, Joseon continued the repatriations by sending envoys under the name hoedap-gyeom-swaehwansa (envoys of reply and repatriation).
links.fit: As an East Asian precedent that put the return of individuals first in postwar negotiations, it supports the assessment that the return of prisoners and forcibly deported children should be the first agenda item (C4). At the same time, only some of those taken away returned, and those who over time settled abroad or whose status changed never came back. The adoption of forcibly deported children and changes to their citizenship follow the same pattern, so the reason to make their return the first item goes beyond humanitarian priority: the longer it waits, the less likely it becomes.
links.limit: The Joseon-Japan negotiations took place in the context of normalizing relations after the war had ended and the regime had changed, and the Tokugawa had a motive to emphasize their break with the Toyotomi regime. In the Russia-Ukraine case, the regime responsible remains the negotiating counterpart, and Russia describes the deportation of children as a protective measure.
sources: Revised Annals of King Seonjo, volume 39, first day of the fourth month of the 38th year of King Seonjo's reign

links.work: Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, "Russia's Systematic Program for the Re-education and Adoption of Ukraine's Children," February 14, 2023
links.idea: Since February 2022, at least 6,000 Ukrainian children have been held in at least 43 facilities in Russia and occupied Crimea. Children with guardians were sent to "re-education" camps, while orphans and children from institutions were placed for adoption or in foster care, and the return of some has been delayed or postponed indefinitely. On March 17, 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants over this issue for President Putin and Russia's commissioner for children's rights.
links.fit: The return of children cannot be settled by a single line in an agreement; it requires a third-party verification system to confirm lists, verify identities, and restore legal status (undoing the grant of Russian citizenship and adoptions). To be effective as the first agenda item, the verification mechanism (the International Committee of the Red Cross, third-country mediators) must be designed before any agreement in principle. And because the issue is the subject of International Criminal Court warrants, Russia has a strong incentive to avoid it as an admission of responsibility.
links.limit: The report's figures are confirmed minimums, and the Ukrainian government's estimates are much higher. Since the report, small numbers of children have been returned through third-country mediation, so individual channels of return may work even without a comprehensive agreement.

links.work: Carl von Clausewitz, On War, Book 7, chapter 5, "The Culminating Point of the Attack," and Book 7, chapter 22, "The Culminating Point of Victory," 1834
links.idea: An attack loses strength as it advances until it reaches a culminating point; beyond that point, it becomes vulnerable to the defender's counterattack. The attacker's key judgment is to stop before passing the culminating point of victory.
links.fit: It agrees with the main assessment that a ceasefire on the current front line is unlikely until Russia concludes that it can no longer bear the cost of taking the rest of Donetsk Oblast. As long as Russia believes it has not reached its culminating point, the attack will continue. Ukraine's bargaining power therefore comes from imposing costs (defense in depth, long-range strikes, economic pressure) that make Russia recognize its culminating point.
links.limit: Clausewitz's culminating point assumes a war of maneuver in which the distance of the advance and the supply lines lengthen. In a war of attrition where the front barely moves, the culminating point shows up less on the battlefield than in finances, recruitment, and defense production, which makes it hard to observe, and belligerents usually recognize it late. Indicators are needed to forecast when Russia will recognize that it has passed its culminating point.
sources: Carl von Clausewitz, Vom Kriege, Book VII, chapters 5 and 22 (1834); trans. Michael Howard and Peter Paret, Princeton University Press, 1976

links.work: James D. Fearon, 「Rationalist Explanations for War」, International Organization 49(3), 1995; Branislav L. Slantchev, 「The Principle of Convergence in Wartime Negotiations」, American Political Science Review 97(4), 2003
links.idea: Even rational states go to war because of information asymmetries and commitment problems. When a future shift in power is expected, the other side cannot trust that a present agreement will be honored later. Slantchev argued that wars end when the two sides' expectations converge through the results on the battlefield.
links.fit: Of the four points of difference between Russia and Ukraine (C5), the troop cap and the exclusion of foreign troops are Russia's solutions to a commitment problem, meant to prevent Ukraine's power from growing in the future; Ukraine's demand for guarantees by great-power troops is the mirror-image solution to the same problem, meant to prevent a renewed Russian invasion. In the Istanbul draft of April 2022, too, Russia proposed capping Ukraine's armed forces at 85,000 and Ukraine at 250,000, and Russia demanded that any action by the guarantors require the unanimous consent of all of them, itself included. The gap is therefore structured less as a set of independent items than as the territorial question plus a pair of mutually exclusive solutions to the commitment problem. Where one side's guarantee is the other side's threat, a concession on any one item does not unlock the others.
links.limit: Fearon's model assumes a single rational actor. If Russia's goal is to deny Ukrainian statehood itself, there may be no bargaining range at all, and the premise of bargaining theory collapses. Territory is divisible in principle, but domestic political constraints such as the annexation clauses of Russia's constitution make it, in practice, indivisible.

links.work: Yevgeny Primakov's principles of foreign policy (from his appointment as foreign minister in 1996); Eugene Rumer, "The Primakov (Not Gerasimov) Doctrine in Action," Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 2019
links.idea: Primakov formulated a multipolar world, Russia's great-power status, primacy in the former Soviet space, and opposition to NATO expansion as the pillars of Russian foreign policy, and Rumer argued that what explains Russia's external behavior in the 2010s is not the much-cited "Gerasimov doctrine" but these Primakov principles. Mark Galeotti, who coined the term "Gerasimov doctrine," himself acknowledged in 2018 that Valery Gerasimov's 2013 article was an observation about Western methods, not Russian doctrine, and the prevailing view among scholars is that the West has overestimated Aleksandr Dugin's influence on policy.
links.fit: The assessment that Russia's best move is to keep its deal-making with Washington going while taking the rest of Donetsk Oblast fits the Primakov tradition. In this tradition, the United States is a peer great power to negotiate with and Ukraine is the object of the deal, and the exclusion of foreign troops is central to the principle of primacy in the former Soviet space, which makes it the item with the least room for concession. At the same time, this reading, which traces Russian behavior to the pursuit of great-power status rather than Dugin-style ideological maximalism, supports the premise of the main assessment that Russia could stop if the costs became unbearable.
links.limit: The Primakov principles explain the direction of Russia's goals but say nothing about the limits of the costs it will bear. Explaining Russian behavior through ideas makes it easy to underestimate economic constraints, elite politics, and the leader's personal judgment. Some argue that the full-scale invasion of 2022, as a means of securing primacy in the former Soviet space, went beyond anything Primakov-style pragmatism would have anticipated.

theory.insight: The analysis of this issue divided the durability of a ceasefire along a single axis, the presence or absence of guarantees by great-power troops, but the material it was checked against shows that this axis covers only half the problem. Seen through Fearon's framework, Ukraine's demand for guarantor troops and Russia's demands for the exclusion of foreign troops and for troop caps are mirror-image solutions to the same commitment problem, so the moment guarantor troops are made a condition of a ceasefire, that condition itself becomes Russia's reason to reject one. Fortna's research on ceasefires, by contrast, shows that even without foreign troops, a demilitarized zone at least two kilometers wide (cutting the risk of renewed war by about 91 percent), joint commissions for dispute resolution, and specific provisions greatly extend a ceasefire's life, while the troop-withdrawal and arms-control provisions Russia demands have no significant effect. Reiter and Poast argue that deterrence comes from a capacity for denial that changes the local balance of power, more than from a symbolic tripwire. Taken together, between the Korean and Minsk models lies a design space for a strong ceasefire without foreign troops: a wide demilitarized zone, third-party monitoring, and joint commissions, combined with Ukraine's own capacity for denial (defense-industrial self-reliance) and Western commitments to sustain arms and funding. Such a design would not collide head-on with Russia's demand to exclude foreign troops while targeting the causes of the Minsk model's failure (the unimplemented demilitarized zone, vague provisions, and powerless monitors). And as Thucydides' Peace of Nicias suggests, a Minsk-style ceasefire may be not an ending separate from the war of attrition but one phase of it, so it would be more accurate to treat a substantial part of U6 in the 2030 distribution of futures as a path back to U1.

The size of the Ming forces that remained during the peace negotiations (1593–1596) and when they withdrew; the volume and chapter of the relevant passage in Jingbirok have not been confirmed

The number of ceasefires in Fortna's sample that had explicit guarantees from outside states; until the original is checked, "no failures" is not translated into a probability

No suitable link was found in Iranian classics or strategic thought. Whether the chapters of Book 7 of Kautilya's Arthashastra on hostages and treaties (hostages as a guarantee device) connect structurally to the tripwire; chapter and section not confirmed

items.who: Ukraine · Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS)
items.q: Could you accept a plan under which Ukraine withdraws from the parts of the Donbas it controls (Kramatorsk, Sloviansk, and others) in exchange for security guarantees from the United States and Europe?
items.read: In the same survey, 59 percent accepted and 31 percent opposed a plan to freeze the war on the current front line without recognizing the occupied territories, with Ukraine receiving large-scale military and financial aid. What Ukrainians reject is not a ceasefire as such but giving up land they still hold and legally recognizing the occupation.
items.caveat: Residents of the occupied territories and refugees abroad are not surveyed. The January 2026 figures are cited from press reports.
sources: January 2026 survey (601 respondents) · cited from NV, January 16, 2026

items.who: Ukraine · Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS)
items.q: Can Ukraine give up some territory to achieve peace quickly and preserve its independence, or should it not give up territory under any circumstances, even if the war lasts longer?
items.latest: May 15–June 3, 2025 (the most recent survey with this question)
items.read: Willingness to give up territory, around 10 percent in the first year of the war, rose to nearly 40 percent by late 2024 and has stalled since. In the June 2025 survey, opposition varied widely depending on what would be given up: 48 percent opposed de facto recognition of the occupation, 68 percent legal recognition, and 78 percent the surrender of unoccupied areas.
items.caveat: This is a different question from the scenario question above, so the two results are not joined into a single time series. Figures before May 2024 are cited from press reports.

items.q: Should military operations continue, or should peace negotiations begin?
items.read: Most Russians want negotiations, but in the same survey 68 percent said they supported the actions of the Russian armed forces. Support for negotiations peaked in February 2026 and has been declining since. Because the question does not ask about terms, support for negotiations cannot be read as consent to territorial concessions.
items.caveat: The Levada Center is an independent polling organization that the Russian government has designated a "foreign agent." Under wartime censorship laws, respondents may hide their true views or decline to answer, so the survey is used as an indicator of direction rather than level. The trend figures were read from charts the center published.

publics.read: Public opinion shows that the ceasefire in the top-ranked combination (B1), a freeze that does not legally cede the occupied territories, falls within what Ukrainians will accept. Withdrawal from the Donbas, by contrast, is rejected by 60 percent even with security guarantees attached, and Russia demands the rest of Donetsk Oblast (C5). That the ranges of agreement public opinion permits in the two countries do not overlap supports, from the side of public opinion, the assessment that a ceasefire is unlikely until Russia concludes that it cannot bear the cost (C1).
publics.watch: If acceptance of the Donbas withdrawal plan in the KIIS survey exceeds 50 percent, a ceasefire that gives up territory will be considered politically possible inside Ukraine, and the ceasefire outlook will be revisited. If continued fighting overtakes negotiations in the Levada survey, the room for agreement on the Russian side will be judged to have narrowed further.

congress.t: Enforcing tariffs under the Russia sanctions law
congress.stage: The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 was signed into law on September 18, 2026. The president must impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas by October 18.
congress.power: Congress made the tariffs mandatory but left the president a way to waive them in the national interest. Any lifting of sanctions on Russia is subject to congressional review.
congress.votes: Senate 86–11 (August 7); House 262–159 (September 16). In the House, 152 Democrats voted no, objecting not to sanctions on Russia but to giving the president more tariff authority.
congress.sides: Supporters argued, in the words of Rep. Michael McCaul, that “you can evade sanctions … but you cannot evade tariffs.” Opponents said the broad waiver provision makes the sanctions effectively optional (Rep. Gregory Meeks).
congress.next: The October 18 deadline for imposing tariffs; whether the president grants waivers, and which countries are targeted.

quotes.role: Representative; former chair, House Foreign Affairs Committee
quotes.body: House floor debate · Congressional Record H5843
quotes.ex: Because, as we have heard from President Zelenskyy's team, you can evade sanctions, which the Russians have done for years, but you cannot evade tariffs. … That is why they are the teeth of this bill. Pursuant to the bill's rule of construction, only the top five importers of Russian oil will be tariffed. If a country falls off of the top-five list, the tariffs are removed.
quotes.full: Mr. McCAUL. Mr. Speaker, I yield myself such time as I may consume. Mr. Speaker, this is a critical time in history, a time my friend Lindsey Graham described as a magic moment, a moment that we cannot afford to waste. America's adversaries--Russia, China, and North Korea--are working together to threaten the free world. Make no mistake, they are watching what we do here today because they know that they will suffer if this bill is passed. Senator Lindsey Graham understood these global threats well, and that is why we spent more than a year working together on this bill. He brought Republicans and Democrats together and secured the White House's support. Today, we have a chance to finish his work, to help end this war in Europe, and to project peace through strength around the globe. I am proud to champion the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, and I thank Mr. Hoyer and our colleagues on both sides of the aisle for their strong support. For me, this is also personal. Lindsey Graham was my friend and my mentor. We shared a fundamental belief: that America is strongest at home when it projects strength abroad. This legislation does exactly that. It targets the money that fuels Russia's war machine. It sanctions Russian officials and oligarchs, banks, and financial institutions, and the shadow fleet that helps keep Russian energy moving. Through precisely targeted tariffs, it also punishes countries providing financial support for the deadliest war in Europe since World War II. Why? Because, as we have heard from President Zelenskyy's team, you can evade sanctions, which the Russians have done for years, but you cannot evade tariffs. In fact, President Zelenskyy's sanction expert, whom I personally met with in Kyiv, told me: Tariffs are a powerful way to amplify the impact of sanctions. That is why they are the teeth of this bill. Pursuant to the bill's rule of construction, only the top five importers of Russian oil will be tariffed. If a country falls off of the top-five list, the tariffs are removed. It incentivizes a race to the bottom. These countries have a choice to make about whether they will continue to sustain Putin's aggression. Putin believes he can keep financing this war indefinitely. We need to change that calculation and bleed his regime economically dry, because the Kremlin has murdered thousands of civilians in cold blood. They've bombed sacred churches and schools. They have kidnapped countless children, tortured and indoctrinated them, and sent them to fight on the front lines against their own country. We have a moral responsibility here today, Mr. Speaker, to bring an end to this suffering, but this is also a matter of national security. If Putin is rewarded for invading a sovereign nation, if he succeeds, he has already told us he will go further. His army will move into Moldova, to Georgia, and the Baltic states. Just like Putin wants to bring back the power of the Soviet Union, also President Xi of China wants to restore Imperial China. These dictators must be deterred before it is too late. This legislation also extends sanctions on Iran, which are set to expire at the end of this year. Again, this is all tied together, and in 2024, I spoke about the Iranian drones being used by Russia to kill Ukrainians. In return, Russia is reportedly providing target information to the IRGC. We cannot look at one part of this threat and ignore the others. This bill leverages our economic strength to make it harder for these regimes to finance aggression. Lindsey Graham once said that this bill would be his greatest achievement. I can think of no better way, Mr. Speaker, to honor his life and his legacy than by passing these tough sanctions, which will force Mr. Putin to the negotiating table. Evil is on the march. History is calling, and now is the time to act. Mr. Speaker, I reserve the balance of my time.

quotes.role: Ranking Democrat, House Foreign Affairs Committee
quotes.body: House floor debate · Congressional Record H5843
quotes.ex: These sanctions that are proposed now, the President of the United States, if this were urgent, could do them right now. … We said let's make sure that our friends in the European Union will not be subject to tariffs. In this bill, my friends from Europe can be tariffed. … Let's make stronger waivers if we really care about the Ukrainian people, so that no President can waive the sanctions that we are putting on Russia. No, can't do that.
quotes.full: Mr. MEEKS. Mr. Speaker, I yield myself such time as I may consume. Mr. Speaker, I rise regrettably to oppose the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. Why? It is a magic moment. It is a moment that we need to take right now. It is a moment that we need to move forward with. Here is why I have to oppose it. Number one, this bill wasn't written by Lindsey Graham. It was written by Donald Trump and Donald Trump's attorneys. We know his attorneys did it because he doesn't know how to write himself, but they wrote this bill. {time} 0920 I say to my Ukrainian friends and to the Ukrainian people: We need to do more. Just last night, we saw Russia again attack the electric grid of Ukraine. These sanctions that are proposed now, the President of the United States, if this were urgent, could do them right now. When you look at the facts and the evidence, what has the President done in all of this time to help Ukraine? He has not done one thing from the very beginning, when he told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that he has no cards, to the time that we gave the red carpet to Putin when he came to the United States. The fact of the matter is, if we just look at recent history, just 2 weeks ago, what did the President do? He took the Finance Minister of Russia to the G20 finance meeting, without any notice to the rest of the Finance Ministers. He has removed sanctions on Russia. Just last week, he removed some sanctions off of Russia. I am saying to my Ukrainian friends: I don't want to give you false hope. I want to give you real hope. Just yesterday, in the Rules Committee, because I wanted to work something out so that we can make sure that we get something done, I asked for some simple things that would give relief to Ukrainians right now. Do you know what would help them right now? Having Patriot missiles to defend themselves from these attacks would help. I put an amendment in. Let's give them $15 billion so that they can purchase and get something that would help themselves and protect their grid. In fact, this House has passed a bill that would have given the Ukrainians money to fix their grid, money to buy more munitions, and tougher sanctions in this bill. We sent it over to the Senate. Unfortunately, the Senate did nothing but go through Mr. Trump and say: You write the bill, and then we will get it passed in the Senate. We said let's make sure that our friends in the European Union will not be subject to tariffs. In this bill, my friends from Europe can be tariffed. Even though we have done nothing, no supplemental to Ukraine, they have stood up and made sure that Ukraine had what it needed to continue this war that has been thrust upon them by the Russians. Let's make sure that our allies and friends cannot be tariffed. I said let's put that in the bill. No, that can't happen. I said, okay, let's have stronger waivers. Let's make sure this President, who has done nothing for Ukraine--there are stronger waivers. We are supposed to be a separate but equal branch of government, not just concede to the executive branch, no [[Page H5844]] matter who is in the White House. Let's make stronger waivers if we really care about the Ukrainian people, so that no President can waive the sanctions that we are putting on Russia. No, can't do that. No secondary tariff. Now, this is to the American people, because we know what is happening with this economy. The President has said himself, proudly, that he is the tariff man. That is what he calls himself. We see what is happening to the economy in the United States of America. We see what is happening with our friend and ally to the north of us, Canada. This President has always said he loves tariffs, and we know the history of what he has done with reference to tariffs to our European allies and our allies everywhere. So, no, I have to come in opposition today to this bill. It does not give the Ukrainians what they need at this moment. They need to have the munitions to protect themselves and continue to do what they are doing to preserve their own country and democracy. Mr. Speaker, I reserve the balance of my time.

quotes.body: House floor debate · Congressional Record H5846
quotes.ex: I share concerns that the tariffs in the bill could backfire. They could harm our trading partners while sparing the main importers of Russian oil like China. The risk of the bill is that an important economy like China could be spared, but tariffs could be used aggressively on smaller U.S. allies. … Despite these design shortcomings I have outlined, I urge a ‘yes’ vote today.
quotes.full: Mr. HILL of Arkansas. Mr. Speaker, I thank Mr. McCaul, and I thank Chairman Mast for their work. Mr. Speaker, for the past decade, and certainly since February 2022, I have consistently advocated for arming the Ukrainians and placing effective sanctions on Russia. My record of supporting Ukraine is strong. Unfortunately, today we are, once again, in my view, presented with a bill that certainly could be better designed, and those points have been made. For example, the sanctions provisions in this bill lack full strategic discipline. The secondary bank sanctions in this bill only target foreign national institutions doing business with sanctioned Russian banks, which can be irrelevant when Russia is clearing energy transactions offshore. Markets have shown little reaction to the bill in terms of the Urals crude price to the Brent price. I share concerns that the tariffs in the bill could backfire. They could harm our trading partners while sparing the main importers of Russian oil like China. The risk of the bill is that an important economy like China could be spared, but tariffs could be used aggressively on smaller U.S. allies. In my view, on these financial points, Congressman Nunn's PEACE Act, which the Financial Services Committee passed virtually unanimously on a bipartisan basis, would be a better design. The bill would cut off Russian energy revenues and channel billions of Russian money to help Ukrainians. Despite these design shortcomings I have outlined, I urge a ``yes'' vote today. I also urge this House floor to bring the PEACE Act up on suspension, and let's really stick it to the Russians. We want to deliver today a loud, resounding message to the Kremlin: End this war. Get out of Ukraine. Focus on rebuilding your shattered international reputation and your destroyed economy. Mr. Speaker, I urge my colleagues to support the bill, and I thank Mr. McCaul for his persistent leadership.

quotes.body: House floor debate · Congressional Record H5846
quotes.ex: If we vote for this bill, it will be a Churchill moment because we will tell the President he needs to do something that he doesn't want to do. He may not do it, and we can't force him to do it … If we fail to pass this bill, there will be cheers in the Kremlin and tears in Kyiv.
quotes.full: Mr. HOYER. Mr. Speaker, I thank the gentleman, my friend, who cosponsored the Ukraine Support Act with me. I am sorry that the Senate won't pass that bill, and I am sorry the President won't sign that bill. The President will sign this bill. This is something we can do. I rise in very strong support of the passage of this legislation. I am, very frankly, in disagreement with the people who have spoken about giving Trump this unfettered power. Trump believes he has unfettered power right now without this bill or any action by the House of Representatives. That is an irrelevant argument. Three-quarters of the Democrats and 87 Members of the Senate--it was 86 votes but McConnell is back--believe that it simply limits to those who are aiding Russia's war effort to additional tariffs under this bill. I disagree with my dear friend that it opens up any country. France just endorsed this bill within the last 24 hours. They would be one of those countries subject to adverse action. We must pass this bill because if we do not pass this bill-- Mr. HOYER. The fact of the matter is that my friend mentioned a Chamberlain moment or a Churchill moment. Let me suggest to you that if we believe the enemy in this case is Trump, it will be a Chamberlain moment. If we vote for this bill, it will be a Churchill moment because we will tell the President he needs to do something that he doesn't want to do. He may not do it, and we can't force him to do it--I would like to force him to do it--but we can say to him to do it because the Congress wants to do it. We have been unanimous on this side, and the Republicans have had the majority of votes on your side almost every time we voted to support Ukraine. If we fail to pass this bill, there will be cheers in the Kremlin and tears in Kyiv. This is a moment when we stand up and say where we are. We can't control where the President is. I disagree with the President, but I agree strongly that it is time for the Members of this House to stand up and say to Russia: You will not continue with this without our adverse action. Mr. Speaker, this is an anti-Russia/pro-Ukraine bill. Let us pass it.

quotes.body: House floor debate · Congressional Record H5847
quotes.ex: The new sanctions on Russia in this bill would be strong and sweeping if they were enforced, but the bill gives Trump the power to simply ignore them. … The bill has a loophole that would allow him to define basically any country as a facilitator of evading Russian sanctions.
quotes.full: Mr. BEYER. Mr. Speaker, I rise to oppose this well-intentioned but terribly flawed bill. All of us on our side strongly support Ukraine, but this would do more harm than good for America and Ukraine. It has three main points: sanctions, tariffs, and symbolism. The new sanctions on Russia in this bill would be strong and sweeping if they were enforced, but the bill gives Trump the power to simply ignore them. That is what he is very likely to do. His criticism of Ukraine and his friendliness to Russia have both been rising recently. He is even calling for more Russian energy exports, the very thing this bill is purported to block. The bill's tariffs are a huge problem. President Trump has abused every Presidential tariff authority--every single one--that Congress has given, often to target our allies. The bill has a loophole that would allow him to define basically any country as a facilitator of evading Russian sanctions. He could then hit them with tariffs of up to 100 percent with no guardrails or oversight and no expiration. It is a much stronger tariff power than those he has already abused, and it will be much harder to challenge in court. Giving him this power, when he has shown us over and over again what he will do with it, would be an incredible mistake. Finally, we are told this bill would be a symbolic win for Ukraine and a show of American support. If this bill passes, I predict Ukraine supporters will regret it. They will be able to say they stood with Ukraine in the immediate aftermath, but when Donald Trump hits our allies with new tariffs and waives sanctions on Russia, the propaganda victory for Putin will be lasting and the damage will be embedded in U.S. law. Meanwhile, the Ukrainian cause will be tied to Trump's widely hated tariffs, deeply unpopular in America already. Further stressing the American pocketbook is not good for Ukraine's long term. We can do better. The House has passed a better bill. With negotiation and compromise, we can pass a stronger bill that truly supports Ukraine and tightens the economic screws on Russia without harming Americans. Mr. Speaker, I urge my colleagues to oppose this misguided bill so we can pass a better one.

strategies.title: The Iran war and Hormuz: what South Korea should protect and what it should give up
strategies.recipient: Government of the Republic of Korea
facts: The war that began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026, is now in its seventh month. Ali Khamenei was killed, and his son Mojtaba succeeded him. After the April cease-fire and the June 17 memorandum of understanding effectively collapsed on July 8 (the MOU formally expired on August 17), the United States reimposed its naval blockade. Iran restricts passage through Hormuz with attacks on merchant ships and with mines, and the U.S. military counters with escorted transits. On September 25, U.S. Central Command said it had turned back 122 merchant ships since the blockade began in April. Estimates of traffic through the strait diverge sharply between ship-tracking data and U.S. government statements. Ship-tracking data in early September showed five to 12 ships a day, roughly 10 percent of normal traffic (about 100 a day). Yet Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on September 28 that about 13 million barrels a day were passing through, and the ship-tracking firm Kpler counted 19 tankers transiting in the week to September 27. Separately, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have captured a U.S. unmanned underwater vehicle.

On September 25, Iran put forward a seven-day roadmap for a cease-fire and the reopening of the strait; Trump rejected it. Natanz and other sites were destroyed again, but about 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent has been beyond IAEA verification since June 2025.

Seventy percent of South Korea's crude oil imports and 35 percent of its naphtha pass through Hormuz, and 64.7 percent of its helium comes from Qatar. Government stockpiles stood at 34 days of actual consumption (about 67 days including private stocks). They fell to 26 days after the coordinated IEA release in March, then rose by eight to nine days' worth once Seoul secured 24 million barrels of crude from the UAE.

In March, 26 South Korean ships were stranded in the Gulf. That month Iran called South Korea a "non-adversarial country" and said it would allow passage subject to prior coordination. After the June MOU, 24 ships had left with Iranian approval by July 1, leaving two ships and 35 South Korean sailors inside the strait (Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries figures as of July 1). In early April, the KOSPI suffered the worst day in its 43-year history and the won fell to a 17-year low. The government responded with a $17 billion supplementary budget, a cap on fuel prices, and an accelerated restart of nuclear reactors.
The Middle East's share of South Korea's crude oil imports fell to 53.1 percent in April 2026 from 65.2 percent a year earlier, as imports from the United States, Canada, and Australia rose.

On September 18, President Lee Jae-myung said there would be no troop deployment that took part or intervened in the war. The next day, the presidential office explained that this was not a rejection of Trump's request regarding Hormuz. Expanding the mission of the Cheonghae Unit, the navy's antipiracy flotilla, is discussed as the most likely option. Separately, South Korea has pledged $20 billion of investment in Texas energy projects.

Iran has not closed the strait; it opens it selectively. Ships from "friendly" countries—China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Malaysia, Thailand, and others—pass after coordination or payment of a toll (one reported case: $2 million per ship), while ships of the United States, Israel, and Western allies are blocked.

The war has badly shrunk Iran's economy. GDP in the first quarter of the Iranian year (March 21 to June 20) was 10.1 percent lower than a year earlier, and crude loadings fell from about two million barrels a day in March to 220,000–250,000 in August. The rial went from about one million to the dollar to more than 2.2 million, and 12-month average inflation stands at 69.9 percent.

Iran's conditions for ending the war, as set out on September 20 by its security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, are an end to the fighting on all fronts including Lebanon, the return of frozen assets, the lifting of the naval blockade, noninterference in Iran's internal affairs, an end to support for opposition forces, and a halt to attacks on Iranian territory. The United States, by contrast, demands first that Iran give up nuclear weapons and allow freedom of navigation through the strait. Iran's position is that it will not discuss the nuclear question until its conditions are met.

On May 4, 2026, the Panamanian-flagged Namu, operated by HMM, was struck in the strait. A South Korean investigation pointed to the possibility of Iranian-made weapons, but the government attributed the attack to "unidentified aerial objects," and Iran denied involvement.

On September 7, 2026, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei warned in a Korean-language post that any country stationing forces in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz or joining military operations there would be regarded as directly supporting the aggressor and would face serious consequences. Two days earlier, a senior Iranian official quoted by Al Mayadeen had said that any South Korean involvement in the strait would amount to direct participation in the war against Iran.

On October 1, the United States sent a carrier strike group and an amphibious ready group to the Middle East, and on October 2 G7 leaders agreed to release 100 million barrels of strategic oil reserves. On October 4, Iran said through parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf that it would not open the strait until seven conditions were met, and its Foreign Ministry said the latest U.S. proposal still put the nuclear question first.

law.title: The legal threshold for deployment
points: Article 60(2) of the Constitution requires the consent of the National Assembly for dispatching the armed forces to foreign states.
Article 5(1) of the Constitution renounces wars of aggression. Interpretations diverge on whether joining an operation to secure the strait counts as self-defense or as taking part in hostilities.

The Cheonghae Unit has operated with the National Assembly's consent for its antipiracy mission. Extending its area of operations to Hormuz has a precedent: in 2020, the unit's independent deployment to Hormuz was handled as an expansion of its area of operations.
law.result: A noncombat expansion (H1) is possible within the existing consent, but a combat deployment (H2) would require new consent from the National Assembly.

responses.lesson: An Iran that calculates with the greatest care would not attack every country alike. It would single out the ships of countries that contribute to securing the strait, in order to split the coalition. Even if Seoul chooses the noncombat expansion (H1), then, it can reduce the price it pays only by stating explicitly that it will not engage in combat and by keeping a separate channel to Iran (H4) open alongside it.
