syn.note: The ratings in the table (Preferred, Acceptable, Uncomfortable, Rejected) are provisional judgments of how readily each country's leadership would accept each of the six futures (I1–I6) through 2030.

reads.t: The future most deciding powers could accept is a cease-fire followed by reopening (I2, I6), but what Iran prefers is an incomplete reopening (I6) that leaves it leverage.
reads.d: The 1988 cease-fire in the Iran-Iraq War held without a peace treaty, and in the Gulf between 2019 and 2023, Iran repeatedly seized selected ships in an "open" strait. Israel's October election and Washington's sense of whether it is winning are variables.

reads.t: South Korea's choices will do little to change the outcome of this war.
reads.d: In that South Korea cannot determine the outcome of the war, the structure is the same as in the Taiwan Strait issue. What Seoul can do is reduce the price it pays in each future—above all, the energy shock.

reads.t: The future in which South Korea loses most is not the war itself but full-scale escalation across the Gulf (I4).
reads.d: Even if the strait reopens, supply will not return if the Gulf producers' facilities are destroyed. The energy transition (H3) is therefore a longer-lasting safeguard than any response aimed at the strait itself.

intent.note: Each party's resolve is judged first by actions that carry costs, not by words.

items.name: Prolonged blockade standoff
items.story: Cease-fires are agreed and collapse in turn, and Hormuz remains unstable, caught between Iranian control and the U.S. blockade. Oil prices and insurance premiums stay high.

Persistently high tanker insurance premiums

A Security Council resolution

items.name: Incomplete reopening

As after the 1988 cease-fire in the Iran-Iraq War and in the Gulf from 2019 to 2023, ships are seized repeatedly in an "open" strait.

Continued demands for tolls or prior coordination
items.why: Assumes that although the strait reopens, insurance premiums and detour costs persist, leaving the income outlook slightly below the baseline.

expect.note: The expected value is the sum of each future's 2030 indicator values weighted by that future's probability. It is calculated separately for each dimension—life and safety, livelihood, freedom, and so on—and the dimensions are not combined.
expect.read: South Koreans' expected livelihood score is 93.9, close to the baseline (93.5), but in the worst future (full-scale escalation across the Gulf) it falls to 93.4. An energy shock could shake South Koreans' livelihoods. The lives of Iran's roughly 90 million people are not entered in this table as numbers. Still, a 10 percent drop in GDP in the first quarter of the war and average inflation approaching 70 percent show that Iranians' livelihoods are already on the side of the worst future.

futures.note: Probabilities and inputs are judgment estimates; ranges are in parentheses. Because South Korea's choices will do little to change the outcome of this war, no separate probabilities are given for the case in which the recommendations are followed. What South Korea's choices change is the price it pays in each future.

ranked.t: Build around the energy transition (H3), keep a separate channel to Iran (H4), and pursue the Cheonghae Unit's expansion (H1) in parallel only on three conditions: its area of operations stays outside the strait and the Gulf, it is not placed in a coalition led by the United States or by Britain and France, and Tehran is notified in advance. This combination does not try to change the probabilities of how the war ends; its aim is to reduce South Korea's exposure to energy shocks and ship detentions. Economic contributions to the United States (H5) serve alongside it as a buffer to soften Washington's demand for troops.
Economic contributions to the United States (H5) soften the demand for a deployment, but Washington can reply that troop contributions are a separate matter.
Riding out the crisis with emergency measures and no deployment (H0) leaves energy vulnerability and friction with the alliance in place.
Deploying combat forces ranks last. It would divide South Korea's forces on the peninsula, make South Korean ships and nationals targets of retaliation, and be hard to reverse.

rank2.tension: What has led Iran to detain ships has been action against Iranian assets and cargo more than participation in combat. The cooperation in enforcing the blockade and sanctions that Washington is likely to ask for therefore collides head-on with the channel to Iran (H4). How far to go in meeting U.S. demands is a line that procedure alone cannot draw.
rank2.undecided: How far to go in meeting the ally's demands is for the National Assembly and the public to decide.

human.note: Revisits the ranking from the strategy evaluation from the standpoint of individual lives.

items.cost: It could arouse U.S. suspicion and carries the burden of going through sanctions-exemption procedures.
items.gain: Helps sustain the livelihoods of Iranians living under the blockade. It is almost the only means by which South Korea can directly help people in this war.

items.client: The core of the top-ranked combination.

items.gain: Keeps the energy shock from falling hardest on the most vulnerable households.

conclusions.t: The most likely future through 2030 is a prolonged blockade standoff (31 percent, range 22–40). The futures in which the strait reopens after a cease-fire add up to 44 percent, but half of that is an incomplete reopening (22 percent) without a formal end to the war, in which Iran keeps detaining selected ships.
conclusions.why: The 1988 cease-fire in the Iran-Iraq War never led to a peace treaty, and from 2019 to 2023 Iran repeatedly seized selected ships even while the strait remained open. The U.S.-Iranian memorandum of understanding of June 17, 2026, collapsed three weeks after it was signed, and Washington, believing it was winning, has since rejected a phased roadmap.
conclusions.flip: If, after a phased agreement is signed, the reopening of the strait and the lifting of the blockade both hold for more than 90 days, the probability of a full reopening will be raised.

conclusions.t: South Korea's choices will do little to change the outcome of this war. The future in which South Korea loses most is not the war itself but an escalation that spreads to all of the Gulf oil producers.
conclusions.why: Even if the strait reopens, crude supplies will not return if the Gulf producers' production and export facilities are destroyed.
conclusions.flip: To be revisited if a South Korean contribution is explicitly made a condition for reopening the strait.

conclusions.t: Measured against the South Korean government's goals, the top-ranked combination is to build around the energy transition (H3), keep a separate channel to Iran (H4), and pursue an expanded mission for the Cheonghae Unit (H1) only if its area of operations is confined to waters outside the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf (the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea).
conclusions.why: In 2020, Japan sent a destroyer while excluding the strait and the Gulf from its area of operations and briefing Iran in advance, winning acceptance from both Washington and Tehran. That same year South Korea chose an independent deployment that extended the Cheonghae Unit's area of operations to Hormuz; this limited Iran's reaction to a diplomatic protest but did not prevent the seizure of the Hankuk Chemi a year later. In September 2026, Iran warned that it would regard any intervention inside the strait as participation in the war.
conclusions.flip: The ranking will be reconsidered if Iran declares even noncombat activity outside the strait a hostile act, or if Washington formally makes participation inside the strait a condition of the alliance.

conclusions.t: Deploying combat forces (H2) ranks last.
conclusions.why: It would divide the forces defending the peninsula, make South Korean ships and nationals targets of retaliation, require new consent from the National Assembly, and be hard to reverse once troops were sent.
conclusions.flip: To be revisited if the North Korean threat diminishes substantially and the operation in the strait becomes a multinational noncombat mission.

conclusions.t: From the standpoint of individual lives, humanitarian aid for Iranians should be added to the diplomatic channel with Iran.
conclusions.why: It is almost the only means by which South Korea can directly help people in this war.
conclusions.flip: If aid is confirmed to be diverted to the Iranian regime, the delivery route will be changed.

conclusions.t: Iran's best move is not to make an enemy of South Korea. But Iran has gained from detaining South Korean ships over frozen funds without ever labeling South Korea an enemy. In wartime, South Korean ships face the same risk of attack as every vessel transiting the strait; the additional risk that South Korea alone bears comes from action against Iranian assets in South Korea and from keeping South Korean warships inside the strait.
conclusions.why: In 2021, the Hankuk Chemi was released only after South Korea agreed to unfreeze $1 billion of the Iranian funds frozen there, and Iran's seizure of two Greek tankers in 2022 followed the same pattern: it aimed to recover Iranian oil that Greek authorities had seized at Washington's request. In May 2026, the HMM-operated Namu was struck before South Korea had any military involvement in the strait. On September 7, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson warned in Korean that any country stationing forces in the strait and the Persian Gulf or joining military operations there would be regarded as directly supporting the aggressor.
conclusions.flip: This assessment is wrong if a South Korean ship that has nothing to do with Iranian assets and stays outside the strait suffers an attack confirmed to be Iran's doing.

conclusions.t: Both the United States and Iran want the strait reopened, and the room for a deal lies in trading the strait's reopening for the lifting of the blockade and sanctions in phases. But such a phased agreement is not stable on its own. For a deal to be reached and to hold, asset transfers through a third country must be executed simultaneously with each side's steps, adjacent fronts such as Lebanon must be explicitly included, and implementation must proceed in stages tied to verification by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
conclusions.why: A phased agreement was already signed once, in the memorandum of understanding of June 17, 2026, but it collapsed within three weeks because it did not cover the Lebanon front. The exchanges that held—the Algiers Accords of 1981 (the release of the U.S. embassy hostages) and the 2023 prisoner swap—were executed simultaneously and in one step, with funds held by a third country. The 2015 nuclear deal (JCPOA), which was divided into several stages, was undone by the Trump administration's withdrawal in 2018. And the 1988 cease-fire in the Iran-Iraq War came only after Iran concluded that military victory was impossible.
conclusions.flip: This assessment is wrong if a single comprehensive deal without phases emerges or if Iran concedes first on the nuclear question.

ranked.t: The best course is to widen passage for non-adversarial countries, prying the United States away from its allies, while pursuing a phased agreement that trades the strait's reopening for the lifting of the blockade and sanctions step by step and defers the nuclear question. The strait is greater leverage when opened selectively than when closed.
If a deal with Washington stalls, hold on to the status quo and wait it out. The limit is how long the economy can hold.
A multilateral framework guaranteed by China would favor Iran, but it cannot come about unless the United States accepts it.
Gulf escalation could upend the board, but it would also cost Iran oil buyers such as China and India.
The nuclear threshold is the ultimate insurance. The moment Iran crosses it, it hands its enemies a pretext for strikes aimed at regime change, so it ranks last.

counter.read: The earlier step that estimated adversaries' responses (step 5) concluded that Iran might view an expanded Cheonghae Unit as siding with the United States and target South Korean ships. Judged by Iran's own goals, its best move is to keep treating South Korea as a non-adversarial country. The precedents show, however, that Iran has detained even non-adversarial countries' ships when there was an asset dispute, and has profited from doing so (the Hankuk Chemi in 2021, the Greek tankers in 2022). Iran's criterion for treating South Korea as an enemy is not whether it joins the fighting but what action it takes against Iranian assets and whether it keeps warships inside the strait.

pairs: South Korea
H3 + H1 + H4 (energy transition, noncombat escort, channel to Iran)
Iran
J2 + J1 (expanded passage for non-adversarial countries and a phased agreement; nuclear issue deferred)
United States (from the deciding powers table)
Press through blockade and airstrikes for resolving the nuclear question first, and ask allies to contribute to securing the strait
twoway.equilibrium: Both the United States and Iran want the strait reopened. The sticking point is what is exchanged first. Iran wants the blockade lifted and its assets returned first and the nuclear question later; the United States demands the nuclear question first. The June 17 memorandum of understanding papered over this question of sequence but collapsed over the Lebanon front. The current equilibrium is therefore a deadlock over sequence somewhere between a prolonged standoff (I1) and a cease-fire (I2). What could break the deadlock are two clocks: Iran's economic clock (crude loadings down 90 percent, the rial collapsing) and America's political clock (the November midterm elections). Reflecting that Gulf escalation (J4) ranks low in Iran's own ordering and that time is running out for its economy, the probability of full-scale escalation across the Gulf (I4) is lowered from 10 percent to 8 percent and that of regime collapse or civil war (I3) is raised from 10 percent to 12 percent.
twoway.zopa: The room for a deal lies in breaking the exchange into phases. In the first phase, the strait's reopening would be traded for the lifting of the blockade, and the removal or downblending of the roughly 440 kilograms of 60 percent enriched uranium would come in the second. The United States would get the outcome it wants—no Iranian bomb—and Iran the claim that it never surrendered its right to enrich. South Korea is not a party to such a deal. But as long as Iran treats it as a non-adversarial country, it has a narrow role in negotiating passage and providing humanitarian aid. This structure, however, was already signed once, in the June MOU, and then collapsed. For a deal to hold this time, it would need simultaneous execution through a third-country escrow, inclusion of the Lebanon front, and phased implementation tied to IAEA verification.
traps: A U.S.-Iranian deal is hostage to the Lebanon front. A single clash between Israel and Hezbollah could bring down the entire agreement on the strait, as it did in June. The next test of this link between the Lebanon front and the strait deal is Israel's election on October 27.

The deeper Iran's economic collapse, the stronger its incentive to deal—but the greater the risk of regime collapse (I3) as well. At the very point at which Washington concludes that a little more pressure will make Iran give in, there may be no one left to negotiate with.

The harder South Korea tries to satisfy both Washington's demands and Iran's treatment of it as a non-adversarial country, the more clearly each side will demand that it choose. Where that choice will show is in the wording of the Cheonghae Unit's mission.

ai.t: AI creates new targets in the Gulf and changes what South Korea stands to gain or lose in each future
ai.stake: Qatar produces about one-third of the world's helium as a by-product of LNG processing, and in 2025 South Korea relied on Qatar for 64.7 percent of its helium imports. In March 2026, two data centers in the UAE were hit directly by Iranian drones, and an AWS facility in Bahrain was damaged by a nearby explosion. The Bahrain facility was attacked again in April, and in July the IRGC claimed a further strike. The U.S. military said it struck more than 13,000 targets in 38 days of air operations before the cease-fire, and the Pentagon's chief digital and AI officer said the Maven system had been used in the campaign.
ai.moves: AI investment in the Gulf has not clearly changed the Gulf states' incentives to avoid escalation. The UAE, the largest AI investor, took the hardest line, and because that hard line emerged after its own data centers were hit, AI assets may have become a reason for retaliation rather than restraint. AI is therefore not factored into the probabilities of this issue's six futures (I1–I6). But by turning data centers into new targets and speeding up the U.S. military's initial strikes, AI has changed the probabilities of how the war unfolds (strikes on Gulf infrastructure, the pace of early attrition). For South Korea, it changes what is gained or lost in each future. In the case of helium, no disruption to South Korean chip production was reported even while Qatar's output was halted for several months in 2026 (thanks to four to six months of inventory, recycling equipment, and diversified suppliers). The damage that actually materialized was in prices, not in halted production. For a helium shortage to stop chip production, the cutoff of Ras Laffan's helium facilities would have to last well beyond the inventory period and alternative suppliers and overland detours would also have to be blocked—a risk that arises only in the extreme case of full-scale escalation across the Gulf (I4).
ai.lever: Adding alternative supply lines and stockpiles for helium and rare gases to the energy transition (H3) would, with the same preparations, reduce the exposure of chip production to helium disruptions. Because the scale of the helium risk depends less on whether supply is cut than on how long the cutoff lasts, stockpile targets should aim to lengthen the period that inventories can cover.

brief.q: Amid the Iran war and the blockade of Hormuz, what should South Korea protect and what should it give up?
brief.a: Build around an energy transition—diversifying sources of crude imports and expanding stockpiles—while keeping a separate diplomatic channel to Iran, and pursue an expanded mission for the Cheonghae Unit only if its area of operations is confined to waters outside the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf. Freezing or disposing of Iranian assets in South Korea and cooperating in enforcing the U.S. blockade and sanctions are the most direct paths to Iranian retaliation.
brief.eq: Both the United States and Iran want the strait reopened, but a deal trading the strait's reopening for the lifting of the blockade and sanctions in phases was signed once, in June 2026, and collapsed within three weeks. Since then Washington, believing it is winning, has rejected a phased roadmap.
brief.human: An energy shock could shake South Koreans' livelihoods. Humanitarian aid is the means by which South Korea can directly help Iranians.

items.name: The Iran-Iraq "Tanker War" and Iran's acceptance of Security Council Resolution 598
items.format: A war on each other's shipping: Iraq first attacked Iranian tankers and terminals, and Iran retaliated against ships linked to Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. On July 20, 1987, the Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 598 (an immediate cease-fire, withdrawal to the borders, and repatriation of prisoners of war), and Iraq promptly accepted it.
items.outcome: Iran held out for nearly a year before accepting it on July 17, 1988, and the cease-fire took effect in August 1988. No peace treaty was ever concluded, and even at the height of the attacks, only about 2 percent of ships transiting the Gulf were damaged.
items.why: Iran's acceptance came only after its military commanders reported that victory was not possible within five years—which is why Khomeini likened accepting it to drinking from a poisoned chalice. What drove the decision was military pessimism more than diplomatic sequencing.
items.differs: Iran did not actually close the strait then; now it controls the strait through selective passage and tolls. And the adversary then was Iraq, whereas now the United States and Israel are direct belligerents.

items.name: U.S. Operation Earnest Will (reflagging and escort of Kuwaiti tankers) and Operation Praying Mantis
items.format: The United States reflagged 11 Kuwaiti tankers under the Stars and Stripes, making them American ships, and the navy escorted them. Mine clearance relied heavily on minesweeping forces from the Netherlands and other allies.
items.outcome: On the first convoy, the Bridgeton struck a mine (July 24, 1987). The Sea Isle City was hit by a Silkworm missile in Kuwaiti waters (October 16, 1987), and the U.S. frigate Samuel B. Roberts also struck a mine (April 14, 1988). The United States retaliated with Operation Nimble Archer (October 19, 1987) and Operation Praying Mantis (April 18, 1988), after which Iranian attacks on neutral shipping dropped sharply. On July 3, 1988, the USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655, killing 290 people.
items.why: The United States, as the escorting power, and Kuwait, as the protected state, immediately became direct Iranian targets. After a series of limited retaliatory strikes, the United States ended up fighting the Iranian navy head-on.
items.differs: Then, the United States claimed the role of protector rather than belligerent; now it is already a party to the war and is enforcing a blockade. The moment South Korea becomes an escorting power, it will stand where Kuwait and the United States stood in 1987.

items.name: The Algiers Accords (release of the hostages and unfreezing of assets)
items.format: Algeria mediated. About $7.955 billion in Iranian assets was moved into an escrow account at the Bank of England, and the Central Bank of Algeria confirmed the release of the hostages and the deposit of the assets simultaneously. Claims disputes were referred to the Iran-United States Claims Tribunal, and a $1 billion security account was set up.
items.outcome: The asset transfer was carried out overnight on January 19–20, 1981, and the hostages were freed just after Reagan's inauguration. The claims tribunal went on to serve as a forum for settling disputes for decades.
items.why: A credible third country certified both sides' performance simultaneously, and because the exchange was completed in a single step, neither side had to rely on the other's later compliance. Iran was also under separate pressure from Iraq's invasion (September 1980).
items.differs: The agenda then consisted only of hostages and assets; now the strait, the blockade, sanctions, the nuclear program, and the Lebanon front are all entangled. Disposing of nuclear material cannot be settled in a single simultaneous exchange.

items.name: From the JPOA interim deal through the JCPOA to the U.S. withdrawal
items.format: The P5+1 and Iran first concluded an interim agreement (the Joint Plan of Action), easing about $7 billion in sanctions in return for a halt to 20 percent enrichment and the dilution of highly enriched stocks. Frozen oil revenues were paid out in installments of $550 million. The JCPOA (July 14, 2015) then adopted an "Implementation Day" structure (January 16, 2016), under which sanctions were eased after the IAEA verified that the nuclear limits were being implemented.
items.outcome: Phased implementation premised on verification did work, but the first Trump administration withdrew from the deal on May 8, 2018. From 2019, Iran scaled back its commitments step by step.
items.why: The deal collapsed not because of how the sequence of implementation was designed but because of U.S. domestic politics and a change of administration. As an executive agreement rather than a treaty, it could not bind the next administration.
items.differs: Washington's negotiator today is the very president who tore up the JCPOA, and Iran's president has said publicly that he has no trust in the United States. Another difference from 2015 is the existence of about 400–440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent.

items.name: The 2019 tanker attacks and seizures: the U.S.-led IMSC and the European-led EMASoH compared
items.format: The IMSC (Operation Sentinel) is an escort arrangement launched in Bahrain by the United States, Britain, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, the UAE, and others. EMASoH/Agenor is a low-intensity surveillance mission designed to avoid escalation; led by France, it drew participants including Belgium, Denmark, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, and Norway, with political support from Germany and Portugal, and was launched on January 20, 2020, with its headquarters in Abu Dhabi.
items.outcome: After Britain detained the Iranian tanker Grace 1 off Gibraltar (July 4, 2019), Iran seized the Stena Impero (July 19, 2019). Greece, an EMASoH participant, handed Iranian oil over to the United States and then had two of its own tankers seized (May 27, 2022); it got the ships back only after promising an apology, compensation, and assurances against a recurrence. Right after the United States seized Iranian oil, the Chevron-chartered Advantage Sweet was seized (April 2023).
items.why: Iran's seizures were tit-for-tat retaliation against specific countries for actions they had taken against Iranian assets and cargo, more than a response to whether they had joined a coalition. EMASoH's defensive design did not invite attacks, but neither did it prevent retaliation arising from asset disputes.
items.differs: The 2019 episode was a peacetime gray-zone confrontation; now there is a full-scale war. Some 30 countries are reportedly considering joining the defensive navigation mission led by Britain and France in 2026, but Iran has warned that it will regard any military presence as support for aggression.

items.name: The Cheonghae Unit's independent deployment to Hormuz in 2020 (compared with Japan's Maritime Self-Defense Force dispatch)
items.format: Rather than joining the IMSC, South Korea deployed independently to Hormuz by expanding the area of operations of its counterpiracy mission in the Gulf of Aden, notifying both Washington and Tehran before the decision. Japan explicitly excluded the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf from its area of operations and operated in the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea on the legal basis of "research and study."
items.outcome: Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Abbas Mousavi, objected that South Korea's decision was unacceptable, but Iran did not immediately retaliate against South Korean ships over the deployment. A year later, however, a South Korean ship was seized while the Cheonghae Unit was on station (see P7, the seizure of the Hankuk Chemi).
items.why: The independent deployment succeeded in keeping Iran's reaction at the diplomatic level, but it did not demonstrate any real ability to protect ships.
items.differs: The year 2020 was a period of intermittent clashes; now there is a full-scale war. On September 5, 2026, a senior Iranian official warned that any South Korean involvement in the strait would amount to direct participation in the aggression against Iran, and on September 7 the Foreign Ministry spokesperson posted a warning to the same effect in Korean. The requirement for National Assembly consent has also been raised again for this deployment.

items.name: The seizure of the Hankuk Chemi and its release linked to frozen funds
items.format: The IRGC seized the South Korean-flagged Hankuk Chemi, citing marine pollution, but an Iranian official said the real hostage was the $7 billion tied up in South Korean banks. South Korea responded by sending diplomats and negotiating; the Cheonghae Unit was dispatched to the scene but could do nothing.
items.outcome: Iran freed most of the crew in February 2021. On February 24, 2021, South Korea agreed to unfreeze at least $1 billion (part of it used to pay Iran's arrears in UN dues), and the ship was released on April 9, 2021.
items.why: Iran seized a South Korean ship over an asset dispute without having labeled South Korea an adversary, and won substantive concessions as a result. For Iran, targeting a South Korean ship turned out to be a gain rather than a cost.
items.differs: The won-denominated funds frozen in South Korea were transferred to Qatar in 2023, removing the direct object of dispute. It has not been confirmed, however, where the $12 billion in frozen assets that Iran is now demanding is held or whether South Korea is involved.

items.name: The 2023 U.S.-Iranian prisoner swap and the transfer of $6 billion in funds frozen in South Korea to Qatar
items.format: After the United States issued a sanctions waiver, won-denominated funds held in South Korea were converted in Switzerland and moved to restricted accounts in Qatar (for humanitarian purchases only, €5.573 billion). Once this was confirmed, a five-for-five prisoner exchange took place simultaneously on September 18, 2023.
items.outcome: The exchange itself was completed. But on October 12, right after Hamas's attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, the United States and Qatar reached a "quiet understanding" that effectively blocked Iran from drawing on the funds.
items.why: A third-country escrow made simultaneous execution possible, but because the stage of actually spending the funds still lay ahead, they were frozen again when an outside shock (Hamas's attack on Israel) hit. For Iran, it became an experience of receiving money it could not spend.
items.differs: This experience, in which later stages were repeatedly reversed, underlies Iran's current demand for sanctions relief and the return of assets up front. Through this precedent, South Korea effectively extricated itself from the frozen-funds issue.

items.name: The "Twelve-Day War" of June 2025 and the verbal cease-fire
items.format: Following Israel's preemptive strikes, the United States struck Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan (June 22). After limited retaliation against Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, Iran entered a cease-fire without any written agreement, following Trump's announcement and Qatari mediation.
items.outcome: Iran's parliament approved a plan to close Hormuz, but the Supreme National Security Council did not carry it out. The whereabouts of about 400–440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent became unclear, and Iran suspended cooperation with the IAEA.
items.why: Both sides, seeking to avoid the costs of escalation, chose to retaliate just enough to save face and then cease fire. But the nuclear question was left entirely unresolved, and eight months later it led to full-scale war.
items.differs: In 2025 the strait card remained a threat; in 2026 it is actually being played. The episode shows a cease-fire without a written agreement failing to prevent the next war.

items.name: The April 2026 cease-fire, the June 17 MOU and its collapse, and the rejection of the September 25 roadmap
items.format: A two-week cease-fire was reached through Pakistani mediation (with Chinese involvement), but the strait remained effectively closed, and on April 12 the United States imposed a naval blockade. The June 17 MOU was a phased agreement: free passage through the strait and mine clearance for 60 days, lifting of the blockade within 30 days, sanctions relief and access to assets, and the nuclear question deferred to follow-on negotiations. Iran's seven-day roadmap of September 25 would have eased assets, sanctions, and the blockade first, on days one through five, reopened the strait on day seven, and included cease-fires in Lebanon and Yemen.
items.outcome: A merchant ship was attacked on June 25 and the United States retaliated on June 27; on July 8 Trump said the MOU was over (it formally expired on August 17), and the blockade resumed. Trump rejected the roadmap, saying Iran wanted a deal "because they are losing so badly." During the MOU period, 23 of 26 South Korean-operated ships got out with Iranian approval (as of June 28).
items.why: The central cause of the collapse was that Article 1 of the MOU did not make clear whether it covered the Israel-Lebanon front. Since then, Washington, judging that it is winning, has turned to rejecting a phased agreement altogether.
items.differs: This precedent is the current situation itself. A phased agreement has already been signed once and collapsed within three weeks.

checks.reason: The Hankuk Chemi case (P7) shows that Iran seized a South Korean ship over an asset dispute without having labeled South Korea an adversary, and gained a concrete payoff—the unfreezing of $1 billion—in return. The subproposition that targeting South Korean ships is costly for Iran is therefore refuted. The Stena Impero, the Greek tankers, and the Advantage Sweet (P5) were all cases of retaliation for specific actions against Iranian assets and cargo, not for joining a coalition. On May 4, 2026, the Panamanian-flagged Namu, operated by South Korea's HMM, was hit by two unmanned aerial vehicles (Washington blamed Iran, Iran denied it, and the South Korean government has withheld judgment on who was responsible), and in early September 2026 Iran warned that any South Korean involvement in the strait (a senior official, September 5) and any military presence or operational participation in the Gulf and the strait (the Foreign Ministry spokesperson, in Korean, September 7) would be treated as joining the aggression.

The defensive design of EMASoH, which the United States did not lead, did help keep participants from being targeted, but Greece, a participant, still had ships seized over an asset dispute (P5). The Cheonghae Unit's independent deployment in 2020 kept Iran's reaction at the diplomatic level but did not prevent the seizure of the Hankuk Chemi a year later (P6, P7). Japan won acceptance from both sides by excluding the strait and the Gulf from its area of operations and briefing Tehran in advance. This time, with Seoul weighing patrol aircraft, a logistics support ship, and a mine-clearing unit, Iran has warned against any military presence in the Gulf and the strait, so an H1 that extends the Cheonghae Unit's area of operations into the strait could clash with the separate channel to Iran (H4).

In Earnest Will, the United States as escort and Kuwait as protected state immediately became targets of mines and missiles, which led to the head-on fighting of Operation Praying Mantis and the mistaken downing of Iran Air Flight 655. Because Iran has already warned, through a senior official on September 5 and in a Korean-language post by its Foreign Ministry spokesperson on September 7, that South Korean involvement in the strait would amount to direct participation in the aggression, sending combat units would immediately undermine the premise of key assessment C6—that Iran will not make an enemy of South Korea. Ranking the deployment of combat forces (H2) last fits the precedents.

A phased agreement was already signed in the MOU of June 17, 2026, but it collapsed within three weeks because the Lebanon front was left out (P10). The proposition that the room for a deal lies in breaking the exchange into phases does not, by itself, explain the conditions under which a deal can be reached and sustained. The exchanges that held (the 1981 Algiers Accords and the 2023 prisoner swap) were one-time simultaneous executions through a third-country escrow, whereas multistage agreements (the JCPOA and the spending stage of the 2023 funds) were overturned by a change of U.S. administration or by an outside shock. Trump's rejection of Iran's September 25 roadmap—which had the same structure as the MOU—on the grounds that Iran was losing also suggests that the current obstacle is not sequencing but differing perceptions of who is winning.

The Iran-Iraq War ended in a cease-fire a year after the resolution was adopted, amid military pessimism, but it remained a cease-fire without a peace treaty (P1). After the JCPOA collapsed, selective seizures recurred in an "open" strait from 2019 to 2023 (P5). Dividing the future into only two branches—cease-fire and reopening, or a prolonged blockade standoff—would miss the intermediate state that has been most common historically (incomplete reopening).

checks.claim: Forecast: an 80 percent probability that Iran will not attack or seize South Korean-flagged or South Korean-operated ships through mid-2027
checks.reason: There are already the 2021 seizure of the Hankuk Chemi and the May 4, 2026, strike on the HMM-operated Namu (responsibility for which is disputed). Iran's Korean-language warning, the prospect of renewed U.S. bombing after the midterm elections, and the debate over expanding the Cheonghae Unit all fall within the forecast period. Given that seven months of war have already produced one event (the strike on the Namu) whose status under this forecast is ambiguous, 80 percent is too high.

checks.claim: Forecast: a 25 percent probability that the United States and Iran will sign a phased agreement by the end of March 2027
checks.reason: In 2026 two signed or declared agreements—the cease-fire and the MOU—emerged within four months, so the base rate for signing as such is not low. Twenty-five percent is a reasonable level that reflects Trump's rejection of the roadmap and the Iranian parliamentary speaker's insistence on seven conditions on October 4. But since both agreements collapsed within weeks, a signing alone carries little policy significance.

precedents.insight: Since 2019, Iran's seizures of ships have been tit-for-tat retaliation for actions specific countries took against Iranian assets and cargo, more than a response to whether they joined a coalition, and both Greece and South Korea recovered their ships through concessions. For South Korea, then, cooperation in enforcing the blockade and sanctions and asset disputes are more direct risk variables than participation in combat. Moreover, of the phased exchange agreements, the only ones that held were one-time simultaneous exchanges through a third-country escrow, and the settlements of 1981 and 1988 came when Iran was under other pressure (Iraq's invasion at the time of the 1981 Algiers Accords, military pessimism at the time of the 1988 cease-fire) or coincided with a change of U.S. administration.
uncertain: Final attribution of the May 4, 2026, strike on HMM's Namu (the South Korean government has withheld judgment, Washington blames Iran, and Iran denies it)
Where the $12 billion in frozen assets Iran is demanding is held, and whether any Iranian funds remain in South Korean financial institutions

The departure of 23 of 26 ships is confirmed as a post-MOU figure as of June 28, 2026; the number that left right after Iran's "non-adversarial" remark in March could not be confirmed. Whether South Korean ships paid tolls is also unconfirmed.
Whether any ships of countries participating in the 2026 defensive navigation mission led by Britain and France have been targeted by Iran
The precise dates for the Resolution 598 cease-fire (reportedly announced on August 8, 1988, and effective on August 20)
Whether the "military presence" Iran has warned against includes patrol aircraft and logistical support outside the strait (in the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea)
Annual statistics showing whether Iranian attacks on shipping increased after escorts began in 1987

links.work: Martin S. Navias & E. R. Hooton, 『Tanker Wars: The Assault on Merchant Shipping During the Iran-Iraq Crisis, 1980-1988』, 1996
links.idea: In the tanker war of 1981 to 1988, 451 merchant ships were attacked (283 by Iraq, 168 by Iran), yet even in the most intense period the attacks never stopped more than 2 percent of the ships transiting the Gulf. Because Iran's own oil exports depended on the same strait, it never carried out its threat to close it.
links.fit: Qualifies the assessment that ranks a prolonged blockade standoff first. By the base rates of the 1980s, a "blockade" persisted not as a physical cutoff but as selective attacks and rising insurance premiums—something close to an incomplete reopening (I6). In 2026, by contrast, ship-tracking data show traffic at a fraction of normal (five to 12 ships a day in early September, roughly 10 percent of the usual 100 or so). The restraint that held Iran back in the 1980s—its own oil exports' dependence on the strait—is gone, and that is a reason to set the probability of a prolonged standoff (I1) higher.
links.limit: The main reason Iran kept the strait open in the 1980s was its dependence on its own exports. In 2026, Iran's exports are already blocked by the U.S. blockade, so closing the strait imposes almost no additional cost on Iran. The 2 percent base rate of the tanker war therefore does not carry over directly to the present, and whether the standoff persists depends on whether the lifting of the U.S. blockade and the reopening of the strait can be made to coincide.
sources: Navias & Hooton, Tanker Wars (London: I.B. Tauris, 1996)

links.work: Michael Horowitz & Dan Reiter, "When Does Aerial Bombing Work? Quantitative Empirical Tests, 1917-1999", Journal of Conflict Resolution 45(2), 2001; Robert A. Pape, 『Bombing to Win』, 1996
links.idea: An analysis of all cases of aerial coercion from 1917 to 1999 found that coercion succeeded when it targeted the adversary's military vulnerability, that civilian vulnerability (punishment) had no effect on the probability of success, and that demanding a change of leadership sharply reduced the success rate. Pape likewise concluded that punishment and decapitation strategies fail and that only denial works.
links.fit: Supports the assessment that assigns a higher probability to a prolonged standoff (I1) than to a cease-fire and full reopening (I2). The more existential the U.S. demands—the regime itself, or giving up nuclear capability—and the more the pressure takes the form of economic blockade and punishment, the lower the base rate at which coercion has produced capitulation.
links.limit: If denial operations that directly destroy Iran's naval and drone forces prove effective, the strait could partly reopen even without a deal, blurring the line between I1 and I6. These studies are also based on 20th-century cases; their samples contain almost no examples of coercion in its current form, which combines precision strikes with a naval blockade.
sources: Robert A. Pape, Bombing to Win: Air Power and Coercion in War (Cornell UP, 1996)

links.work: Ibn Khaldun, The Muqaddimah, Chapters 2–3 (especially Chapter 3, Sections 1 and 12), 1377; Benjamin F. Jones and Benjamin A. Olken, "Hit or Miss? The Effect of Assassinations on Institutions and War," AEJ: Macroeconomics 1(2), 2009
links.idea: Ibn Khaldun held that royal authority rests on group solidarity (asabiyya) and that dynasties fall when weakening internal cohesion coincides with the rise of a challenger with stronger cohesion. Jones and Olken, analyzing 298 assassination attempts on leaders from 1875 to 2004, reported that successful assassinations of autocrats raised the probability of a transition to democracy by 13 percentage points (from a base rate of 4.2 percent) but intensified moderate-intensity wars.
links.fit: Qualifies the 12 percent assigned to regime collapse or civil war (I3). In Ibn Khaldun's framework, collapse requires not only outside blows but a cohesive alternative force. In Iran, the core cohesive groups—the IRGC and the clerical networks—may rally under foreign attack, while the opposition is fragmented. The fall of the Pahlavi monarchy in 1979 was possible because the clerical network supplied an alternative asabiyya.
links.limit: Jones and Olken's results show that a leader's death can significantly accelerate institutional change, so with Ali Khamenei killed in the February 2026 strikes, there is also a case for putting I3 above 12 percent. Ibn Khaldun's three-generation (roughly 120-year) cycle was framed for tribally based dynasties and cannot be transposed directly onto a modern theocracy that combines bureaucratic, military, and religious organizations.
sources: Ibn Khaldun, The Muqaddimah, trans. Franz Rosenthal (Princeton UP, 1958), Ch. III §1, §12

links.work: Mancur Olson & Richard Zeckhauser, "An Economic Theory of Alliances", Review of Economics and Statistics 48(3), 1966
links.idea: When the security an alliance provides is a public good, a small member's contribution barely changes the outcome, so small members bear little and large members bear a disproportionate share—"exploitation of the great by the small."
links.fit: Provides theoretical support for the assessment that South Korea's choices will do little to change the outcome of the war. Because reopening the strait is in the nature of a public good, whether South Korea contributes militarily affects the politics of burden-sharing more than the outcome of the war.
links.limit: That South Korea's choices cannot change the war's outcome does not mean they have no consequences. If free-riding becomes visible, the costs surface on other fronts—U.S. pressure on the alliance, defense cost-sharing negotiations, links to tariffs. What South Korea's choices change, in other words, is not the outcome in the Gulf but the U.S.-South Korean relationship and Iran's choice of targets. Later research (Sandler and Hartley, among others) found that the exploitation hypothesis weakens when a good such as deterrence is not purely public but carries private benefits.

links.work: Lutz Kilian, "Not All Oil Price Shocks Are Alike: Disentangling Demand and Supply Shocks in the Crude Oil Market", American Economic Review 99(3), 2009
links.idea: When oil price shocks are decomposed into supply shocks, global aggregate demand shocks, and precautionary demand shocks driven by anxiety about future supply, it is the precautionary demand created by anxiety about future supply, more than actual supply losses, that pushes oil prices up most sharply and most immediately.
links.fit: Supports the assessment that the future in which South Korea loses most is not the war itself but full-scale escalation across the Gulf. Escalation would endanger Saudi, Emirati, and Qatari production and export facilities themselves, setting off an explosion of precautionary demand, and would also threaten the routes around Hormuz (Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline and the UAE's Fujairah pipeline). In the 2026 shock, Asian gas prices rose 80 percent while U.S. prices rose only 13 percent—a sign of how Asian LNG importers such as South Korea bear the heaviest costs of escalation.
links.limit: In the 2026 shock, IEA members' release of about 400 million barrels of reserves, bypass pipelines, and lower Chinese demand shrank the net shortfall from about 20 million barrels a day to about 12 million. The market's capacity to absorb shocks may partly offset the costs of escalation, and the size of South Korea's losses depends not only on external conditions but on its policies on stockpiles and diversifying suppliers.
sources: Lutz Kilian, American Economic Review 99(3): 1053-1069, 2009, doi:10.1257/aer.99.3.1053

links.work: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VII, Chapter 1 (the six measures of foreign policy), compiled between the fourth century BCE and the early centuries CE; English translation by R. Shamasastry, 1915
links.idea: Of the six measures—peace, war, neutrality, marching, seeking protection, and the double policy—Kautilya advised choosing the one that builds up one's own forts, buildings, and trade routes while obstructing the same works of the enemy. Neutrality is the measure for when the enemy cannot harm you and you cannot destroy the enemy.
links.fit: Supports the combination built around the energy transition (H3). Kautilya's criterion is not who wins but whether one's own base grows relatively stronger, and the energy transition is a move that strengthens South Korea's base regardless of how the war goes. A combination that pairs seeking protection from the United States (a limited expansion of the Cheonghae Unit) with de facto neutrality toward Iran (a separate channel) corresponds to combining two of his six measures: seeking protection and neutrality.
links.limit: Kautilya's condition for neutrality—that the enemy cannot harm you—does not hold for South Korea. Iran can detain South Korean ships, so South Korea's neutrality is not a safe neutrality but a costly one. His system also presupposes a mandala (a circular structure of alliances) among neighboring states and does not directly address a distant middle power being drawn into an ally's war.
sources: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VII, Ch. 1, trans. R. Shamasastry (1915)

links.work: Glenn H. Snyder, "The Security Dilemma in Alliance Politics", World Politics 36(4), 1984
links.idea: Allies choose between the risk of abandonment and the risk of entrapment. Strengthening commitment to an ally reduces the risk of abandonment but increases the risk of being dragged into the ally's conflicts; weakening commitment does the opposite.
links.fit: Supports, with a caveat, confining the Cheonghae Unit's expanded area of operations to waters outside the strait and the Gulf. Limiting the area of operations is a compromise that lowers the risk of entrapment while signaling a minimum of commitment. Japan's cabinet decision of December 27, 2019, which set the Self-Defense Forces' area of activity as the high seas of the Gulf of Oman, the northern Arabian Sea, and the eastern Gulf of Aden while excluding the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, is a precedent for the same compromise.
links.limit: Snyder's dilemma also implies that a compromise leaves both risks in place. If Washington sees a limited contribution as a lack of commitment, the risk of abandonment (pressure over defense costs and tariffs) rises; if Iran regards operations even outside the strait as joining the war, the risk of entrapment remains. In 2020 South Korea extended the Cheonghae Unit's area of operations to Hormuz, but that was a phase of intermittent clashes; 2026 is a phase of full-scale war, so the same decision means something different.

links.work: Machiavelli, The Prince, Chapter 21, 1532
links.idea: When two powerful parties fight, neutrality is usually harmful. The winner does not trust those who failed to help in its hour of need, and the loser will not take in those who did not stand with it. The one who is not your friend asks for your neutrality, while your friend asks you to take up arms on its side.
links.fit: A case against the combination that keeps a separate channel to Iran. If the United States emerges as the winner of this war, South Korea's dual track will stand as a record of insufficient commitment; if Iran holds out, South Korea may be remembered as a country that sided with the United States. Key assessment C6—that Iran's best move is to keep treating South Korea as a non-adversarial country—maps exactly onto Machiavelli's observation that it is the one who is not your friend who asks for your neutrality.
links.limit: Machiavelli assumed a system of Italian city-states in which the victor could attack a neutral directly. Whatever the outcome of the war, Iran's ability to punish South Korea militarily is limited to detentions at sea, and the United States would find it hard to abandon South Korea within its alliance system. The dual track of King Gwanghae of Joseon (see the Gwanghae case linked to key assessment C4), which in the short run averted an invasion by the Later Jin, is also a counterexample to Machiavelli's generalization.
sources: Niccolò Machiavelli, Il Principe, cap. XXI (1532); English translation by Harvey C. Mansfield, The Prince, U of Chicago Press, 1985

links.work: Clausewitz, On War, Book 1, Chapter 1, Section 11, 1832
links.idea: The political purpose of a war determines its military objective and the amount of effort to be committed. The smaller the political purpose, the weaker the motive and the smaller the commitment should be.
links.fit: Supports the assessment that ranks the deployment of combat forces (H2) last. South Korea's political purpose is not regime change in Iran or a solution to the nuclear question but energy supply and the safety of its own ships, so the effort proportionate to that purpose is protecting shipping lanes and keeping diplomatic channels open, not joining the fighting.
links.limit: Clausewitz assumed the purposes of a single state. In coalition wars, an ally's political purposes often raise the level of effort expected of a smaller state. If South Korea's political purpose includes managing the U.S.-South Korean alliance, the size of the proportionate effort changes as well.
sources: Carl von Clausewitz, Vom Kriege, Buch 1, Kap. 1, §11 (1832); English translation by Howard & Paret, On War, Princeton UP, 1976

links.work: Annals of Gwanghaegun (Gwanghaegun ilgi); Han Myung-gi, Gwanghaegun: A Monarch of Outstanding Foreign Policy, 2000—the Battle of Sarhu (Simha) in 1619 and Gang Hong-rip's surrender
links.idea: In response to Ming China's demand for troops, King Gwanghae sent some 10,000 men under Gang Hong-rip (13,000 to 17,000 by some records), but at the Battle of Sarhu the Joseon army surrendered to the Later Jin after heavy losses. Tradition holds that Gwanghae issued a secret order to act according to how the situation developed. This dual track was used as a justification for the 1623 coup that installed King Injo (betrayal of loyalty to the Ming), and the invasions of 1627 and 1636 followed under the subsequent pro-Ming line.
links.fit: Qualifies the assessment that ranks the deployment of combat forces last. When an ally's demands are strong, refusing to send troops may be impossible, and the historical response combined a minimal deployment with avoidance of combat. The lesson of this case is that Gwanghae's dual track was brought down not by an external enemy but by attacks on his legitimacy at home.
links.limit: Whether Gwanghae's secret order existed and the nature of Gang Hong-rip's surrender remain disputed among scholars (Kye Seung-beom and others regard the secret order as a weakly supported later account). Seventeenth-century Joseon was a tributary state of the Ming, whereas South Korea is a sovereign ally; and the Later Jin was a neighbor, whereas Iran cannot invade South Korea directly.
sources: Annals of Gwanghaegun, entries for the third and fourth months of the 11th year of his reign (1619)
Han Myung-gi, Gwanghaegun: A Monarch of Outstanding Foreign Policy (Yeoksa Bipyeongsa, 2000)

links.work: Sung Chul Jung, "More Unstable Internally, More Reliable Externally: South Korea's Participation in the Vietnam War", Korean Journal of International Studies 14(1), 2016; Min Yong Lee, "The Vietnam War: South Korea's Search for National Security", in Kim & Vogel eds., 『The Park Chung Hee Era』, 2011
links.idea: From 1965 to 1973, South Korea sent up to about 50,000 troops to Vietnam (70 percent or more of the non-U.S. allied forces in Vietnam from 1965 to 1970); 3,094 were killed by February 1970. In return it gained about $516 million in economic benefits from 1965 to 1969, along with the continued presence of U.S. Forces Korea and continued aid.
links.fit: Qualifies the assessment that ranks the deployment of combat forces last. In modern South Korean history, combat deployments have been used to buy alliance commitments, and they did bring economic and security gains. The ranking of a combat deployment (H2) could change if it were judged not by the outcome of this war but by what it gains in the U.S.-South Korean relationship.
links.limit: Even while South Korean troops were in Vietnam, the Nixon administration withdrew the U.S. 7th Infantry Division from South Korea in 1971. Commitments bought with combat deployments did not last in the face of a shift in U.S. strategy. And unlike in Vietnam, Iran can detain South Korean ships directly, so the costs of a deployment would fall immediately on South Korea's domestic economy and shipping.

links.work: Dursun Peksen, "Better or Worse? The Effect of Economic Sanctions on Human Rights", Journal of Peace Research 46(1), 2009
links.idea: Economic sanctions worsen rather than improve human rights in target states, and the more comprehensive the sanctions, the greater the deterioration. Their burden falls more heavily on ordinary people and vulnerable groups than on the leadership.
links.fit: Supports the assessment (C5) that humanitarian aid for Iranians should be added to the diplomatic channel with Iran. There is substantial empirical evidence that blockades and sanctions wreck the lives of ordinary people before they wreck the regime. In 2023 South Korea took part in moving frozen funds through Switzerland to Qatar and placing them in restricted accounts for humanitarian purchases, so it has already operated, once, a structure that links humanitarian aid to a diplomatic channel.
links.limit: As Pape (1997) pointed out, sanctions so rarely achieve their aims that causal identification in research on their effects is difficult. And the Qatari accounts set up in 2023 were frozen again by U.S.-Qatari agreement after Hamas's attack on October 7. A humanitarian channel can be closed by decisions of the United States and the custodian country rather than South Korea.
sources: Robert A. Pape, "Why Economic Sanctions Do Not Work," International Security 22(2): 90-136, 1997

links.work: Nathan Nunn & Nancy Qian, "US Food Aid and Civil Conflict", American Economic Review 104(6), 2014
links.idea: An analysis of U.S. food aid from 1971 to 2006 found that increases in aid raised the incidence and lengthened the duration of civil conflict in recipient countries. The proposed mechanisms are that aid is captured by armed groups or becomes a resource for war.
links.fit: Qualifies the assessment (C5) that humanitarian aid should be added to the diplomatic channel with Iran. In a phase of regime collapse or civil war (I3), aid delivered through government channels could flow to the IRGC or its affiliated foundations (bonyads) and become a resource for war. Who receives the aid and how its distribution is monitored must be settled in advance.
links.limit: The robustness of this result is disputed. Christian and Barrett (2017 onward) argued that the effect is overestimated because of trend problems in the instrumental variable. The sample also consists mainly of food aid to low-income countries, which is hard to apply directly to medical aid to a middle-income country such as Iran.

links.work: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama (The Book of Government), late 11th century; the "circle of justice" maxim attributed to the Sasanian king Ardashir
links.idea: The "circle of justice" of Persian statecraft holds that there is no power without an army, no army without wealth, no wealth without cultivation, and no cultivation without justice and good government. The legitimacy of rule comes from keeping the people's livelihoods intact.
links.fit: Examines key assessment C5 on humanitarian aid through the logic of Iran's internal politics. Because humanitarian aid that sustains people's livelihoods keeps the links of the "circle of justice" intact, the Iranian regime could present it as part of its own capacity to govern, and it could ease popular discontent with the regime. Humanitarian aid thus helps the people while also shoring up the regime's legitimacy.
links.limit: Whether this effect harms South Korea depends on its goals. If South Korea's goal is not regime change but stability in the strait and the safety of its ships, the effect of averting an abrupt regime collapse (I3) could actually serve its interests. The maxim is, moreover, an ideal of medieval Persian kingship, not evidence that the modern Iranian regime actually follows it.
sources: Nizam al-Mulk, The Book of Government or Rules for Kings (Siyar al-Muluk / Siyasat-nama), trans. Hubert Darke (Routledge, 1960; reissued)
Jennifer London, "The Circle of Justice," History of Political Thought 32(3), 2011
Linda T. Darling, A History of Social Justice and Political Power in the Middle East: The Circle of Justice from Mesopotamia to Globalization (Routledge, 2013)

links.work: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence, Chapters 1–2, 1966
links.idea: The power to hurt is bargaining power when it is held in reserve rather than used. For compellence to succeed, the demand must be specific, and there must be an assurance that the pain will stop if the adversary complies.
links.fit: Provides theoretical support for the assessment that Iran profited from detentions without labeling South Korea an enemy. The detention of the Hankuk Chemi on January 4, 2021, was ostensibly about pollution but was tied to a specific demand concerning the funds frozen in South Korea, and the ship was reportedly released on April 9 in step with talks on unfreezing them. The combination of a specific demand and the prospect of release is classic compellence.
links.limit: In a phase of full-scale war, selective compellence is hard to distinguish from denial operations against the strait as a whole. In 2026, traffic through the strait has nearly stopped, so the risk to South Korean ships depends more on the state of the strait as a whole than on anything South Korea itself does. And since most of the funds frozen in South Korea were moved to Qatar in 2023, the motive for an asset-linked detention like that of 2021 depends on how many Iranian assets remain in South Korea.
sources: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence (Yale UP, 1966), Ch. 1-2

links.work: Navias and Hooton, Tanker Wars, 1996—Iran's choice of targets and the reflagging of Kuwaiti tankers (Operation Earnest Will, 1987–1988)
links.idea: In the tanker war, Iran's attacks concentrated on ships linked to Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, which supported Iraq. When Kuwaiti tankers were reflagged as American ships and placed under U.S. Navy escort, the Bridgeton, in the first convoy, struck a mine on July 24, 1987.
links.fit: Supports the assessment (C6) that the additional risk South Korea alone bears comes from action against Iranian assets and from keeping warships inside the strait. Iran chose its targets not by whether a country was hostile but by how much it was helping the enemy's war effort, and the very fact of providing military escort raised a ship's value as a target.
links.limit: The reflagging and escort operation, together with U.S. military responses such as Operation Praying Mantis in 1988, ultimately helped deter Iranian attacks. That a military presence did not only raise risks but also had a deterrent effect is a caution against a one-dimensional reading. Moreover, Iran was not then at war with the United States directly; in 2026 it is in direct combat with the United States, so any military force that enters the strait could become a target.

links.work: James D. Fearon, "Rationalist Explanations for War", International Organization 49(3), 1995
links.idea: One reason two rational states fail to find a bargain better than war is the commitment problem. If the balance of power shifts while an agreement is being implemented, the side that concedes first fears that the other will break its promises later.
links.fit: Supports the assessment (C7) that a phased agreement is not stable on its own. If Iran opens the strait first, it loses bargaining power; if the United States lifts the blockade and unfreezes assets first, it loses bargaining power. When Iran's security chief said in September 2026 that there would be no step-by-step process, he was expressing this problem. Simultaneous execution is a device for reducing it.
links.limit: Fearon's model assumes unitary rational actors. In practice, U.S.-Iranian agreements have collapsed because of domestic political turnover (the U.S. withdrawal from the JCPOA in 2018) or events on other fronts (the refreezing of the Qatari accounts after October 7, 2023). Commitment problems arise not only from shifts in power but from changes of government and linkages between events.

links.work: Virginia Page Fortna, 『Peace Time: Cease-Fire Agreements and the Durability of Peace』, 2004
links.idea: An analysis of all cease-fires in interstate wars ending between 1946 and 1994 found that the stronger the mechanisms in an agreement—demilitarized zones, third-party guarantees, peacekeeping and international monitoring, joint commissions for resolving disputes—the longer the cease-fire lasted. The parties invested in strong mechanisms precisely when peace was most precarious.
links.fit: Supports the conditions in key assessment C7: simultaneous execution of asset transfers through a third country, explicit inclusion of adjacent fronts, and phased implementation tied to IAEA verification. These conditions correspond, respectively, to Fortna's third-party guarantees, international monitoring, and clearly defined scope of agreement.
links.limit: Fortna's strongest mechanism, the demilitarized zone, is hard to apply to a maritime chokepoint: a strait is not a space where lines can be drawn and forces separated. Her sample also consists of conventional interstate wars and contains almost no multifront cease-fires involving nonstate proxies such as Hezbollah in Lebanon. The JCPOA had both IAEA verification and phased implementation, yet it collapsed with the U.S. withdrawal.

links.work: Radi Al Yasin, Sulh al-Hasan (The Peace Treaty of Imam Hasan), written in the early 1950s; Persian translation by Ali Khamenei, The Peace of Imam Hasan: The Most Glorious Heroic Flexibility in History, 1969; Khamenei's speech to the IRGC, September 17, 2013
links.idea: Shiite tradition interprets the peace that Imam Hasan made with Muawiya in 661 not as capitulation but as a tactical concession endured for a larger purpose. In translating the book, Khamenei gave it the phrase "heroic flexibility," and ahead of the 2013 nuclear talks he said that a wrestler may show flexibility for technical reasons without forgetting who his opponent is.
links.fit: Adds a basis in Iran's internal legitimacy to the assessment (C7) that both the United States and Iran want the strait reopened and that there is room for a deal. The Iranian regime already possesses a traditional vocabulary with which to justify a phased agreement without abandoning its ideology. The 2015 JCPOA was an application of it.
links.limit: The same tradition defines an agreement not as permanent peace but as a conditional truce, which actually reinforces the agreement's instability. Moreover, Ali Khamenei, who legitimized this vocabulary, was killed in the February 2026 strikes and succeeded by his son Mojtaba, and it has not been confirmed whether the new leadership will use the same logic. In September, Iran's security chief denied that there would be a step-by-step process.

theory.insight: The key point that emerges from the contrast with the tanker war is that the restraint that kept the strait open in the 1980s is gone in 2026. Then, because Iran's own oil exports had to pass through the same strait, it limited its attacks to within 2 percent of traffic. In 2026, Iran's exports are already blocked by the U.S. blockade, so closing the strait has become a bargaining tool that costs Iran almost nothing more. Reopening can therefore happen only if Iran's opening of the strait and the U.S. lifting of the blockade occur simultaneously, which means that a simultaneous exchange is structurally required, more than the phased agreement described in key assessment C7. Historically, moreover, what broke U.S.-Iranian agreements was less Iranian violations than changes of administration on the U.S. side (the 2018 withdrawal from the JCPOA) and events on other fronts (the refreezing of the Qatari accounts after October 7, 2023). The conditions for stability that key assessment C7 sets out (asset transfers, inclusion of adjacent fronts, IAEA verification) are mainly devices for securing Iranian compliance; a device to guard against reversal on the U.S. side is missing. This matters for South Korea. As the 2021 detention of the Hankuk Chemi shows, Iran targets countries that actually hold its assets, and since 2023 most of the funds frozen in South Korea have been moved to Qatar. South Korea's own asset risk will be determined by how many Iranian assets remain in South Korea and by whether, under a new deal, South Korea again serves as a custodian of assets or a transfer route. If the structure is one in which the blame falls on the custodian when a deal is reversed for reasons on the U.S. side, South Korea would reduce its risk by staying out of the transfer route or by completing any transfer irreversibly.
uncertain: The exact sample size of Horowitz and Reiter (2001) could not be confirmed from the abstract.

Whether Gholz and Press, "Protecting 'The Prize'" (Security Studies 19(3), 2010), treated a closure of Hormuz as an exception to market adjustment could not be confirmed from the original, so the link was excluded. The author of the rebuttal in the same journal, "The Enduring Vulnerabilities of Oil Markets" (22(1), 2013), could not be confirmed either.

The statement that the Hankuk Chemi's release was directly linked to an agreement to unfreeze $1 billion is based on Wikipedia; the South Korean government may not have officially acknowledged the link.

The size of Joseon's 1619 expeditionary force (10,000 to some 17,000) and the existence of Gwanghae's secret order vary by source and scholarly view. The original text in the National Institute of Korean History's historical content could not be checked because the site could not be reached.
The year of the first edition of the Arabic original of Sulh al-Hasan (reportedly the early 1950s) could not be confirmed. WikiShia lists only a 1991 Beirut edition.

The amount of Iranian assets remaining in South Korean financial institutions after the 2023 transfer to Qatar could not be confirmed.

items.q: What do you think about sending South Korean forces and assets to the Strait of Hormuz?
items.read: In a survey with three options conducted right after a South Korean ship was struck in May 2026, 48 percent favored a deployment premised on escorting South Korean ships, 16 percent a deployment to support U.S. military operations, and 24 percent opposed any deployment. Most South Koreans oppose a deployment, but when the mission is confined to escorting South Korean ships, support outnumbers opposition two to one; the line that divides public opinion is not whether to deploy but the nature of the mission. In the September survey, 69 percent of Democratic Party supporters opposed a deployment, while 50 percent of People Power Party supporters favored it.
items.caveat: Because the three surveys asked different questions, they are not joined into a single time series. Other organizations' September 2026 surveys also found opposition ahead (NBS: 45 percent to 36 percent; Hankyoreh and the Korean Association of Party Studies: 57.8 percent to 28.2 percent; both figures cited from press reports).

items.who: United States · Quinnipiac University, Gallup, Pew Research Center
items.q: Do you support U.S. military action against Iran?
items.latest: Quinnipiac, July 23–27, 2026; 963 respondents (most recent survey with the question on support for military action)
items.read: Support for U.S. military action against Iran fell short of a majority from the start of the war and has declined since. In the same July survey, 74 percent opposed sending ground troops; Gallup's June survey put approval at 34 percent; and in Pew Research Center's March survey, 59 percent said the use of force was the wrong decision. The administration faces domestic pressure to hurry toward a deal rather than escalate, which supports the motive for a phased agreement (C7).
items.caveat: The three organizations used different questions and populations (registered voters, adults), so their figures are not joined. Quinnipiac's September 2026 surveys used different questions and are not joined to the trend above. In the September 3–6 survey (970 respondents), 39 percent favored keeping forces in place while negotiating, 30 percent withdrawing without negotiations, and 22 percent expanding operations; in the September 24–27 survey (1,032 respondents), 28 percent approved of the president's handling of Iran (66 percent disapproved).

items.q: If the war with Iran has in fact ended, to what extent does that serve Israel's security interests?
items.series: Serves them little or not at all: total 59 · Jewish respondents about 64 · Arab respondents 48.5
items.read: Most Israelis do not see an end to the war as good for their security. This suggests the Israeli government has domestic room to unsettle a deal on adjacent fronts such as Lebanon, adding weight to the assessment (C7) that adjacent fronts must be written into any agreement.
items.caveat: No earlier comparison for the same question was found, and the question was not repeated later. In other Israel Democracy Institute questions, 38 percent said Israel's security situation had improved since the Iran war (June 28–July 1, 2026; 754 respondents), and the most common response on Iran, at 37 percent, was that Israel should avoid military involvement and respond only when attacked (July 28–August 2, 2026; 751 respondents).

items.q: Views on the ideal political system and on the U.S.-Israeli military operations
items.series: Prefer a change of political system about 47 · support the Islamic Republic 13 · see the military operations as aggression about 42
items.read: Far more respondents want a change of system than support the Islamic Republic, but more than 40 percent also regard the U.S.-Israeli attacks as aggression. Discontent with the regime does not translate into support for foreign military action.
items.caveat: Conducted online through VPNs by an organization based abroad, the survey skews toward internet users, and responding under an authoritarian regime carries risks. It is used only as an indicator of direction.
sources: GAMAAN (Group for Analyzing and Measuring Attitudes in Iran), released July 27, 2026, https://gamaan.org/

publics.read: South Korean public opinion accepts a deployment limited to escort duty and rejects participation in combat, which shows that the top-ranked combination—pursuing the Cheonghae Unit's expanded mission only if it is confined to waters outside the strait (C3) and ranking a combat deployment last (C4)—lies within the range of domestic acceptance. American opinion does not support escalation, and Israeli opinion does not welcome an end to the war. With the domestic conditions of the side that wants to hurry a deal and the side that could unsettle one pointing in opposite directions, public opinion also supports the assessment that mechanisms to protect a deal must be spelled out.
publics.watch: If support for a deployment overtakes opposition in Gallup Korea surveys—especially after another South Korean ship has been attacked—domestic constraints on expanding the Cheonghae Unit's mission will be considered to have eased.

congress.t: A deployment to the Strait of Hormuz
congress.stage: The government told the National Assembly that no decision had been made on a specific contribution (September 10). The Foreign Ministry reported that it had been reviewing options for a contribution since the crisis began and had been in contact with the United States, Britain and France (September 17).
congress.power: Sending South Korean troops abroad requires the National Assembly's consent (Article 60(2) of the Constitution).
congress.votes: With 161 seats, the Democratic Party holds a majority on its own and could pass a consent motion without other parties. The real variable is opinion within the ruling party.
congress.sides: Ruling-party members called for consultation with the Assembly in advance and said consent would not come easily unless the safety of South Korean citizens was assured. A Rebuilding Korea Party member suspected that the government's visits to the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain were preparation for a deployment, and People Power Party members criticized the government for not stating a clear position.
congress.next: Whether the government submits a consent motion for a new deployment or for changing an existing one.

congress.stage: The House has passed three resolutions in 2026 limiting the president's military action against Iran, but the Senate rejected one, 49–50, on September 24.
congress.power: Congress can try to limit military action through a resolution, but overriding a presidential veto takes two-thirds of both chambers. No military action has ever been halted by such a resolution.
congress.votes: Seven Republicans voted yes in the House on September 15; in the Senate on September 24, four Republicans voted yes and one Democrat voted no.
congress.next: Another attempt at a Senate vote; the balance of seats after the November 3 midterm elections.
