strategies.title: The U.S.-China contest over AI and chips: how long South Korea can use its leverage, and where
strategies.recipient: Government of the Republic of Korea
facts: During Xi Jinping's visit to the United States (September 24–25, 2026), Washington and Beijing pushed back the expiration of the tariff truce set by the Busan agreement (October 30, 2025) by two months, from November 10, 2026, to January 10, 2027. They also agreed on mutual tariff cuts worth about $30 billion and a new channel for dialogue on AI, with the next meeting set for November 2026. Neither side's statement mentioned any change to export controls on semiconductors.

In a Federal Register notice on September 2, 2025, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revoked the validated end-user (VEU) status of Samsung Electronics' NAND plant in Xi'an and SK hynix's DRAM plant in Wuxi and NAND plant in Dalian, effective December 31, 2025. On December 30, 2025, it issued annual equipment licenses valid only for 2026. The licenses cover only equipment needed to maintain and run existing lines, exclude tools for expansion or technology upgrades, and expire on December 31, 2026.

According to TrendForce (March 27, 2026), the Chinese plants accounted in 2025 for roughly 30 to 35 percent of Samsung Electronics' NAND output, 40 to 45 percent of SK hynix's NAND output, and 35 to 40 percent of SK hynix's DRAM output. Investment in 2025 rose 67.5 percent from the previous year at Samsung's Xi'an plant, to 465.4 billion won; 102 percent at SK hynix's Wuxi plant, to 581 billion won; and 52 percent at Dalian, to 440.6 billion won. The Wuxi plant moved its DRAM process from 1z to 1a.

Reuters reported on August 4, 2026 (U.S. time), that Samsung Electronics and SK hynix had for about two years been testing whether etching equipment from China's AMEC could be used in their Chinese plants. Both companies denied running such tests. The same report estimated that Chinese vendors would hold 25 to 30 percent of China's wafer-equipment market (about $28 billion) in 2026.

The Korea-U.S. Joint Fact Sheet (November 14, 2025) set the tariff on ordinary Korean goods at 15 percent. On Section 232 tariffs on semiconductors, the United States said it intends to provide terms "no less favorable than terms that may be offered in a future agreement covering a volume of semiconductor trade at least as large as Korea's." Korea's investment pledge to the United States totals $350 billion: $200 billion in strategic investment (capped at $20 billion a year) and $150 billion in shipbuilding cooperation.

On January 14, 2026, President Trump issued a Section 232 proclamation imposing a 25 percent tariff on a narrowly defined set of high-performance chips, including Nvidia's H200 and AMD's MI325X, effective January 15, 2026. The proclamation called for a report on the market for data-center semiconductors by July 1, 2026. On September 2, 2026, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick signaled a second phase that would broaden the tariffs, saying that companies that build in the United States would pay nothing and those that do not should expect to pay to enter the U.S. market. No rates or timetable have been announced.

In January 2026, Lutnick said: "Everyone who wants to build memory has two choices: They can pay a 100% tariff, or they can build in America." Yet South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said on August 19, 2026, that Korean companies have no plans to invest in memory production in the United States, and SK hynix's plant in Indiana (more than $4 billion) is an HBM packaging facility, not a wafer fab.

In Washington on September 3, 2026, Kim Jung-kwan, South Korea's minister of trade, industry and resources, said of U.S. semiconductor tariffs that Washington had already said it would provide treatment no less favorable than competing countries receive, and that discussions were under way in that spirit. The first project under Korea's U.S. investment pledge (a $22.3 billion gas-fired combined-cycle power plant in Texas) was reported to the National Assembly on September 22, 2026, but as of September 27 its formal announcement had been delayed by internal U.S. procedures.

After the U.S. Supreme Court struck down tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) on February 20, 2026, Washington imposed temporary tariffs under Section 122 of the Trade Act (February 24 to July 24, 2026) and then, from July 24, 2026, Section 301 tariffs, set at 12.5 percent for South Korea. Korean press reports say DRAM, NAND, and HBM are excluded. But the semiconductor findings of a Section 301 investigation into "structural excess capacity and production" covering 16 economies, including South Korea (opened March 11, 2026), have not yet been issued.

On December 8, 2025, President Trump allowed sales of the H200 to China on condition that the United States receive 25 percent of the revenue. A BIS rule in January 2026 shifted the licensing policy from a presumption of denial to case-by-case review, subject to conditions: sales to China capped at 50 percent of U.S. sales volume, third-party performance testing in the United States, and end-user certification.

In mid-January 2026, China's customs administration issued guidance that effectively barred imports of the H200, and the authorities told Chinese companies not to buy the chip except when unavoidable. ByteDance and Tencent each took first delivery of about 10,000 units in the summer of 2026, but Nvidia's data-center revenue from China remains below 1 percent of the total, and the company wrote down $400 million in H200 inventory.

On May 31, 2026, BIS issued guidance requiring export licenses for Nvidia Blackwell-class chips shipped to subsidiaries of China-headquartered companies located outside China, such as in Malaysia. The measure closes a workaround that opened after the AI Diffusion Rule was rescinded in May 2025.

A BIS rule of December 2, 2024, made exports of HBM (HBM2E and above) to China subject to licensing. SemiAnalysis estimated that Samsung shipped about 11.4 million HBM stacks to China, including about seven million in the month between the rule's announcement and its entry into force, and that China held an inventory of about 13 million foreign-made HBM stacks.

According to IDC data (reported by Reuters in April 2026), Chinese vendors held 41 percent and Nvidia 55 percent of China's AI accelerator market of about four million units in 2025, with Huawei shipping about 812,000 units. Bernstein projects the Chinese vendors' share will reach about 80 percent in 2026.

client.name: Government of the Republic of Korea
client.note: Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are private companies, so investment and the disposition of their plants are for the two companies to decide. The government's tools are trade negotiations, diplomacy, permits, fiscal measures, and approval of technology exports. The ranking of goals below is Clisa Geopolitics' interpretation, based on the government's statements that the dichotomy of anmi gyeongjung ("security with the United States, economy with China") no longer holds (August 2025 and June 2026) and that Korean companies have no plans to invest in memory production in the United States (August 19, 2026).

alts.name: Staying the course (keep the Chinese plants under annual licenses)
alts.desc: Run the Chinese plants at existing process nodes and existing capacity under the annual equipment licenses in effect since 2026. No expansion or upgrades; new advanced investment goes to Korea and to packaging in the United States. Negotiate tariffs case by case, relying on the "no less favorable" treatment clause of the Korea-U.S. agreement.

eff.safety: No change.
eff.living: Exports and jobs hold for now, but uncertainty over licenses and tariffs recurs every year.

alts.loser: Employees of the Chinese plants, whose fate hangs on the annual license renewal

G2.t: The Chinese plants fall further behind each year

G4.t: Operations continue, but depend on a license every year

alts.name: Align fully with U.S. controls and withdraw from the Chinese plants in stages
alts.desc: Conform in practice to U.S. export controls across the board, and wind down the Chinese plants over several years through output cuts, sales, and closures, with no new investment. Bring Korean exports of equipment and technology to China in line with U.S. standards.

eff.safety: No change.
eff.living: Relocating 30 to 45 percent of memory output brings costs and supply gaps along the way.

alts.loser: Local staff at the Chinese plants and Korean suppliers operating in China

G1.t: Maximizes trust within the control regime

G2.t: Hands the Chinese market to CXMT and YMTC

G4.t: Loses the Chinese plants and market

G5.t: Greatest risk of retaliation on rare earths and materials

alts.name: Get the renewal criteria for the Chinese plants in writing, and let the companies manage their own exposure
alts.desc: Since the 2026 licenses already bar expansion and upgrades, a pledge not to expand or upgrade would be no new concession. Instead, Seoul should lock in the scope of the process transitions already carried out (236-layer NAND at Xi'an, DDR5 at Wuxi) and ask in writing for the scope of maintenance and replacement equipment, the criteria for renewal review, and deadlines for issuing licenses. The share of production in China should be reduced as the companies' own risk management, not traded with Washington as a bargaining chip. TSMC, which has only about 3 percent of its capacity in China, received the same annual license for its Nanjing plant, so a multiyear license guarantee should not be expected.

eff.safety: No change.
eff.living: The Chinese plants lose value gradually, but an abrupt rupture is avoided.

alts.loser: Local jobs at the Chinese plants, which shrink over time

G1.t: Makes outcomes within the control regime more predictable

G5.t: Written criteria, once disclosed, could become a target under China's State Council Decree No. 835

ev.feas: Medium (Washington wants to keep its discretion to change license terms each year as leverage)

alts.prob: Medium (Washington wants to keep its discretion to change license terms each year as leverage)

alts.name: Bring Chinese equipment into the Chinese plants on a large scale
alts.desc: In case shipments of U.S. equipment are blocked, introduce etching and deposition tools from AMEC and other Chinese vendors as substitutes on a large scale. Reuters reported in August 2026 that the two companies had for about two years been testing Chinese equipment in preparation for U.S. restrictions; both companies denied it. Limited testing against the risk that maintenance or parts supply is cut off can be seen as insurance, but large-scale adoption is different in kind, because it puts the entire U.S. license at stake.

eff.safety: No change.
eff.living: The Chinese plants keep running, but if U.S. licenses are shaken, even domestic production is put at risk.

alts.loser: Workers at domestic plants hit by tighter U.S. licensing

G1.t: Hurts U.S. license reviews and sours congressional sentiment

G5.t: Eases equipment procurement, but only for the Chinese plants

alts.name: Use memory supply as leverage to trade investment for tariff relief, and keep front-end fabrication at home
alts.desc: Citing the HBM shortage and the "no less favorable" treatment clause of the Korea-U.S. agreement, win recognition for U.S. investment in packaging, R&D, foundry, power, and the like in exchange for tariff exemptions, while keeping front-end memory fabrication in Korea. Use the U.S.-Taiwan agreement (duty-free imports of up to 2.5 times the new U.S. production capacity under construction) as the benchmark. Use multiyear supply contracts signed during the boom with U.S. buyers (Nvidia and the hyperscalers) to lock in tariff and license terms, building a constituency in Washington with a stake in the supply of Korean memory.

eff.safety: No change.
eff.living: Export terms stabilize and domestic investment continues.

alts.loser: Domestic projects pushed back when funding for U.S. investment competes with investment at home

G1.t: Delivering on investment pledges builds trust in the alliance

ev.feas: Medium (collides head-on with the commerce secretary's principle that companies must build in America or pay tariffs)

alts.prob: Medium (collides head-on with the commerce secretary's principle that companies must build in America or pay tariffs)

alts.name: Build front-end memory fabs in the United States
alts.desc: As the commerce secretary demands, build DRAM and NAND wafer fabs in the United States and receive tariff exemptions. Construction costs are estimated at about twice those in Korea, and the fabs would take five years or more to come online.

eff.safety: No change.
eff.living: Tariff risk disappears, but domestic investment and jobs move to the United States.

alts.loser: Future jobs in Korea's semiconductor investment regions

G2.t: Higher costs and the burden of protecting technology

alts.name: Double insurance for supply chains: institutionalize Korea-China supply-chain dialogue and diversify critical minerals
alts.desc: Institutionalize the Korea-China supply-chain hotline and fast-track rare-earth licensing to manage in advance the risk of administrative delays in Chinese licenses, and expand stockpiles. In parallel, pursue the long-term task, which will take years, of reducing dependence on China for heavy rare earths (about 90 percent) through critical-minerals cooperation with Australia, the United States, and others. After 2010, it took Japan nearly five years to cut its dependence on China for rare earths from about 90 percent to about 60 percent. By not signing the G7 critical minerals declaration in June 2026, South Korea has already leaned toward dialogue with China.

G4.t: Opens a channel of communication with China

alts.desc: Join WAICO, launched on July 16, 2026, as an observer or in a similar capacity, as insurance for maintaining ties with the Chinese market. No one in South Korea has been found to advocate this publicly.

eff.living: If access to U.S. supply chains is restricted, exports and jobs are badly shaken.

alts.loser: Workers at chip and AI companies that depend on the U.S. market

alts.desc: The equipment and materials suppliers (Japan and the Netherlands) and the memory and foundry producers (South Korea and Taiwan) coordinate their responses to U.S. tariffs and demands for allied alignment, and share intelligence and stockpiles against Chinese retaliation.

responses.note: Assumes each counterpart responds as shrewdly as possible.

rows.USA: The State Department and congressional hawks welcome it. The White House, worried about a shock to memory supply and rising prices, is cautious about the pace of withdrawal.
rows.CHN: Delays export licenses for rare earths and gallium as a warning, and tries to absorb the departing plants' equipment and staff through acquisition offers.
rows.JPN: Sees Korean companies' exit from their Chinese plants as lower demand for Japanese equipment and materials.

rows.USA: BIS wants to keep its discretion to change license terms each year. It may partly accept written renewal criteria, but could take issue with the process transitions already carried out.
rows.CHN: Waits and watches as long as the plants keep running. If license criteria set in writing with Washington come to light, it could invoke State Council Decree No. 835 to challenge Korean companies' compliance with U.S. controls.
rows.JPN: No direct stake.

rows.USA: The most negative. Congress demands tighter license terms and limits on equipment servicing, and U.S. equipment makers push back as well.
rows.CHN: The option it welcomes most. It offers quiet support and refrains from public fanfare.
rows.JPN: Worries that its equipment will be replaced by Chinese tools in Korean plants.

rows.USA: The Commerce Department is likely to consider investment without front-end fabs insufficient. But the U.S.-Taiwan agreement and the "no less favorable" treatment clause make an outright rejection difficult, so the negotiation ultimately narrows to the size of the investment.
rows.CHN: Waits and watches. As long as the Chinese plants keep running, its interests do not collide.
rows.JPN: No direct stake.

rows.USA: Welcomes it and rewards it with tariff exemptions and subsidies.
rows.CHN: Criticizes it but refrains from direct retaliation, since U.S. fabs will take five years or more to come online and are compatible with keeping the Chinese plants.
rows.JPN: Japan, which has invited Korean companies to produce in Japan, ends up competing with the United States to attract production.

rows.USA: Welcomes minerals diversification but is wary if Korea-China dialogue looks like a back channel around U.S. controls.
rows.CHN: Responds eagerly to institutionalizing the dialogue, and may tighten enforcement against indirect imports routed through third countries.
rows.JPN: Welcomes minerals cooperation.

rows.USA: Pushes back hard and considers restricting supply-chain access and imposing penalties in licensing.
rows.CHN: Welcomes it loudly and offers rewards such as wider market access.
rows.JPN: Sees a crack in U.S.-Japan-South Korea coordination.

rows.USA: Welcomes it as cooperation among allies, but if the joint response turns into a common front in tariff negotiations, tries to split it into separate bilateral talks.
rows.CHN: Sees it as a U.S.-Japan-South Korea technology alliance and is wary. It is already enforcing a ban on exports of dual-use items to Japan (January 2026).
rows.JPN: Welcomes it. But Taiwan has already reached a separate agreement with the United States, so the four countries are out of step.

responses.lesson: A United States calculating as shrewdly as possible would not press South Korea on everything at once. It would work separate tracks: tariffs (the Commerce Department's Section 232 route), annual licenses (BIS, within Commerce), bloc cohesion (the State Department), and legislation on allied alignment (Congress), using a concession won on one track as a springboard for new demands on another. A China making the same calculation would not strike at South Korea as a whole but would keep it close, while using targeted measures to show where the red lines are, aimed at companies that cooperate with U.S. investigations or at statements about Taiwan. The costs South Korea bears will therefore come less from across-the-board retaliation than from the many separate negotiations each power opens and from targeted measures against individual companies.

items.means: Export controls (annual licenses, the Foreign Direct Product Rule), Section 232 tariffs, CHIPS Act subsidies, legislation on allied alignment
items.frame: Treats advanced AI computing power as a national-security matter and seeks to slow China's catch-up. It also treats chips as an industrial-policy project of moving production to the United States, and the Trump administration uses controls as a bargaining chip and a way to capture revenue (25 percent of H200 sales).

Bring semiconductor production, including memory, to the United States

items.strategy: Block leading-edge products and equipment while selling products a generation behind under conditions. Tie tariff exemptions to investment in the United States to draw production over, and keep allied companies' Chinese plants under annual licenses to freeze their technology level.

Conditional H200 licenses with 25 percent of revenue going to the U.S. government (2025-12-08; rule in January 2026)

syn.note: The ratings in the table (Preferred, Acceptable, Uncomfortable, Rejected) are provisional assessments of how readily each country's leadership would accept each of the four futures to 2030 (M1–M4).

reads.t: The future most deciding powers can accept is managed separation (M1).
reads.d: The U.S. administration holds on to both controls and deals, China believes time is on its side, and Japan and the Netherlands protect their companies' sales in China. The evidence: the U.S.-China summit in September 2026 extended the tariff truce to January 10, 2027, and kept chip controls off the agenda.

reads.t: South Korea's choices affect the price it pays in each future more than which future arrives.
reads.d: Which future arrives will turn on the struggle between Congress and the administration in Washington, extensions of the U.S.-China truce, and how fast CXMT catches up. What South Korea can change are the terms of U.S. equipment licenses and chip tariffs, and how hard the shock would be if rare-earth supplies were cut off.

reads.t: The future in which South Korea loses most depends on timing: through 2027, it is intensified pressure from both sides (M3), especially if U.S. tariffs force front-end memory fabrication to relocate; from 2028 on, it is accelerated Chinese substitution (M4).
reads.d: Chinese substitution proceeds in every future; M4 is the case in which it moves fast enough to change the game. New capacity at CXMT and YMTC is expected to be absorbed by Chinese AI demand through 2027, so what erodes first is not global prices but the share of the Chinese market held by the Korean plants. In the dispute that led to the 1986 U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Agreement, the biggest winner was a third producer outside the rules (South Korea in the 1990s); in the 2020s, Chinese companies occupy that position.

intent.note: In the table, "Said" means official announcements and statements, and "Did" means concrete measures that carry a cost. Only items relevant to this issue are included.
intent.read: In the United States, words (tighter controls) and deeds (allowing H200 sales, keeping controls off the agenda) diverge; in China, words (openness) and deeds (targeted coercion, stockpiling coercive tools) diverge. Washington's next move should therefore be read as depending on whether the administration or Congress takes the lead, and Beijing's on which line South Korea crosses.

why.risk: Uses the same value (50) as the Korean Peninsula issue.
why.gni: Uses the same basis as the Iran issue (2025 per capita gross national income).

wellbeing.status: Calculated for South Koreans only. Local staff at the Chinese plants and workers at suppliers will be added once the underlying data are confirmed.

facts.ROK: About one-quarter (2025 full year, $173.4 billion); 47.8% (September 1–20, 2026, monthly figure during the boom)
facts.src: Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources and Korea Customs Service statistics (as reported)

facts.k: Exports to China and to the United States
facts.src: Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources, monthly trade data

items.name: Managed separation
items.story: U.S. controls stay in place, and the annual licenses are renewed each year. Korea's plants in China make only limited process transitions with no expansion, and their share of total output declines gradually; chip tariffs settle into exemptions tied to investment in the United States. Washington and Beijing keep extending the tariff truce and leave rare-earth controls suspended. CXMT steadily gains share in commodity memory.
items.test: If none of the tests for transactional easing (M2), intensified pressure from both sides (M3), or accelerated Chinese substitution (M4) is met, the outcome counts as managed separation (M1). If several are met, M3 takes precedence, then M4, then M2.
signs: Renewal of the annual licenses
Another extension of the truce
Section 232 tariff exemptions tied to investment
items.why: Assumes South Koreans' incomes follow the baseline projection (57 million won per capita in 2030).

items.name: Transactional easing
items.story: Washington and Beijing strike a bigger deal that partly loosens AI chip sales and equipment controls, and process upgrades at Korean companies' Chinese plants are permitted. Rare-earth controls are withdrawn. Korean memory holds on to the Chinese market, but China catches up faster too.
items.test: By 2030, the United States permits process upgrades at Korean companies' Chinese plants or grants multiyear blanket licenses, and China withdraws its October 2025 expansion of rare-earth controls.
signs: Controls appear on the agenda of the U.S.-China AI dialogue
Multiyear licenses or restoration of validated end-user (VEU) status
items.why: Assumes the value of the Chinese market and the Chinese plants holds, so South Koreans' incomes run slightly above the baseline projection.

items.name: Intensified pressure from both sides
items.story: Congress legislates to force allies to join controls on China and equipment and services controls widen, or Section 232 tariffs are set high on memory, forcing front-end fabrication to move to the United States. China revives rare-earth controls and, invoking State Council Decree No. 835, targets companies that comply with U.S. controls. Korean companies are caught between the laws of the two countries.
items.test: By 2030, one of the following occurs: output at Korean companies' Chinese plants falls by half or more because of U.S. licensing problems; China maintains measures targeting a Korean chipmaker or its subsidiaries for six months or longer; or the United States imposes a tariff of 25 percent or more on memory without giving South Korea an investment-linked exemption.
signs: Passage of the MATCH Act
Delayed or tightened 2027 licenses
Application of Decree No. 835
The Section 232 tariff rate on memory
items.why: Assumes South Koreans' incomes run about 4 percent below the baseline projection because of losses in the Chinese market and plants, cutoffs in materials supply, and tariffs. This figure is an assumption of this analysis, not survey data. Scarcer memory and higher prices offset part of the loss.

items.name: Accelerated Chinese substitution
items.story: Chinese substitution proceeds in every future, but in this one its speed changes the game. From 2028 on, CXMT and YMTC win large shares of commodity memory, and HBM, too, reaches self-sufficiency. Korean memory's share of the Chinese market shrinks first, then commodity memory prices fall, and the value of the Chinese plants quietly collapses.
items.test: In any quarter of 2029, Chinese companies' combined share of global DRAM revenue reaches 25 percent or more, or YMTC's share of NAND revenue reaches 25 percent or more (per Counterpoint or TrendForce).
signs: CXMT begins volume production of HBM3
CXMT's share tops 15 percent
Chinese AI accelerators adopt domestic HBM
items.why: Assumes falling commodity memory prices and market share for Korean companies leave South Koreans' incomes about 2.5 percent below the baseline projection. This figure is an assumption of this analysis.

futures.note: Probabilities and inputs are the analyst's judgment estimates, with ranges in parentheses. Because South Korea's choices barely change which future arrives, no separate probabilities are given for the case in which the recommendations are followed. What South Korea's choices change is the price it pays in each future.

expect.note: The expected value is the sum of each future's 2030 index value weighted by that future's probability. It is calculated separately for each dimension, such as life and safety or livelihood, and the dimensions are not added together.
expect.read: South Koreans' expected livelihood score is 94.0, above the baseline (93.5), but it stays at 93.8 under intensified pressure from both sides (M3). This issue's impact falls mainly on livelihoods, through an export structure in which semiconductors account for about a quarter of annual exports and close to half of monthly exports during the boom. The harm to local staff at the Chinese plants and to small and midsize manufacturers that depend on materials does not show up in this average.

ranked.t: Build around a deal trading U.S. investment for tariff relief (A4) while keeping front-end memory fabrication at home, and use multiyear supply contracts signed with U.S. buyers during the boom to create a constituency in Washington with a stake in the supply of Korean memory. On the Chinese plants, offer no new concessions; ask Washington to put renewal-review criteria and licensing deadlines in writing, and let the companies manage their own exposure (A2). Prepare for rare-earth and materials risk through Korea-China dialogue and stockpiles in the short term and minerals diversification in the long term (A6). The combination aims to lock in the terms of U.S. chip tariffs and equipment licenses for the Chinese plants while the HBM shortage lasts.
Coordination with Japan, Taiwan, and the Netherlands (A8) is a supporting tool. Taiwan has already reached a separate agreement with the United States, so the room for a common front is narrow.
Staying the course (A0) leaves Seoul dragged along by annual license renewals and tariff talks, and wastes the window in which the HBM shortage gives it favorable bargaining conditions.

Front-end fabs in the United States (A5) are the last card, to be played if Section 232 tariffs on memory are set high. Played first, it would give away the domestic production base and still lose leverage in tariff talks. After the United States imposed antidumping duties on Korean DRAM in 1993, Korean companies built DRAM plants in the United States, but those plants were later closed or converted to other uses.
Full withdrawal (A1) brings the cost of relocating 30 to 45 percent of memory output and invites rare-earth retaliation. It should not be chosen unless Washington forces it.

Large-scale adoption of Chinese equipment (A3) would put the entire U.S. equipment license at risk for the sake of protecting the Chinese plants. It should be distinguished from limited testing against disruptions in maintenance and parts supply.
Joining WAICO (A7) ranks last. It gains nothing to offset the cost of losing access to U.S. supply chains.

rank2.tension: Korean companies' Chinese plants carried out process transitions in 2025–2026 (236-layer NAND at Xi'an, DDR5 at Wuxi), which already sit uneasily with BIS's policy of allowing no upgrades. The harder Seoul pushes for written renewal criteria, the more these transitions surface as an issue; and the more closely companies follow written U.S. criteria, the more that compliance could become grounds for sanctions under China's State Council Decree No. 835. No established procedure settles the line between a permitted process transition and a prohibited upgrade.
rank2.undecided: The government cannot make investment decisions on the companies' behalf. The disposition of the Chinese plants and the form of U.S. investment and supply contracts will ultimately be decided by the two companies' boards, and how to divide funding between U.S. and domestic investment is for the National Assembly and the public to decide.

human.note: Reexamines the strategy rankings from the standpoint of individual lives.

items.clisa: Urge the companies to match the pace at which they reduce production in China to the time needed to adjust local employment, and put in place support for expatriate managers facing legal risk (China's State Council Decree No. 835).
items.cost: Production in China is reduced more slowly.
items.gain: Individuals caught between U.S. and Chinese law are spared sudden layoffs and legal disputes.

items.clisa: Design rare-earth and materials stockpiles and emergency licensing channels so that small and midsize manufacturers can use them before large companies.
items.cost: Funding for stockpiles and allocation procedures.
items.gain: Keeps the shock of licensing delays from falling hardest on the companies with the least bargaining power and on their workers.

items.clisa: Same assessment. If the card must be played, a jobs plan for the domestic investment regions should come with it.
items.gain: Protects future jobs in the domestic investment regions.

conclusions.t: The most likely future through 2030 is managed separation (40 percent, range 30–50 percent). Intensified pressure from both sides is put at 25 percent, accelerated Chinese substitution at 20 percent, and transactional easing at 15 percent.
conclusions.why: The U.S. administration wants to hold on to both controls and deals (allowing H200 sales, keeping chip controls off the agenda at the September summit), while Congress seeks to legislate allied participation in controls on China, so policy tilts decisively in neither direction. In their first year (2026), the annual U.S. licenses allowed existing production to continue, and the U.S.-China tariff truce keeps being extended for short periods (from November 10, 2026, to January 10, 2027). The thresholds for intensified pressure from both sides (M3) are measures targeting a Korean chipmaker that last six months or longer, a halving of output because of licensing problems, or memory tariffs of 25 percent or more with no investment-linked exemption.
conclusions.flip: If the annual licenses for 2027 are denied or even the maintenance of existing processes is restricted, or if the MATCH Act is enacted, intensified pressure from both sides (M3) becomes the most likely future.

conclusions.t: The leverage of Korean memory moves differently by segment. In commodity DRAM and in the Chinese market it is already shrinking, but HBM's leverage over U.S. AI demand may hold or grow through 2027, while the shortage lasts. The terms of tariffs and licenses need to be locked in before new HBM supply catches up with demand, which current reporting suggests will happen in 2027–2028.
conclusions.why: SK hynix began volume shipments of HBM4 in the second quarter of 2026, both companies have said the shortage will last through 2027, and there are reports that their 2027 capacity is already sold out. Meanwhile, CXMT's DRAM share rose from 4 percent to 10 percent in a year (9.5 percent by TrendForce's count), and the current price surge earned CXMT a net profit of 77.6 billion yuan in the first half of 2026. CXMT's HBM3 yields remain at 25 to 30 percent. Apple is seeking assurances that CXMT will not be added to the Entity List, a sign that U.S. buyers, too, want to keep alternative sources open. Greater leverage, however, does not automatically translate into favorable terms: even with South Korea holding the edge in memory, Washington has not withdrawn its threat of memory tariffs.
conclusions.flip: If CXMT's HBM volume production is confirmed within 2027 or the memory shortage eases before 2027, the timeline moves earlier. If CXMT's share stalls in the low teens, it moves later.

conclusions.t: Toward South Korea as a whole, China's default is co-optation, but it pairs this with tools for pressuring selected companies in ways it can deny. Its threshold for applying pressure is lower than formal South Korean alignment with U.S. equipment controls on China: measures targeting particular companies or sectors could follow merely from Korean companies cooperating with U.S. investigations or defense policy, or from the South Korean government making remarks about Taiwan.
conclusions.why: China's recommendations for its 15th Five-Year Plan call for both self-reliance and attracting foreign investment, and keeping the Korean plants in place serves both. In its retaliation over THAAD in 2016–2017, China left alone the Korean memory on which its own manufacturers depended, and in its 2023 sanctions on Micron, it targeted only an American company, choosing products for which alternative suppliers existed. But its sanctions on Hanwha Ocean's U.S. subsidiaries in October 2025 were imposed on the grounds that the company had cooperated with a U.S. Section 301 investigation under the Trade Act, and after the Japanese prime minister's remarks on Taiwan, Japan faced a ban on dual-use exports (2026-01) and an antidumping case on chip materials (2026-09). South Korea did not sign the G7 critical minerals declaration in June 2026, a sign that China's co-optation and latent threats already constrain Seoul's choices. Memory was spared retaliation in 2017 because there was no alternative supplier, and that irreplaceability is eroding as CXMT grows.
conclusions.flip: If China puts a Korean chipmaker or its subsidiaries on a sanctions or control list, or singles out South Korea for delays in rare-earth licenses, coercion should be treated as its default move.

conclusions.t: The Chinese plants of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are leverage for both Washington and Beijing. Since U.S. equipment licenses became annual, the plants' value is reset each year by U.S. discretion and the U.S.-China truce, and the process transitions already carried out (236-layer NAND at Xi'an, DDR5 at Wuxi) could become an issue in the 2027 license renewal.
conclusions.why: By revoking validated end-user (VEU) status and switching to one-year licenses, Washington gained a tool for adjusting the terms every year, and it gave TSMC's Nanjing plant, which accounts for only about 3 percent of TSMC's capacity, the same one-year license. Samsung's Xi'an plant has moved to 236-layer NAND and SK hynix's Wuxi plant to DDR5, and the companies raised their 2025 investment in China by 52 to 102 percent. With Decree No. 835, China created a legal basis for sanctioning companies that comply with U.S. controls. As the Nexperia (Netherlands) and Hanwha Ocean cases show, measures against companies from countries caught between Washington and Beijing were lifted thanks to agreements between the U.S. and Chinese leaders rather than to the responses of those countries.
conclusions.flip: If Washington restores multiyear blanket licenses or a status equivalent to VEU, or if a provision is enacted that excludes by law the Chinese plants of companies whose parents are headquartered outside countries of concern (such as Section 6 of the amended MATCH Act), the premise of year-to-year discretion no longer holds.

conclusions.t: The top-ranked combination builds around a deal trading U.S. investment for tariff relief (A4) while keeping front-end memory fabrication at home, and uses multiyear supply contracts with U.S. buyers to create a constituency in Washington with a stake in the supply of Korean memory. On the Chinese plants, it offers no new concessions, asks Washington for written license-renewal criteria, and leaves the companies to manage the share of production in China themselves (A2). It prepares for rare-earth and materials risk through dialogue and stockpiles in the short term and diversified sourcing in the long term (A6). Large-scale adoption of Chinese equipment (A3) and joining WAICO (A7) rank last.
conclusions.why: Ranking the South Korean government's goals as alliance trust, technological lead, and domestic production base, this combination loses heavily on none of them. Because a ban on expansion and upgrades at the Chinese plants is already a condition of the U.S. licenses, a pledge not to expand or upgrade is not a card to trade. And as Britain's abandonment of the China differential in 1957 and the removal of the GAIN AI Act from the National Defense Authorization Act in 2025 after lobbying by Nvidia show, what actually moved controls was commercial interest more than exchanges between governments. That the Netherlands and Japan negotiated a narrower scope when they joined U.S. equipment controls on China in 2023 suggests that South Korea, too, has room to win written licensing criteria, if not multiyear guarantees. The experience of absorbing Japan's 2019 export restrictions on chip materials through alternative sourcing shows that alternative sourcing works; that it took Japan nearly five years after 2010 to reduce its dependence on China for rare earths shows that diversification is no short-term fix.
conclusions.flip: If Section 232 tariffs on memory are set high and investment-linked exemptions recognize only front-end fabs, front-end fabs in the United States (A5) should be reconsidered.

conclusions.t: U.S. demands are not one demand. The Commerce Department's tariff-and-investment track (Section 232) seeks relocation of production; the export-control track run by BIS, also within Commerce, seeks to block expansion and upgrades at the Chinese plants; the White House wants deals; and Congress wants allied alignment written into law. A concession on one track does not automatically reduce demands on another, and trades across tracks happen only rarely, by presidential decision.
conclusions.why: Even after South Korea concluded its investment-and-tariff agreement with the United States on July 30, 2025, BIS announced the revocation of VEU status on August 29, and the commerce secretary demanded in January and on September 2, 2026, that memory plants move to the United States. The White House allowed H200 sales and took controls off the negotiating table at the September summit. The MATCH Act passed the House Foreign Affairs Committee 44–0 on April 22, 2026, but floor passage has not been confirmed. Nvidia succeeded in getting the GAIN AI Act dropped from the National Defense Authorization Act.
conclusions.flip: If the president announces chip tariffs and controls bundled in a single agreement, the premise of track-by-track negotiation no longer holds.

conclusions.t: Measured by individual lives, this issue's impact falls mainly on livelihoods. The first to be shaken are local staff and expatriate managers at the Chinese plants, and small and midsize manufacturers that use rare earths and materials.
conclusions.why: Semiconductors accounted for about a quarter of South Korea's exports in 2025 and close to half of monthly exports in the second half of 2026, at the height of the memory boom, so the shock could be larger if intensified pressure coincides with a turn in the price cycle. This analysis assumes that if intensified pressure from both sides (M3) materializes, South Koreans' incomes will be about 4 percent below the baseline projection. The shock of the THAAD retaliation, too, reached the livelihoods of local staff and suppliers first, and the shock of the rare-earth crisis was passed on to downstream users through prices.

predictions.q: By the end of January 2027, the United States issues 2027 equipment licenses for all of Samsung's Xi'an plant and SK hynix's Wuxi and Dalian plants
By the end of June 2027, Samsung Electronics or SK hynix formally announces construction of a memory wafer fab in the United States
predictions.note: A sign that the investment-for-tariffs trade (A4) is blocked

predictions.q: By the end of June 2027, China's Ministry of Commerce adds a Korean company or its subsidiary to a control or sanctions list, or reinstates the sanctions on Hanwha Ocean's subsidiaries
predictions.note: A sign that the assessment that China singles out particular companies for pressure (C3) is being borne out

falsify: If China puts a Korean chipmaker on a sanctions list or singles out South Korea for delays in rare-earth licenses, the assessment of China's response (C3) and the supply-chain double insurance (A6) within the top-ranked combination will be reconsidered.
If Section 232 tariffs on memory are set high and only front-end fabs among U.S. investments qualify for exemptions, front-end fabs in the United States (A5) will move up the ranking.
If a blockade or quarantine begins in the Taiwan Strait, this issue will follow the course of the Taiwan Strait issue.

counter.name: China (AI and Chips)
counter.note: This evaluation is not a recommendation to China. It is "China's best move" judged against goals drawn from China's own documents and actions. The goals are taken from the Outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan, adopted by the National People's Congress in March 2026, and the readout of the Korea-China summit on January 5, 2026; their order is Clisa Geopolitics' interpretation.

goals.t: High-level self-reliance and strength in science and technology
goals.d: Achieve decisive breakthroughs across the entire chain of core technologies, including integrated circuits, through "extraordinary measures." Designates semiconductors as a pillar industry.
goals.src: Outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (adopted by the National People's Congress, 2026-03): "采取超常规措施，全链条推动集成电路…关键核心技术攻关取得决定性突破" (take extraordinary measures to drive decisive breakthroughs across full chains in integrated circuits and other core technologies). The first task in the 15th Five-Year Plan for the electronic information manufacturing industry, issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the National Development and Reform Commission (2026-09-15), is a full-chain push on integrated circuits. https://www.jingyuan.gov.cn/zfxxgk/bmhxzxxgk/xzxxgk/xlx/fdzdgknr/ghjh/art/2026/art_d8d5760fb44d4717b30a46328dc7be44.html ; https://www.nbd.com.cn/articles/2026-09-15/4582184.html

goals.t: Self-reliance, control, and security in industrial and supply chains
goals.d: Build systems for assessing and responding to supply-chain security risks, and keep strengthening China's competitive edge in rare earths, rare metals, and the like. Improve the export-control system.
goals.src: 15th Five-Year Plan outline: "提升产业链自主可控水平" (raise the level of self-reliance and control in industrial chains), "持续增强稀土、稀有金属、超硬材料等竞争优势" (keep strengthening competitive advantages in rare earths, rare metals, superhard materials, and the like), "完善出口管制体系" (improve the export-control system). https://www.jingyuan.gov.cn/zfxxgk/bmhxzxxgk/xzxxgk/xlx/fdzdgknr/ghjh/art/2026/art_d8d5760fb44d4717b30a46328dc7be44.html

goals.t: High-standard opening up and attracting foreign investment
goals.d: Attract and use more foreign investment, and fully implement national treatment for foreign-invested enterprises. The Chinese fabs of Samsung and SK are sources of jobs, tax revenue, exports, and technology spillovers.
goals.src: 15th Five-Year Plan outline: "更大力度吸引和利用外资" (step up efforts to attract and use foreign investment), "全面落实外资企业国民待遇" (fully implement national treatment for foreign-invested enterprises). https://www.jingyuan.gov.cn/zfxxgk/bmhxzxxgk/xzxxgk/xlx/fdzdgknr/ghjh/art/2026/art_d8d5760fb44d4717b30a46328dc7be44.html

goals.t: Prevent U.S.-led bloc formation and oppose protectionism
goals.d: Keep South Korea from being fully absorbed into a U.S. technology bloc, and draw it into a front for multilateralism and against protectionism. Offer WAICO as an alternative framework.
goals.src: Xi Jinping–Lee Jae-myung meeting (2026-01-05), Chinese readout: both countries "should stand firmly on the right side of history and make correct strategic choices"; China and the ROK "should jointly oppose protectionism, practice true multilateralism." https://www.fmprc.gov.cn/eng/xw/zyxw/202601/t20260105_11806810.html ; https://english.www.gov.cn/news/202607/17/content_WS6a59a226c6d00ca5f9a0c432.html

goals.d: Fully implement the AI Plus initiative and explore paths to AGI. Securing HBM and other high-performance memory is the bottleneck.
goals.src: 15th Five-Year Plan outline: "全面实施‘人工智能+’行动" (fully implement the AI Plus initiative). https://triviumchina.com/research/chinas-15th-five-year-plan-puts-ai-and-semiconductors-at-the-center-of-tech-self-reliance/

goals.t: Stability in Northeast Asia and managing ties with South Korea
goals.d: Safeguard peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and in Northeast Asia, and extend Korea-China industrial-chain cooperation to emerging fields such as AI and green industries.
goals.src: Xi Jinping–Lee Jae-myung meeting (2026-01-05): "safeguard peace and stability of Northeast Asia"; "deeply integrated industrial and supply chains." https://www.fmprc.gov.cn/eng/xw/zyxw/202601/t20260105_11806810.html

alts.name: Status quo: selective conciliation while stockpiling tools
ev: No direct effect on the pace of self-reliance
Korean fabs keep supplying Chinese downstream industries, and rare-earth leverage is preserved
Signals that foreign investment is welcome to stay
With stable relations, South Korea keeps hedging, delaying its full absorption into the U.S. technology bloc
HBM remains blocked by U.S. controls
Fits the momentum of shuttle diplomacy between the two leaders
alts.feas: Very high. It costs almost nothing and is already under way.

alts.name: Active co-optation: market and investment incentives and offers of institutional cooperation
ev: Gains technology spillovers as Korean fabs expand local sourcing and equipment testing
Korean fabs staying in China contribute to supply stability
Precisely fits the goal of attracting foreign investment
Strengthens the view in South Korea that the Chinese market cannot be given up
alts.feas: High. Tools include the second phase of the Korea-China FTA, dialogue on export controls, and easing visa rules and curbs on Korean pop culture. But because U.S. controls determine South Korea's choices, the effect is limited.

alts.name: Warning signals and administrative delays
ev: Displays leverage through delays in rare-earth licenses
Deterrent and backlash effects cancel out
alts.feas: High. As the 63 percent drop in South Korea's imports of samarium for defense use after China placed heavy rare earths under licensing in April 2025 shows, this can be done without formal sanctions.

alts.name: Targeted sanctions on specific Korean companies (the Hanwha model)
ev: Sends a warning to foreign-invested companies in general
Sets an example but pushes South Korea toward the United States
Creates uncertainty in sourcing Korean memory
alts.feas: Medium. There is a precedent: sanctions on five U.S. subsidiaries of Hanwha Ocean in October 2025 (suspended for one year from November 2025). Targets tend to be limited to subsidiaries with U.S. ties.

alts.name: Across-the-board economic retaliation (THAAD-style)
ev: Chinese industry takes a hit as supplies of Korean materials and memory are cut off
Accelerates the flight of foreign investment
Pushes South Korea decisively into the U.S. camp
Sourcing of memory for AI servers worsens
alts.feas: Low. There is the precedent of the THAAD retaliation in 2016–2017, but semiconductors are something China cannot replace. It would be considered only if South Korea crossed a line on Taiwan or on export controls against China.

alts.name: Localization pressure and faster domestic substitution
ev: Korean fabs' adoption of Chinese equipment and preferential treatment for CXMT and YMTC directly speed up self-reliance
Raises the level of self-reliance and control
Could look like discrimination against foreign-invested companies
Anchoring Korean fabs in China's ecosystem is offset by heightened U.S. wariness
If done quietly, little effect on the relationship
alts.feas: High. Procurement preferences, subsidies, and encouragement to test domestic equipment are already in place. The testing of AMEC equipment by Korean companies reported by Reuters (which both companies deny) can be seen as one result.

alts.name: Acquiring Korean assets in China and absorbing their workforce
ev: Gains fab and packaging facilities along with operating staff and know-how in one stroke
Puts production capacity under Chinese ownership
Looks like a case of foreign investment pulling out
Turns South Korea's exit from China to China's advantage
Depends on how the deal is structured
alts.feas: Low to medium. Chinese funds and companies are mentioned as potential buyers of a stake in the Chongqing packaging plant, but the sale of a front-end fab is blocked by the South Korean government's approval requirement for exports of national core technologies and by the risk of U.S. sanctions.

ranked.t: Lead with co-optation to keep South Korea close (J1) and selective conciliation (J0), and show the threshold with targeted sanctions (J3) on individual companies that cooperate with U.S. investigations and controls. This is the move that serves China's goals of technological self-reliance (G1), self-reliant supply chains (G2), and attracting foreign investment (G3) at once, without damaging relations with South Korea as a whole.

Expand the adoption of Chinese equipment and materials (J5) through procurement preferences and subsidies. If Reuters' report is accurate, the Korean plants' testing of Chinese equipment is a hedge the companies chose themselves, so China has no reason to publicize it.
Keep warning signals such as licensing delays (J2) in reserve, for use when South Korea crosses a line. They require no formal sanctions.
Treat the acquisition of Korean assets and absorption of their workforce (J6) as an opportunity when assets come up for sale.
THAAD-style across-the-board retaliation (J4) ranks last, because semiconductors are something China cannot yet replace with its own products.

counter.read: The earlier estimate of responses (step 5) assumed China would retaliate if South Korea aligned with the United States. Judged by China's own goals, however, its best move toward South Korea as a whole is co-optation, not across-the-board coercion. Even in its THAAD retaliation, China left alone the Korean memory on which its own manufacturers depended. But China does not choose between co-optation and coercion; it uses both. The sanctions on Hanwha Ocean's U.S. subsidiaries (October 2025) were triggered solely by one company's cooperation with a U.S. Section 301 investigation, and Japan faced a ban on dual-use exports and an antidumping case on chip materials after its prime minister's remarks on Taiwan. China's threshold for coercion is lower than formal South Korean alignment with U.S. equipment controls on China, and the more substitution capacity CXMT acquires, the more memory itself becomes a potential target.

pairs: South Korea
A4 + A2 + A6 (investment-for-tariffs trade with multiyear supply contracts, written renewal criteria, supply-chain insurance)
China
J0 + J1 (+ J3) (co-optation and selective conciliation, targeted sanctions on companies that cooperate with the United States)
United States (from the deciding-powers table)
Uses tariffs to win production in the United States and annual licenses to block expansion and upgrades at the Chinese plants, while Congress pushes to write allied alignment into law
twoway.equilibrium: Washington and Beijing both prefer that Korean companies' Chinese plants keep running without expansion rather than close. Washington preserves supply stability while freezing the plants' technology level; Beijing holds on to foreign capital and output until CXMT and YMTC can meet domestic demand. For China, this coexistence is merely a choice for the transition period. The current state is not a complete freeze but a "limited coexistence," in which limited process transitions continue within the scope of existing equipment, and the point where those transitions collide with BIS's policy of allowing no upgrades could become the issue in the 2027 renewal. Two deadlines coincide: the expiration of the annual U.S. licenses on December 31, 2026, and the end of the U.S.-China tariff truce on January 10, 2027.
twoway.zopa: South Korea's room for a deal with Washington does not lie in a pledge not to expand or upgrade. A ban on expansion and upgrades is already a condition of the U.S. licenses, so it is no new concession, and TSMC, which has held its exposure in China to about 3 percent of its capacity at Nanjing, received only the same annual license. The room lies in two places. One is to get in writing at least the review criteria and issuance deadlines within the discretion the U.S. government holds each year. The other is commercial interests within the United States. As the collapse of COCOM's China differential in 1957, the withdrawal of the Siberian pipeline sanctions in 1982, and the removal of the GAIN AI Act from the National Defense Authorization Act in 2025 show, it was commercial interests that actually moved controls. Multiyear supply contracts signed with U.S. buyers during the boom create a constituency in Washington with a stake in the supply of Korean memory.
traps: China's State Council Decree No. 835 allows compliance with U.S. controls by companies in China to be treated as grounds for sanctions. The more closely Korean companies' Chinese plants observe U.S. license conditions, the greater their risk of violating Chinese law.

Bringing in Chinese equipment on a large scale to protect the Chinese plants (A3) would unsettle the entire U.S. equipment license. Equipment is where what the two countries want from the Korean plants collides most directly.

Greater leverage does not automatically translate into favorable terms. Even with South Korea holding the edge in memory, Washington has not withdrawn its threat of memory tariffs. And like the price floor in the 1986 U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Agreement, the current price surge cuts both ways: it is funding CXMT's catch-up (net profit of 77.6 billion yuan in the first half of 2026).

brief.q: Caught between U.S. tariffs and controls on one side and China's market and minerals on the other, when and where should South Korea use the leverage of memory?
brief.a: Through 2027, while the HBM shortage lasts, Seoul should lock in the terms of U.S. chip-tariff exemptions in return for recognition of its U.S. investment, and keep front-end memory fabrication at home. Multiyear supply contracts with Nvidia and other U.S. buyers would create a constituency in Washington with a stake in the supply of Korean memory. On the Chinese plants, Seoul should offer no new concessions and ask Washington for written license-renewal criteria, while the companies manage the share of production in China themselves. For rare earths and materials, it should rely on dialogue with China and stockpiles in the short term and on diversified sourcing in the long term. Large-scale adoption of Chinese equipment, or joining the China-led World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO), would put the entire U.S. equipment license at risk.
brief.eq: Washington and Beijing both prefer that the Chinese plants of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix keep running without expansion rather than shut down. The value of this "limited coexistence" will be reset at two points: when the annual U.S. licenses expire at the end of 2026, and when the U.S.-China tariff truce ends in January 2027.
brief.human: This issue could shake South Koreans' livelihoods. Semiconductors made up about a quarter of South Korea's exports in 2025 and close to half of monthly exports during the boom, so stronger U.S. and Chinese pressure would lower the income outlook for South Koreans as a whole. The first to be shaken are local staff and expatriate managers at the Chinese plants, and small and midsize manufacturers that use rare earths and materials.

items.name: COCOM multilateral export controls, the collapse of the "China differential," and the Toshiba-Kongsberg affair
items.format: A gentlemen's agreement, not based on any treaty, launched under U.S. leadership in January 1950. Members set lists of strategic goods by unanimity, and each country enforced them under its own domestic law. In 1952, CHINCOM was created to apply stricter controls on China than on the Soviet Union (the "China differential"), and Japan joined the same year.
items.outcome: When Britain unilaterally abandoned the stricter controls on China in May 1957, other European countries followed, and the differential effectively disappeared. In 1987 it came to light that between 1982 and 1984 Toshiba Machine had used disguised transactions to deliver eight machine tools fitted with Kongsberg numerical controllers to the Soviet Union; Toshiba's chairman and president resigned, Japan stiffened penalties under its Foreign Exchange Act, and Congress imposed sanctions restricting imports of Toshiba products. COCOM was dissolved in March 1994 and replaced in 1996 by the less binding Wassenaar Arrangement.
items.why: Cohesion held only when the threat perception was shared and Washington compensated allies' commercial losses with aid and market access. Unanimity and uneven national enforcement made leakage constant, and when security tensions eased, commercial interests outran controls. The Toshiba affair is a case in which the threat of U.S. retaliation after detection forced an ally to tighten enforcement.
items.differs: The communist bloc then was a separate bloc cut off from Western economies, whereas in 2026 China is one of South Korea's largest markets, absorbing about a fifth of its total exports, and a major buyer of its chips. The countries targeted then had no means of retaliation, whereas China today holds counter-control tools such as rare earths and gallium. South Korea was not a member of COCOM; it is now a member of the Wassenaar Arrangement.

items.name: The 1980 grain embargo against the Soviet Union and the 1982 extraterritorial sanctions on the Siberian pipeline
items.format: The Carter administration restricted grain exports in January 1980 in response to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. The Reagan administration responded to martial law in Poland by suspending licenses for oil and gas equipment in December 1981, and on June 18, 1982, extended the ban to products of U.S. companies' European subsidiaries and of European companies holding U.S. technology licenses. Applied extraterritorially and retroactively, the measure covered some 20 companies in West Germany, France, Italy, and Britain.
items.outcome: The grain embargo had little effect as the Soviet Union switched to suppliers such as Argentina; it merely depressed U.S. grain prices and was lifted on April 24, 1981. In response to the pipeline sanctions, Britain issued orders not to comply under the Protection of Trading Interests Act, France directed its companies to fulfill their contracts, and West Germany and Italy also refused. The equipment left European ports in August 1982, and on November 13, 1982, Washington lifted the sanctions, citing an agreement on a joint review of East-West trade. The pipeline was completed on schedule in 1984.
items.why: Alternative suppliers existed, and European governments jointly defended contracts and jobs at the national level. Once extraterritorial and retroactive application became a question of allied sovereignty, Washington's legitimacy weakened. The asymmetry, in which the costs of the sanctions fell on allies while the United States bore none itself, drove the defections.
items.differs: In the 2020s, Washington has institutionalized extraterritorial reach through the Foreign Direct Product Rule (FDPR) and the Entity List, and Europe and Japan ultimately fell in line. South Korea, unlike Europe in 1982, does not belong to a bloc with collective legal countermeasures (such as the EU Blocking Statute). And unlike pipeline equipment in 1982, chip equipment and design software have almost no alternative suppliers outside the United States.

items.name: The U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Agreement, the decline of Japanese DRAM, and the rise of South Korea
items.format: On September 2, 1986, Washington and Tokyo signed a five-year agreement. Japan pledged to prevent dumping, including in third-country markets (through price monitoring), and to open its market, and a confidential side letter set a target of about 20 percent for the foreign share of the Japanese market. In April 1987, citing violations of the agreement, the United States imposed 100 percent tariffs on $300 million worth of Japanese products. The agreement was renewed in 1991 and expired in July 1996.
items.outcome: Between 1978 and 1987, Japan's share of the global semiconductor market rose from 28 percent to 50 percent, while the U.S. share fell from 55 percent to 44 percent. The 20 percent foreign-share target was reached at the end of 1992, but no new memory makers emerged in the United States. South Korea, which was not covered by the anti-dumping provisions, became the biggest beneficiary, and Samsung Electronics became the world's largest DRAM maker in 1992.
items.why: The price floor protected Japanese companies' margins but weakened their incentive to expand, and Korean companies increased investment under that price umbrella. Japan, dependent on the United States for its security, had little room to refuse the agreement, and the strong yen after the 1985 Plaza Accord eroded its cost competitiveness at the same time.
items.differs: South Korea then was a latecomer outside the rules that found a niche, whereas in 2026 it is a principal party, home to the world's top two memory makers, and a direct target of U.S. demands linking tariffs to investment. The position of a third party outside the rules may now be taken by China's CXMT and YMTC.

items.name: China's 2010 rare-earth customs delays against Japan and Japan's reduced dependence
items.format: After a Chinese fishing boat collided with Japanese coast guard vessels near the Senkakus on September 7, 2010, and its captain was detained, reports followed that China was delaying customs clearance of rare earths bound for Japan without any official announcement. China had already sharply cut export quotas that year. In October 2010, Japan passed a supplementary budget of 100 billion yen and invested in Australia's Lynas through JOGMEC and Sojitz, and in 2012 it filed a WTO complaint together with the United States and the EU (DS431).
items.outcome: The captain was released on September 24, 2010. Rare-earth prices rose about tenfold within a year. Japan's dependence on China fell from about 90 percent to about 60 percent, and its use of rare earths fell to half the 2010 level. The WTO ruled definitively against China in 2014, and China abolished its quotas in 2015. However, a trade-data study (CEPR) found no clear drop in Japanese imports in the second half of 2010, raising the possibility that the embargo's reality was exaggerated.
items.why: The coercion's real effect came less from cutting off volumes than from price spikes and fear, which prompted Japanese industry to cut demand, substitute, and invest in overseas equity stakes, weakening China's long-term leverage. Informal measures offered deniability but no legal defense at the WTO.
items.differs: China's 2025 controls are a formal licensing system based on its 2020 Export Control Law, and China now dominates refining and magnet production as well, making substitution harder. South Korea has not built up the 15 years of stockpiling and overseas mining stakes that Japan has.

items.name: China's THAAD retaliation (group tours, Lotte, the ban on Korean culture)
items.format: South Korea decided in July 2016 to deploy THAAD with U.S. forces in Korea. While denying any formal sanctions, China banned group tours to South Korea by verbal instruction from March 15, 2017; by August 2017 it had shut 74 of Lotte's 112 hypermarkets in China, which had provided the deployment site, on the pretext of fire inspections; and it blocked broadcast and performance permits for Korean content.
items.outcome: Chinese visitors to South Korea fell 48 percent, from 8.07 million in 2016 to 4.17 million in 2017. Hyundai Motor's 2017 sales in China fell by more than 300,000 vehicles from the previous year. Lotte withdrew from retail in China in 2018. Estimates of the losses range from more than $10 billion (KEI) to about $15.6 billion (the Asan Forum). Yet Korea-China trade grew about 15 percent in 2017, and semiconductors were not targeted. The dispute was patched up on October 31, 2017, with South Korea's statement of the "three no's"; THAAD stayed, and group tours resumed only in August 2023.
items.why: China minimized its own costs by targeting only sectors with ample substitutes, direct consumer contact, and broad regulatory discretion. It left alone the Korean memory on which its own manufacturers depended. The coercion failed to achieve its goal of reversing the deployment, but it won a statement that South Korea would not deploy additional batteries, join U.S. missile defense, or form a trilateral alliance with the United States and Japan, constraining Seoul's future options.
items.differs: In 2017, China had no substitute for Korean memory, but by 2026 CXMT has grown into the world's fourth-largest DRAM maker, so memory, too, could become a target of selective pressure. And Korean companies' fabs in China (30 to 40 percent of SK hynix's memory output and about a third of Samsung's NAND) sit under Chinese regulatory discretion.

items.name: Japan's export restrictions on South Korea (hydrogen fluoride, photoresist, fluorinated polyimide) and the localization of materials, parts, and equipment
items.format: On July 4, 2019, Japan moved three semiconductor materials from general to individual licensing, and on August 28, 2019, it removed South Korea from its list of preferred export destinations (the "white list"). The stated reason was inadequate export controls, but the background was the October 2018 Supreme Court ruling on forced labor. South Korea filed a WTO complaint in September 2019 (DS590) and gave notice that it would terminate GSOMIA, then suspended that notice on November 22, 2019; it raised its budget for materials, parts, and equipment from 827 billion won in 2019 to 2.1 trillion won in 2020.
items.outcome: Japanese exports of hydrogen fluoride to South Korea are estimated to have fallen 87.9 percent because of the restrictions, but declines in photoresist and fluorinated polyimide were negligible as Japan partly allowed general licenses. No significant disruption of South Korean chip production or change in profitability was observed. Imports of hydrogen fluoride from Japan fell 66 percent, from $36.3 million to $12.5 million, and dependence on Japan for 100 key items fell from 30.9 percent in 2019 to 24.9 percent in 2021. Shares of the Japanese suppliers Stella Chemifa and Morita fell 16 to 20 percent. Right after the Japan-South Korea summit in March 2023, Japan lifted the restrictions and South Korea withdrew its WTO complaint, and in July 2023 Japan returned South Korea to the white list.
items.why: The controlled items were commodity chemicals with alternative suppliers in Taiwan, the United States, Belgium, and elsewhere, and with potential for domestic production. Japan actually issued licenses, so there was no total cutoff, and Japanese suppliers bore the cost of losing customers. Washington, wanting to restore U.S.-Japan-South Korea cooperation, acted as mediator. Dependence on Japan for the most advanced materials, such as high-purity EUV photoresist, remained.
items.differs: In 2019, the country imposing controls, Japan, was a U.S. ally like South Korea, and Washington was the mediator. In 2026, the pressure comes from the United States (equipment, design software, tariffs) and China (rare earths, markets), and the United States is itself a party. Irreplaceable items (EUV equipment, U.S. EDA software) are involved, so much of the pressure cannot be absorbed through localization.

items.name: U.S. sanctions on Huawei (the Entity List and FDPR) and the Kirin 9000S
items.format: The United States put Huawei on the Entity List on May 16, 2019, and amended the Foreign Direct Product Rule (FDPR) on May 15 and August 17, 2020, to block supplies to Huawei of chips made in third countries with U.S. equipment and software. TSMC stopped supplying Huawei from September 14, 2020, and Samsung Electronics and SK hynix also halted memory shipments. A temporary general license remained in place until August 2020, giving Huawei time to stockpile.
items.outcome: Huawei's revenue fell about 29 percent, from 891.4 billion yuan in 2020 to 636.8 billion yuan in 2021, and its consumer business shrank by about half. But in August 2023 it launched the Mate 60 Pro with the Kirin 9000S, made on SMIC's 7nm-class process, and its 2025 revenue of 880.9 billion yuan approached the 2020 peak. Constraints on yields and volumes at advanced nodes persist.
items.why: The FDPR exploited the irreplaceability of U.S. equipment and EDA to bind even third-country companies, so its short-term effect was large. But a huge domestic market, government support, advance stockpiling, and business diversification combined to rally China's supply chain, and the controls only slowed China's catch-up without stopping it.
items.differs: In 2020, Korean companies bore the indirect cost of losing a customer, whereas the 2026 controls apply directly to their own fabs in China and their exports to China. The Huawei case also shows that the more China adapts to U.S. controls, the greater the pressure to replace Korean products in China.

items.name: The Netherlands and Japan join U.S. equipment controls, and ASML's sales in China
items.format: On January 27, 2023, the United States, Japan, and the Netherlands agreed, without any public document, that Japan and the Netherlands would join U.S. equipment controls. Japan put controls on 23 items into effect on July 23, 2023, and the Netherlands placed advanced DUV immersion lithography tools (NXT:2000i and above) under licensing on September 1, 2023, extending it to some 1970i and 1980i models from January 2024. Neither country adopted the U.S. rules barring "U.S. persons" from supporting Chinese fabs or the limits on maintenance.
items.outcome: ASML's share of sales from China jumped from 14 percent in 2022 to 29 percent in 2023 on front-loaded purchases and was still 36 percent in the fourth quarter of 2025, before plunging to 19 percent in the first quarter of 2026. Chinese companies are estimated to have stockpiled several years' worth of equipment, and localization, such as SMEE's 28nm lithography tool, is under way. ASML's CEO has publicly criticized tighter controls as backfiring by accelerating China's self-reliance.
items.why: Allied alignment was achieved, but it was implemented quietly and in stages, with gaps between announcement and implementation that let Chinese companies buy equipment in advance. The Netherlands and Japan aligned under the threat of extraterritorial FDPR enforcement but kept the scope narrower than Washington's to protect their companies' interests. Alignment, in other words, was not wholesale acceptance but negotiated partial acceptance.
items.differs: The Netherlands and Japan, as suppliers of irreplaceable equipment, sided with the controlling powers. South Korea, as a buyer of equipment and a producer in China, is closer to being a target of controls, and its equipment industry, being less irreplaceable, has little bargaining power to extract a price for aligning.

items.name: China's counter-controls on critical minerals (gallium, germanium, graphite, rare earths) and the Busan truce
items.format: China placed gallium and germanium under licensing on August 1, 2023, and graphite on December 1, 2023, and banned exports of gallium, germanium, and antimony to the United States on December 3, 2024. On April 4, 2025, in response to U.S. tariffs, it placed seven heavy rare earths under licensing, and on October 9, 2025, it announced five more, along with extraterritorial rules covering third-country products containing Chinese rare earths.
items.outcome: U.S. imports of gallium and germanium fell 77 percent and 68 percent, respectively, between 2021 and 2024, but indirect inflows via Belgium and elsewhere were detected. Chinese exports of yttrium to the United States plunged from 333 tons to 17 tons, comparing the eight months before and after the controls. After the U.S.-China summit in Busan on October 30, 2025, China suspended for one year, from November 10, 2025, to November 10, 2026, its October 2025 expansion of rare-earth controls and its export ban on the United States, and the United States suspended BIS's 50 percent affiliates rule for one year. The April 2025 measures remain in force, and at the Beijing summit in May 2026, too, the two sides' statements on rare earths diverged.
items.why: Because China's monopoly on refining and magnet production made short-term substitution impossible, its counter-controls extracted a real concession: the suspension of a U.S. control measure (the affiliates rule). Still, there was leakage through diversion, inventories, and recycling, and in the long run the controls are spurring Western investment in alternatives.
items.differs: South Korea was not a direct target, but the extraterritorial rules could affect Korean batteries and chips containing Chinese materials that are exported to the United States. South Korea sat outside the U.S.-China negotiating table, accepting the results of the suspension, and the suspension's expiration date (November 10, 2026) is approaching.

items.name: China's sanctions on Micron and the U.S. request not to fill the gap
items.format: On May 21, 2023, the Cyberspace Administration of China declared that Micron's products had failed a cybersecurity review and barred operators of critical information infrastructure from buying them. Shortly before, in April 2023, it was reported that Washington had asked the South Korean government to keep Korean companies from filling the gap Micron left in China.
items.outcome: Micron's revenue from mainland China was $3.4 billion, about 12 percent of its total, and Micron was reported in October 2025 to have decided to exit the business of supplying server chips for data centers in China. It kept selling chips for automotive and mobile uses and to customers with operations abroad, such as Lenovo. The gap was divided among Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and the state-backed CXMT and YMTC.
items.why: China kept its own costs down by selectively excluding only an American company in products with alternative suppliers. The sanction took the form of a cybersecurity review rather than an export control, leaving room to deny it was retaliation. The South Korean government neither publicly accepted nor rejected the U.S. request, and the companies responded according to market logic.
items.differs: South Korea gained a windfall in 2023, but much of the benefit went to Chinese companies, which could erode Korean companies' position in China over the long run. The possibility that the same format (a security review) will be applied to Korean companies in the future cannot be ruled out.

items.name: The granting and revocation of VEU status for Samsung's Xi'an plant, SK hynix's Wuxi and Dalian plants, and TSMC Nanjing
items.format: When it introduced controls on advanced chip equipment on October 7, 2022, the United States gave Korean companies' fabs in China a one-year reprieve, and in October 2023 it granted them validated end-user (VEU) status indefinitely. SK hynix completed its acquisition of Intel's NAND business and Dalian plant, announced in October 2020, in two stages: the first in December 2021 and the second ($1.9 billion) on March 27, 2025. On August 29, 2025, Washington announced that it would revoke the VEU status of Samsung's, SK's, and Intel's Chinese subsidiaries, and on September 2, 2025, that of TSMC Nanjing, effective December 31, 2025.
items.outcome: On December 30, 2025, Washington approved Samsung's and SK's equipment shipments for 2026 under annual licenses, allowing existing production to be maintained but barring equipment for expansion or process upgrades. As of 2025, China is estimated to account for 30 to 35 percent of Samsung's NAND output and for 35 to 40 percent of SK hynix's DRAM and 40 to 45 percent of its NAND output; TSMC Nanjing accounts for about 3 percent of TSMC's total capacity. In August 2026, reports emerged that Samsung and SK had tested China's AMEC equipment, which both companies denied.
items.why: For Washington, Korean companies' fabs in China carry both the supply-stability benefit of "Chinese production by non-Chinese companies" and the risk of technology transfer.
